a0406: Course home / Phase 4 · Teaching Machines to See Finding objects in a picture (YOLO) Lesson 4.6 75 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Explain the grid-and-anchor design that turns detection into a dense prediction problem and state what every number in the output tensor means Compute Intersection-over-Union between boxes and implement non-maximum suppression from scratch Build a minimal YOLO-style head on top of a pretrained backbone, including the classification, objectness, and box-regression losses Read a detection metric row (precision@0.5, recall, mAP@0.5, mAP@0.5:0.95) and pick which knob to turn next Before you start Needs : Phase 4 Lesson 03 (CNNs), Phase 4 Lesson 04 (Telling images apart: classification), Phase 4 Lesson 05 (Transfer Learning) Type : Build. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Detection is classification plus regression, run at every position in a feature map, then cleaned up with non-maximum suppression. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Anchor "Box prior" A pre-defined box shape at each grid cell from which the network predicts deltas instead of absolute coordinates IoU "Overlap" Intersection-over-union of two boxes; the universal similarity measure in detection NMS "Deduplicate" Greedy algorithm that keeps highest-score predictions and removes overlapping ones above a threshold Objectness "Is there something here" Per-anchor, per-cell scalar predicting whether an object is centred in that cell Grid stride "Downsample factor" Pixels per grid cell; a 416-px input with a 13-grid head has stride 32 mAP "Mean average precision" Average of the area under the precision-recall curve, averaged over classes and (for COCO) IoU thresholds AP@0.5 "PASCAL VOC AP" Average precision with IoU threshold 0.5; the lenient version of the metric mAP@0.5:0.95 "COCO AP" Average over IoU thresholds 0.5..0.95 step 0.05; the strict version and current community standard The problem In plain words first A detector answers "what is in this image, and where?" with a list of boxes, each with a class and a confidence score. YOLO does it in one pass: it lays a grid over the image, and every grid cell predicts a few boxes as small adjustments to preset shapes ( anchors ), plus how likely each box holds an object and of which class. Because neighbouring cells often find the same object, a final step called non-maximum suppression keeps the most confident box and deletes its near-duplicates. Overlap between boxes is measured with IoU . Classification says "this image is a dog." Detection says "there is a dog at pixels (112, 40, 280, 210), there is a cat at (400, 180, 560, 310), and nothing else in the frame." That one structural change — predicting a variable number of labelled boxes instead of one label per image — is what every autonomous system, every surveillance product, every document layout parser, and every factory vision line depends on. Detection is also where every engineering trade-off in vision shows up at once. You want boxes that are accurate (regression head), you want the right class for each box (classification head), you want the model to know when there is nothing to detect (objectness score), and you want exactly one prediction per real object (non-maximum suppression). Miss any of these and the pipeline either misses objects, reports hallucinated boxes, or predicts the same object fifteen times in slightly different positions. YOLO (You Only Look Once, Redmon et al. 2016) was the design that made all of this run in real time by doing it with a single forward pass of a conv net, and the same structural decisions are still the backbone of modern detectors (YOLOv8, YOLOv9, YOLO-NAS, RT-DETR). Learn the core and every variant becomes a rearrangement of the same parts. Idea 1 · Detection as dense prediction A classifier outputs C numbers per image. A YOLO-style detector outputs (S x S x (5 + C)) numbers per image, where S is the spatial grid size. Each of the S * S grid cells predicts B boxes. For each box: 4 numbers describe geometry: tx, ty, tw, th . 1 number is the objectness score: "is there an object centred in this cell?" C numbers are class probabilities. Total per cell: B * (5 + C) . For VOC with S=13, B=2, C=20 , that is 50 numbers per cell. Idea 2 · Why grids and anchors Plain regression would predict (x, y, w, h) for every object as an absolute coordinate. That is hard for a conv network because translating the image should not translate all predictions by the same amount — each object is spatially anchored. The grid answers this by assigning each ground-truth box to the grid cell its centre falls in; only that cell is responsible for that object. Anchors address a second problem. A 3x3 conv cannot easily regress a 500-pixel-wide box out of a 16-pixel receptive field feature cell. Instead, we pre-define B prior box shapes (anchors) per cell and predict small deltas from each anchor. The model learns to pick the right anchor and nudge it rather than regress from nothing. Copy Modern detectors often use FPN with different anchor sets per resolution — small anchors on shallow high-resolution maps, large anchors on deep low-resolution maps. Same idea, more scales. Idea 3 · Decoding predictions The raw tx, ty, tw, th are not box coordinates; they are regression targets to be transformed before plotting: centre y width height ​ = ( σ ( t x ​ ) + cell x ​ ) ⋅ stride = ( σ ( t y ​ ) + cell y ​ ) ⋅ stride = anchor w ​ ⋅ exp ( t w ​ ) = anchor h ​ ⋅ exp ( t h ​ ) ​ sigmoid keeps centre offsets inside the cell. exp lets the width scale freely from the anchor without a sign flip. stride scales the grid coordinates back to pixels. This is the YOLOv2/v3 decode. Later versions changed the details (YOLOv5 bounds the width as anchor × (2σ(t_w))² so it cannot explode, and YOLOv8 drops anchors altogether), but every version still decodes raw outputs relative to the grid cell. Worked example Decoding one prediction by hand A 416 × 416 image with stride 32 gives a 13 × 13 grid. Cell uses the medium anchor (75 × 170) and outputs : centre centre width = 150 , height = 170 So the box is in ​ , y 1 ​ , x 2 ​ , y 2 ​ ) pixels. A raw output of zero means "the anchor shape, centred in the cell". Idea 4 · IoU Detection's universal similarity metric between two boxes: ( A ∪ B ) area ( A ∩ B ) ​ means identical; means no overlap. IoU between the prediction and the ground-truth box is what decides whether a prediction counts as a true positive (typically ). IoU between two predictions is what NMS uses to deduplicate. Worked example IoU by hand Boxes and each have area 100. They overlap in the square from to , area 25. The union is , so . Shifting one box by half its width in both directions already drops IoU far below the usual 0.5 match threshold: IoU is strict. Check your mental model ✗ "NMS is a fixed O(N log N) step." ✓ Sorting is O(N log N), but each kept box is compared with every box still left, so the worst case is O(N²). With thousands of candidates this is why detectors cap the number of boxes before NMS. ✗ "A lower NMS threshold is always cleaner." ✓ It removes duplicates more aggressively, but also deletes genuinely different objects that overlap, such as people standing in a crowd. ✗ "A detector run on an empty or noise image returns nothing." ✓ The pretrained Faster R-CNN under "Use it" returns 9 boxes for pure random noise. Always apply a score threshold and evaluate on images without objects too. Idea 5 · Non-maximum suppression A conv network trained on adjacent anchors will often predict overlapping boxes for the same object. NMS keeps the highest-confidence prediction and deletes any other prediction with IoU above a threshold. Copy Typical threshold: 0.45 for object detection. Recent detectors replace standard NMS with soft-NMS , DIoU-NMS , or learn the suppression directly (RT-DETR) but the structural purpose is the same. Predict before you run Under "Use it", a pretrained Faster R-CNN looks at a photo of a garbage truck with a person in the cab and a wheelie bin beside it. With NMS switched off and a score threshold of 0.3, how many boxes do you expect, and how many after NMS at IoU 0.5? (Solution P1.) Idea 6 · The loss YOLO loss is three losses added with weights: + + + ​ λ coord ​ ⋅ L box ​ ( pred , target , where obj = 1 ) λ obj ​ ⋅ L obj ​ ( pred , 1 , where obj = 1 ) λ noobj ​ ⋅ L obj ​ ( pred , 0 , where obj = 0 ) λ cls ​ ⋅ L cls ​ ( pred , target , where obj = 1 ) ​ Only cells that contain an object contribute to the box-regression and classification losses. Cells without objects contribute only to the objectness loss (teaching the model to stay silent). lambda_noobj is usually small (~0.5) because the vast majority of cells are empty and would otherwise dominate the total loss. Modern variants swap MSE box loss for CIoU / DIoU (which optimise IoU directly), use focal loss for class imbalance, and balance objectness with quality focal loss. The three-component structure is unchanged. Idea 7 · Detection metrics Accuracy does not transfer to detection. Four numbers that do: Precision@IoU=0.5 — of the predictions counted as positives, how many are actually correct. Recall@IoU=0.5 — of the real objects, how many did we find. A detector that is strong on mAP@0.5 but weak on mAP@0.5:0.95 is localising roughly but not tightly; fix with better box-regression loss. A detector with high precision and low recall is too conservative; lower the confidence threshold or increase the objectness weight. The same idea as a formula IoU. For boxes and , , with . a0407: Course home / Phase 4 · Teaching Machines to See Labelling every pixel (U-Net) Lesson 4.7 75 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Distinguish semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentation and pick the right task for a given problem Build a U-Net from scratch in PyTorch with encoder blocks, a bottleneck, a decoder with transposed convolutions, and skip connections Implement pixel-wise cross-entropy, Dice loss, and the combined loss that is the current default for medical and industrial segmentation Read IoU and Dice metrics per class and diagnose whether a bad score comes from small-object recall, boundary accuracy, or class imbalance Before you start Needs : Phase 4 Lesson 03 (CNNs), Phase 4 Lesson 04 (Telling images apart: classification) Type : Build. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Segmentation is classification at every pixel. U-Net makes it work by pairing a downsampling encoder with an upsampling decoder and wiring skip connections between them. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Semantic segmentation "Label every pixel" Per-pixel classification into C classes; instances of the same class merge Instance segmentation "Label every object" Separates distinct instances of the same class; foreground-only Panoptic segmentation "Semantic + instance" Every pixel gets a class; every thing instance also gets a unique id Skip connection "U-Net bridge" Concatenation of encoder features into matching-resolution decoder features; preserves high-frequency detail Transposed conv "Deconvolution" Learnable upsampling; can produce checkerboard artifacts Dice loss "Overlap loss" 1 - 2 mIoU "Mean intersection over union" Average IoU across classes; the community-standard metric for segmentation Boundary F1 "Boundary accuracy" F1 score computed on boundary pixels only; matters for precision-critical tasks The problem In plain words first A classifier gives one label per image. A segmentation model gives a label to every pixel : this pixel is road, that one is car, that one is sky. U-Net does this with two halves shaped like a U. The left half shrinks the image step by step to understand what is in it; the right half grows it back to full size to say where . Bridges called skip connections carry the fine detail from the left half straight across to the right half, so edges come out sharp. You score the result by how much the predicted mask overlaps the true one (IoU or Dice), not by plain pixel accuracy. Classification outputs one label per image. Detection outputs a handful of boxes per image. Segmentation outputs one label per pixel. For an input of size H x W , the output is a tensor of shape H x W (semantic) or H x W x N_instances (instance). That is millions of predictions per image, not one. The structure of segmentation is why it powers almost every dense-prediction vision product: medical imaging (tumour masks), autonomous driving (road, lane, obstacle), satellite (building footprints, crop boundaries), document parsing (layout zones), robotics (graspable regions). None of those tasks can be solved by putting a box around the object; they need the exact silhouette. The architectural problem is simple to state and not simple to solve: you need the network to see the global context of an image (what kind of scene is this) and the local pixel detail (exactly which pixel is road vs pavement) simultaneously. A standard CNN compresses spatially to gain context, which throws away the detail. U-Net was the design that got both. Idea 1 · Semantic vs instance vs panoptic Semantic says "this pixel is road, that pixel is car." Two cars next to each other collapse into a single blob. Instance says "this pixel is car #3, that pixel is car #5." Ignores background stuff ("stuff" = sky, road, grass). Panoptic unifies both: every pixel gets a class label, every instance gets a unique id, stuff and things both segmented. This lesson covers semantic. The next lesson (Mask R-CNN) covers instance. Idea 2 · The U-Net shape The encoder halves spatial resolution four times and doubles channels. The decoder reverses: doubles spatial resolution four times and halves channels. The skip connections concatenate matching encoder features with decoder features at every resolution. The final 1x1 conv maps 64 -> num_classes at full resolution. Why skip connections are necessary: the decoder has seen only small feature maps by the time it tries to output pixel-level predictions. Without the skips it cannot localise edges accurately because that information was compressed away in the encoder. Skip connections hand it the high-resolution feature maps the encoder computed on the way down. Idea 3 · Transposed vs bilinear upsample The decoder has to expand spatial dimensions. Two options: Transposed convolution ( nn.ConvTranspose2d ) — learnable upsample. Historical U-Net default. Can produce checkerboard artifacts if stride and kernel size do not divide evenly. Bilinear upsample + 3x3 conv — smooth upsample followed by a conv. Fewer artifacts, fewer parameters, now the modern default. Both appear in the wild. For a first U-Net, bilinear is safer. Idea 4 · Cross-entropy on a pixel grid For semantic segmentation with classes, the model output is (N, C, H, W) . The target is (N, H, W) with integer class IDs. Cross-entropy is identical to the classification case, just applied at every spatial position: mean ​ [ − lo g ( softmax ( logits [ n , : , h , w ]) [ target [ n , h , w ]] ) ] F.cross_entropy in PyTorch handles this shape natively. No reshape needed. Idea 5 · Dice loss and why you need it Cross-entropy treats every pixel equally. That is wrong when one class dominates the frame (medical imaging: 99% background, 1% tumour). The network can score 99% accuracy by predicting background everywhere and still be useless. Dice loss solves this by directly optimising the overlap between predicted and true mask: ( p , y ) Dice loss ​ ​ = ∑ p + ∑ y + ϵ 2 ∑ ( p ⋅ y ) ​ = 1 − Dice ​ where p is the sigmoid/softmax probability map for a class and y is the binary ground-truth mask. The loss is zero only when the overlap is perfect. Because it is a ratio per class, a class covering 1% of the image counts as much as one covering 90%, which makes Dice far less sensitive to class imbalance (not immune: tiny masks give noisy Dice gradients). In practice, use the combined loss : ​ + λ ⋅ L dice ​ ( λ ≈ 1 ) Cross-entropy gives stable gradients early in training; Dice focuses the tail of training on actually matching the mask shape. This combination is the medical-imaging default and hard to beat on any class-imbalanced dataset. Worked example Dice and IoU by hand A predicted tumour mask covers 30 pixels, the true mask covers 40, and they share 20. IoU 20 ​ = 50 20 ​ = 0.40 Dice 2 × 20 ​ = 70 40 ​ = 0.571 Check the conversion: . Same ranking, different scale: Dice always reads higher than IoU except at 0 and 1. Now the trap. In a 64 × 64 scan (4,096 pixels) the tumour covers 41 pixels, 1%. A model that predicts "background" everywhere is right on 4,055 pixels: 99.0% pixel accuracy , and tumour IoU and Dice of exactly 0. Idea 6 · Evaluation metrics Pixel accuracy — percent of pixels predicted correctly. Cheap. Broken on imbalanced data for the same reason as accuracy in classification. IoU per class — intersection over union for each class's mask; average across classes = mIoU. Dice (F1 on pixels) — similar to IoU; . Medical imaging prefers Dice, driving community prefers IoU; they are monotonically related. Boundary F1 — measures how close predicted boundaries are to ground-truth boundaries, penalising even small shifts. Important for high-precision tasks like semiconductor inspection. Report IoU per class, not just mIoU. Mean IoU hides a class at 15% when nine others are at 85%. Check your mental model ✗ "99% pixel accuracy means the segmentation works." ✓ On imbalanced images, predicting all background reaches that. Read IoU or Dice per class. ✗ "Skip connections are an optional speed trick." ✓ They carry the full-resolution detail the encoder threw away. Under "Use it", zeroing them costs about 0.2 IoU on the same data and training budget. ✗ "Dice and IoU can disagree about which model is better." ✓ For one mask they are linked by Dice = 2·IoU / (1 + IoU), so they rank models the same way. Averaged over many images or classes they can differ slightly. Idea 7 · Input resolution trade-off U-Net's encoder halves resolution four times, so the skip connections line up exactly only when the input is divisible by 16. Other sizes need padding or the resize in the up block (Step 2). Medical images are often 512x512 or 1024x1024. Autonomous-driving crops are 2048x1024. The memory cost of U-Net scales with H * W * C_max , and at 1024x1024 with 1024 bottleneck channels the forward pass already uses gigabytes of VRAM. Two standard workarounds: 1. Tile the input — process 256x256 tiles with overlap and stitch. 2. Replace the bottleneck with dilated convolutions that keep spatial resolution higher but widen receptive field (the DeepLab family). For a first model, a 256x256 input with a 64-channel-base U-Net trains comfortably on 8 GB VRAM. The same idea as a formula Per-pixel classification. With logits ​ for classes at every pixel, the cross-entropy is averaged over all positions: 1 ​ ∑ h , w ​ lo g p y h w ​ , h , w ​ . Rare classes cover few pixels and contribute little, so they are under-learned. Dice. For a predicted mask and ground truth , 2∣ P ∩ G ∣ ​ , L Dice ​ = 1 − ∑ i ​ p i ​ + ∑ i ​ g i ​ + ϵ 2 ∑ i ​ p i ​ g i ​ + ϵ ​ with soft probabilities ​ . It measures overlap relative to the object's own size, so a small object counts as much as a large one; training often sums cross-entropy and Dice. IoU and Dice are related: , and mIoU averages IoU over classes. Upsampling. A transposed convolution produces ​ = ( n − 1 ) s − 2 p + k positions; with , it doubles the size exactly. Bilinear upsampling followed by a convolution avoids the checkerboard artefacts that overlapping transposed kernels can cause. U-Net skips. The decoder at each scale concatenates the encoder's feature map of the same size, restoring the spatial detail that downsampling threw away. a0408: Course home / Phase 4 · Teaching Machines to See Separating each object (Mask R-CNN) Lesson 4.8 75 min Build + Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Trace the Mask R-CNN architecture end-to-end: backbone, FPN, RPN, RoIAlign, box head, mask head Implement RoIAlign from scratch and explain why RoIPool is no longer used Use the torchvision maskrcnn_resnet50_fpn_v2 pretrained model for production-quality instance masks and read its output format correctly Fine-tune Mask R-CNN on a small custom dataset by replacing the box and mask heads and keeping the backbone frozen Before you start Needs : Phase 4 Lesson 06 (YOLO), Phase 4 Lesson 07 (U-Net) Type : Build + Learn. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Add a tiny mask branch to a Faster R-CNN detector and you have instance segmentation. The hard part is RoIAlign, and it is harder than it looks. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Mask R-CNN "Detection plus masks" Faster R-CNN + a small FCN head that predicts a 28x28 mask per proposal per class FPN "Feature pyramid" Top-down + lateral connections that give every stride level C channels of semantic-rich features RPN "Region proposer" A small conv head that produces ~1000 object/no-object proposals per image RoIAlign "No-rounding crop" Bilinearly samples a fixed-size feature grid from any float-coordinate box RoIPool "Pre-2017 crop" Same purpose as RoIAlign but rounds box coordinates; obsolete Mask AP "Instance mAP" Average precision computed with mask IoU instead of box IoU; the COCO instance segmentation metric Binary mask head "Per-class mask" Predicts one binary mask per class for each proposal; only the predicted class's channel is kept Background class "Class 0" The catch-all "no object" class; indices for real classes start at 1 The problem In plain words first Semantic segmentation colours every dog pixel "dog". Instance segmentation also says which dog: dog number 1 and dog number 2 get separate masks. Mask R-CNN gets there by starting from an object detector. The detector finds a box around each object; then, for each box, a small extra network paints a mask of the object inside that box. The fiddly part is cutting a fixed-size patch of features out of a box whose edges fall between pixels; RoIAlign does that cut without rounding, and that turns out to matter a lot. Semantic segmentation gives you one mask per class. Instance segmentation gives you one mask per object, even when two objects share a class. Counting individuals, tracking across frames, and measuring things (the bounding box of each brick in a wall, each cell in a microscope image) all demand instance segmentation. Mask R-CNN (He et al., 2017) solved this by reframing instance segmentation as detection-plus-a-mask. The design was so clean that for the next five years almost every instance segmentation paper was a Mask R-CNN variant, and it remains a common, well-supported baseline in torchvision and Detectron2. The hard engineering problem is sampling: how do you crop a fixed-size feature region out of a proposal box whose corners do not align with pixel boundaries? Getting that wrong costs several mAP points: in the Mask R-CNN paper's ablation, replacing the old rounding crop (RoIPool) with RoIAlign raised COCO mask AP from 26.9 to 30.2, and by 7.3 points on a stride-32 backbone. RoIAlign is the answer. Idea 1 · The architecture Five pieces to understand: Backbone — ResNet-50 or ResNet-101 trained on ImageNet. Produces a hierarchy of feature maps at strides 4, 8, 16, 32. FPN (Feature Pyramid Network) — top-down + lateral connections that give every level C channels of semantic-rich features. Detection queries the FPN level matching the object size. RPN (Region Proposal Network) — a small conv head that, at every anchor position, predicts "is there an object here?" and "how do I refine the box?". Produces ~1000 proposals per image. RoIAlign — samples a fixed-size (e.g. 7x7) feature patch from any box on any FPN level. Bilinear sampling, no quantisation. Heads — two-layer box head that refines the box and picks a class, plus a small conv head that outputs a 28x28 binary mask for each proposal. Idea 2 · Why RoIAlign, not RoIPool The original Fast R-CNN used RoIPool, which splits a proposal box into a grid, takes the maximum feature in each cell, and rounds all coordinates to integers. That rounding misaligns the feature map from the input pixel coordinates by up to a full feature-map pixel — small on a 224x224 image, catastrophic when the feature map is stride 32. Copy RoIAlign lifts mask AP by about 3 points on COCO for free, with most of the gain at the strict IoU 0.75 threshold. Every detector that crops features out of boxes now uses it (Faster R-CNN, Mask R-CNN and Cascade R-CNN in torchvision and Detectron2). Newer one-stage and transformer models such as YOLO segmentation heads and Mask2Former avoid per-box crops altogether. Worked example Rounding, by hand A box edge at image x = 170 on a stride-16 feature map sits at feature x = 170 / 16 = 10.625. RoIPool rounds it to 11. That is 0.375 feature pixels off, which is 0.375 × 16 = 6 image pixels . Rounding can be off by up to half a feature pixel, 8 image pixels, at each edge, and then the bin boundaries are rounded again. RoIAlign keeps 10.625 and reads the feature map there by bilinear interpolation: 37.5% of feature column 10 and 62.5% of column 11 (in the simple case where values sit on whole columns). Eight pixels is invisible on a 400-pixel bus and is a third of a 24-pixel mask for a distant pedestrian. That is why the gain shows up most at the strict IoU 0.75 threshold. See it drawn See it measured A feature map whose value is simply its own x coordinate, so the output tells you where the crop read from. Slide a box right one image pixel at a time and read the first output cell from torchvision's roi_pool and roi_align . Show the code that draws this Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output RoIAlign's output moves smoothly with the box: shift the box 1 pixel and the features shift 1/16 of a feature pixel. RoIPool's output is a staircase. It ignores the box moving 15 pixels, then jumps a whole feature pixel (16 image pixels) at once. Its gradients are equally blocky, so the box and mask heads cannot learn sub-16-pixel precision through it. Idea 3 · The RPN in one paragraph At every position of a feature map, place K anchor boxes of different sizes and shapes. Predict an objectness score for each anchor and a regression offset to turn the anchor into a better-fitting box. Keep the top ~1,000 boxes by score, apply NMS at IoU 0.7, and hand the survivors to the heads. The RPN is trained with its own mini-loss — the same structure as the YOLO loss from Lesson 6, just with two classes (object / no object). Idea 4 · The mask head For each proposal (after RoIAlign) the mask head is a tiny FCN: four 3x3 convs, a 2x deconv, a final 1x1 conv that produces num_classes output channels at 28x28 resolution. Only the channel corresponding to the predicted class is kept; the others are ignored. This decouples mask prediction from classification. Upsample the 28x28 mask to the proposal's original pixel size to produce the final binary mask. Check your mental model ✗ "The mask head decides the class too." ✓ It predicts one mask per class and only the channel of the class chosen by the box head is used. Classification and mask shape are learned separately. ✗ "The 28 × 28 mask limits outlines to 28 pixels of detail across the whole image." ✓ It is 28 × 28 per box , then resized to the box. A small object gets fine detail; a huge object gets a coarser outline. ✗ "A pretrained detector on an empty image returns nothing." ✓ Step 4 feeds random noise and gets 60 detections back, each with a mask. Score thresholds are part of the model. Idea 5 · Losses Mask R-CNN has five losses added together: ​ + L rpn_box ​ + L box_cls ​ + L box_reg ​ + L mask ​ L_rpn_cls , L_rpn_box — objectness + box regression for the RPN proposals. L_box_cls — cross-entropy over (C+1) classes (including background) on the head's classifier. L_box_reg — smooth L1 on the head's box refinement. L_mask — per-pixel binary cross-entropy on the 28x28 mask output. Each loss has its own default weight; the torchvision implementation exposes them as constructor arguments. Idea 6 · Output format torchvision.models.detection.maskrcnn_resnet50_fpn_v2 returns a list of dicts, one per image: Copy The mask is full image resolution already. The 28x28 head output has been upsampled internally. The same idea as a formula Anchors and box targets. The region proposal network places anchors at every feature-map position and predicts, for each, an objectness score and offsets to the true box: ​ = w a ​ x − x a ​ ​ , t y ​ = h a ​ y − y a ​ ​ , t w ​ = lo g w a ​ w ​ , t h ​ = lo g h a ​ h ​ normalised by the anchor's size so that one regressor handles all scales. RoIAlign. Each proposal is divided into a fixed grid (for example for boxes, for masks); in each bin, a few points are sampled at their exact fractional positions with bilinear interpolation and averaged. RoIPool instead rounded the box and bin edges to whole feature cells; with a stride of 16 pixels, a rounding of half a cell is an 8-pixel shift, harmless for classification but ruinous for masks. Losses. For each sampled proposal, ​ + L box ​ + L mask ​ where the mask loss is a per-pixel binary cross-entropy on a mask, computed only for the ground-truth class's channel: classes do not compete for pixels, the classification head decides the class. Output. Per detected instance: a box, a class, a score and a mask, resized from to the box and thresholded at 0.5. Step 1 · RoIAlign from scratch This is the one component of Mask R-CNN that is simpler to understand as code than as prose. Copy Every number is at a bilinearly-sampled position. No rounding, no quantisation, no dropped gradients. (Solution B1.) Use it: the same idea with real libraries The full training loop for Mask R-CNN in torchvision is 40 lines and does not change meaningfully between tasks — swap datasets and go. Copy The targets list must have per-image dicts with boxes , labels , and masks (as (num_instances, H, W) binary tensors). The model returns a dict of five losses during training and a list of predictions during eval, keyed on model.training . The semantic view cannot tell you there are two dogs, how big each one is, or which pixels belong to which; the instance view can, because every mask comes from its own detected box. Where the dogs touch, each pixel is assigned per box, so the two masks can overlap slightly (the printed count). Panoptic segmentation forbids that overlap; Mask R-CNN does not. Recap What to keep from this lesson Mask R-CNN = Faster R-CNN (backbone, FPN, RPN, box head) + a small mask head per box. RoIAlign crops box features with bilinear sampling instead of rounding; about 3 mask AP on COCO, more at strict IoU. The mask head predicts a 28 × 28 mask per class per box; the box head's class picks which one is used. Outputs: boxes, 1-based labels, scores and full-resolution soft masks to threshold at 0.5. To fine-tune, replace both predictors with num_classes including background, and freeze the backbone on small data. Solutions Solution P1 · Two masks, not one blob Two masks above 0.5, one per dog, each with its own box (the printed lines give the scores and sizes). A semantic model outputs a single map in which every dog pixel has the label "dog": it would show one dog-shaped region, or two touching ones, with no way to say how many dogs there are. Solution B1 · A mask head for the wrong classes The old mask predictor still outputs 91 channels for COCO's classes. At inference Mask R-CNN picks the channel matching the predicted label, so your class 3 reads COCO's channel 3 ("car"), and during training the mask loss is computed against those mismatched channels. Nothing crashes as long as your labels stay below 91, but the masks are trained through a head sized for another label set. Replace both predictors whenever the class list changes, and check model.roi_heads.mask_predictor.mask_fcn_logits.out_channels == num_classes . Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Instance segmentation in practice. Ultralytics YOLO segmentation models, RF-DETR's segmentation variant and Mask2Former are the usual deployed choices; Mask R-CNN (Detectron2) remains a reference. Promptable segmentation for labelling. SAM 2 and SAM 3 are built into annotation tools (CVAT, Label Studio, Roboflow) so a click or a text prompt produces a mask, which is now how most segmentation datasets are labelled. a0409: Course home / Phase 4 · Teaching Machines to See Making images with two rival networks (GANs) Lesson 4.9 75 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Explain the minimax game between generator and discriminator and why the equilibrium corresponds to $p_{\text{model}} = p_{\text{data}}$ Implement a DCGAN in PyTorch and get it to generate coherent 32x32 synthetic images in under 60 lines Stabilise GAN training with the three standard tricks: non-saturating loss, spectral norm, TTUR (two-timescale update rule) Read training curves that distinguish healthy convergence from mode collapse, oscillation, and discriminator-wins-completely Before you start Needs : Phase 4 Lesson 03 (CNNs), Phase 3 Lesson 06 (Optimisers: SGD, momentum and Adam), Phase 3 Lesson 07 (Stopping a network from memorising) Type : Build. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line A GAN is two neural networks in a fixed game. One draws, one critiques. They get better together until the drawings fool the critic. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Generator (G) "The draws-stuff net" Maps noise to images; trained to fool the discriminator Discriminator (D) "The critic" Binary classifier; trained to distinguish real from generated images Minimax "The game" min over G, max over D of an adversarial loss; equilibrium is $p_G = p_{\text{data}}$ Non-saturating loss "The numerically sane version" G's loss is $-\log(D(G(z)))$ instead of $\log(1 - D(G(z)))$ to avoid vanishing gradients early in training Mode collapse "Generator makes one thing" G produces only a small subset of the data distribution; fix with SN, minibatch discrimination, or larger batch TTUR "Two learning rates" D learns faster than G, typically by a factor of 2-4; stabilises training Spectral norm "1-Lipschitz layer" A weight-normalisation that bounds each layer's Lipschitz constant; stops D from becoming arbitrarily steep FID "Fréchet Inception Distance" Distance between Inception-v3 feature distributions of real and generated sets; the standard evaluation metric The problem In plain words first A GAN is two networks playing a game. The generator turns random numbers into an image. The discriminator looks at an image and guesses "real" or "fake". The discriminator is trained to catch fakes; the generator is trained to fool it. Neither ever sees a "correct" image to copy pixel by pixel. The generator only learns from how the critic reacts, and if the game goes well, its images end up looking like they came from the real data. Classification teaches a network to map images to labels. Generation inverts the problem: sample new images that look like they came from the same distribution. There is no "correct" output you can diff against; there is only a distribution you want to mimic. The standard loss functions (MSE, cross-entropy) cannot measure "did this sample come from the real distribution." Minimising per-pixel error produces blurry averages, not realistic samples. The breakthrough was to learn the loss: train a second network whose job is to tell real from fake, and use its judgement to push the generator. GANs (Goodfellow et al., 2014) defined that framework. By 2018 StyleGAN was producing 1024x1024 faces indistinguishable from photographs. Diffusion models have since taken the throne on quality and controllability, but GAN ideas live on inside them: the autoencoder that gives Stable Diffusion its latent space is trained with an adversarial (GAN) loss, and fast one-step image generators are distilled with one too. Idea 1 · The two networks The generator G takes a vector of noise z and outputs an image. The discriminator D takes an image and outputs a single scalar: the probability that the image is real. Idea 2 · The game G wants D to be wrong. D wants to be right. Formally: min ​ D max ​ E x ​ [ lo g D ( x )] + E z ​ [ lo g ( 1 − D ( G ( z )))] Read right to left: D is maximising accuracy on real ( log D(real) ) and fake ( log (1 - D(fake)) ) images. G is minimising D's accuracy on fakes — it wants D(G(z)) to be high. Goodfellow proved that this minimax has a global equilibrium where p_G = p_data , D outputs 0.5 everywhere, and the Jensen-Shannon divergence between generated and real distributions is zero. The hard part is getting there. Worked example What the losses read at the finish line At the ideal equilibrium D outputs 0.5 for every image, real or fake. With this lesson's losses (D's loss is the sum of its real and fake terms): ​ = − ln 0.5 − ln ( 1 − 0.5 ) = 2 ln 2 ≈ 1.386 ​ = − ln 0.5 = ln 2 ≈ 0.693 So healthy GAN losses hover around a level; they do not head to zero like a classifier's. In Step 4's printout D sits near 0.1 and G near 4: D is winning comfortably, which is normal early on and a warning sign if it never changes. Idea 3 · Non-saturating loss The form above is numerically unstable. Early in training, D(G(z)) is near zero for every fake, so log(1 - D(G(z))) has vanishing gradients with respect to G. The fix: flip G's loss. ​ L G ​ ​ = − E x ​ [ lo g D ( x )] − E z ​ [ lo g ( 1 − D ( G ( z )))] = − E z ​ [ lo g D ( G ( z ))] (non-saturating) ​ Now when D(G(z)) is near zero, G's loss is large and its gradient is informative. Most GANs since use this variant or a close relative such as the hinge or Wasserstein loss. See it drawn See the gradients Each loss as a function of D's verdict on a fake, , with its gradient with respect to D's logit worked out by autograd. Early in training D easily spots fakes, so is near 0: the left edge is where training starts. Show the code that draws this Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Both losses push in the same direction: make D believe the fake. But at the start, where , the saturating loss has a gradient of almost zero and the generator barely moves. The non-saturating loss has its steepest gradient exactly there. It is the same game with a better-shaped signal for the player who is losing. Idea 4 · DCGAN architecture rules Radford, Metz, Chintala (2015) distilled years of failed experiments into five rules that make GAN training stable: Replace pooling with strided convs (both nets). Use batch norm in both generator and discriminator, except output of G and input of D. Remove fully connected layers on deeper architectures. G uses ReLU on all layers except output (tanh for output in [-1, 1]). D uses LeakyReLU (negative_slope=0.2) on all layers. Later GANs (BigGAN, StyleGAN, GigaGAN) replaced many of these pieces, for example batch norm gave way to other normalisations, but the strided-convolution, no-pooling skeleton survived. Idea 5 · Failure modes and their signatures Mode collapse : G finds one image that fools D and produces only that. Fix: add minibatch discrimination, spectral norm, or label-conditioning. Discriminator wins : D becomes too strong too fast, G's gradients vanish. Fix: smaller D, lower D learning rate, or apply label smoothing on the real labels. Oscillation : the two nets trade wins without ever approaching equilibrium. Fix: TTUR (D learns faster than G by a factor of 2-4), or switch to Wasserstein loss. Check your mental model ✗ "Falling GAN losses mean the images are improving." ✓ The losses measure the game, not quality. D's loss falling towards 0 usually means D is winning. Look at samples. ✗ "Mode collapse means every sample is identical." ✓ Often it is partial: the samples vary, but cover only part of the data, such as a few colours out of many. Compare statistics of real and generated sets. ✗ "The generator learns by copying training images." ✓ It never sees one. Its only signal is the gradient that flows back through D's verdict. Idea 6 · Evaluation GANs have no ground truth, so how do you know they are working? Sample inspection — just look at 64 samples at the end of every epoch. Non-negotiable. FID (Fréchet Inception Distance) — distance between Inception-v3 feature distributions of real and generated sets. Lower is better. Community standard. Inception Score — older, more brittle; prefer FID. Precision/Recall for generative models — measures quality (precision) and coverage (recall) separately. More informative than FID alone. For a small synthetic-data run, sample inspection is enough. The same idea as a formula The game. A generator maps noise ​ to images; a discriminator outputs the probability that its input is real: min ​ D max ​ E x ∼ p data ​ ​ [ lo g D ( x )] + E z ∼ p z ​ ​ [ lo g ( 1 − D ( G ( z )))] What the optimum means. For a fixed , the best discriminator is ( x ) = p data ​ ( x ) + p g ​ ( x ) p data ​ ( x ) ​ . Substituting it, the generator minimises ​ ∥ p g ​ ) , a divergence that is zero only when ​ = p data ​ , where = 2 1 ​ everywhere. Non-saturating loss. Early on easily rejects fakes, , and is flat there, so gets almost no gradient. In practice instead minimises , which has the same fixed point and a strong gradient exactly when is losing. Evaluation. The Fréchet Inception Distance compares Gaussian fits (mean , covariance ) to Inception features of real and generated images: ​ − μ g ​ ∥ 2 + Tr ( Σ r ​ + Σ g ​ − 2 ( Σ r ​ Σ g ​ ) 1/2 ) lower is better; it rewards both quality and diversity, and needs thousands of samples to be stable. Mode collapse is mapping many to the same few outputs: the discriminator is fooled locally, the distribution is not matched. Step 1 · Generator A small DCGAN generator that takes 64-dim noise and produces a 32x32 image. Copy Four transposed convs, each with kernel_size=4, stride=2, padding=1 so they cleanly double spatial size. Output activations in [-1, 1] via tanh. Step 2 · Discriminator Mirror of the generator. LeakyReLU, strided convs, ends with a scalar logit. Copy The last conv reduces a 4x4 feature map to 1x1 . Output is a single scalar per image; apply sigmoid only during loss computation. Step 3 · Training step Alternate: update D once, then G once, every batch. Copy G(z).detach() in the D step stops D's loss from flowing back into G. Without it, loss_d.backward() also fills G's gradients with "make fakes easier to spot". Here opt_g.zero_grad() clears them before the G step, so forgetting it only wastes compute; in a loop that zeroes gradients once per iteration, those gradients would push G the wrong way. Step 4 · Full training loop on synthetic shapes Copy What you should see Copy Copy Adam(lr=2e-4, betas=(0.5, 0.999)) is the DCGAN default — the low beta1 keeps the momentum term from stabilising the adversarial game too much. Predict before you run Under "Use it" the same DCGAN trains for 30 epochs (about 950 updates) on the 2,000 circles. The real circles have random colours and a radius between 6 and 12 pixels. Do you expect clean circles at the end? Will the generated colours be as varied as the real ones? (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose In train_step , change the G loss to -F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(d_fake, torch.zeros_like(d_fake)) , which is the original minimax form . Use the picture under Idea 3 to predict what happens in the first epochs. (Solution B1.) Step 5 · Sampling Copy Always switch to eval mode before sampling. For DCGAN this matters because batch norm running stats are used instead of the batch's stats. Step 6 · Spectral normalisation A drop-in replacement for BN in the discriminator. It divides each weight by an estimate of its largest singular value (one step of power iteration per forward pass), which keeps each layer's Lipschitz constant close to 1 so D cannot become arbitrarily steep. It often fixes "D wins too hard" failures. Copy Swap Discriminator for build_sn_discriminator() and you often do not need the TTUR trick. Spectral norm is the easiest single robustness upgrade you can apply. Use it: the same idea with real libraries For serious generation, use pretrained weights or switch to diffusion. Two standard libraries: torch_fidelity computes FID / IS on your generator without writing custom eval code. pytorch-gan-zoo (legacy) and StudioGAN ship tested implementations of DCGAN, WGAN-GP, SN-GAN, StyleGAN, and BigGAN. GANs remain a common choice where one fast forward pass matters: real-time generation, style transfer, and paired or unpaired image-to-image translation (Pix2Pix, CycleGAN). Distilled one-step diffusion models now compete there too, and diffusion leads on photorealism and text conditioning. Recap What to keep from this lesson A GAN trains a generator and a discriminator against each other; G only learns through D's gradients. Use the non-saturating G loss: its gradient is strongest exactly when G is losing. DCGAN rules: strided convs, batch norm, ReLU in G, LeakyReLU in D, tanh output, Adam with beta1 = 0.5. GAN losses oscillate around a level; judge progress with samples and statistics or FID. Watch for D winning, oscillation and (partial) mode collapse; spectral norm and TTUR are the first fixes. Solutions Solution P1 · Blobs, with too little colour variety Not clean circles: 30 epochs on CPU gives coloured blobs with ragged edges. The average radius matches the real data but the sizes vary more, and the colours are less varied than the real data's, as the printed colour spread shows. Longer training, a bigger model or spectral norm improve both, but GANs rarely cover the full variety of the data without help. Solution B1 · A generator that cannot start At the start D rejects fakes confidently, so is close to 0. The picture under Idea 3 shows the gradient of is nearly zero there, so G barely changes while D keeps improving, which pushes even closer to 0. Training can stall with noise as output. The non-saturating loss gives the largest push in exactly this situation. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) GANs as parts, not whole generators. Diffusion replaced GANs for general image generation, but adversarial losses remain inside production systems: the VAE decoders of latent-diffusion models, few-step distilled generators (SDXL Turbo's adversarial diffusion distillation) and speech vocoders such as HiFi-GAN (Lesson 6.7). Super-resolution. Real-ESRGAN and similar GAN upscalers are still widely used in image and video tools. Sources: Adversarial Diffusion Distillation , Latent diffusion (VAE with adversarial loss) , Real-ESRGAN . Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line A diffusion model learns to denoise. Train it to remove a tiny bit of noise from a noisy image, repeat that backwards a thousand times, and you have an image generator. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Forward process "Add noise over time" Fixed Markov chain that corrupts an image into Gaussian noise over $T$ steps Reverse process "Denoise step by step" Learned distribution that walks back from noise to image Epsilon prediction "Predict the noise" The training target: epsilon_theta(x_t, t) predicts the noise added at step $t$ Beta schedule "Noise amounts" Sequence of $T$ small variances that define how much noise enters per step $\bar{\alpha}_t$ "Cumulative retain factor" Product of $(1 - \beta_s)$ up to time $t$; bigger $t$ means less signal left DDPM sampler "Ancestral, stochastic" Samples each $x_{t-1}$ from its conditional Gaussian; 1000 steps DDIM sampler "Deterministic, fast" Rewrites sampling as a deterministic ODE; 20-100 steps with similar quality Time conditioning "Tell the model which t" Sinusoidal embedding of $t$ injected into the U-Net so it knows the noise level The problem In plain words first Take a photo and sprinkle a little random noise on it, then a little more, a thousand times, until nothing but static is left. That direction is easy and needs no learning. A diffusion model learns the opposite direction: shown a noisy image and told how noisy it is, it guesses the noise so it can be subtracted. Start from pure static, remove a little predicted noise a thousand times, and an image appears that was never in the training set. Training is just "guess the noise" with a squared-error loss, which is why it is so much calmer than a GAN. GANs generate one-shot: noise in, image out, one forward pass. They are fast and hard to train. Diffusion models generate iteratively: start from pure noise, denoise in small steps, image emerges. They are slow and easy to train. For the last five years the latter property has dominated: any small team can train a diffusion model and get reasonable samples; GAN training is a craft you learn over years of failed runs. Beyond training stability, diffusion's iterative structure is what unlocks everything modern image generation does: text conditioning, inpainting, image editing, super-resolution, controllable style. Each step of the sampling loop is a place to inject a new constraint. That hook is why Stable Diffusion, Imagen and DALL-E 3 are diffusion models, as are most controllable image tools. (Not all: OpenAI describes GPT-4o's image generation as autoregressive.) This lesson builds the minimal DDPM: forward noising, backward denoising, training loop. Idea 4 · The training loss For every training step: Sample a real image x_0 . Sample a timestep t uniformly from . Sample noise epsilon ~ N(0, I) . Compute x_t = sqrt(alpha_bar_t) * x_0 + sqrt(1 - alpha_bar_t) * epsilon . Predict epsilon_theta(x_t, t) with the network. Minimise || epsilon - epsilon_theta(x_t, t) ||^2 . That is it. The neural network learns to predict the noise at any timestep. The loss is MSE. There is no adversarial game, no collapse, no oscillation. Each training example uses one random and one forward pass. ✗ "The sampler should remove noise only; adding fresh noise each step is a bug." ✓ In DDPM the fresh noise is part of the maths. Copy The key is that even though the reverse conditional is not known in closed form in general, for this specific Gaussian forward process it is. The ugly-looking coefficients are what Bayes' rule gives you. Idea 6 · Why 1000 steps The forward noise schedule is chosen so each step adds just enough noise that the reverse step is nearly Gaussian. Too few steps and the reverse step is far from Gaussian, the network cannot model it well. Too many steps and sampling becomes expensive with diminishing gain. with a linear schedule is the DDPM default. Idea 7 · DDIM: 20x faster sampling Training is the same. Sampling changes. DDIM (Song et al., 2020) defines a deterministic reverse process that skips timesteps without retraining. Sampling in 50 steps with DDIM gives near-1000-step DDPM quality. Production systems use DDIM or faster solvers (DPM-Solver, Euler), or distilled models that need only a few steps. Recap What to keep from this lesson Forward process: a fixed schedule of small Gaussian noise steps; the closed form jumps to any directly. Training: pick a random , noise the image, and regress the noise with MSE. No adversary. DDPM sampling walks back all steps, adding fresh noise each step; DDIM skips steps deterministically. Fewer sampler steps trade a little quality for a lot of speed. The denoiser must know (time embedding) and must see far enough to coordinate whole shapes. Solutions Solution P1 · More steps, closer fit DDPM with 1,000 steps fits best, and DDIM improves as its step count rises from 10 to 200 (compare the printed distances). DDIM's selling point is not beating DDPM but getting close with 20 to 100 times fewer network calls, and on large image models the gap at 50 steps is usually small. With only 10 steps the shape is still there but noticeably looser. Solution B1 · Everything collapses to one point Without the fresh noise, each step moves the sample towards the average clean point consistent with it, and repeating that 1,000 times drags every starting point to nearly the same spot: the spread drops to almost zero. The fresh noise in DDPM is what keeps samples spread over the whole distribution. DDIM removes it legitimately only because it also changes the update coefficients to match. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Stable Diffusion is a DDPM that runs in the latent space of a pretrained VAE, conditioned on text via cross-attention, sampled with a fast deterministic ODE solver, and steered by classifier-free guidance. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Latent diffusion "Diffuse in latents" Run the entire DDPM in the VAE latent space (4x64x64) instead of pixel space (3x512x512); 48x fewer values to denoise VAE scale factor "0.18215" Constant that rescales the VAE's raw latent to roughly unit variance; 0.18215 for SD 1.x and 2.x, 0.13025 for SDXL; diffusers reads it from vae.config.scaling_factor Classifier-free guidance "CFG" Mix conditional and unconditional noise predictions; the single most impactful inference knob Scheduler "Sampler" The algorithm that turns noise + model predictions into a denoised latent trajectory LoRA "Low-rank adapter" Small rank-decomposition matrices that fine-tune attention layers without touching base weights Cross-attention "Text-image attention" Attention from latent tokens to text tokens; injects prompt information at every U-Net level ControlNet "Structure conditioning" A separately-trained adapter that steers SD with an extra input (canny, depth, pose, segmentation) DPM-Solver++ "The default scheduler" Second-order deterministic ODE solver; a common default at 20-30 steps The problem In plain words first Stable Diffusion is the previous lesson's denoiser with three practical upgrades. First, it does not denoise the full photo: a separate network (the VAE ) squeezes a 512 × 512 image into a small 64 × 64 grid of numbers, the diffusion happens there, and the VAE turns the result back into pixels. Second, the denoiser reads your prompt through a text encoder and cross-attention , so "a dog on a skateboard" shapes every step. Third, classifier-free guidance turns up how strongly the prompt is obeyed. Everything else, from image-to-image to LoRA fine-tuning, is a small variation on that pipeline. Training a DDPM directly on 512x512 RGB images is expensive. Every training step backprops through a U-Net that sees 3x512x512 = 786,432 input values, and sampling takes 50+ forward passes through that same U-Net. Even in latent space, Stable Diffusion v1 took about 150,000 A100 GPU-hours to train, according to its model card; in pixel space every one of those training steps, and every sampling step afterwards, would be far more expensive. The trick that made open-weight text-to-image practical was latent diffusion (Rombach et al., CVPR 2022). Train a VAE that maps a 3x512x512 image to a 4x64x64 latent tensor and back, then do the diffusion in that latent space. The number of values the denoiser handles drops by (3*512*512)/(4*64*64) = 48x , and since a U-Net's cost grows with spatial size, every training and sampling step gets cheaper by a similar order of magnitude. Almost every modern image-generation model — SDXL, SD3, FLUX, HunyuanDiT, Wan-Video — is a latent diffusion (or latent flow-matching) model with variations on the autoencoder, the denoiser (U-Net or DiT), and the text conditioning. Learn Stable Diffusion and you have learnt the template. Idea 1 · The pipeline VAE — frozen autoencoder. Encoder turns image into latents (used for img2img and training). Decoder turns latents back into an image. Text encoder — CLIP text encoder (SD 1.x/2.x), CLIP-L + CLIP-G (SDXL), or T5-XXL (SD3/FLUX). Produces a sequence of token embeddings. U-Net — the denoiser. Has cross-attention layers that attend from latents to the text embedding at every resolution level. Scheduler — the sampling algorithm (DDIM, Euler, DPM-Solver++). Picks sigmas, blends predicted noise back into the latent. Safety checker — optional NSFW / illegal-content filter on the output image. Worked example The 48x, by hand A 512 × 512 RGB image holds numbers. Its SD latent is numbers: each side shrinks 8 times (because ) and the channels go from 3 to 4. . The U-Net never sees a pixel. It denoises those 16,384 numbers 25 to 50 times, and the VAE decoder runs once at the end to turn the result into an image. Idea 2 · Classifier-free guidance (CFG) Plain text conditioning learns epsilon_theta(x_t, t, c) for every prompt c . CFG trains the same network with c dropped 10% of the time (replaced by an empty embedding), giving a single model that predicts both the conditional and the unconditional noise. At inference: ​ + w ⋅ ( ϵ cond ​ − ϵ uncond ​ ) w is the guidance scale. w=0 is unconditional, w=1 is plain conditional, w>1 pushes the output toward being "more conditioned on the prompt" at the cost of diversity. SD default is w=7.5 . CFG is the reason text-to-image works at production quality. Without it, prompts bias the output weakly; with it, prompts dominate. Check your mental model ✗ "Higher guidance is always better: the image matches the prompt more." ✓ It matches more narrowly . Past a point, samples lose variety, then leave the data distribution: over-saturated, over-sharpened images. The picture under "Use it" shows both effects. ✗ "CFG needs a separate unconditional model." ✓ One network, trained with the prompt dropped about 10% of the time, gives both predictions. It costs two forward passes per step at inference (usually batched together). ✗ "The 4 × 64 × 64 latent is an abstract code with no picture in it." ✓ It is still a small spatial map. The latent channels under "Use it" show the puppies' outline clearly. Idea 3 · Latent space geometry The VAE's 4-channel latent is not just a compressed image. It is still spatial (roughly a picture 8 times smaller, with 4 channels instead of 3), but only a thin set of latents decodes to natural images, and that set is what the diffusion U-Net spends its entire modelling budget on. Decoding a random 4x64x64 latent does not produce a random-looking image — it produces garbage, because only a specific submanifold of latents decodes to valid images. Two consequences: Img2img = encode image to latent, add partial noise, run the denoiser, decode. Image structure survives because only part of the noise schedule is applied, so the coarse layout is still in the latent; the prompt steers the details that the noise erased. Inpainting = same as img2img but the denoiser only updates masked regions; unmasked regions are kept at the encoded latent. Dedicated inpainting models such as stable-diffusion-inpainting go further: their U-Net takes 9 input channels (the noisy latent, the mask, and the latent of the masked image) so it sees the surroundings it must match. Worked example How much does img2img actually denoise? With strength=0.6 and num_inference_steps=50 , the pipeline noises the encoded photo to the point 60% of the way into the schedule, then runs only the last denoising steps. strength=1.0 starts from pure noise, which is why it ignores the input (Exercise 2), and strength=0.2 runs 10 steps on a barely noised latent, which can only change fine detail. Idea 4 · The U-Net architecture The SD U-Net is a big version of the TinyUNet from Lesson 4.10 scaled up, with three ingredients used far more heavily: Transformer blocks at every spatial resolution, containing self-attention + cross-attention to the text embedding. Time embedding via MLP on sinusoidal encoding. Skip connections between encoder and decoder at matching resolutions. Total parameters in SD 1.5: ~860M. SDXL: ~2.6B. FLUX: ~12B. (FLUX replaces the U-Net with a transformer.) Idea 5 · LoRA fine-tuning Full fine-tuning of Stable Diffusion needs 20+ GB of VRAM and updates 860M parameters. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) keeps the base model frozen and injects small rank-decomposition matrices into the attention layers. A LoRA adapter for SD is typically 10-50 MB, trains in 10-60 minutes on a single consumer GPU, and loads at inference time as a drop-in modification. Copy LoRA is how almost every community fine-tune is distributed. CivitAI and Hugging Face host huge libraries of them. Idea 6 · Schedulers you will see DDIM — deterministic, ~50 steps, simple. Euler ancestral — stochastic, 30-50 steps, slightly more creative samples. DPM-Solver++ 2M Karras — deterministic, 20-30 steps, production default. LCM / TCD / Turbo — consistency models and distilled variants; 1-4 steps at the cost of some quality. Swapping schedulers is a one-line change in diffusers and sometimes fixes sample issues without any retraining. The same idea as a formula Work in a latent space. A VAE encoder compresses a image to a latent (8× smaller per side): numbers become , 48 times fewer, and diffusion runs there. The decoder turns the final latent back into pixels. It gets the class (0 or 1) as an input, replaced by a "no class" token 10% of the time, exactly the CFG training recipe. Sampling uses DDIM with 50 steps and the CFG formula from Idea 2. At the samples are pushed so hard away from "what the unconditional model expects" that they leave the data altogether (the distance to data jumps). In images that shows up as over-saturated colours and harsh contrast, which is why Stable Diffusion defaults to 7.5, not 30. Img2img and inpainting reuse the same denoiser on a partly noised encoded image. LoRA trains small low-rank matrices in the attention layers and leaves the base model frozen. Solutions Solution P1 · Narrower, then wrong At samples fall on both moons (the label is ignored). From almost all land on the class-0 moon. As grows they crowd into a shrinking part of that moon, and at they drift off the data entirely. Guidance trades diversity for adherence, and too much of it leaves the distribution: the 2-D version of an over-cooked Stable Diffusion image. Solution B1 · Latents at the wrong scale The printed raw latent standard deviation is about 4.6, not 1. The noise schedule assumes data of roughly unit scale, so at every timestep the "clean" part of ​ is about 4.6 times too large relative to the noise. The model learns a different problem from the one the pretrained U-Net and the scheduler expect, and at inference its outputs decode to washed-out or blown-out images. Nothing errors; the constant is a contract between the VAE, the schedule and the U-Net. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Which Stable Diffusion people run. a0412: Course home / Phase 4 · Teaching Machines to See Understanding video over time Lesson 4.12 45 min Learn + Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Distinguish the three main video-modelling approaches (2D+pool, 3D conv, spatio-temporal transformer) and predict their cost and accuracy trade-offs Implement frame sampling, temporal pooling, and a 2D+pool baseline classifier in PyTorch Explain why I3D's "inflated" 3D kernels transfer well from ImageNet weights and what a factorised (2+1)D conv does differently Read the standard action-recognition datasets and metrics: Kinetics-400/600, UCF101, Something-Something V2; top-1 accuracy at the clip and video level Before you start Needs : Phase 4 Lesson 03 (CNNs), Phase 4 Lesson 04 (Telling images apart: classification) Type : Learn + Build. Time : about 45 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line A video is a sequence of images plus the physics that connects them. Every video model either treats time as an extra axis (3D conv), a sequence to attend over (transformer), or a feature to extract once and pool (2D+pool). Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means 2D + pool "Per-frame classifier" Run a 2D CNN on every sampled frame, average-pool features across time, classify 3D convolution "Spatio-temporal kernel" Kernel that convolves over (T, H, W); can model motion natively Inflation "Lift 2D weights to 3D" Initialise 3D conv weights by repeating a 2D conv's weights along the new time axis, then divide by kernel_T to preserve activation scale (2+1)D "Factorised conv" Split 3D into 2D spatial + 1D temporal; same parameter budget, extra non-linearity between Divided attention "Time then space" Transformer block with two attentions per layer: one over tokens at the same frame, one over tokens at the same position Clip "T-frame window" A sampled subsequence of T frames; the unit a video model consumes Clip vs video accuracy "Two eval settings" Clip = one sample per video, video = average across multiple sampled clips Kinetics "The ImageNet of video" 400-700 action classes, 300k+ YouTube clips, the standard video pretraining corpus The problem In plain words first A video is a stack of images in order. The easy way to classify one is to look at a few frames separately with an image model and average what it sees; that works when a single frame already shows the answer, such as "this is swimming". It fails when the answer is the motion : a door opening and a door closing contain the same frames in opposite order. To see motion a model has to look across neighbouring frames at once, with a 3D convolution or with attention across time. A 30-second video at 30 fps is 900 images. Naively, video classification is image classification run 900 times followed by some kind of aggregation. That works when the action is visible in almost every frame (sports, cooking, exercise videos) and fails badly when the action is defined by motion itself: "pushing something from left to right" looks like two still objects in every single frame. The core question for every video architecture is: when does temporal structure get modelled, and how? The answer drives everything else — compute cost, pretraining strategy, whether you can reuse ImageNet weights, what datasets the model trains on. This lesson is deliberately shorter than the static-image lessons. The core image machinery is already in place, and video understanding is mostly about the temporal story: sampling, modelling, and aggregating. Idea 1 · The three architectural families Idea 2 · 2D + pool Take a 2D CNN (ResNet, EfficientNet, ViT). Run it independently on every sampled frame. Average (or max-pool, or attention-pool) the per-frame embeddings. Feed the pooled vector to a classifier. Pros: - ImageNet pretraining transfers directly. - Simplest to implement. - Cheap: T frames * single-image inference cost. Cons: - Cannot model motion. Action = aggregate of appearances. - Temporal pooling is order-invariant; "open door" and "close door" look the same. When to use: appearance-heavy tasks, transfer learning on small video datasets, initial baselines. Worked example Why averaging cannot see direction A ball crosses the frame left to right in 4 frames: ​ , f 2 ​ , f 3 ​ , f 4 ​ . The 2D network turns each into a feature vector ​ … e 4 ​ , and the pooled video feature is = 4 1 ​ ( e 1 ​ + e 2 ​ + e 3 ​ + e 4 ​ ) The right-to-left video is the same frames in reverse, ​ , f 3 ​ , f 2 ​ , f 1 ​ , so its pooled feature is 1 ​ ( e 4 ​ + e 3 ​ + e 2 ​ + e 1 ​ ) : identical , because addition does not care about order. No amount of training can make the classifier tell them apart. Under "Use it" this exact situation gives FramePool 50% accuracy on a two-class problem. Idea 3 · 3D convolutions Replace 2D (H, W) kernels with 3D (T, H, W) kernels. The network convolves over both space and time. Early family: C3D, I3D, SlowFast. I3D trick: take a pretrained 2D ImageNet model, "inflate" each 2D kernel by copying it along a new time axis. A 3x3 2D conv becomes a 3x3x3 3D conv. This gives the 3D model strong pretrained weights instead of training from scratch. Pros: - Directly models motion. - I3D inflation gives free transfer learning. Cons: - About 3x the FLOPs of the 2D network run frame by frame, because each 3x3 kernel becomes 3x3x3. - Temporal kernels are small; long-range motion needs a pyramid or dual-stream approach. When to use: action recognition where motion is the signal (Something-Something V2, Kinetics with motion-heavy classes). Idea 4 · Spatio-temporal transformers Tokenise the video into a grid of space-time patches and attend across all of them. TimeSformer, ViViT, Video Swin, VideoMAE. Attention patterns that matter: - Joint — one big attention over (t, h, w). Quadratic in T*H*W ; expensive. - Divided — two attentions per block: one over time, one over space. Far cheaper than joint attention, because each token attends to T tokens in time plus H·W in space instead of all T·H·W. - Factorised — time attention alternates with space attention across blocks. Pros: - Top accuracy on most major benchmarks. - Transfers from image transformers (ViT) via patch inflation. - Supports long-context video via sparse attention. Cons: - Compute-hungry. - Requires careful attention pattern choice or runtime balloons. When to use: large datasets, high-fidelity video understanding, multi-modal video+text tasks. Check your mental model ✗ "A better image backbone will fix 2D+pool on motion tasks." ✓ Mean pooling is order-invariant. If the classes differ only in frame order, the pooled features are identical whatever the backbone. ✗ "(2+1)D saves parameters over 3D." ✓ Step 4's mid_c is chosen to match the 3D parameter count (see the worked example under Idea 5). The gain is the extra non-linearity, not size. ✗ "Joint space-time attention is the most accurate, so always use it." ✓ Its cost grows with the square of T·H·W tokens. Divided or factorised attention is the usual compromise. Idea 5 · Frame sampling A 10-second clip at 30 fps is 300 frames; feeding all 300 to any model is wasteful. Standard strategies: Uniform sampling — pick T frames evenly across the clip. Default for 2D+pool. Dense sampling — random contiguous T-frame window. Common for 3D convs because motion requires neighbouring frames. Multi-clip — sample multiple T-frame windows from the same video, classify each, average predictions at test time. T is usually 8, 16, 32, or 64. Higher T = more temporal signal at more compute. Worked example The (2+1)D parameter budget For a 3 × 3 × 3 convolution from 64 to 64 channels, a full 3D kernel has weights. Step 4 picks 64 ⋅ 64 ⋅ 27 ​ = 768 110 , 592 ​ = 144 so the spatial part has weights and the temporal part : a total of 110,592 , exactly the same. With other channel counts the integer division leaves it a few weights short. Idea 6 · Evaluation Two levels: - Clip-level accuracy — model sees one T-frame clip, reports top-k. - Video-level accuracy — average clip-level predictions across multiple clips per video; higher and more stable. Always report both. A model that scores 78% clip / 82% video is relying heavily on test-time averaging; one that scores 80% / 81% is more robust per-clip. Idea 7 · Datasets you will meet Kinetics-400 / 600 / 700 — the general-purpose action dataset. About 300k clips for Kinetics-400 and 650k for Kinetics-700; YouTube URLs (many now dead). Something-Something V2 — motion-defined actions ("moving X from left to right"). 2D+pool does poorly on it, because the class is the direction of motion. UCF-101 , HMDB-51 — older, smaller, still reported. AVA — action localisation in space and time; harder than classification. The same idea as a formula Three ways to add time. 2D + pool: run an image model on each of sampled frames and average (or attend over) the feature vectors. Cost times one image; no motion inside a frame pair is modelled. 3D convolution: a ​ × k h ​ × k w ​ kernel spans time too, with ​ k h ​ k w ​ C in ​ C out ​ weights; a kernel has three times the weights and cost of its image counterpart. Spatio-temporal transformer: cut the clip into tubelets of pixels, giving T ​ ⋅ p H ​ ⋅ p W ​ tokens 16 frames at with tubelets: tokens, eight times an image's 196, and full attention costs : 64 times as much. Factorised ("divided") attention attends over space within each frame and over time at each position, + T / t ) pairs instead of . Frame sampling. Uniform sampling of frames from takes indices 1 ​ ) N / K ⌋ ; dense sampling takes consecutive frames at a fixed stride. For long videos, the sampling decides what the model can see at all. Evaluation. Clip-level top-1 accuracy on single clips, and video-level accuracy averaging predictions over several clips and crops ("multi-view testing"). Step 1 · Frame sampler Uniform and dense samplers that work on a list of frames (or a video tensor). Copy Both return T indices that you use to slice the video tensor. Step 2 · A 2D+pool baseline Run a 2D ResNet-18 over every frame, average-pool features, classify. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Eleven million parameters, ImageNet pretrained, runs per-frame, averages, classifies. This baseline is often within 5-10 points of proper 3D models on appearance-heavy tasks — sometimes better, because it reuses a stronger ImageNet backbone. Predict before you run Under "Use it", FramePool (ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18) and a small network built from Step 4's Conv2Plus1D blocks both learn to tell "ball moving right" from "ball moving left". Every left-moving video is an exact time-reversal of a right-moving one. What test accuracy do you expect from each? (Solution P1.) Step 3 · An I3D-style inflated 3D conv Turn a single 2D conv into a 3D conv by repeating weights along a new time axis. Copy What you should see Copy Copy The division by time_kernel keeps the activation magnitudes roughly constant — important for not breaking batch-norm statistics on the first pass. Break it on purpose In inflate_2d_to_3d , delete / time_kernel . Feed a clip where every frame is the same image (a "boring video"). How does the 3D conv's output compare with the original 2D conv on that image? (Solution B1.) Step 4 · Factorised (2+1)D conv Split a 3D conv into a 2D (spatial) and a 1D (temporal) conv. Same receptive field and, with the mid_c chosen below, the same number of parameters as the full 3D conv, but with an extra non-linearity in between. The R(2+1)D paper found this more accurate and easier to optimise. Copy What you should see Copy Copy A full R(2+1)D network is the same as a ResNet-18 with every 3x3 conv replaced by Conv2Plus1D . Use it: the same idea with real libraries Two libraries cover production video work: torchvision.models.video — R(2+1)D, MViT, Swin3D with pretrained Kinetics weights. Same API as image models. pytorchvideo (Meta) — model zoo, data loaders for Kinetics / SSv2 / AVA, standard transforms. For Vision-Language video models (video captioning, video QA), use transformers : VideoMAE , TimeSformer and ViViT for classification, and video-language models such as LlavaNextVideo and VideoLlava . See it drawn See it: appearance versus motion 400 training and 200 test clips of 8 frames, 64 × 64. Each shows one coloured ball sliding right; its exact time-reversal is added as "sliding left". First, the lesson's FramePool . Show the code that draws this Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output FramePool sits at exactly 50%, a coin flip, and the logits for a clip and its reversal agree to within floating-point rounding (about 1e-7). The two rows of frames contain the same eight images, so after averaging there is literally nothing left that differs. This is the worked example under Idea 2, run for real. See it drawn Now a model that sees time The same data, with a small network made of three of Step 4's Conv2Plus1D blocks (about 43,000 parameters, trained from scratch, against FramePool's 11 million pretrained ones). Show the code that draws this Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output A network with about 260 times fewer parameters and no pretraining gets the direction right on every test clip within two or three epochs, because its temporal kernels compare neighbouring frames. Pretraining and size buy nothing when the architecture throws the signal away. On real datasets the gap is smaller (most action classes also have tell-tale appearance), but on motion-defined datasets like Something-Something V2 this is exactly the story. Recap What to keep from this lesson Three families: 2D+pool, 3D (or (2+1)D) convolution, and space-time transformers. Mean pooling over frames is order-invariant: it cannot see direction or sequence. Inflation reuses 2D ImageNet weights in 3D by repeating them over time and dividing by the time size. (2+1)D splits a 3D kernel into spatial then temporal parts at the same parameter budget. Sample frames uniformly or densely, and report clip-level and video-level accuracy. Solutions Solution P1 · 50% versus nearly 100% FramePool scores exactly 50%: every test clip has a twin with the same frames in reverse order and the opposite label, and mean pooling gives both twins the same features. The tiny (2+1)D network reaches 100% by its third epoch. Size and ImageNet pretraining cannot compensate for an architecture that discards order. Solution B1 · Activations three times too large On a clip whose frames are all identical, the inflated conv adds up three copies of the same 2D response, one per time tap. Dividing by time_kernel turns that sum back into the original 2D output, which is why inflation preserves ImageNet behaviour on static content. Without the division every activation is 3 times larger at the first layer, the batch-norm statistics learned in 2D no longer match, and the effect compounds layer after layer. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Video understanding through VLMs. Gemini accepts long videos directly, and open models such as Qwen3-VL (2025) handle hours of video with timestamps; many production video-search and summarisation features use them instead of trained temporal classifiers. Dedicated video models still matter for real-time or on-device work: action recognition with VideoMAE-style encoders, and video embedding services (TwelveLabs, Vertex AI multimodal embeddings) for search. Sources: Gemini video understanding , Qwen3-VL , VideoMAE , TwelveLabs .
