a0413: Course home / Phase 4 · Teaching Machines to See Seeing in 3D: point clouds and NeRFs Lesson 4.13 45 min Learn + Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Distinguish explicit (point cloud, mesh, voxel) and implicit (signed distance field, NeRF) 3D representations and when each is used Understand PointNet's symmetric-function trick that makes a neural network permutation-invariant over an unordered set of points Trace a NeRF forward pass: ray casting, volumetric rendering, positional encoding, MLP density+colour head Use nerfstudio or instant-ngp for pretrained 3D reconstruction from a small set of posed images Before you start Needs : Phase 4 Lesson 03 (CNNs), Phase 1 Lesson 12 (Shapes, axes and broadcasting with tensors) Type : Learn + Build. Time : about 45 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line 3D vision comes in two flavours. Point clouds are the sensor's raw output. NeRFs are the learned volumetric field. Both answer "what is where in space." Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Point cloud "3D points from LIDAR" Unordered set of (x, y, z) + optional features per point PointNet "First neural net on point clouds" Shared MLP per point + symmetric (max) pool; permutation-invariant by construction NeRF "MLP that is the scene" Network mapping (x, y, z, dir) to (density, colour); rendered by ray casting Positional encoding "Fourier features" Encode each coordinate into sin/cos at multiple frequencies to overcome MLP low-frequency bias Volumetric rendering "Ray integration" Composite samples along a ray into a single pixel using transmittance and alpha Instant-NGP "Hash-grid NeRF" Replaces NeRF's coordinate MLP with a multi-resolution hash grid; 100-1000x faster 3D Gaussian splatting "Millions of Gaussians" Scene = collection of 3D Gaussians; renders in real time, trains in minutes SDF "Signed distance field" Function returning signed distance to the nearest surface; another implicit representation The problem In plain words first There are two common ways to hold a 3D scene in a computer. A point cloud is just a list of 3D points, the raw output of a LIDAR or depth camera; the list has no order, so a network must give the same answer however the points are shuffled. A NeRF stores the scene inside a small neural network: give it a position and a viewing direction, and it says how solid the space is there and what colour it looks. To render a picture you shoot a ray through each pixel, ask the network about points along the ray, and blend the answers. Train it on a few photos with known camera positions and it can render views no camera ever took. A camera produces a 2D image. A LIDAR produces a set of 3D points with no ordering. A structure-from-motion pipeline produces a sparse cloud of 3D keypoints. A NeRF reconstructs an entire 3D scene from a handful of posed images. All of these are "vision" but none of them look like the dense tensor a CNN wants. 3D vision matters because almost every high-value robot task runs in 3D: grasping, obstacle avoidance, navigation, AR occlusion, 3D content capture. A vision engineer who only understands 2D images is locked out of the fastest-growing slice of the field (AR/VR content, robotics, autonomous driving stacks, NeRF-based 3D reconstruction for real-estate or construction). The two representations dominate for different reasons. Point clouds are what sensors give you for free. NeRFs and their successors (3D Gaussian splatting, neural SDFs) are what you get when you ask a neural network to learn a scene. Idea 1 · Point clouds A point cloud is an unordered set of points in , optionally each with features (colour, intensity, normal). Copy No grid, no connectivity. Two properties make this hard for neural networks: Permutation invariance — the output must not depend on point order. Variable N — a single model must handle clouds of different sizes. PointNet (Qi et al., 2017) solved both with one idea: apply a shared MLP to every point, then aggregate with a symmetric function (max pool). The result is a fixed-size vector that does not depend on order. max ​ MLP ( p ) This is the entire core of PointNet. Deeper variants (PointNet++, Point Transformer) add hierarchical sampling and local aggregation but the symmetric-function trick is unchanged. Worked example Why max is order-proof Three points pass through the shared MLP and come out as 2-number features: , , . Max-pooling each feature over the points gives . List the points in any of the 6 possible orders and you still get , because max, like sum and mean, ignores order. Flattening instead, , changes with every reordering, so a network built on it would give 6 different answers for the same object. Idea 2 · The PointNet architecture "Shared MLP" means the same MLP runs on every point independently. Implemented as a 1x1 conv over the point dimension for efficiency. Idea 3 · Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) NeRFs (Mildenhall et al., 2020) took the question "can we reconstruct a 3D scene from N photos?" and answered with a neural network that is the scene. The network maps (x, y, z, viewing_direction) to (density, colour) . Rendering a new view is a ray-casting loop over this network. Copy A loss compares the rendered pixel to the ground-truth pixel in the training photos. Backprop through the rendering step updates the MLP. No 3D ground truth, no explicit geometry — the scene is stored in the MLP weights. Idea 4 · Positional encoding in NeRF A vanilla MLP on (x, y, z) cannot represent high-frequency details because MLPs are spectrally biased toward low frequencies. NeRF fixes this by encoding each coordinate into a Fourier feature vector before the MLP: π p ) , cos ( 2 0 π p ) , sin ( 2 1 π p ) , cos ( 2 1 π p ) , … ) Up to frequency levels. This is the same trick transformers use for positions, and it appears again in diffusion time conditioning ( Lesson 4.10 ). Without it, NeRFs look blurry. Idea 5 · Volumetric rendering T i ​ δ i ​ ​ = i ∑ ​ T i ​ ( 1 − exp ( − σ i ​ δ i ​ ) ) c i ​ = exp ( − j < i ∑ ​ σ j ​ δ j ​ ) = t i + 1 ​ − t i ​ ​ T_i is transmittance — how much light survives to point . (1 - exp(-sigma_i * delta_i)) is the opacity at point . c_i is the colour. The final pixel is a weighted sum along the ray. Worked example One ray, two samples A ray meets two samples apart: first a thin red haze with ​ = 2 , then a dense blue surface with ​ = 10 . Sample 1: opacity = 0.632 , transmittance ​ = 1 , weight . Sample 2: opacity = 0.993 , transmittance ​ = e − 1 = 0.368 , weight . The pixel is : mostly red, because the haze in front absorbs 63% of the light before it reaches the blue surface. The weights sum to 0.998, so almost nothing of the background shows through. Check your mental model ✗ "A NeRF stores a 3D model, like a mesh, inside the network." ✓ It stores a function: density and colour at any point. Surfaces are only where density happens to be high. ✗ "Training needs 3D ground truth." ✓ Only photos and their camera poses. The loss compares rendered pixels with real pixels; geometry appears because it is the only consistent explanation of every view. ✗ "More view-direction detail is always better." ✓ With few views, a high-frequency direction encoding lets the network paint each training view separately and generalise badly (see "Try it yourself" under "Use it"). Idea 6 · What replaced NeRFs Pure NeRFs are slow to train (hours) and slow to render (seconds per image). The lineage since: Instant-NGP (2022) — hash-grid encoding replaces the MLP's position input; trains in seconds. Mip-NeRF 360 — handles unbounded scenes and anti-aliasing. 3D Gaussian Splatting (2023) — replaces the volumetric field with millions of 3D Gaussians; trains in minutes, renders in real time. Now the most widely used of these for real-time view synthesis. Many products that started with NeRFs now use Gaussian splatting, which Lesson 4.22 covers. The volumetric rendering idea from NeRF carries over. Idea 7 · Datasets and benchmarks ShapeNet — classification and segmentation of 3D CAD models as point clouds. ScanNet — real indoor scans for segmentation. KITTI — outdoor LIDAR point clouds for autonomous driving. NeRF Synthetic / Blended MVS — posed-image datasets for view synthesis. Mip-NeRF 360 dataset — unbounded real scenes. The same idea as a formula Point clouds are sets. A cloud of points has no natural order, so a classifier must give the same answer for any permutation. PointNet achieves it with a symmetric function: ​ , … , x n ​ ) = γ ( i = 1 max n ​ h ( x i ​ ) ) a shared MLP on every point, an element-wise max over points, and a final MLP . The max picks, for each feature, the most extreme point, so a few critical points determine the output. Volume rendering (NeRF). A network maps a 3-D position and viewing direction to a density and a colour . Along a camera ray, with samples spaced ​ apart, ∑ ​ T i ​ ( 1 − e − σ i ​ δ i ​ ) c i ​ , T i ​ = exp ( − j < i ∑ ​ σ j ​ δ j ​ ) ​ δ i ​ is the chance the ray stops in sample , and ​ the chance it got that far. Everything is differentiable, so the network is trained by comparing rendered and real pixels. Positional encoding. MLPs struggle to represent fine detail from raw coordinates, so each coordinate is expanded to π p ) , cos ( 2 k π p ) ) k = 0 L − 1 ​ , with for positions in the original NeRF: 60 numbers per point instead of 3. Cost. Rendering one image with 192 samples per ray needs over 120 million network evaluations, which is why rasterised Gaussian splatting (Lesson 4.22) replaced NeRF for real-time use. For deployment, 3D Gaussian splatting has largely replaced pure NeRFs: it renders in real time (the paper reports over 100 frames per second at 1080p) where NeRFs of similar quality took seconds per frame, with comparable reconstruction quality. A NeRF built from this lesson's positional_encoding , TinyNeRF and volumetric_render learns the scene from those pixels alone, then renders a held-out viewpoint. One change to TinyNeRF : density goes through softplus instead of relu (see "Break it on purpose"). The depth panels are the striking part. Nobody gave the network any 3D information, yet its depth for the sphere pixels matches the ray tracer's true depth to within about 0.12 units on average, with the blue sphere correctly nearer than the orange one. Geometry emerges because a consistent 3D density is the simplest way to explain all 24 photos at once. Make it your own Try it yourself Change L_dir=1 to L_dir=4 , the lesson's default, and rerun. The training loss gets even lower but the held-out PSNR drops sharply (in our run, to about 16 dB, with washed-out colours): with high-frequency direction features and only two rings of cameras, the network paints each training direction separately instead of learning one colour per surface point. Real NeRFs keep direction detail but train on 100 or more views. Recap What to keep from this lesson Point clouds are unordered sets; PointNet's shared MLP plus max pooling makes the output order-independent. A NeRF maps position and view direction to density and colour; rendering integrates along camera rays. Volumetric rendering weights each sample by its opacity times the light that survived to reach it. Positional encoding lets an MLP represent fine detail; too much of it for view direction overfits. Gaussian splatting is the faster successor; the volumetric idea carries over. Solutions Solution P1 · Blurry but right, with real depth The render is recognisable but soft (about 23 dB PSNR on the printed line), because 24 images of 32 × 32 pixels are very little data. The depth map matches the true depth closely (the printed error is about 0.12 units, with the camera 4 units away), even though no depth was ever given: the network found a 3D density that explains every photo, and depth falls out of it. Solution B1 · All density dies At the start every sample has some density, so each ray is partly opaque and the render is far from the white background. The fastest way to reduce the loss is to push density down everywhere, and once relu receives a negative input its output and its gradient are exactly zero. When we trained the unmodified TinyNeRF this way, density went to zero everywhere within a few hundred steps and the network rendered a black image from then on, with no gradient to recover. softplus is never exactly zero and always has a gradient, which is why later NeRF variants such as mip-NeRF use it. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Point clouds in production. Autonomous vehicles and robots process LiDAR point clouds (Waymo's and others' open datasets), and phones with LiDAR (iPhone Pro) produce them for AR and scanning; Open3D and PyTorch3D are common libraries. NeRF gave way to Gaussian splatting in most products that capture 3-D scenes from photos (Lesson 4.22), because splats render in real time; NeRF ideas remain in research and some mapping systems. a0414: Course home / Phase 4 · Teaching Machines to See Reading images as patches (ViT) Lesson 4.14 45 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Implement patch embedding, learned positional embedding, class token, and transformer encoder blocks from scratch to build a minimal ViT Explain why ViT was thought to need massive pretraining data until DeiT and MAE proved otherwise Compare ViT, Swin, and ConvNeXt on their architectural priors (none, local window attention, conv backbone) Fine-tune a pretrained ViT on a small dataset using timm and the standard linear-probe / fine-tune recipe Before you start Needs : Phase 7 Lesson 02 (Self-Attention), Phase 4 Lesson 04 (Telling images apart: classification) Type : Build. Time : about 45 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Cut the image into patches, treat each patch as a word, run a standard transformer. Don't look back. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Patch embedding "The first conv" A conv with kernel size = stride = patch size; turns the image into a grid of token embeddings Class token "[CLS]" A learned vector prepended to the token sequence; its final output is the global image representation Positional embedding "Learned pos" A learned vector added to every token so the transformer knows where each patch came from Pre-LN "LayerNorm before sublayer" The stable transformer variant: x + sublayer(LN(x)) instead of LN(x + sublayer(x)) Multi-head attention "Parallel attention" Standard transformer attention split into num_heads independent subspaces, concatenated afterwards ViT-B/16 "Base, patch 16" The canonical size: dim=768, depth=12, heads=12, patch_size=16, image=224; ~86M params DeiT "Data-efficient ViT" ViT trained on ImageNet-1k alone with strong augmentation; proved large pretraining datasets are not strictly required MAE "Masked autoencoder" Self-supervised pretraining: mask 75% of patches, reconstruct; a widely used ViT pretraining recipe The problem In plain words first A Vision Transformer cuts an image into a grid of small square patches, say 16 × 16 pixels each, and treats every patch like a word in a sentence. Each patch becomes a vector, a learned "where am I" vector is added so the model knows its position, and a standard transformer lets every patch look at every other patch through attention. An extra "summary" token collects the result for classification. There is no convolution and no built-in idea that nearby pixels belong together, so a ViT has to learn that from data, which is why it needs more data or more help than a CNN. For a decade, convolution was synonymous with computer vision. CNNs had strong inductive biases — locality, translation equivariance — that nobody thought you could replace. Then Dosovitskiy et al. (2020) showed that a plain transformer applied to flattened image patches, with no convolutional machinery at all, could match or beat the best CNNs at scale. The catch was "at scale." ViT on ImageNet-1k lost to ResNet. ViT pretrained on ImageNet-21k or JFT-300M then fine-tuned on ImageNet-1k beat it. The conclusion was that transformers lacked useful priors but could learn them from enough data. Subsequent work (DeiT, MAE, DINO) showed that with the right training recipes — strong augmentation, self-supervised pretraining, distillation — ViTs train fine on small data too. Pure CNNs remain competitive, especially on edge devices (ConvNeXt is a strong example), but transformers now lead most other areas: segmentation (Mask2Former, SegFormer), detection (DETR, RT-DETR), multimodal (CLIP, SigLIP), video (VideoMAE, VJEPA). The ViT block structure is the one to know. Idea 1 · The pipeline Seven steps. Patches -> tokens -> attention -> classifier. Variants such as DeiT, Swin and MAE pretraining change one or two of the seven and leave the rest alone. Idea 2 · Patch embedding The first conv is the secret. Kernel size 16, stride 16, so a 224x224 image becomes a 14x14 grid of 16x16 patches, each projected to a 768-dim embedding. That single conv both patchifies and linearly projects. Copy 196 patches = 196 tokens. Each token's feature dimension is 768 (ViT-B), 1024 (ViT-L), or 1280 (ViT-H). Worked example Counting tokens and weights A 224 × 224 image with 16 × 16 patches gives patches per side, patches. With the class token, 197 tokens. Each patch holds numbers. ViT-B projects it to 768 dimensions too, so the patch-embedding conv is a matrix plus 768 biases: 590,592 weights, under 1% of ViT-B's 86M. Attention compares every token with every other: ≈ 38 , 800 pairs per head per layer. Halve the patch size to 8 and there are 784 patches, about 16 times as many pairs (Idea 7). Idea 3 · Class token A single learned vector prepended to the sequence: Copy After N transformer blocks, the [CLS] output is the global image representation. Classification head reads only this one vector. Idea 4 · Positional embedding Transformers have no built-in notion of spatial position. Add a learned vector to every token: Copy The embedding is a parameter of the model; gradient-based training adapts it to 2D image structure. Fixed 2D sine-cosine embeddings work about as well and are what MAE uses; newer models often use relative schemes such as 2D RoPE instead. See it drawn See what the positions learned Each panel takes one patch position in the pretrained ViT-B/16 loaded under "Use it" and colours every other position by how similar their learned positional embeddings are (cosine similarity). Show the code that draws this Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Nobody told the model the image is a 2D grid; it got 196 independent vectors to learn. Yet each position's embedding ends up most similar to its neighbours, and also to positions in the same row and column (the bright cross through each square). Training on images taught the model that the patches form a grid. This is the same picture as Figure 7 of the ViT paper. Idea 5 · Transformer encoder block Standard. Multi-head self-attention, MLP, residual connections, pre-LayerNorm. Copy ViT-B/16 stacks 12 of these blocks, each with 12 attention heads, totalling 86M parameters. Check your mental model ✗ "The class token sees only its own patch." ✓ It has no patch. It is a learned extra token whose output, after attending to every patch in every layer, summarises the image. ✗ "Without positional embeddings, a ViT just gets a bit less accurate." ✓ It becomes blind to arrangement: shuffling the patches gives exactly the same output (see "Break it on purpose"). ✗ "Attention maps show what the model is looking at." ✓ Sometimes. In large ViTs the last layers often attend to a few low-information background patches used as scratch space (see "Use it"). Idea 6 · Why pre-LN Early transformers used post-LN ( x = LN(x + sublayer(x)) ) and struggled to train past 6-8 layers without warmup. Pre-LN ( x = x + sublayer(LN(x)) ) trains deeper networks stably without warmup. Almost every ViT and modern LLM uses pre-normalisation (Swin-V2 is a notable exception, with a modified post-norm). Idea 7 · Patch size trade-off 16x16 patches -> 196 tokens, standard. 32x32 patches -> 49 tokens, faster but lower resolution. 8x8 patches -> 784 tokens, finer but ) attention cost scales badly. Bigger patches = fewer tokens = faster but less spatial detail. SwinV2 uses 4x4 patches in hierarchical windows. Idea 8 · DeiT's recipe for training ViT on ImageNet-1k The original ViT needed JFT-300M to beat CNNs. DeiT (Touvron et al., 2020) trained ViT-B to 81.8% top-1 on ImageNet-1k alone with four changes: Heavy augmentation: RandAugment, Mixup, CutMix, Random Erasing. Stochastic depth (drop entire blocks at random during training). Repeated augmentation (same image sampled 3 times per batch). Distillation from a CNN teacher (optional, lifts accuracy further). Every modern ViT training recipe descends from DeiT. Predict before you run Under "Use it" a small CNN (95,000 parameters) and a small ViT (809,000 parameters, patch size 4) train for 8 epochs on just 5,000 CIFAR-10 images with the same optimiser and flip augmentation. Which scores higher on held-out images? (Solution P1.) Idea 9 · Swin vs ConvNeXt Swin (Liu et al., 2021) — window-based attention. Each block attends within a local window; alternating blocks shift the window to mix information across windows. Brings back a CNN-like locality prior while keeping the attention operator. ConvNeXt (Liu et al., 2022) — redesigned CNN that matches Swin's architecture choices (depthwise convs, LayerNorm, GELU, inverted bottleneck). Showed that the gap is not "attention vs convolution" but "modern training recipe + architecture." In 2026, ConvNeXt-V2 and Swin-V2 are both production-grade; the right choice depends on your inference stack (ConvNeXt compiles better for edge) and pretraining corpus. Idea 10 · MAE pretraining Masked Autoencoder (He et al., 2022): mask 75% of patches at random, train the encoder to process only the visible 25%, train a small decoder to reconstruct the masked patches from the encoder's output. After pretraining, discard the decoder and fine-tune the encoder. MAE pretraining on ImageNet-1k alone let ViT-H reach 87.8% top-1, and MAE became one of the standard self-supervised recipes alongside DINO-style methods. The same idea as a formula Patches become tokens. An image cut into patches gives H ​ ⋅ P W ​ patches, each flattened to P 2 C numbers For and : = 196 patches of numbers, each multiplied by a learned matrix (equivalently a convolution with stride 16). A learned class token is prepended and learned position embeddings are added: the encoder sees 197 vectors. Encoder block (pre-LN, as in every modern ViT): Normalising inside each branch leaves the residual stream untouched, so gradients pass straight through it; post-LN puts a normalisation on the stream itself and needs careful warm-up to train deep stacks. Patch size and cost. Attention costs D ) per layer. Halving to 8 quadruples to 784 and multiplies attention cost by 16, for finer detail. MAE pretraining. Hide a random 75% of the patches, run the encoder on the 49 visible ones only (about a quarter of the encoder's compute), and train a light decoder to reconstruct the hidden pixels; the loss is computed on the masked patches only. Step 1 · Patch embedding Copy One conv, one flatten, one transpose. That is the entire image-to-tokens step. Step 2 · Transformer block Pre-LN, multi-head self-attention, MLP with GELU, residual connections. Step 3 · The ViT Copy What you should see Copy Copy About 2.8M parameters — a tiny ViT tractable on CPU. Real ViT-B is 86M; same class definition with dim=768, depth=12, num_heads=12 . Break it on purpose In ViT.forward , delete x = x + self.pos_embed . Then cut a photo into its patches, shuffle them into a jigsaw, and run the photo and the jigsaw through the model. What happens? Under "Use it" this is done to the pretrained ViT-B by zeroing its positional embedding. (Solution B1.) Step 4 · Sanity check — single image inference Copy What you should see Copy Copy Should run without error. Probabilities sum to 1. Use it: the same idea with real libraries timm ships every ViT variant with ImageNet pretrained weights. One line: Copy timm is the most widely used library for vision backbones. Supports ViT, DeiT, Swin, Swin-V2, ConvNeXt, ConvNeXt-V2, MaxViT, MViT, EfficientFormer, and dozens of others under the same API. For multi-modal work (image + text), transformers ships CLIP, SigLIP, BLIP-2, LLaVA. The image encoder in all of those is a ViT variant. See it drawn Where does a pretrained ViT attend? The ImageNet-trained ViT-B/16 on three photos. Each heat map shows how much the class token attends to each patch, averaged over the 12 heads, in an early block (3) and the last block (12). Show the code that draws this Copy What you should see Copy Copy See it drawn See the broken version The same pretrained ViT-B on the first photo and on a jigsaw of it (its 196 patches shuffled), first as trained, then with its positional embedding set to zero. Show the code that draws this Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Reading these outputs The attention maps. The model classifies each photo correctly. In block 3 the class token spreads its attention widely, with clear focus on the dog in the first photo. In block 12 a few patches in the background take a large share of it: the top 3 of 196 patches get roughly 30 to 45% (an even spread would give them 1.5%). This is a known behaviour of large ViTs (Darcet et al., 2023, "Vision Transformers Need Registers"): the model repurposes a few uninformative background patches to hold global information. The lesson: an attention map is not an explanation of what the model "looked at". The jigsaw. As trained, the model still calls the jigsaw an English springer, from fur texture alone, but its confidence halves (90% to 46%): arrangement matters to it. With the positional embedding zeroed, photo and jigsaw get identical probabilities up to rounding, because the transformer now treats the patches as an unordered set. It is also badly broken, calling both a space shuttle, since it was trained to rely on positions. See it drawn Small data: CNN versus ViT 5,000 CIFAR-10 training images and 2,000 test images, both models trained 8 epochs with AdamW and random horizontal flips. First the CNN. Copy What you should see Copy Copy See it drawn Then the ViT The lesson's ViT class sized for 32 × 32 inputs: 4 × 4 patches (64 tokens), width 128, depth 4. Show the code that draws this Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output With only 5,000 images the CNN wins on test accuracy despite having about a ninth of the parameters, and it is ahead on training accuracy too: in the same 8 epochs the ViT has not even fitted the training images as well. The CNN gets locality and translation equivariance for free from its convolutions; the ViT has to discover that nearby pixels belong together from the data itself, which takes more examples and more updates. This is the effect DeiT's augmentation recipe and MAE pretraining were designed to overcome, and why fine-tuning a pretrained ViT is the usual way to use one on a small dataset. Recap What to keep from this lesson A ViT turns an image into a sequence of patch tokens with one strided conv, adds a class token and positional embeddings, and runs a transformer. Positional embeddings carry all the information about arrangement; without them the model sees a bag of patches. Pre-norm residual blocks: attention then MLP, each wrapped as x + f(LN(x)) . ViTs have weak built-in priors, so they need large data, heavy augmentation (DeiT) or self-supervised pretraining (MAE). Attention maps are suggestive, not explanations; large ViTs park attention on a few background tokens. Solutions Solution P1 · The CNN wins on small data The CNN reaches the higher test accuracy (the printed numbers), even though the ViT has about nine times as many parameters. The ViT also trails on training accuracy: without the built-in assumptions of a convolution it learns more slowly from the same images. With hundreds of thousands of images, or with pretraining, the order flips. Solution B1 · A bag of patches With the positional embedding zeroed, the jigsaw and the original get identical probabilities up to rounding. Attention is permutation-equivariant: shuffle the input tokens and the outputs shuffle the same way. The class token reads a weighted sum over all of them, which does not depend on their order. Position is the only place the model learns where a patch was, so deleting it makes the model unable to tell a face from a scrambled face. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) ViTs are the default vision backbone in foundation models: SigLIP 2 (2025) is the image encoder of many vision-language models, Gemma 3 uses a SigLIP encoder, and DINOv2 and DINOv3 are ViTs. Efficient attention for images. FlashAttention and native-resolution patching (NaViT-style packing in Qwen-VL and SigLIP 2's NaFlex variant) let ViTs handle large and oddly shaped images. a0415: Course home / Phase 4 · Teaching Machines to See Vision on small devices, in real time Lesson 4.15 75 min Learn + Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Measure inference latency, peak memory, and throughput for any PyTorch model, and read the FLOPs / params / latency trade-off Quantise a vision model to INT8 using PyTorch's post-training quantisation and verify accuracy loss < 1% Export to ONNX and compile with ONNX Runtime or TensorRT; name the three most common export failures and their fixes Explain when to pick MobileNetV3, EfficientNet-Lite, ConvNeXt-Tiny, or MobileViT for an edge constraint Before you start Needs : Phase 4 Lesson 04 (Telling images apart: classification), Phase 10 Lesson 11 (Quantization) Type : Learn + Build. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Edge inference is the discipline of getting a 90%-accurate model to run at 30 fps on a device with 2 GB of RAM. Every percentage point of accuracy is traded against milliseconds of latency. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Latency "How fast" Time from input to output; p50/p95/p99 percentiles, not mean FLOPs "Model size" Floating-point ops per forward pass; rough proxy for compute cost INT8 quantisation "8-bit" Replace FP32 weights/activations with 8-bit integers; ~4x smaller, 2-4x faster PTQ "Post-training quantisation" Quantise a trained model without retraining; easy, usually enough QAT "Quantisation-aware training" Simulate quantisation during training; best accuracy, requires labelled data ONNX "The neutral format" Model exchange format supported by every mainstream inference runtime TensorRT "NVIDIA compiler" Compiles ONNX into an optimised engine for NVIDIA GPUs Distillation "Teacher -> student" Train a small model to mimic a big model's logits; recovers most lost accuracy The problem In plain words first A model that works on a big training machine still has to run somewhere small: a phone, a camera, a car. Edge deployment is the job of making it fit. You measure first (how many milliseconds per image, how much memory), then pull three levers: pick a smaller architecture, store the numbers in 8-bit integers instead of 32-bit floats ( quantisation ), and run it with an inference engine built for the target hardware. The one rule that never changes: measure on the device, because estimates such as FLOP counts often point the wrong way. A training-time vision model is a floating-point monster. 100M parameters, 10 GFLOPs per forward pass, 2 GB of VRAM. None of that fits on a phone, a car's infotainment unit, an industrial camera, or a drone. Shipping a vision system means fitting the same predictions into a budget that is 100x smaller. Three knobs do most of the work: model choice (a smaller architecture with the same recipe), quantisation (INT8 instead of FP32), and the inference runtime (ONNX Runtime, TensorRT, Core ML, TFLite). Getting them right is the difference between a demo that runs on a workstation and a product that ships on a $30 camera module. This lesson sets up the measurement discipline first (you cannot optimise what you cannot measure), then walks the three knobs. The goal is not to learn every edge runtime but to know what levers exist and how to verify each one does what you think. Idea 1 · The three budgets Latency : p50, p95, p99. Reporting only p50 (or the mean) hides tail behaviour that matters for real-time systems. Peak memory : the maximum the device ever sees, not the steady-state average. Matters because OOMs are fatal on embedded targets. Power / energy : millijoules per inference on a battery-powered device. Often proxied by CPU/GPU utilisation * time. A table of (model, latency, memory, accuracy) is what an edge decision is made from. Every cell is measured on the target device, not the workstation. Worked example A 30 fps budget At 30 frames per second each frame has ms. On the CPU under "Use it", ResNet-18's median (p50) latency is close to that, but its p95 is around 40 ms: one frame in twenty would arrive late and the video would stutter. That is why edge budgets are written against p95 or p99, not the mean. Memory works the same way. ResNet-18 has 11.7M parameters; at 4 bytes each that is MB of weights, and at 1 byte each (INT8) 11.7 MB. The file sizes printed under "Use it" match. Idea 2 · Measurement discipline Three rules that every edge profile should follow: Warm up the model with 5-10 dummy forward passes before measuring. Cold caches and JIT compilation produce unrepresentative first numbers. Synchronise GPU workloads with torch.cuda.synchronize() before and after the timed block. Without this you measure kernel dispatch, not kernel execution. Fix input sizes to the production resolution. Latency on 224x224 is not latency on 512x512. Idea 3 · FLOPs as a proxy FLOPs (floating-point operations per inference) is a cheap, device-independent proxy for latency. Useful for architecture comparison, misleading as absolute wall-clock. A model with 10% more FLOPs can be 2x faster in practice because it uses hardware-friendly ops (depthwise convs compile well, large 7x7 convs do not). Rule: use FLOPs for architecture search, use on-device latency for deployment decisions. Check your mental model ✗ "Fewer FLOPs means faster." ✓ Under "Use it", EfficientNet-B0 needs about a fifth of ResNet-18's FLOPs and is slower on this CPU: depthwise convolutions and squeeze-excitation do little arithmetic per byte of memory moved. ✗ "Quantisation always costs accuracy." ✓ It usually costs a little, but on 300 test images the INT8 ResNet-18 under "Use it" scores within noise of the FP32 one. ✗ "ONNX Runtime is always faster than PyTorch." ✓ It depends on model, hardware and settings. On this CPU the two were within a few milliseconds for FP32 ResNet-18. Benchmark both. Idea 4 · Quantisation in one paragraph Replace FP32 weights and activations with INT8. Model size drops 4x, memory bandwidth drops 4x, compute drops 2-4x on hardware that has INT8 kernels (modern mobile SoCs, recent x86 CPUs, and NVIDIA GPUs since Turing). Accuracy loss on vision tasks is typically 0.1-1 percentage points with post-training static quantisation. Types: Dynamic — quantise weights to INT8, activations computed in FP. Easy, small speedup. Static (post-training) — quantise weights + calibrate activation ranges on a small calibration set. Much faster than dynamic. Quantisation-aware training (QAT) — simulate quantisation during training so the model learns around it. Best accuracy, needs labelled data. For vision, post-training static quantisation gives 95% of the benefit with 5% of the effort. Use QAT only when accuracy loss from PTQ is unacceptable. Predict before you run Under "Use it", this lesson's quantise_ptq converts an ImageNet ResNet-18 to INT8 after calibrating on 64 images. Guess the INT8 model's speed-up on CPU, its file size relative to FP32, and its change in accuracy. (Solution P1.) Idea 5 · Pruning and distillation Pruning — remove unimportant weights (magnitude-based) or channels (structured). Works well on overparameterised models; less useful on already-compact architectures. Distillation — train a small student to mimic a large teacher's logits. Often recovers most of the accuracy lost by shrinking the model. Standard for production edge models. Idea 6 · The inference runtimes PyTorch eager — slow, not for deployment. Use for development only. TorchScript — legacy. Superseded by torch.compile and ONNX export. ONNX Runtime — the neutral runtime. CPU, CUDA, CoreML, TensorRT, OpenVINO all have ONNX providers. Start here. TensorRT — NVIDIA's compiler. Best latency on NVIDIA GPUs (workstation and Jetson). Integrates with ONNX Runtime or standalone. Core ML — Apple's runtime for iOS/macOS. Needs .mlmodel or .mlpackage . TFLite — Google's runtime for Android/ARM. Needs .tflite . OpenVINO — Intel's runtime for CPU/VPU. Needs .xml + .bin . In practice: export PyTorch -> ONNX -> pick the runtime for the target. ONNX is the lingua franca. Idea 7 · Edge architecture picker Budget Model Why < 3M params MobileNetV3-Small Compiles everywhere, good baseline 3-10M EfficientNet-Lite0 (4.7M) or MobileViT-S (5.6M) Strong accuracy per parameter; Lite0 is built for TFLite, MobileViT adds attention 10-30M ConvNeXt-Tiny (28.6M) High ImageNet accuracy from plain, CPU-friendly ops 10-30M Swin-V2-Tiny (28.3M) If the runtime supports window attention well Quantise all of these to INT8 unless you have a specific reason not to. The same idea as a formula Latency, throughput, memory. Report latency as percentiles over many timed runs after warm-up, at the batch size you will serve (often 1); throughput = batch size / latency for one batch. FLOPs are a rough proxy only: memory traffic, kernel launches and unsupported operators often dominate on small devices. Quantisation. Map a real tensor to -bit integers with a scale and zero point : − 1 ) , x ^ = s ( q − z ) , s = 2 b − 1 x m a x ​ − x m i n ​ ​ Each value is off by at most . int8 weights take a quarter of fp32's memory, and int8 arithmetic runs several times faster on hardware that supports it. Per-channel scales (one per output channel) keep the error small when channels have very different ranges. Depthwise-separable convolution (MobileNet) replaces a convolution's C in ​ C out ​ multiply-adds per position by C in ​ + C in ​ C out ​ : a ratio of ​ 1 ​ + k 2 1 ​ , about 8–9 times fewer for kernels. Distillation. Train a small student to match a large teacher's softened probabilities: ​ ) + a T 2 KL ( softmax ( z t ​ / T ) ∥ softmax ( z s ​ / T ) ) The temperature exposes how the teacher ranks the wrong classes; keeps the gradient scale comparable. Step 1 · Measure latency correctly Copy Warm up, synchronise, use time.perf_counter() . Report percentiles, not just mean. Step 2 · Parameter and FLOP counts Copy For real projects use fvcore.nn.FlopCountAnalysis or ptflops ; they handle every module type correctly. Break it on purpose flops_estimate counts a Linear layer as 2 * in_features * out_features , once. ConvNeXt applies its Linear layers to every spatial position of a feature map. What does that do to its FLOP count? The table under "Use it" prints both. (Solution B1.) Step 3 · Post-training static quantisation Copy Four steps: configure, prepare (insert observers), calibrate with real data, convert (swap in INT8 modules). The model must be ready for it first: QuantStub and DeQuantStub around the float parts, and Conv -> BN -> ReLU fused into one module with torch.ao.quantization.fuse_modules . torchvision's models.quantization versions come ready, which is how "Use it" runs this function. Note that these eager-mode torch.ao.quantization APIs are deprecated in current PyTorch in favour of the torchao library: they still work, as shown below, but new projects should start with torchao . Step 4 · Export to ONNX Copy dynamic_axes lets you run the ONNX model with any batch size. In current PyTorch, torch.onnx.export uses the newer dynamo=True exporter by default, which writes opset 18; when it cannot convert down to the requested 17 it says so and keeps 18, and it stores the weights in a separate model.onnx.data file. Pass dynamo=False if a runtime needs opset 17 exactly. "Use it" exports and runs this function for real. Step 5 · Benchmark and compare regimes Copy Run the same function for resnet50 , efficientnet_v2_s , and convnext_tiny and you have the comparison table you need for a deployment decision. Use it: the same idea with real libraries Production stacks converge on one of three paths: Web / serverless : PyTorch -> ONNX -> ONNX Runtime (CPU or CUDA provider). Easiest, good enough for most. NVIDIA edge (Jetson, GPU server) : PyTorch -> ONNX -> TensorRT. Best latency, biggest engineering effort. Mobile : PyTorch -> ONNX -> Core ML (iOS) or TFLite (Android). Quantise before export. For measurement, torch-tb-profiler , nvprof / nsys , and Instruments on macOS give layer-by-layer breakdowns. benchmark_app (OpenVINO) and trtexec (TensorRT) give standalone CLI numbers. Solutions Solution P1 · Faster, smaller, about as accurate On this CPU the INT8 model runs several times faster (the printed p50s), its file is about a quarter of the FP32 file (one byte per weight instead of four), and top-1 changes by a point or two, which on 300 images is within noise. The speed-up is larger than the textbook 2-4x because the INT8 version also fuses Conv, BN and ReLU and uses optimised x86 INT8 kernels; on other hardware the gain differs. Solution B1 · ConvNeXt looks cheaper than it is ConvNeXt's blocks use Linear layers as pointwise convolutions on every position of the feature map, so each one does in_features * out_features multiply-adds per position, not once. flops_estimate counts them once, so it reports ConvNeXt-Tiny at a fraction of its real cost; the per-position count in the table is several times larger. ResNet-18, whose only Linear is the final classifier, is unaffected. Always check an estimator on a model whose true FLOPs you know, or use fvcore / ptflops . a0416: Course home / Phase 4 · Teaching Machines to See Build a complete vision pipeline Lesson 4.16 120 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Design a production vision pipeline that detects objects, classifies them, and emits structured JSON — with every failure path handled Plug a detector (Mask R-CNN or YOLO), a classifier (ConvNeXt-Tiny), and a data contract (Pydantic) into one service Benchmark the end-to-end pipeline and identify the first bottleneck (usually preprocessing, then the detector) Ship a minimal FastAPI service that accepts an image upload, runs the pipeline, and returns detections with classifications Before you start Needs : Phase 4 Lessons 01-15 Type : Build. Time : about 120 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line A production vision system is a chain of models and rules stitched with data contracts. The pieces are already in this phase; the capstone wires them together end-to-end. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Pipeline "The system" An ordered chain of preprocessing, inference, and postprocessing steps with a typed interface between each pair Data contract "The schema" Pydantic / dataclass definitions that every stage input and output conforms to; catches integration bugs at the boundary Preprocessing "Before the model" Decoding, colour conversion, resizing, normalising; usually the biggest CPU time sink Postprocessing "After the model" NMS, mask resize, threshold, RLE encode; cheap on GPU, expensive on CPU Microbatcher "Collect then forward" Aggregator that waits a fixed window for multiple requests, runs a single batched forward pass Trace ID "Request id" Per-request identifier logged at every stage so slow requests can be traced end-to-end Failure code "Named error" Specific error code per failure class instead of generic 500; enables client retry logic Health check "Readiness probe" Cheap endpoint that reports whether the service can answer; loadbalancers rely on this The problem In plain words first A real vision product is several models in a row with plumbing in between: decode the uploaded photo, find objects with a detector, cut each object out, name it with a classifier, and send back a tidy JSON answer. Most bugs in such systems are not inside the models but in the plumbing: a box in the wrong format, a crop without the normalisation the classifier expects, a missing score threshold. This capstone builds that chain, and the experiments below find two real bugs of exactly that kind in it. Individual vision models are useful; vision products are chains of them. A retail shelf audit is a detector plus a product classifier plus a price-OCR pipeline. Autonomous driving is a 2D detector plus a 3D detector plus a segmenter plus a tracker plus a planner. A medical pre-screen is a segmenter plus a region classifier plus a clinician UI. Wiring those chains is the part that separates a ML prototype from a product. Every interface between models is a new place for bugs. Every coordinate transform, every normalisation, every mask resize is a silent-failure candidate. A pipeline is as strong as its weakest interface. This capstone sets up the minimum viable pipeline: detection + classification + structured output + a serving layer. Everything else in Phase 4 slots into this skeleton: swap Mask R-CNN for YOLOv8, add an OCR head, add a segmentation branch, add a tracker. The architecture is stable; the pieces are pluggable. Idea 1 · The pipeline Seven stages. The two model stages are expensive; the five other stages are where the bugs live. Idea 2 · Data contracts with Pydantic Every model boundary becomes a typed object. This turns silent failures into loud ones. Copy When a detector returns boxes in (cx, cy, w, h) instead of (x1, y1, x2, y2) , Pydantic's validation fails at the boundary and you find out immediately instead of debugging a downstream crop that silently returns empty regions. Worked example One box through the plumbing The detector returns the float box on a 600 × 400 image. int() truncates it to , then clamping keeps ​ = min ( 400 , 400 ) = 400 . The crop is pixels wide and tall. Resizing to 224 × 224 stretches the width by and squeezes the height by : the object is distorted by a factor of . Classifiers are trained on undistorted images, so production pipelines often pad the crop to a square first. None of this raises an error. Every step is a place where a pipeline can be quietly wrong. Idea 3 · Where latency goes Three truths hold in nearly every vision pipeline: Preprocessing is easy to forget. Decoding JPEGs, converting colour spaces and resizing large camera frames are CPU-bound and can rival a small model. (In this lesson's pipeline the Mask R-CNN detector dwarfs them, as "Use it" measures.) The detector dominates GPU time. 70-90% of GPU time is in the detection forward pass. Postprocessing (NMS, RLE encode/decode) is cheap on GPU, expensive on CPU. Always profile with the actual target. Knowing the distribution is what turns optimisation into a prioritised list. Idea 4 · Failure modes Empty detections — return empty list, do not crash. Log. Out-of-bounds boxes — clamp to image size before cropping. Tiny crops — skip classification for boxes smaller than the classifier's minimum input. Corrupt upload — 400 response with a specific error code, not 500. Model load failure — fail at service startup, not at first request. A production pipeline handles each of these without writing generic try/except that hides the failure. Every failure gets a named code and a response. Check your mental model ✗ "Pydantic will reject a box in the wrong format." ✓ Only if you write that rule. Tuple[float, float, float, float] accepts (cx, cy, w, h) just as happily as (x1, y1, x2, y2) . "Use it" shows it and adds a validator. ✗ "Detectors return only confident detections." ✓ torchvision's Mask R-CNN keeps everything above a score of 0.05 by default, so the pipeline must apply its own threshold. ✗ "If each model works on its own, the pipeline works." ✓ The interfaces must match too: each model expects its own preprocessing. Idea 5 · Batching A production service serves multiple clients. Batching detections and classifications across requests multiplies throughput. The trade-off: extra latency from waiting for a batch to fill. Typical setup: collect requests for up to 20ms, batch together, process, distribute responses. torchserve and triton do this natively; small services with predictable load roll their own micro-batcher. The same idea as a formula Where the time goes. End-to-end latency is a sum: ​ = t decode ​ + t preprocess ​ + t queue ​ + t model ​ + t postprocess ​ + t network ​ Image decoding and resizing on the CPU often cost as much as the model on a GPU; measure each term separately before optimising. Batching. If one forward pass on a batch of takes (a fixed overhead plus a per-image cost ), throughput is B ​ ⟶ b 1 ​ as B grows so batching pays when is large compared with , as on GPUs. Dynamic batching waits up to a maximum delay to fill a batch, so each request's latency grows by up to in exchange for throughput. Capacity. By Little's law, requests per second at latency means requests in flight; the server must hold that many in memory and the GPU must keep up with on average, with headroom for the peak. Contracts. A request schema fixes types and ranges (image size limits, allowed formats) so that bad inputs fail fast with a clear error at the boundary instead of deep inside the model. Recap What to keep from this lesson A vision product is a chain: decode, detect, crop, classify, serialise, serve. CVAT, Label Studio and Roboflow (with SAM-assisted labelling) for annotation, and Voxel51's FiftyOne for finding label errors and duplicates; most of a vision project's time goes here. Serving. a0417: Course home / Phase 4 · Teaching Machines to See Learning to see without labels (SimCLR, DINO, MAE) Lesson 4.17 75 min Learn + Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Trace the three major self-supervised families — contrastive (SimCLR), teacher-student (DINO), masked reconstruction (MAE) — and state what each one optimises Implement an InfoNCE loss from scratch and explain why a batch of 512 works but a batch of 32 fails Explain why MAE's 75% masking ratio is not arbitrary and how it differs from BERT's 15% for text Use DINOv2 or MAE ImageNet checkpoints for linear probing and zero-shot retrieval Before you start Needs : Phase 4 Lesson 04 (Telling images apart: classification), Phase 4 Lesson 14 (ViT) Type : Learn + Build. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Labels are the bottleneck of supervised vision. Self-supervised pretraining removes them: learn visual features from 100M unlabelled images, fine-tune on 10k labelled ones. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Self-supervised "Label-free" A pretext task that produces useful representations from unlabelled data Pretext task "The fake task" The objective used during SSL (reconstruct patches, match views); discarded after pretraining Linear probe "Frozen encoder + linear head" Standard SSL evaluation: train only a linear classifier on top of frozen features InfoNCE "Contrastive loss" softmax over cosine similarities; positive pair is the target class, all others are negatives EMA teacher "Moving-average teacher" Teacher whose weights are an exponential moving average of the student's; used by BYOL, MoCo, DINO Mask ratio "% of patches hidden" Fraction of patches masked during MAE; 75% for vision, 15% for text Representation collapse "Constant output" SSL failure where the encoder outputs a constant vector for all inputs; prevented by centring, sharpening, or negatives DINOv2 "Production SSL backbone" Meta's 2023 self-supervised ViT, a widely used general-purpose feature extractor; succeeded by DINOv3 (2025) The problem In plain words first Labelling millions of images is slow and expensive, but unlabelled images are everywhere. Self-supervised learning invents a task whose answer comes from the image itself, so no human labels are needed: recognise that two different crops come from the same photo ( contrastive learning, SimCLR), match the answers of a slowly-updated copy of yourself ( teacher-student , DINO), or fill in hidden patches ( masked reconstruction , MAE). The task is thrown away afterwards; what remains is an encoder whose features are good enough that a simple classifier on top, trained with a handful of labels, works well. Supervised ImageNet has 1.3M labelled images, which took years of crowd-sourced labelling to build. Medical and industrial datasets are smaller and even more expensive to label. Every vision team asks: can we pretrain on cheap unlabelled data — YouTube frames, web crawls, webcam footage, satellite sweeps — and then fine-tune on a small labelled set? Self-supervised learning is the answer. A modern self-supervised ViT pretrained without labels reaches or beats supervised ImageNet accuracy when fine-tuned. It also transfers better to downstream tasks (detection, segmentation, depth) than supervised pretraining. DINOv2 (Meta, 2023) and MAE (Meta, 2022) became standard sources of transferable vision features, and DINOv3 (Meta, 2025) scales the DINO recipe further. The conceptual shift is that the pretext task — the thing the model is trained to do — does not have to be the downstream task. What matters is that it forces the model to learn useful features. Predict the colour of grayscale images, rotate images and ask the model to classify the rotation, mask patches and reconstruct them — all have worked. The three approaches that scale are contrastive learning, teacher-student distillation, and masked reconstruction. Idea 1 · Three families Idea 2 · Contrastive learning (SimCLR) Take one image, apply two random augmentations, get two views. Feed both through the same encoder plus a projection head. Minimise a loss that says "these two embeddings should be close" and "this embedding should be far from every other image's embeddings in the batch." Copy This is the InfoNCE loss. It requires many negatives per positive, so batch size matters — SimCLR needs 512-8192. MoCo introduced a momentum queue of past batches to decouple negative count from batch size. Worked example InfoNCE by hand One view ​ has cosine similarity 0.9 with its partner and 0.1 and 0.2 with the two other views in a tiny batch. At the logits are . Loss + e 1 + e 2 e 9 ​ = lo g ( 1 + e − 8 + e − 7 ) = 0.0012 . At the logits are . Loss + e − 0.7 ) = lo g 1.946 = 0.666 . The same similarities give a loss 500 times smaller at the low temperature: decides how sharply "closest" must beat "close". A cold temperature focuses the gradient on the hardest negatives, which is why it needs many of them. Idea 3 · Teacher-student (DINO) Two networks with the same architecture: student and teacher. The teacher is an exponential moving average (EMA) of the student's weights. Both see augmented views of the image. The student's output is trained to match the teacher's — no explicit negatives. Copy Why it does not collapse to "predict a constant": the teacher's output is centred (subtract per-dimension mean) and sharpened (divide by small temperature). Centering prevents one dimension from dominating; sharpening prevents output collapse to uniform. DINO is what DINOv2 scales up, on 142M curated images. Its features set the state of the art for frozen-feature retrieval and dense prediction when released; DINOv3 (2025) pushed further with a 7B-parameter model trained on 1.7 billion images. Check your mental model ✗ "Self-supervised means unsupervised clustering." ✓ It is ordinary supervised training on a task whose labels come from the data itself: which crops match, what the hidden patches looked like. ✗ "Without negatives, teacher-student training must collapse." ✓ It would, except that DINO centres and sharpens the teacher's outputs and updates the teacher slowly (EMA). Remove those and it does collapse (Exercise 2). ✗ "The pretext task is what you deploy." ✓ The pretext head is discarded; only the encoder's features are kept. Idea 4 · Masked reconstruction (MAE) Mask 75% of patches of a ViT input. Pass only the visible 25% through the encoder. A small decoder receives the encoder's output plus mask tokens at masked positions, and is trained to reconstruct the pixels of the masked patches. Copy Key design choices that make MAE work: 75% mask ratio — high. Forces the encoder to learn semantic features; reconstructing 25% would be near-trivial (neighbouring pixels are so correlated that a CNN could nail it). Asymmetric encoder/decoder — the big ViT encoder only sees visible patches; a small decoder (8-layer, 512-dim) handles reconstruction. Pretraining runs 3x or more faster than feeding every patch through the encoder. Pixel-space reconstruction target — simpler than BEiT's tokenised target and works better on ViT. After pretraining, discard the decoder. The encoder is the feature extractor. Idea 5 · Why 75% and not 15% BERT masks 15% of tokens. MAE masks 75%. The difference is information density. Natural language has high entropy per token. Predicting 15% of tokens is still hard because each masked position has many plausible completions. Image patches have low entropy — an unmasked neighbourhood often determines the masked patch's pixels almost exactly. To make prediction require semantic understanding, you have to mask aggressively. 75% is high enough that simple spatial extrapolation cannot solve the task; the encoder must represent the image content. Idea 6 · Linear-probe evaluation After self-supervised pretraining, the standard evaluation is a linear probe : freeze the encoder, train a single linear classifier on top on ImageNet labels. Reports top-1 accuracy. SimCLR ResNet-50: ~71% (2020) DINO ViT-S/16: ~77% (2021) MAE ViT-L/16: ~76% (2022) DINOv2 ViT-g/14: ~86% (2023) Linear probe is a pure measure of feature quality; fine-tuning typically adds 2-5 points but also mixes in the effect of head retraining. Images are redundant: with 15% hidden (BERT's rate for text), nearby visible patches give the answer away. Linear probe. Freeze the encoder, train a linear classifier on its features: the standard measure of how linearly organised the learned representation is. Time : about 45 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Train an image encoder and a text encoder together so that matching (image, caption) pairs land at the same point in a shared space. That is the whole trick. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Two-tower "Dual encoder" Separate image and text encoders ending in a shared-dim projection head Zero-shot "No task-specific training" Classify into classes described only by text at inference; no labels touched Temperature / logit_scale "tau" Learned scalar that scales the similarity matrix before softmax Prompt template "A photo of a {}" Natural-language wrapper around class names; averaging many templates boosts zero-shot accuracy CLIP "Image+text model" The 2021 OpenAI model; vocabulary of the field in 2026 SigLIP "Sigmoid CLIP" Swaps softmax for per-pair sigmoid; trains better at small batches OpenCLIP "Open reproduction" Community-trained CLIP variants on LAION; production default for open-source pipelines VLM "Vision-language model" A CLIP-family encoder plus an LLM, trained to answer questions about images The problem In plain words first CLIP learns from hundreds of millions of photos with their captions. It has two encoders, one for images and one for text, and trains them so that a photo and its own caption end up as nearby points in the same space, while mismatched pairs end up far apart. Afterwards you can classify an image into categories nobody trained it on: write each category as a sentence ("a photo of a parachute"), encode the sentences, and pick the one closest to the image. That is called zero-shot classification. Traditional classifiers are closed-vocabulary: a 1000-class ImageNet model can only predict 1000 labels. Every new category requires labelled data and a retrained head. CLIP (Radford et al., OpenAI 2021) showed that training on 400M (image, caption) pairs scraped from the web produces a model that can classify into any set of categories at inference, described purely in natural language. You give it a new class by writing a sentence. That capability — zero-shot transfer — is why so many vision systems now start from a CLIP-family checkpoint. Detection (Grounding DINO, OWL-ViT), segmentation (CLIPSeg, SAM), retrieval, content moderation, VLMs, and text-to-image generation all build on CLIP-style joint embeddings. Idea 1 · Two towers Both encoders end with a linear projection to the same embedding dimension (512 for CLIP ViT-B/32, 768 for CLIP ViT-L/14). L2-normalise and compute cosine similarity. Idea 2 · The objective Given a batch of (image, caption) pairs, build an similarity matrix. Train both encoders so the diagonal (matching pairs) has high similarity and off-diagonals (non-matching) have low similarity. Copy Symmetric because both image-to-text and text-to-image retrieval should work. tau (temperature) is typically learned as a scalar parameter, initialised to 0.07. Worked example One row of the matrix A batch has 3 pairs. Image 1's cosine similarities with the three captions are ; its own caption is the first. With CLIP's starting temperature, , the logits are . + e 0.71 + e 1.43 e 4.29 ​ = 73.0 + 2.0 + 4.2 73.0 ​ = 0.92 so this row's loss is . A cosine of only 0.30 is enough to be "clearly the match", because only the ranking within the batch matters. The text-to-image direction does the same for every column, and the two losses are averaged. Idea 3 · SigLIP: a better loss SigLIP (Zhai et al., 2023) replaced the softmax with per-pair sigmoid: y ij ​ ​ = pairs mean ​ lo g ( 1 + exp ( − y ij ​ ⋅ sim ij ​ ) ) = { + 1 − 1 ​ if matching otherwise ​ ​ Per-pair loss removes the batch-level normalisation that CLIP requires. SigLIP trains better at small batch sizes and matches or exceeds CLIP at equal data. Idea 4 · Zero-shot classification Given a trained CLIP: For each class, compose a prompt: "a photo of a {class}". Encode all class prompts with the text encoder -> T shape (C, d). Encode the test image -> I shape (1, d). Similarity = I @ T.T shape (1, C). Argmax -> predicted class. Prompt engineering matters. OpenAI published 80 prompt templates for ImageNet ("a photo of a {}", "a blurry photo of a {}", "a sketch of a {}", ...). Average the embeddings of all templates per class for an extra 1-3% top-1 accuracy. Check your mental model ✗ "Zero-shot means the model never saw that kind of image." ✓ It never saw labels for your classes . It almost certainly saw many web photos of dogs with captions saying so. ✗ "The prompt wording does not matter; only the class name does." ✓ It can matter, mostly for ambiguous names on large class lists. On the 10 easy classes under "Use it" the three prompt styles score within half a point of each other, which is itself worth knowing. ✗ "A cosine similarity of 0.3 is a weak match." ✓ Absolute CLIP similarities are small; what counts is which candidate is highest (see the worked example). Idea 5 · Where CLIP-style models are used in 2026 Zero-shot classification — direct use. Image retrieval — encode all images once, embed query at inference. Text-conditioned detection — Grounding DINO, OWL-ViT wrap a CLIP text tower around a detector. Text-conditioned segmentation — CLIPSeg; the original SAM paper explored text prompts through CLIP embeddings, and SAM 3 (Lesson 4.24) makes text prompts a core feature. VLMs — LLaVA, Qwen-VL, InternVL wire a CLIP-family vision encoder into an LLM. Text-to-image gen — Stable Diffusion 1.x and 2.x condition on CLIP text embeddings, and SDXL on two CLIP text encoders. Once you have a shared embedding space, every vision+language task becomes a distance computation. The same idea as a formula Two towers, one space. An image encoder and a text encoder produce L2-normalised embeddings ​ = f ( x i ​ ) and ​ = g ( t j ​ ) . For a batch of matching pairs, the similarity matrix is ​ = τ u i ​ ⋅ v j ​ ​ with a learned temperature . CLIP's loss is the average of two cross-entropies: each image must pick its own caption from the in the row, and each caption its image from the column; the diagonal holds the correct pairs. SigLIP replaces the softmax over the batch with an independent binary decision for every pair: 1 ​ i , j ∑ ​ lo g σ ( z ij ​ ( t u i ​ ⋅ v j ​ + b ) ) , z ij ​ = + 1 if i = j , − 1 otherwise with learned scale and bias . No normalisation across the batch is needed, so the loss works well at small batch sizes and is cheaper to distribute. Zero-shot classification. Embed a prompt per class ("a photo of a dog") and predict ​ u ⋅ v c ​ ; averaging the embeddings of several prompt templates per class usually adds a few points of accuracy. Retrieval is the same score used the other way: rank all images by ​ ⋅ v for a text query. Step 1 · A tiny two-tower model Real CLIP is ViT + transformer. Here it classifies a photo from ImageNet's validation set: Copy What you should see Copy Copy SigLIP is newer and trains better at small batch sizes; SigLIP 2 (2025) improves it further, and many recent vision-language models use a SigLIP image encoder: google/siglip-base-patch16-224 . Hugging Face ships both families. See it drawn Real CLIP on ImageNet classes OpenCLIP ViT-B/32 classifies 300 photos into Imagenette's 10 ImageNet classes with no training, using three kinds of prompt. Show the code that draws this Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Without a single training label CLIP sorts these photos into the 10 classes with high accuracy, and the puppies photo puts almost all its probability on "English springer". The three prompt styles all land at about 99% here, with the bare class name marginally ahead: these 10 classes are so distinct that wording barely matters. The gains from templates and ensembles that Idea 4 describes were measured on all 1,000 ImageNet classes, where many names are ambiguous ("crane" the bird or the machine); measure on your own class list before assuming either way. On harder or more specialised lists (medical scans, rare species) zero-shot accuracy drops a lot, and a linear probe or fine-tuning on a few labelled examples is the next step. Recap What to keep from this lesson CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder so matching pairs are close in one shared space. The loss is a symmetric cross-entropy over the batch similarity matrix; SigLIP uses a per-pair sigmoid instead. Zero-shot classification: encode one prompt per class, pick the most similar to the image. Prompt templates and ensembles help on large, ambiguous class lists; only relative similarity matters. CLIP-family encoders power retrieval, open-vocabulary detection and segmentation, and vision-language models. Solutions Solution P1 · Almost perfect on unseen concepts Far above chance: nearly 100% on the five concepts never seen in training, about the same as on the seen ones. The towers learned a general mapping from both views into a shared space, not a lookup table of 15 classes, so a new concept's caption lands next to that concept's images automatically. Real CLIP works for the same reason, with language as the bridge. Solution B1 · Text-to-image retrieval With only the image-to-text term, each image learns to pick its caption out of the batch, but nothing asks each caption to pick its image out of the batch. Zero-shot classification (image in, best caption out) barely notices. Search in the other direction, "find the images matching this text", is what weakens, because the text embeddings are never trained to rank images. The symmetric average keeps both directions useful. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) SigLIP 2 and OpenCLIP models are the common open image-text encoders; SigLIP replaced CLIP's softmax loss with a sigmoid loss and is the vision encoder in many VLMs. Multimodal embeddings as a service. Vertex AI multimodal embeddings, Cohere Embed v4 and Gemini Embedding 2 put images and text in one vector space for search, the CLIP idea in production. Sources: SigLIP 2 , OpenCLIP , Vertex AI multimodal embeddings , Gemini Embedding 2 . Time : about 45 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line OCR is a three-stage pipeline — detect text boxes, recognise the characters, then lay them out. Every modern OCR system reorders these stages or merges them. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means OCR "Text from pixels" Turning image regions into character sequences CTC "Alignment-free loss" Loss that trains a sequence model without per-timestep labels; marginalises over alignments CRNN "Classic OCR model" Conv feature extractor + BiLSTM + CTC; the 2015 baseline still used in production Donut "End-to-end OCR" ViT encoder + text decoder; emits JSON directly from image Layout parsing "Find regions" Detect and label Title/Table/Figure/Paragraph regions in a document Reading order "Text sequence" Ordering of recognised regions into a sentence; trivial for Latin, non-trivial for mixed layouts CER / WER "Error rates" Levenshtein distance / reference length at character or word granularity VLM-OCR "LLM that reads" A vision-language model trained or prompted for OCR tasks; the strongest option on complex documents The problem In plain words first OCR turns pictures of text into text. The classic recipe has three steps: find where the text is, read each line, then put the pieces in reading order. Reading a line is the clever part: a network slides along the line and, at every small step, guesses which character is there, or "nothing" (a special blank ). A rule then merges repeated guesses and drops the blanks, so "hh_ee_ll_ll_oo" becomes "hello". The training loss behind this, CTC , does not need to know which pixel column belongs to which letter. Newer models skip the steps and read a whole document straight into structured data, such as JSON for a receipt. Images full of text are everywhere: receipts, invoices, IDs, scanned books, forms, whiteboards, signs, screenshots. Extracting structured data from them — not just the characters, but "this is the total amount" — is one of the highest-value applied-vision problems. The field splits into three skill layers: OCR proper : turn pixels into text. Layout parsing : group OCR output into regions (title, body, table, header). Document understanding : extract structured fields ("invoice_total = $42.50") from layout. Each layer has classical and modern approaches, and the gap between "I want text from an image" and "I need the total amount from this receipt" is bigger than most teams realise. Idea 1 · The classical pipeline Text detection produces per-line or per-word quadrilaterals. Recognition crops each region to a fixed height, runs a CNN + BiLSTM + CTC to produce a character sequence. Layout rebuilds reading order (top-to-bottom, left-to-right for Latin; different for Arabic, Japanese). Idea 2 · CTC in one paragraph OCR recognition produces a variable-length sequence from a fixed-length feature map. CTC (Graves et al., 2006) lets you train this without character-level alignment. The model outputs a distribution over (vocab + blank) at every time step; CTC loss marginalises over all alignments that reduce to the target text after merging repeats and removing blanks. Copy CTC is the reason CRNN worked in 2015 and it still trains many production line recognisers, PaddleOCR's among them. Worked example Counting alignments Say the target is "ab" and the network outputs frames. Every 3-frame string that collapses to "ab" is a valid alignment: aab , abb , _ab , a_b , ab_ Five of them. CTC's loss is of the sum of their probabilities, computed efficiently by dynamic programming instead of listing them. Now the target "aa": aa_ ... collapses to "a", not "aa", because repeats merge. The only valid 3-frame alignment is a_a : a blank must sit between repeated letters. That is why a recogniser needs at least as many frames as characters plus one per repeated pair, and why the "ll" in "hello" costs an extra frame. Check your mental model ✗ "CTC needs to know which frames belong to which character." ✓ It sums over every alignment that collapses to the target, so only the text label is needed. ✗ "The blank is just a space character." ✓ Blank means "no new character here". A real space is an ordinary symbol in the vocabulary. ✗ "End-to-end document models read text perfectly." ✓ Under "Use it", Donut reads every number on a receipt correctly and still files the shop's name as a menu item. Idea 3 · Modern end-to-end models Donut (Kim et al., 2022) — a ViT encoder + a text decoder; reads an image and emits JSON directly. No text detector, no layout module. TrOCR — ViT + transformer decoder for line-level OCR. OCR-capable vision-language models — general VLMs such as Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL, and OCR-specialised ones such as GOT-OCR 2.0, olmOCR, PaddleOCR-VL and DeepSeek-OCR; the strongest results on complex documents (tables, formulas, mixed layouts), at a much higher compute cost. PaddleOCR — classical DB + CRNN pipeline in a mature production package; still the open-source workhorse. End-to-end models need more data and compute but skip the error accumulation of multi-stage pipelines. Idea 4 · Layout parsing For structured documents, run a layout model (LayoutLMv3, or a detector trained on the DocLayNet dataset) that labels each region: Title, Paragraph, Figure, Table, Footnote. Reading order then becomes "iterate through regions in layout order, concatenate." For forms, use Key-Value extraction models (Donut for visually-rich documents, LayoutLMv3 for plain scans). They take image + detected text + positions and predict structured key-value pairs. Idea 5 · Evaluation metrics Character Error Rate (CER) — Levenshtein distance / length of reference. Lower is better. Production target: < 2% on clean scans. Word Error Rate (WER) — same at the word level. F1 on structured fields — for key-value tasks; measures whether {invoice_total: 42.50} appears correctly. Edit distance on JSON — for end-to-end document parsing; the Donut paper introduced normalised tree edit distance. The same idea as a formula CTC. A recogniser emits, at each of time steps, a distribution over characters plus a blank . An alignment of length maps to text by : merge repeated symbols, then delete blanks, so hh∅e∅ll∅l∅oo → hello (the blank between the two l s keeps them apart). The probability of a transcript sums over every alignment that produces it: ( y ) ∑ ​ t = 1 ∏ T ​ p ( π t ​ ∣ x ) computed by dynamic programming in ; training minimises without needing character positions. Greedy decoding takes the best symbol at each step and applies . Error rates. With substitutions, deletions and insertions in the minimum edit between prediction and reference of characters (or words), S + D + I ​ , WER the same over words They can exceed 100% when there are many insertions. One wrong character in a 6-letter word is a CER of 17% but a WER of 100% for that word. End-to-end models (TrOCR, Donut, and the vision-language OCR models of 2025–2026) generate text token by token with a decoder instead, and are evaluated with the same CER and WER, plus field-level exact match for documents. Step 1 · CTC loss + greedy decoder Copy F.ctc_loss uses the efficient CuDNN implementation when available. The greedy decoder is simpler than a beam search and usually within 1% CER of it. Step 2 · Tiny CRNN recogniser Minimal CNN + BiLSTM for line OCR. Copy Fixed-height input (the CNN max-pools height to 1). Width is the time dimension for CTC. Step 3 · Synthetic OCR Generate black-on-white strings for an end-to-end smoke test. Each character becomes a column of six bars that spell its vocabulary index in binary. The image must carry the character's identity: if every character were the same blank box, the model could not tell a from x , and the loss would stall. Copy What you should see Copy Copy A real OCR dataset adds fonts, noise, rotation, blur, and colour. The pipeline above is identical. Predict before you run Under "Use it" the TinyCRNN trains for 600 steps on random strings of 3 to 7 characters from all 36 glyphs, then reads 200 strings it has never seen.
