You would expect stuttering output such as "hheello". Run it under "Use it" on the trained model, look at the heat map there, and explain what you see. (Solution B1.) Step 4 · Training sketch Copy Loss should drop from double digits to near zero within 400 steps on this trivial synthetic data (it ended at 0.007 when this page was built; see "Use it"). code/main.py runs the same loop on its own string set and then decodes three test strings. Use it: the same idea with real libraries Three production paths: PaddleOCR — mature, fast, multilingual. Usage: paddleocr.PaddleOCR(lang="en").predict(image_path) in PaddleOCR 3.x (older 2.x code calls .ocr(image_path) , now deprecated). EasyOCR — Python-native, multilingual, PyTorch backbone. Tesseract — classical; still useful for old scanned documents when models struggle. For end-to-end document parsing, use Donut or a VLM: Copy For receipts, invoices, and forms with repeatable structure, fine-tune Donut. For arbitrary documents or OCR with reasoning, use a vision-language model such as Qwen2.5-VL or an OCR-specialised one, and check its cost per page. See it drawn Train and read Step 4 above ran 400 steps on two fixed strings; here is its final loss, then a fresh TinyCRNN trained on random strings and tested on new ones. Show the code that draws this Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Even a tiny CRNN reads unseen strings of this synthetic font essentially without errors after 600 steps: the task is easy by design, but the pipeline is the real one. The heat map shows how CTC reads "hello": each character lights up on exactly one frame , and blank fills every other frame, including the frames between the two l's. This "peaky" pattern is typical of trained CTC models: one frame per character is the cheapest way to make the probability of the right collapse high. That is also why the broken decoder ("without merging repeats") reads the same words here. See it drawn Donut reads a receipt The naver-clova-ix/donut-base-finetuned-cord-v2 model from the code above (fine-tuned on Indonesian shop receipts) on a receipt drawn here with PIL. No text detector, no OCR engine: image in, JSON out. Show the code that draws this Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Every quantity and price is right, and so are subtotal, tax, total, cash and change, all read from pixels with no separate OCR step. The mistakes are structural: Donut treats the shop name "CAFE ROSSO" as a menu item and pushes "Cappuccino" into the wrong field. It was fine-tuned on receipts with a different layout, and it has learned where things usually are rather than what a shop name is. This is why production document pipelines validate extracted fields (does subtotal plus tax equal total?) and fine-tune on their own documents. Recap What to keep from this lesson OCR = detect text regions, recognise each line, restore reading order; layout parsing and field extraction come on top. A CRNN turns a line into a sequence of per-frame character probabilities; CTC trains it without alignments. Decoding merges repeats, then drops blanks; repeated letters need a blank between them. Measure CER and WER for text, field-level F1 for extracted data. End-to-end models (Donut, VLMs) read straight to JSON but still make structural mistakes; validate the fields. Solutions Solution P1 · Near zero Close to 0% CER on unseen strings (the printed value). The synthetic font encodes each character as a clean binary bar pattern, so the task is easy; the point is that the same CNN + BiLSTM + CTC pipeline generalises to strings it never saw, because it learned characters, not whole words. Real fonts, noise and blur push CER up and the training set size with it. Solution B1 · No stutter, thanks to peaky outputs The broken decoder still reads "hello", "coffee" and "1000" correctly, because this trained model never predicts the same character on two neighbouring frames: each character gets one frame, separated by blanks (the heat map). The bug is real but hidden. Early in training, on blurry real text, or with a model trained differently, characters do spread over several frames, and then the broken decoder stutters ("hheelllo"). A decoder test on one well-trained model can pass while the code is wrong; test it on hand-written frame sequences such as h h _ e e l _ l o o too. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Document AI services. AWS Textract, Azure AI Document Intelligence and Google Document AI extract text, tables and forms at scale; Mistral OCR (2025) is an API built on a vision-language model. Open pipelines. PaddleOCR 3.0 (2025, with PP-OCRv5 and PP-StructureV3) and IBM's Docling convert PDFs and scans into structured text and tables; Tesseract remains for simple printed text. VLMs read documents. Gemini, GPT and Claude models, and open models such as Qwen3-VL, extract fields from documents directly, often with a JSON schema; check numbers and tables, where they still slip. Sources: PaddleOCR 3.0 , Docling , Mistral OCR , Azure Document Intelligence , AWS Textract . a0420: Course home / Phase 4 · Teaching Machines to See Finding similar images Lesson 4.20 45 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Explain triplet, contrastive, and proxy-based metric learning losses and pick the right one for a given dataset Implement L2-normalisation and cosine similarity correctly and audit the difference between "same item" and "same class" retrieval Build a FAISS index, query it by text and by image, and report recall@K for a held-out query set Use DINOv2, CLIP, and SigLIP as off-the-shelf embedding backbones and know when each wins Before you start Needs : Phase 4 Lesson 14 (ViT), Phase 4 Lesson 18 (CLIP) Type : Build. Time : about 45 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line A retrieval system ranks candidates by a distance in embedding space. Metric learning is the discipline of shaping that space so the distances mean what you want. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Metric learning "Shape the space" Training an encoder so distances in its output space reflect a target similarity Triplet loss "Pull and push" $L = \max(0, d(a, p) - d(a, n) + \text{margin})$; the canonical metric-learning loss Semi-hard mining "Useful negatives" Negatives further from the anchor than the positive but within margin; empirically the most informative Proxy-based loss "Class prototypes" One learned proxy per class; cross-entropy over similarity-to-proxies; no pair mining Recall@K "Top-K hit rate" Fraction of queries with at least one correct result in the top K Instance retrieval "Find this exact thing" Fine-grained matching; off-the-shelf features usually underperform FAISS "The NN library" Facebook's nearest-neighbour library; supports exact and approximate indexes HNSW "Graph index" Hierarchical navigable small world; fast approximate NN with small memory overhead The problem In plain words first Retrieval means "find the items most like this one". Each image (or text) becomes a list of numbers, an embedding , and similar things should get nearby embeddings. Search is then just finding the nearest points, which a library such as FAISS does quickly even for millions of items. Metric learning is how you train the embedding so that "nearby" means what your product needs: same class, same exact product, or same person. The scorecard is recall@K: for what fraction of queries does a correct match appear in the top K results? Retrieval is everywhere in production vision: duplicate detection, reverse image search, visual search ("find similar products"), face re-identification, person re-ID for surveillance, instance-level matching for e-commerce. The product question is always the same: "given this query image, rank my catalogue." Two design decisions shape the whole system. The embedding — what model produces the vectors. The index — how to find nearest neighbours at scale. Both are commodity in 2026 (DINOv2 for the embedding, FAISS for the index), which raises the bar: the hard part is defining what counts as similar for your application, then shaping the embedding space so the distances match. That shaping is metric learning. It is a small but high-leverage discipline. Idea 1 · Retrieval at a glance Idea 2 · The four loss families Loss Requires Pros Cons Contrastive (anchor, positive) + negatives Simple, works with any pair label Slow to converge without many negatives Triplet (anchor, positive, negative) Intuitive; direct margin control Hard-triplet mining is expensive NT-Xent / InfoNCE Pairs + batch-mined negatives Scales to large batches Needs big batch or momentum queue Proxy-based (ProxyNCA) Class labels only Fast, stable, no mining Can overfit to proxies on small datasets For most production use cases, start with a pretrained backbone and only add a metric-learning fine-tune if the off-the-shelf embeddings underperform on your test set. Idea 3 · Triplet loss formally − ∥ f ( a ) − f ( n ) ∥ 2 + margin ) Pull anchor a close to positive p , push it away from negative n , with a margin that ensures a gap. The three-image structure generalises to any similarity ordering. Mining matters: easy triplets ( n already far from a ) contribute zero loss; only hard triplets teach the network. Semi-hard mining ( n further than p but within margin) is the FaceNet recipe (2015) and remains a common default. Worked example One triplet by hand Unit-length embeddings: anchor , positive , negative , margin 0.2. Using plain distances as Step 1's code does: + 0. 6 2 ​ = 0.632 + 0. 8 2 ​ = 0.894 loss The negative is already farther than the positive by more than the margin, so this triplet teaches nothing. Swap in a harder negative : , loss . That is a semi-hard negative: farther than the positive, but inside the margin. Note the formula above squares the distances while Step 1 does not; both are used, and the margin means different things in each. Idea 4 · Cosine similarity vs L2 Two metrics, two conventions: Cosine : angle between vectors. Requires L2-normalised embeddings. L2 : Euclidean distance. Works on raw or normalised embeddings, but is usually paired with L2-normalised + squared L2. For most modern nets the two are equivalent: ||a - b||^2 = 2 - 2 cos(a, b) when ||a|| = ||b|| = 1 . Pick the convention that matches your embedding training; mixing them silently changes what "nearest" means. Check your mental model ✗ "Higher recall@10 means a better search engine." ✓ It means the right item is somewhere in the top 10. If users only look at the first result, recall@1 is the number that matters. ✗ "Off-the-shelf embeddings are enough for any retrieval task." ✓ For category-level search they often are (see "Use it"). For "this exact product" they usually need metric-learning fine-tuning. ✗ "Cosine and L2 search can give different neighbours on normalised vectors." ✓ With unit vectors, = 2 − 2 cos ( a , b ) , so the rankings are identical. They differ only on unnormalised vectors. Idea 5 · Recall@K The standard retrieval metric: Copy Report recall@1, @5, @10 side by side. A recall@10 above 0.95 with recall@1 below 0.5 means the embedding space has the right structure but the ranking is noisy — try longer fine-tunes or a re-ranking step. For duplicate detection, precision@K matters more because every false positive is a user-visible mistake. For visual search, recall@K is the product signal. Idea 6 · FAISS in one paragraph Facebook AI Similarity Search. The de-facto library for nearest-neighbour search. Three index choices: IndexFlatIP / IndexFlatL2 — brute force, exact, no training. Use up to ~1M vectors. IndexIVFFlat — partition into K cells, search only the closest few cells. Approximate, fast, needs training data. IndexHNSW — graph-based, fastest for many queries, large index size. For 100k vectors you probably want IndexFlatIP on cosine similarity. For 10M you want IndexIVFFlat . For 100M+ combined with product quantisation ( IndexIVFPQ ). Idea 7 · Instance-level vs category-level retrieval Two very different problems with the same name: Category-level — "find cats in my catalogue." Class-conditional similarity; off-the-shelf CLIP / DINOv2 embeddings work well. Instance-level — "find this exact product in my catalogue." Needs fine-grained discrimination between visually similar objects of the same class; off-the-shelf embeddings under-perform; fine-tuning with metric learning matters. Always ask which one you are solving before picking a model. The same idea as a formula Triplet loss. For an anchor , a positive (same identity) and a negative , with distance and margin : Zero once the negative is at least farther than the positive. Most random triplets are already satisfied and give no gradient, so training mines hard or semi-hard negatives in each batch. Normalised embeddings. For unit vectors = 2 − 2 u ⋅ v , so ranking by L2 distance and by cosine similarity agree; production systems normalise once and use the inner product. Recall@K. The fraction of queries whose correct match appears among the top results. It is the right metric when a person or a later model will look at a short list. Approximate search. An exact search over vectors of dimension costs per query. An IVF index clusters the database into ​ cells and scans only the ​ nearest cells, about a fraction ​ / n list ​ of the vectors. Product quantisation compresses each vector by splitting it into sub-vectors and storing an 8-bit codebook index for each: a 768-dimensional float32 vector (3,072 bytes) becomes 96 bytes with , a 32-fold saving. Step 1 · Triplet loss Copy One line. Works on L2-normalised or raw embeddings. Step 2 · Semi-hard mining Given a batch of embeddings and labels, find the hardest semi-hard negative for each anchor. Copy Each anchor gets the hardest positive in-class and a semi-hard negative that is further than the positive but within margin. Step 3 · Recall@K Copy Top-k by inner product on L2-normalised embeddings equals top-k by cosine. Report the mean proportion of queries with at least one correct neighbour. Step 4 · Putting it together Copy After a few hundred steps the embedding clusters form one cluster per class. Predict before you run The toy data has 6 classes of 128-number vectors. Step 4 trains for 200 steps. What recall@1 do you expect on fresh samples before training (a random encoder) and after? (Solution P1.) That is the honest baseline to beat. After triplet training the classes become tight, separate clusters and recall@1 rises to nearly perfect. Always report the untrained or off-the-shelf baseline next to the fine-tuned number; a large-looking final score can hide a small gain. Break it on purpose In Encoder.forward , return self.net(x) without F.normalize , train as in Step 4, and evaluate with recall_at_k , which ranks by inner product. What can go wrong? (Solution B1.) Use it: the same idea with real libraries Production stacks in 2026: DINOv2 + FAISS — general-purpose visual retrieval. Works off-the-shelf. CLIP + FAISS — when queries are text. Fine-tuned DINOv2 + FAISS — instance-level retrieval, face re-ID, fashion, e-commerce. Milvus / Weaviate / Qdrant — vector databases that add storage, filtering and replication around approximate nearest-neighbour indexes such as HNSW (Milvus can also use FAISS internally). For SOTA instance retrieval, the recipe is: DINOv2 backbone, add an embedding head, fine-tune with a triplet or InfoNCE loss on instance-labelled pairs, index in FAISS. See it drawn Off-the-shelf embeddings + FAISS 300 gallery photos and 100 separate query photos from ImageNet's validation set (10 classes). Each photo is embedded by DINOv2-base and by OpenCLIP ViT-B/32, the vectors are L2-normalised and put in a FAISS IndexFlatIP (exact inner-product search), and recall@K counts a hit when a retrieved photo has the query's class. First DINOv2. Copy What you should see Copy Copy See it drawn Then CLIP, which can also search by text Show the code that draws this Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output On these 10 clearly different ImageNet classes, both off-the-shelf models retrieve a photo of the right class first for nearly every query, with no training: category-level retrieval is largely solved by pretrained embeddings, which is why the lesson says to measure them before fine-tuning anything. The text queries search the same FAISS index with CLIP's text tower, and the cosine scores above each photo are small numbers (around 0.3) even for good matches, as Lesson 4.18 explained. What these numbers do not tell you is how either model does on instance-level search ("this exact jacket"), which needs its own labelled test set. Recap What to keep from this lesson Retrieval ranks items by distance between embeddings; metric learning shapes the embedding space. Triplet loss pulls positives closer than negatives by a margin; only hard and semi-hard triplets produce gradient. Normalise embeddings and keep one convention: on unit vectors, cosine and L2 rank identically. Report recall@1, @5, @10 and always the untrained or off-the-shelf baseline. FAISS IndexFlatIP is exact and enough for about a million vectors; IVF, HNSW and PQ trade accuracy for scale. Solutions Solution P1 · A strong baseline, then near-perfect The random encoder already gets a recall@1 far above the 1-in-6 chance level, because the inputs themselves cluster by class and a random network keeps much of that structure. After 200 triplet steps recall@1 is close to 1. Both numbers are printed above the plot; the gap between them, not the final number alone, is what training bought. Solution B1 · Long vectors win Without normalisation, inner-product ranking rewards vectors that are simply long : a gallery item with a large norm can top the list for every query regardless of direction. The triplet loss on raw distances also lets the network shrink or blow up norms instead of arranging directions. Recall can still look fine on easy data, which is what makes the bug dangerous. Normalise, or rank by L2 distance consistently with how you trained. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Image search runs on embeddings and ANN indexes. Products from visual shopping search to photo libraries use CLIP/SigLIP or DINO embeddings in FAISS or a vector database (Lesson 2.6). Metric learning in faces and products. ArcFace-style margin losses remain the standard for face recognition and product re-identification; libraries such as InsightFace and pytorch-metric-learning implement them. Sources: FAISS , ArcFace , InsightFace , pytorch-metric-learning . a0421: Course home / Phase 4 · Teaching Machines to See Finding body joints and poses Lesson 4.21 45 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Distinguish top-down and bottom-up pose estimation and state when each is used Regress heatmaps for K keypoints with a Gaussian-per-keypoint target and extract keypoint coordinates at inference Explain Part Affinity Fields (PAFs) and how bottom-up pipelines associate keypoints into instances Use MediaPipe Pose or MMPose for production keypoint estimation and understand their output format Before you start Needs : Phase 4 Lesson 06 (Detection), Phase 4 Lesson 07 (U-Net) Type : Build. Time : about 45 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line A pose is a set of ordered keypoints. A keypoint detector is a heatmap regressor. Everything else is bookkeeping. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Keypoint "A landmark" A specific ordered point on an object (joint, corner, feature) Pose "The skeleton" An ordered set of keypoints belonging to one instance Top-down "Detect then pose" Two-stage pipeline: person detector + per-crop keypoint model; highest accuracy Bottom-up "Pose first, group later" Single-pass all-keypoint prediction + grouping; constant time in crowd size Heatmap "Gaussian target" H x W tensor per keypoint with peak at the true location; the preferred regression target PAF "Part Affinity Field" 2-channel unit vector field encoding limb directions; used to group keypoints into instances OKS "Keypoint IoU" Object Keypoint Similarity; the COCO metric for pose HRNet "High-Resolution Net" A long-standard top-down keypoint architecture that keeps high-resolution features throughout; ViTPose now often scores higher The problem In plain words first Pose estimation finds a fixed list of points on each object, such as the 17 joints COCO uses for a human body (nose, eyes, shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, ankles), always in the same order. The usual trick is not to predict coordinates directly but to predict one "heat map" per point: an image that is bright where the network thinks that point is. The brightest pixel gives the location. With several people in the picture you either find each person first and then their joints ( top-down ), or find all joints first and then work out which belong together ( bottom-up ). Keypoint tasks hide under many names: human pose (17 body joints), face landmarks (68 or 478 points), hand (21 points), animal pose, robotic object pose, medical anatomy landmarks. Every one of them shares the same structure: detect K discrete points on an object and output their (x, y) coordinates. Pose estimation is the foundation of motion capture, fitness apps, sports analytics, gesture control, animation, AR try-on, and robotic grasping. The 2D case is mature; 3D pose (estimating joint positions in world coordinates from a single camera) is the current research frontier. The engineering question is scale. A single-image, single-person pose is a 20ms problem. Multi-person pose in a crowd at 30 fps is a different problem with different architectures. Idea 1 · Top-down vs bottom-up Top-down — detect people first, then run a per-person keypoint model on each crop. Highest accuracy; scales linearly with number of people. Bottom-up — one forward pass predicts all keypoints plus an association field; group them. Constant time regardless of crowd size. Top-down (HRNet, ViTPose) is the accuracy leader; bottom-up (OpenPose, HigherHRNet) is the throughput leader for crowded scenes. Idea 2 · Heatmap regression Instead of regressing (x, y) directly, predict an H x W heatmap per keypoint with a Gaussian blob centred at the true location. ( x − cx k ​ ) 2 + ( y − cy k ​ ) 2 ​ ) At inference, the argmax of each heatmap is the predicted keypoint location. Why heatmaps work better than direct regression: the network's spatial structure (conv feature map) aligns naturally with spatial output. Gaussian targets also regularise — a small localisation error produces a small loss, not zero. Idea 3 · Sub-pixel localisation Argmax gives integer coordinates. For sub-pixel precision, refine by fitting a parabola to the argmax and its neighbours, or shift the argmax a quarter pixel toward the higher neighbour: dx = 0.25 * sign(heatmap[y, x+1] - heatmap[y, x-1]) , and the same for dy (the rule used by Hourglass and SimpleBaseline). The lesson's code/main.py multiplies by the difference instead of its sign, which moves the estimate only a few hundredths of a pixel; the visual after this idea measures all three. Worked example Sub-pixel by hand A Gaussian heat map with has its true peak at . The pixel values around it are /8 = 0.783 , /8 = 0.980 , /8 = 0.956 . Argmax says 32, an error of 0.4. The quarter-pixel rule sees and moves to 32.25 (error 0.15). The lesson's 0.25 * (h(33) - h(31)) moves by , to 32.04 (error 0.36), almost no help. Fitting a parabola to the log values is exact for a clean Gaussian: ln h ( 33 ) − ln h ( 31 ) ​ = 2 ( − 0.040 + 0.045 + 0.245 ) − 0.045 + 0.245 ​ = 0.40 See it drawn See it measured 2,000 Gaussian heat maps ( , 64 × 64) with random sub-pixel centres, decoded four ways. Multiplying by the raw difference barely helps, because neighbouring values of a smooth Gaussian differ by only a few tenths. The quarter-pixel sign rule halves the error, and the log-parabola recovers the centre almost exactly on these clean maps. Real predicted heat maps are noisy, which is why methods such as DARK smooth the map before fitting. Idea 4 · Part Affinity Fields (PAFs) OpenPose's trick for bottom-up association. For each pair of connected keypoints (e.g. left shoulder to left elbow), predict a 2-channel field that encodes the unit vector pointing from one to the other. To associate a shoulder with its elbow, integrate the PAF along the line connecting candidate pairs; the pair with the highest integral is matched. Copy Elegant and scales to arbitrary crowd sizes without per-person crops. Idea 5 · COCO keypoints The standard body-pose dataset: 17 keypoints per person, PCK (Percentage of Correct Keypoints) and OKS (Object Keypoint Similarity) as metrics. OKS is the keypoint analogue of IoU and is what COCO mAP@OKS reports. Check your mental model ✗ "A heat map per keypoint is just a fancier way to regress coordinates." ✓ It keeps the output spatial like the features, and it can express doubt: two bright spots mean "it is one of these two places". ✗ "Keypoints only need to be visible to be learnable." ✓ They must be distinguishable : channel k must be able to tell its point from the others. "Use it" shows what happens when they are not. ✗ "Top-down is always more accurate, so always use it." ✓ Its cost grows with the number of people; in a crowd at 30 fps, bottom-up or one-stage models win. Idea 6 · 2D vs 3D 2D pose — image coordinates; solved at production quality (MediaPipe, HRNet, ViTPose). 3D pose — world / camera coordinates; still active research. Common approaches: Lift 2D predictions to 3D with a small MLP (VideoPose3D). Direct 3D regression from image (PyMAF, MHFormer). Multi-view setups (CMU Panoptic) for ground truth. The same idea as a formula Heatmap targets. For a keypoint at , the network is trained to output, on an grid, ( u − x ) 2 + ( v − y ) 2 ​ ) with of 1–3 heatmap pixels, using a mean-squared error. A smooth target gives nearby pixels partial credit, which is easier to learn than one hot pixel. Sub-pixel decoding. The arg-max is only accurate to one heatmap cell, which at a stride of 4 is 4 image pixels. Fitting a parabola through the peak and its two neighbours ​ , h 0 ​ , h + 1 ​ refines the position by ​ − 2 h 0 ​ + h + 1 ​ ) h − 1 ​ − h + 1 ​ ​ ∈ ( − 2 1 ​ , 2 1 ​ ) (in each axis), then the position is multiplied by the stride. Evaluation (COCO). Object keypoint similarity compares predicted and true keypoints with the object's scale and a per-keypoint tolerance ​ : ​ 1 [ v i ​ > 0 ] ∑ i ​ exp ( − d i 2 ​ / ( 2 s 2 k i 2 ​ ) ) 1 [ v i ​ > 0 ] ​ It plays the role IoU plays for boxes; AP is computed at OKS thresholds from 0.50 to 0.95. Wrists get a larger tolerance than eyes because annotators disagree more about them. Real pose datasets have the same requirement in a subtler form: a left wrist must look different from a right wrist in context, and flipping an image during augmentation must also swap the left and right labels. Keypoint R-CNN is top-down inside one network: it finds person boxes, then predicts a heat map per keypoint inside each box (56 × 56, through RoIAlign as in Lesson 4.8), which is why its cost grows with the number of people. Recap What to keep from this lesson A pose is an ordered set of keypoints; each keypoint gets its own heat map, and the argmax gives its location. Refine the argmax to sub-pixel precision; a quarter-pixel shift or a log-parabola fit beats plain argmax. Keypoints must be distinguishable for heat-map regression to work, and augmentations must keep left and right consistent. Top-down (detect, then pose each crop) leads on accuracy; bottom-up (keypoints plus grouping, e.g. PAFs) scales to crowds. COCO uses 17 keypoints and OKS-based mAP. Solutions Solution P1 · Twenty pixels versus half a pixel On the lesson's data the average error is well over 10 pixels (the printed value; the data is random, so it varies a little from run to run), because each channel guesses which square is its own. With colour-coded keypoints it drops to under a pixel. The network, the loss and the training are identical; only whether the task is solvable changed. Solution B1 · Nothing identifies the keypoints Nothing in the image says which square is keypoint 0. The best the network can do under MSE is to put a smaller blob on every square in every channel, the average of the four possibilities. The loss still falls, because blobs in the right places beat a blank map, so the training curve looks healthy while the coordinates are wrong. The fix is to make keypoints distinguishable (colour here; anatomy and context in real images) or to switch to a set-based loss that does not care about order. Google's MediaPipe (pose, hands, face landmarks on phones and the web), Ultralytics YOLO pose models, MMPose's RTMPose for real time, and Apple's Vision framework (body and hand pose) on iOS. Uses. Fitness and physiotherapy apps, sports analytics, sign-language and gesture interfaces, and ergonomics in factories. a0422: Course home / Phase 4 · Teaching Machines to See 3D scenes from Gaussian splats Lesson 4.22 90 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Explain why 3D Gaussian Splatting displaced NeRF for most real-time photorealistic 3D reconstruction State the six per-Gaussian parameters (position, rotation quaternion, scale, opacity, spherical harmonics colour, optional feature) and how many floats each contributes Implement a 2D Gaussian splatting rasterizer from scratch using alpha compositing, then show how the 3D case projects to the same loop Use nerfstudio , gsplat , or SuperSplat to reconstruct a scene from 20-50 photos and export to the KHR_gaussian_splatting glTF extension or the OpenUSD 26.03 UsdVolParticleField3DGaussianSplat schema Before you start Needs : Phase 4 Lesson 13 (3D Vision & NeRF), Phase 1 Lesson 12 (Shapes, axes and broadcasting with tensors), Phase 4 Lesson 10 (Diffusion basics optional) Type : Build. Time : about 90 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line A scene is a cloud of millions of 3D Gaussians. Each one has a position, orientation, scale, opacity, and a colour that depends on viewing direction. Rasterise them, backprop through the rasterisation, done. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means 3DGS "Gaussian splats" Explicit scene representation as millions of 3D Gaussians with per-Gaussian position, rotation, scale, opacity, SH colour Covariance "Shape of the Gaussian" Sigma = R S S^T R^T ; orientation and anisotropic scale of one Gaussian Alpha compositing "Back-to-front blend" Same equation as NeRF's volumetric render, now over an explicit sparse set Densification "Clone and split" Adaptive addition of new Gaussians where reconstruction is under-fit Pruning "Delete low-opacity" Remove Gaussians that have collapsed to near-zero opacity during training Spherical harmonics "View-dependent colour" Fourier basis on the sphere; stores colour as a function of viewing direction Splatfacto "nerfstudio's 3DGS" The easiest path to training 3DGS in 2026 KHR_gaussian_splatting "glTF standard" Khronos 2026 extension that makes 3DGS portable across viewers and engines The problem In plain words first Gaussian splatting describes a 3D scene as a cloud of soft, coloured, see-through blobs. Each blob is a 3D Gaussian: it has a centre, a size and stretch in each direction, an orientation, a colour and an opacity. To draw a picture, every blob is flattened onto the screen as a 2D ellipse, and the ellipses are blended front to back, exactly like layers of tinted glass. Because each step is differentiable, the blobs can be moved, stretched and recoloured by gradient descent until the rendered pictures match real photos. Unlike a NeRF there is no network to query per pixel, so rendering is fast enough for real time. A NeRF stores a scene as the weights of an MLP. Every rendered pixel is hundreds of MLP queries along a ray. Training takes hours, rendering takes seconds, and the weights cannot be edited — if you want to move a chair inside a scene, you have to retrain. 3D Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkühler, Drettakis, SIGGRAPH 2023) replaced all of that. A scene is an explicit set of 3D Gaussians. Rendering is GPU rasterisation at 100+ fps. Training takes minutes. Editing is direct: translate a subset of Gaussians and you have moved the chair. By 2026 the Khronos Group has ratified a glTF extension for Gaussian splats, OpenUSD 26.03 ships a Gaussian splat schema, Zillow and Apartments.com render real estate with them, and most new research papers on 3D reconstruction are variants on the core 3DGS idea. The mental model is simple, the math has enough moving parts that most introductions start at rasterisation and skip past the projections and spherical harmonics. This lesson builds the whole thing — a 2D version first, then the 3D extension. Idea 1 · What a Gaussian carries One 3D Gaussian is a parametric blob in space with these attributes: Copy Rotation + scale build a 3x3 covariance: Sigma = R S S^T R^T . That is the shape of the Gaussian in 3D. Spherical harmonics let the colour change with viewing direction — specular highlights, subtle sheen, view-dependent glow — without storing per-view textures. With SH degree 3 you get 16 coefficients per colour channel, 48 floats per Gaussian for colour alone. A scene typically has 1-5 million Gaussians. Each stores roughly 60 floats (3 + 4 + 3 + 1 + 48 + misc). At 4 bytes per float that is about 240 bytes per Gaussian, so a five-million-Gaussian scene needs about 1.2 GB uncompressed: much more than a NeRF's few-megabyte MLP, which is the price of real-time rendering. Quantised formats ( .splat , SPZ, glTF with compression) shrink it several-fold. Worked example Counting the floats Per Gaussian: position 3, rotation quaternion 4, log-scales 3, opacity 1, and spherical-harmonic colour up to degree 3: = 16 coefficients for each of 3 colour channels, . Total floats, bytes. 1 million Gaussians: 236 MB. 5 million: 1.18 GB. Dropping view dependence (degree 0, 3 colour floats instead of 48): bytes, 4.2 times smaller. That is the first knob compressed formats turn: most of a splat file is the view-dependent colour. Idea 2 · Rasterisation, not ray marching Five steps, all GPU-friendly. No MLP query per pixel. The original paper reports well over 100 frames per second at 1080p on a single high-end GPU. Idea 3 · The projection step The 3D Gaussian at world position mu with 3D covariance Sigma projects to a 2D Gaussian at screen position mu' with 2D covariance Sigma' : Σ ′ W J ​ = project ( μ ) = J W Σ W T J T ( 2 × 2 ) = viewing transform (rotation + translation of camera) = Jacobian of the perspective projection at μ ′ ​ The 2D Gaussian's footprint is an ellipse whose axes are the eigenvectors of Sigma' . Every pixel inside that ellipse receives the Gaussian's contribution, weighted by exp(-0.5 * (p - mu')^T Sigma'^-1 (p - mu')) . Idea 4 · The alpha-compositing rule For one pixel, the Gaussians that cover it are sorted back-to-front (or equivalently front-to-back with inverted formula). Colour is composited with the same equation as every semi-transparent rasteriser since the 1980s: ​ T i ​ α i ​ c i ​ ​ = i ∑ ​ α i ​ T i ​ c i ​ = j < i ∏ ​ ( 1 − α j ​ ) = opacity i ​ ⋅ exp ( − 0.5 d T Σ ′ − 1 d ) = eval_SH ( SH i ​ , view_direction ) ​ ​ transmittance up to i local contribution view-dependent colour ​ This is the same equation as NeRF's volumetric render , just over an explicit sparse set of Gaussians instead of dense samples along a ray. That identity is why rendered quality matches NeRF — both are integrating the same radiance-field equation. Check your mental model ✗ "A Gaussian splat is a point with a colour." ✓ It is a soft 3D ellipsoid with its own shape and transparency; overlapping ellipsoids blend. ✗ "Splatting needs a neural network at render time." ✓ It only projects, sorts and blends explicit primitives. The learning is gradient descent on their parameters. ✗ "The draw order does not matter, the colours just add up." ✓ Front-to-back order decides who hides whom; "Use it" renders a trained scene with the order reversed. Idea 5 · Why this is differentiable Every step — projection, tile assignment, alpha compositing, SH evaluation — is differentiable with respect to the Gaussian parameters. Given a ground-truth image, compute rendered pixel loss, backprop through the rasteriser, update all (mu, q, s, alpha, c_lm) by gradient descent. Over ~30,000 iterations the Gaussians find their right positions, scales, and colours. Idea 6 · Densification and pruning A fixed set of Gaussians cannot cover a complex scene. Training includes two adaptive mechanisms: Clone a Gaussian at its current position when its gradient magnitude is high but its scale is small — the reconstruction needs more detail here. Split a large-scale Gaussian into two smaller ones when its gradient is high — one big Gaussian is too smooth to fit the region. Prune Gaussians whose opacity drops below a threshold — they are not contributing. Densification runs every iterations. A scene typically grows from ~100k initial Gaussians (seeded from SfM points) to 1-5M at the end of training. Idea 7 · Spherical harmonics in one paragraph View-dependent colour is a function c(direction) on the unit sphere. Spherical harmonics are the sphere's Fourier basis. Truncate at degree L and you get (L+1)^2 basis functions per channel. Evaluating the colour for a new view is a dot product between the learned SH coefficients and the basis evaluated at the viewing direction. Degree 0 = one coefficient = constant colour. Degree 3 = 16 coefficients = enough to capture Lambertian shading, specular, and mild reflection. SD Gaussian Splatting papers use degree 3 by default. Idea 8 · The 2026 production stack Copy Idea 9 · 4D and generative variants 4D Gaussian Splatting — Gaussians are functions of time; used for volumetric video (Framestore's work on the 2025 film Superman , A$AP Rocky's "Helicopter" video). Generative splats — text-to-splat models (Marble by World Labs) that hallucinate entire scenes. 3D Gaussian Unscented Transform — NVIDIA NuRec's variant for autonomous driving simulation. The same idea as a formula One Gaussian. Each primitive has a centre , a covariance , an opacity and a colour; its density at is 1 ​ ( x − μ ) ⊤ Σ − 1 ( x − μ ) ) . To keep a valid covariance during optimisation it is built from a rotation (a unit quaternion) and per-axis scales: R ⊤ Projection. With the world-to-camera transform and the Jacobian of the perspective projection at , the 2-D footprint on screen is the Gaussian with covariance = J W Σ W ⊤ J ⊤ (its top-left block). Compositing. Sorted front to back, the Gaussians covering a pixel blend as ∑ ​ c i ​ α i ​ j < i ∏ ​ ( 1 − α j ​ ) , α i ​ = o i ​ G i ′ ​ ( pixel ) the same form as NeRF's volume rendering, but over a short list of splats per pixel instead of hundreds of network evaluations per ray, so it rasterises in real time and every term is differentiable. Size. With degree-3 spherical harmonics for view-dependent colour (16 coefficients per channel, 48 numbers), each Gaussian stores floats: position, scale, rotation, opacity, colour. A scene of 3 million Gaussians is about 700 MB in float32, which is why compression and pruning matter for deployment. Step 1 · A 2D Gaussian We first build a 2D rasteriser. The 3D case reduces to it after projection. Copy einsum does the quadratic form diff^T Sigma^-1 diff for every (Gaussian, pixel) pair. Step 2 · 2D splatting rasteriser Alpha-compositing front-to-back. Depth in 2D is meaningless, so we use a learned per-Gaussian scalar for order. Copy Not fast — a real implementation uses tile-based CUDA kernels — but exactly the right math and fully differentiable. Step 3 · A trainable 2D splat scene Copy log_scale , opacity_logit , and colour_logits are all unconstrained parameters mapped through the right activation at render time. This is the standard pattern for every 3DGS implementation. Step 4 · Fit 2D Gaussians to a target image Copy What you should see Copy Copy See it drawn See the fitted splats The target, the 64 trained Gaussians rendered by rasterise_2d , and the same Gaussians drawn as ellipses (one standard deviation) to show their shapes. Over 200 steps the 64 Gaussians settle into the two shapes. That is the entire idea — gradient-descent on explicit geometric primitives. Step 5 · From 2D to 3D The 3D extension keeps the same loop. The additions: Per-Gaussian rotation is a quaternion instead of a single angle. Covariance is R S S^T R^T with R built from the quaternion and S = diag(exp(log_scale)) . Projection (mu, Sigma) -> (mu', Sigma') uses the camera extrinsics and the Jacobian of the perspective projection at mu . Colour becomes a spherical-harmonics expansion; evaluate it at the viewing direction. Depth-sort is from actual camera-space z instead of a learned scalar. Every production implementation ( gsplat , inria/gaussian-splatting , nerfstudio ) does exactly this on the GPU with tile-based CUDA kernels. Step 6 · Spherical harmonics evaluation The SH basis up to degree 3 has 16 terms per channel. Evaluation: Copy Learned sh_coeffs store the "colour in every direction" for that Gaussian. At render time you evaluate against the current view direction and get a 3-vector RGB. Recap What to keep from this lesson A 3D Gaussian carries a position, rotation, scale, opacity and view-dependent colour, about 59 floats. Rendering projects each Gaussian to a 2D ellipse with = J W Σ W T J T and alpha-composites front to back. The compositing equation is NeRF's volume rendering applied to explicit primitives. Everything is differentiable, so the primitives are fitted to photos by gradient descent, with densification and pruning. Splats render in real time but take much more storage than a NeRF; compressed formats and glTF/USD standards now exist. Solutions Solution P1 · Yes, and quickly Yes: the held-out render shows all three spheres in the right places at about 30 dB PSNR (printed), blurrier at the edges than the truth. Each training view constrains where the Gaussians can be; a blob in the wrong place would show up wrongly in other views, so only a consistent 3D arrangement fits all 24. Solution B1 · Back paints over front The front-to-back formula gives the first Gaussian in the list full weight and dims everything after it. Sorting far-to-near therefore lets the farthest Gaussians cover the nearer ones: the green sphere hidden behind the orange one shows through on top of it, and the PSNR drops (the printed second line). The more the scene overlaps itself, the worse it gets. The trained parameters are fine; only the order is wrong, which is why real rasterisers sort by depth for every view. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Splats in products. Capture apps (Niantic's Scaniverse, Polycam, Luma) and viewers (PlayCanvas SuperSplat) create and share Gaussian splats from phone video; game engines and web viewers render them in real time. A standard file format. Khronos announced a glTF extension for Gaussian splats (2025–2026), so splats can travel between tools like ordinary 3-D assets. Tooling. nerfstudio's gsplat library is a common open implementation for training splats. Sources: Khronos glTF Gaussian splatting , gsplat , SuperSplat , Scaniverse . a0423: Course home / Phase 4 · Teaching Machines to See Diffusion transformers and straight-line flows Lesson 4.23 75 min Learn + Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Trace the evolution from U-Net DDPM (Lesson 10) to Diffusion Transformer (DiT), MMDiT (SD3), and single+double-stream DiT (FLUX) Explain rectified flow: why a straight-line trajectory between noise and data lets models sample in 20 steps instead of 1000 Implement a tiny DiT block and a rectified-flow training loop, both under 100 lines Distinguish model variants (SD3, FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.1-schnell, Z-Image, Qwen-Image) by architecture, parameter count, and licensing Before you start Needs : Phase 4 Lesson 10 (Diffusion DDPM), Phase 4 Lesson 14 (ViT), Phase 7 Lesson 02 (Self-Attention) Type : Learn + Build. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line The U-Net is not the secret of diffusion. Replace it with a transformer, swap the noise schedule for a straight-line flow, and suddenly you have SD3, FLUX, and most recent text-to-image models. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means DiT "Diffusion transformer" Transformer that replaces the U-Net as the diffusion denoiser; operates on patchified latents AdaLN "Adaptive layer norm" Timestep/text conditioning via learned scale, shift, gate applied after LayerNorm; standard in every modern DiT MMDiT "Multi-modal DiT (SD3)" Separate weight streams for text and image tokens that share a joint self-attention Single-stream / double-stream "FLUX trick" First $N$ blocks double-stream (separate weights per modality), later blocks single-stream (concat + shared weights) for efficiency Rectified flow "Straight-line noise-to-data" Linear interpolation between data and noise; network predicts velocity; fewer ODE steps needed at inference Velocity target "epsilon - x_0" The regression target in rectified flow; points from clean data to noise CFG guidance "classifier-free guidance" Mix conditional and unconditional predictions; still used in rectified-flow models Schnell / turbo / LCM "1-4 step distillation" Small-step variants distilled from full-quality models; production real-time The problem In plain words first Two upgrades turned 2022's diffusion models into today's. First, the denoiser: the U-Net is replaced by a transformer that treats patches of the latent image as tokens (a Diffusion Transformer , DiT). Second, the path from noise to image: instead of a curved, many-step noising schedule, the model learns to move each noisy sample along a straight line towards a clean image ( rectified flow ). Straight paths can be followed in big steps, so sampling needs 20 or so steps instead of hundreds. Stable Diffusion 3, FLUX and most recent open models combine both. Lesson 4.10 built a DDPM with a U-Net denoiser. That recipe dominated 2020-2023: U-Net + beta schedule + noise-prediction loss. It produced Stable Diffusion 1.5 and 2.1 and DALL-E 2. The leading open text-to-image models have moved past it. Stable Diffusion 3, FLUX, Z-Image, Qwen-Image, HunyuanImage — none use a U-Net. They use Diffusion Transformers (DiT). SD3 and FLUX also swap the DDPM noise schedule for rectified flow, which straightens the path from noise to data and enables 1-4 step inference with consistency or distilled variants. The shift matters because it is the reason diffusion-based image generation became controllable, prompt-accurate (SD3 and its successors render legible text far more reliably), and production-fast. Understanding DiT + rectified flow is understanding the 2026 generative-image stack. Idea 1 · From U-Net to transformer DiT (Peebles & Xie, 2023) — replace the U-Net with a ViT-like transformer on latent patches. Conditioning via adaptive layer norm (AdaLN). MMDiT (SD3, Esser et al., 2024) — two streams with separate weights for text and image tokens that share a joint attention. FLUX (Black Forest Labs, 2024) — first N blocks double-stream like SD3, later blocks concatenate and share weights (single-stream) for efficiency at higher depth. Z-Image (2025) — an efficient single-stream DiT at 6B parameters that challenges "scale at all costs". Idea 2 · Rectified flow in one paragraph DDPM defines the forward process as a noisy SDE where x_t is increasingly corrupted. The learned reverse is a second SDE, solved by 1000 small steps. Rectified flow defines a straight-line interpolation between clean data and pure noise: ​ = ( 1 − t ) x 0 ​ + t ϵ , t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] Train a network to predict the velocity v_theta(x_t, t) = epsilon - x_0 — the forward direction along the straight-line path from clean data to noise ( dx_t/dt ). During sampling, you integrate this velocity backward to step from noise toward data. The resulting ODE is much closer to a straight line, so far fewer integration steps are needed to sample. SD3 calls this Rectified Flow Matching . FLUX, Z-Image, and most 2026 models use the same objective. Typical inference: 20-30 Euler steps (deterministic) vs 50+ DDIM steps in the old DDPM regime. Distilled / turbo / schnell / LCM variants take it down to 1-4 steps. Worked example One Euler step by hand A 1-number "image": clean value ​ = 2 , noise draw . At : ​ = ( 1 − 0.75 ) × 2 + 0.75 × ( − 1 ) = 0.5 − 0.75 = − 0.25 The velocity target is ​ = − 1 − 2 = − 3 , the same at every : the path is a straight line. If the model predicts exactly, one Euler step from to gives , the clean value, in a single jump. In practice the model only sees ​ , not which ​ , ϵ ) pair produced it, so it predicts the average velocity over all pairs that pass through that point; averaged paths bend, and that is why a few steps are still needed. Check your mental model ✗ "Rectified flow paths are perfectly straight, so one step is enough." ✓ Each training pair's path is straight, but the learned field averages many crossing paths and is curved. "Use it" shows one step lands every sample near the middle of the data. ✗ "A transformer denoiser needs a new training objective." ✓ DiT changes the network only. The same DiT can be trained with noise prediction or with velocity prediction. ✗ "Rectified flow removes the need for classifier-free guidance." ✓ Guidance is about conditioning, not the path; SD3 and FLUX.1-dev still use it (schnell is distilled to work without it). Idea 3 · AdaLN conditioning DiTs condition on timestep and class/text via adaptive layer norm : predict scale and shift from the conditioning vector and apply them after LayerNorm. Much cleaner than FiLM-style modulation in U-Nets and standard in DiTs. Copy Idea 4 · Text encoders in SD3 and FLUX SD3 uses three text encoders: two CLIP models + T5-XXL. Embeddings concatenated and fed to the image stream as text conditioning. FLUX uses one CLIP-L + T5-XXL. Qwen-Image / Z-Image variants use their own in-house text encoders aligned with their base LLMs. The text encoder is a big part of why SD3/FLUX reason about prompts so much better than SD1.5. T5-XXL alone is 4.7B params. Idea 5 · Classifier-free guidance still holds Rectified flow changes the sampler, not the conditioning. Classifier-free guidance (drop text with 10% probability during training, mix conditional and unconditional predictions at inference) works identically with rectified flow. Most 2026 models use guidance scale 3.5-5 — lower than SD1.5's 7.5 because rectified-flow models follow prompts more tightly by default. Idea 6 · Consistency, Turbo, Schnell, LCM Four names for the same idea: distil a slow many-step model into a fast few-step model. LCM (Latent Consistency Model) — train a student that predicts the final x_0 from any intermediate x_t in one step. SDXL Turbo / FLUX schnell — 1-4 step models trained with adversarial diffusion distillation. SD Turbo — the same adversarial diffusion distillation as SDXL Turbo, applied to SD 2.1. Production serving of any new model ships both a "full quality" checkpoint and a "turbo / schnell" variant. Schnell ("fast" in German, Black Forest Labs' convention) runs in 1-4 steps and fits real-time pipelines. Idea 7 · Model landscape in 2026 Model Size Architecture License Stable Diffusion 3 Medium 2B MMDiT SAI Community Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large 8B MMDiT SAI Community FLUX.1-dev 12B Double + Single Stream DiT non-commercial FLUX.1-schnell 12B same, distilled Apache 2.0 FLUX.2 (late 2025) 32B ([dev]) iterated FLUX.1 varies by variant ([dev] non-commercial) Z-Image 6B S3-DiT (Scalable Single-Stream) permissive Qwen-Image ~20B DiT + Qwen text tower Apache 2.0 HunyuanImage-3.0 ~80B (mixture of experts) multimodal autoregressive + diffusion Tencent community licence Sizes and licences change quickly, so check each model card. As a rough guide: FLUX.1-schnell and Z-Image are popular when a permissive licence and speed matter, and the larger FLUX.2 and Qwen-Image models when quality matters most. Idea 8 · Why this phase shift matters DDPM + U-Net worked. DiT + rectified flow works better, faster, and scales more cleanly . The transition parallels the one from RNNs to transformers in NLP: both architectures solved the same problem, but transformers scaled and now dominate. Every 2026 paper on image, video, or 3D generation uses a DiT-shaped denoiser and usually a rectified flow objective. U-Net DDPM is now primarily pedagogical ( Lesson 4.10 ). The same idea as a formula Rectified flow. Join a data sample ​ and noise with a straight line, ​ = ( 1 − t ) x 0 ​ + t ε for . Its velocity is constant, d x t ​ ​ = ε − x 0 ​ , and a network learns to predict it: ​ , ε , t ​ ​ v θ ​ ( x t ​ , t , c ) − ( ε − x 0 ​ ) ​ 2 Sampling integrates backwards from noise at , for example with Euler steps ​ = x t ​ − Δ v θ ​ ( x t ​ , t , c ) . Straighter paths need fewer steps; SD3 and FLUX are trained this way, and distilled variants (Turbo, Schnell, LCM) sample in 1–4 steps. AdaLN conditioning. Solution B1 · Noise stays noise Training defined as clean data and as pure noise, and the velocity points from data towards noise. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Production generators are diffusion transformers trained with flow matching. a0424: Course home / Phase 4 · Teaching Machines to See Segmenting anything you can name (SAM 3) Lesson 4.24 60 min Use + Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Distinguish SAM (visual prompts only), Grounded SAM / SAM 2 (detector + SAM), and SAM 3 (native text prompts via Promptable Concept Segmentation) Explain the SAM 3 architecture: shared backbone + image detector + memory-based video tracker + presence head + decoupled detector-tracker design Use Hugging Face transformers SAM 3 integration for text-prompted detection, segmentation, and video tracking Pick between SAM 3, Grounded SAM 2, YOLO-World, and SAM-MI based on latency, concept complexity, and deployment target Before you start Needs : Phase 4 Lesson 07 (U-Net), Phase 4 Lesson 08 (Mask R-CNN), Phase 4 Lesson 18 (CLIP) Type : Use + Build. Time : about 60 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Give a model a text prompt and an image and get masks for every matching object. SAM 3 made that a single forward pass. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Open-vocabulary segmentation "Segment by text" Produce masks for objects described in natural language, not a fixed label set PCS "Promptable Concept Segmentation" SAM 3's core task — given a noun-phrase or image exemplar, segment all matching instances Concept prompt "The text input" Short noun phrase or image exemplar; not a full sentence Presence head "Is it here?" SAM 3 module that decides whether the concept exists in the image before localisation SA-CO "SAM 3 benchmark" 270K-concept open-vocabulary segmentation benchmark; 50x larger than prior open-vocab benchmarks Object Multiplex "SAM 3.1 update" Shared-memory multi-object tracking; fast joint tracking of many instances Grounded SAM 2 "Modular pipeline" Detector + SAM 2 cascade; still relevant when detector swap matters SAM-MI "Efficient SAM variant" Mask Injection for 1.6x speedup over Grounded-SAM The problem In plain words first The original Segment Anything Model (SAM) cuts out whatever you point at: click a spot or draw a box and it returns that object's mask. It does not understand words. To get "every dog in this photo" you first needed a text-aware detector to find the dogs, then SAM to cut each one out (a "Grounded SAM" pipeline). SAM 3 does both in one model: give it a short phrase such as "yellow school bus" and it returns a mask for every matching object, and it first asks whether the thing is in the picture at all, so it can return nothing when the answer is no. The 2023 SAM was a visual-prompt-only model: you click a point or draw a box and it returns a mask. For "give me all the oranges in this photo" you needed a detector (Grounding DINO) to produce boxes, then SAM to segment each. Grounded SAM turned this into a pipeline, but it was a cascade of two frozen models with inevitable error accumulation. SAM 3 (Meta, Nov 2025, ICLR 2026) collapsed the cascade. It accepts a short noun phrase or an image exemplar as prompt and returns all matching masks and instance IDs in a single forward pass. That is Promptable Concept Segmentation (PCS) . Combined with the March 2026 Object Multiplex update (SAM 3.1), it tracks multiple instances of the same concept through video efficiently. This lesson is about the structural shift this represents. 2D seg, detection, and text-image grounding have merged into one model. The production question is no longer "which pipeline do I chain together" but "which promptable model handles my use case end-to-end." Idea 1 · The three generations Idea 2 · Promptable Concept Segmentation A "concept prompt" is a short noun phrase ( "yellow school bus" , "striped red umbrella" , "hand holding a mug" ) or an image exemplar. The model returns segmentation masks for every instance in the image that matches the concept, plus a unique instance ID per match. This differs from classic visual-prompt SAM in three ways: No per-instance prompting required — one text prompt returns all matches. Open-vocabulary — the concept can be anything describable in natural language. Returns multiple instances at once rather than one mask per prompt. Idea 3 · Key architectural pieces Shared backbone — a single ViT processes the image. Both the detector head and the memory-based tracker read from it. Presence head — predicts whether the concept is present in the image at all. Decouples "is this here?" from "where is it?". Reduces false positives on absent concepts. Decoupled detector-tracker — image-level detection and video-level tracking have separate heads so they do not interfere. Memory bank — stores per-instance features across frames for video tracking (same mechanism SAM 2 used). Worked example Why a presence head helps Suppose a detector scores 300 candidate regions for the prompt "giraffe" in a photo with no giraffe, and each region independently has a 0.2% chance of scoring above the 0.35 threshold by accident. The chance that none does is = 0.55 : almost half the giraffe-free photos still get at least one false giraffe. A presence head answers "is there a giraffe at all?" once per image. If it says no with high confidence, every region is suppressed together, and the per-region scores only have to sort out where , not whether . "Use it" shows the false-positive case on a real photo. Check your mental model ✗ "Open-vocabulary means the model understands any sentence." ✓ SAM 3 expects short noun phrases ("striped red umbrella"), not instructions or questions; long prompts are better handled by a vision-language model in front of it. ✗ "A text-prompted detector returns nothing when the object is absent." ✓ Without a presence check it often returns its best guess anyway. "Use it" asks for a giraffe in a photo of two puppies. ✗ "Segmentation quality comes from the detector." ✓ In a modular pipeline the detector decides which objects and SAM decides the mask ; errors in either show up in the result. Idea 4 · Training at scale SAM 3 was trained on 4 million unique concepts generated by a data engine that iteratively annotates and corrects using AI + human review. The new SA-CO benchmark contains 270K unique concepts, 50x larger than prior benchmarks. SAM 3 reaches 75-80% of human performance on SA-CO and doubles existing systems on image + video PCS. Idea 5 · SAM 3.1 Object Multiplex March 2026 update: Object Multiplex introduces a shared-memory mechanism for joint tracking of many instances of the same concept at once. Previously, tracking N instances meant N separate memory banks. Multiplex collapses that into one shared memory with per-instance queries. Result: substantially faster multi-object tracking without sacrificing accuracy. Idea 6 · Where Grounded SAM still matters in 2026 When you need a specific open-vocabulary detector swapped in (DINO-X, Florence-2). When the SAM 3 license (gated on HF) is a blocker. When you need more control over the detector threshold than SAM 3 exposes. For research / ablation work on the detector component. Modular pipelines still have a place. For most production work, SAM 3 is the simpler answer. Idea 7 · YOLO-World vs SAM 3 YOLO-World — open-vocabulary detector only (no masks). Real-time. Best when you need boxes at high fps. SAM 3 — full segmentation + tracking. Slower but richer output. Production split: YOLO-World for fast detection-only pipelines (robotics navigation, fast dashboards), SAM 3 for anything that needs masks or tracking. Idea 8 · SAM-MI efficiency SAM-MI (2025-2026) addresses SAM's decoder bottleneck. Key ideas: Text-guided sparse point prompting — samples a few well-chosen point prompts for SAM instead of a dense grid, which speeds up mask generation. Shallow mask aggregation — merges partial masks to reduce SAM's tendency to over-segment. Decoupled mask injection — injects SAM's masks as guidance separately into low-frequency and high-frequency features. Result, as reported in the SAM-MI paper: a 1.6× speedup and a 16.7% relative mIoU improvement over Grounded-SAM on the MESS benchmark. Idea 9 · Output format for the three models All return the same general structure (boxes + labels + scores + masks + IDs), which is helpful — your pipeline downstream does not have to branch on which model ran. The same idea as a formula Promptable segmentation. An image encoder runs once per image, (in the original SAM, a input becomes a grid of embeddings); prompts (points, boxes, a text concept) are encoded into a few tokens ; a light decoder maps to masks and a predicted quality score. Because the heavy encoder is shared, each new prompt costs only milliseconds. Ambiguity. One click can mean a part or a whole object, so the decoder outputs several masks (three in SAM) with predicted IoUs and the best is chosen, or all are shown. Training loss. For predicted mask logits against the ground truth, a weighted sum of focal and Dice loss (SAM used a 20 : 1 ratio), plus a mean-squared error between the predicted and the actual IoU of each mask. Scoring masks. Mask IoU over pixels. A stability score measures how much a mask changes when its logit threshold moves: ​ , M > − δ ​ ) ; masks that change little are kept in automatic mode. Concept prompts (SAM 3) return every instance matching a noun phrase, each with its own mask and identity, so the output is a variable-length list, not one mask. Output size. A mask is booleans; for transmission it is usually stored as run-length encoding (COCO RLE), often 10–100 times smaller. a0425: Course home / Phase 4 · Teaching Machines to See How vision-language models are wired Lesson 4.25 75 min Learn + Use Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do State the ViT-MLP-LLM architecture and explain what each of the three components contributes Compare Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5, LLaVA-Next, and GLM-4.6V on parameter count, context length, and benchmark performance Explain DeepStack: why multi-level ViT features tighten vision-language alignment better than a single last-layer feature Measure VLM hallucination in production with Cross-Modal Error Rate (CMER) and act on the signal Before you start Needs : Phase 4 Lesson 14 (ViT), Phase 4 Lesson 18 (CLIP), Phase 7 Lesson 02 (Self-Attention) Type : Learn + Use. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line A vision encoder converts an image into tokens. An MLP projector maps those tokens into the LLM's embedding space. A language model does the rest. That pattern, ViT-MLP-LLM, underlies almost every open VLM today. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means ViT-MLP-LLM "The VLM pattern" Vision encoder + projector + language model; the standard open-VLM layout Projector "The bridge" 2-4 layer MLP (or Q-former) that maps vision tokens into LLM embedding space DeepStack "Qwen3-VL feature trick" Multi-level ViT features stacked rather than last-layer only Image token " placeholder" Special token in the text stream replaced by projected vision embeddings CMER "Hallucination KPI" Cross-Modal Error Rate; high when text confidence is high but image-text similarity is low Visual agent "VLM that clicks" VLM operating GUIs (OSWorld, mobile, web) with tool calls Q-former "Fixed-count token bridge" BLIP-2 style projector producing a fixed number of visual query tokens Alignment / pre-training / instruction tuning "Three stages" Standard VLM training pipeline The problem In plain words first A vision-language model (VLM) is a chatbot that can look at pictures. It has three parts. An image encoder (a ViT, often from CLIP or SigLIP) turns the picture into a few hundred or thousand vectors, one per patch. A small projector network converts those vectors into the same format as the language model's word embeddings. The language model then reads the "image words" followed by your question, and writes the answer word by word. Because the language model is fluent, it can also be fluently wrong about the picture; checking answers against the image is part of using VLMs well. CLIP (Phase 4 Lesson 4.18 ) gives you a shared embedding space for images and text, which is enough for zero-shot classification and retrieval. It cannot answer "how many red cars are in this image?" because CLIP does not generate text — it only scores similarities. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) — Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5, LLaVA-Next, GLM-4.6V — bolt a CLIP-family image encoder to a full language model. The model sees an image plus a question and generates an answer. The strongest open-weight VLMs now report scores close to leading closed models on many multimodal benchmarks (MMMU, MMBench, DocVQA, ChartQA, MathVista, OSWorld). The trio of pieces (ViT, projector, LLM) is the standard. The differences between models are in which ViT, which projector, which LLM, the training data, and the alignment recipe. Once you understand the pattern, swapping any component is mechanical. Idea 1 · The ViT-MLP-LLM architecture Vision encoder — a pretrained ViT (CLIP-L/14, SigLIP, DINOv3, or a fine-tuned variant). Produces patch tokens. Projector — a small module (2-4 layer MLP, or a Q-former) that maps vision tokens into the LLM's embedding dimension. It is the only part trained from scratch, so it is always trained; how much of the encoder and LLM is also unfrozen depends on the stage (Idea 3). LLM — a decoder-only language model (Qwen3, Llama, Mistral, GLM, InternLM). Reads the vision + text tokens in sequence, generates text. All three pieces are trainable in principle. In practice the first stage trains only the projector, which is cheap; later stages usually unfreeze the LLM and often the encoder too, which is where most of the compute goes. Worked example How many tokens is a picture? A ViT with 14-pixel patches on a 448 × 448 image produces = 3 2 2 = 1 , 024 patch tokens. Many VLMs then merge neighbouring tokens (a 2 × 2 merge gives 256) before the projector, because every image token costs the language model as much as a word: it takes part in attention for the whole answer. High-resolution inputs are often cut into tiles, each encoded separately, so one photo can cost a thousand tokens or more. The small VLM under "Use it" prints its count: about a thousand image tokens for one 500 × 461 photo, against about 20 for the question. Check your mental model ✗ "The LLM sees the pixels." ✓ It sees projected vectors placed where the <image> tokens were. It never sees pixels, which is one reason fine details like small text can be lost. ✗ "A fluent answer is a grounded answer." ✓ The language model will write a confident sentence whether or not the image supports it. "Use it" shows a small VLM naming the wrong instrument. ✗ "The projector is a big part of the model." ✓ It is usually tiny: about 7M of the 228M parameters in the model under "Use it". Idea 2 · DeepStack Vanilla projection uses only the last ViT layer. DeepStack (Qwen3-VL) samples features from multiple ViT depths and stacks them. Deeper layers carry high-level semantics; shallower layers carry fine-grained spatial and textural information. Feeding both into the LLM closes the gap between "what does the image contain" (semantics) and "where exactly" (spatial grounding). Idea 3 · Three training stages Modern VLMs train in stages: Alignment — freeze ViT and LLM. Train only the projector on image-caption pairs. Teaches the projector to map vision space into language space. Pre-training — unfreeze everything. Train on large-scale interleaved image-text data (500M+ pairs). Builds the model's visual knowledge. Instruction tuning — fine-tune on curated (image, question, answer) triples. Teaches conversational behaviour and task formats. This is what turns a "vision-aware LM" into a usable assistant. Most LoRA fine-tunes target stage 3 with a small labelled dataset. Idea 4 · Model family comparison (early 2026) Model Params Vision encoder LLM Context Strengths Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B (MoE) 235B (22B active) custom ViT + DeepStack Qwen3 256K General SOTA, GUI agent Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B (MoE) 30B (3B active) custom ViT + DeepStack Qwen3 256K Smaller MoE alternative Qwen3-VL-8B (dense) 8B custom ViT Qwen3 128K Production dense default InternVL3.5-38B 38B InternViT-6B Qwen3 + GPT-OSS 128K Strong MMBench / MMVet InternVL3.5-241B-A28B 241B (28B active) InternViT-6B Qwen3 128K Competitive with GPT-4o LLaVA-OneVision-72B 72B SigLIP Qwen2 32K Open, well-documented recipe GLM-4.6V 106B (plus a 9B Flash variant) custom GLM 128K Open weights, native tool calling MiniCPM-V-2.6 8B SigLIP Qwen2-7B 32K Edge-friendly Idea 5 · Visual agents Qwen3-VL-235B was reported at release among the strongest models on OSWorld — a benchmark for visual agents that operate GUIs (desktop, mobile, web). The model sees a screenshot, understands the UI, and emits actions (click, type, scroll). Combined with tools, it closes the loop on common desktop tasks. This is what most 2026 "AI PC" demos run under the hood. Idea 6 · Agentic capabilities + RoPE variants VLMs need to know when a frame is in a video. Qwen3-VL evolved from T-RoPE (temporal rotary position embeddings) to text-based time alignment — explicit timestamp text tokens interleaved with video frames. The model sees " <timestamp 00:32> frame, prompt" and can reason about temporal relationships. Idea 7 · The alignment problem Web-crawled image-text pairs often contain captions that are not fully grounded in the image. A VLM trained on such data learns to hallucinate — fabricate objects, misread numbers, invent relationships. In production this is the dominant failure mode. One simple way to track it is a cross-modal error rate (CMER) , a monitoring heuristic rather than a standard benchmark: Copy High CMER means the model is confidently saying things not grounded in the image. The value of such a signal is not that it fixes the model but that it lets you route suspicious outputs to human review. How well it works depends entirely on the checker; "Use it" tries one and shows its limits. Idea 8 · Fine-tuning with LoRA / QLoRA Full fine-tuning of a 70B VLM is out of reach for most teams. LoRA (rank 16-64) on attention + projector layers, or QLoRA with 4-bit base weights, fits on a single A100 / H100. Cost: 5,000-50,000 examples, $100-$5,000 in compute, 2-10 hours of training. Idea 9 · Spatial reasoning is still weak Spatial reasoning (above-below, left-right, counting, distance) remains a weak spot on dedicated benchmarks, with VLMs well below human accuracy. If your use case depends on "which object is on top of which," validate heavily — generic VLM performance is below human. Better-than-VLM alternatives for pure spatial tasks: a specialised keypoint / pose estimator, a depth model, or a detection model with box geometry post-processed. Training stages. (1) Align: freeze the vision encoder and the language model, train only the projector on image–caption pairs. (2) Instruction-tune: unfreeze the language model (and often the encoder) on visual question answering and dialogue. (3) Preference or reinforcement tuning to reduce hallucination.
