Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Weigh a trade-off You can spend your data budget on one of two things: have a strong proprietary model write captions for two million images, or pay people to describe seven hundred thousand images in detail by speaking for a minute or more about each one. Which do you choose for a new vision-language model, and what is the evidence? Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Pay the people. The reference result is a model trained on 712K densely captioned images and no distilled captions that beat a much larger model on 11 of 11 benchmarks. Dense human captions carry 5 to 10 times the information of a short web caption and stay grounded in the image, while distilled captions inherit the hallucinations of the model that wrote them; about 12 percent of crawled pairs already describe things that are not in the image. Caption density beats caption quantity, which beats distillation convenience. The evidence. The dense-caption recipe: annotators described each image for one to three minutes in speech, transcribed to text, which gave 712K densely captioned images. The 72B model trained on them beat a 90B competitor on every one of 11 benchmarks. The difference was not architecture. Two other datasets followed the same path with mixed human and synthetic captions, and the trend across them is that density wins. The first visual instruction set was written by a text-only model from captions and boxes without seeing the image, 158k turns; it worked to unlock dialogue, with noise. Why density beats volume. A dense caption of 80 to 300 tokens names objects, counts, relations, text in the image and context; a web alt text names one thing. For alignment and instruction tuning the model learns from what the caption says about the image, so the information per image is the currency, not the image count. Why distillation is risky. The writing model does not see what it does not see. It hallucinates plausible content, and the student learns to hallucinate with the same confidence. A benchmark built from similar data does not punish it; production users do. When distillation still has a place. Bootstrapping a new domain fast, before human data arrives. Generating questions and answers from a human-written caption, which keeps the grounding in the caption. Filtered: score each synthetic caption against the image with a contrastive checker and drop the ungrounded tail. What to do with the budget. Dense human captions for the alignment and instruction stages, task-specific instruction data on top, and synthetic data only where a human caption anchors it. Measure grounding on a held-out human-labelled set, not only benchmark accuracy. Plausible wrong answers. "Two million captions beat seven hundred thousand; more data wins." The reference result beat a larger model with fewer, denser, grounded captions; volume of thin or hallucinated captions is no substitute. "The strong model's captions are better than what annotators write." They are longer than web captions but not grounded; the model describes what it expects, and the student learns the same habit. "Caption quality only matters for captioning tasks." The reference model gained on every benchmark, reasoning and reading included, because the alignment stage learned more about each image. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why did the speech-based collection matter? Expected: people say far more in a minute than they type, so the captions are long and specific at a cost that scales. (level 3) How do you check that a synthetic caption is grounded? Expected: embed the image and the caption with a contrastive checker and flag low similarity, then read a sample; drop or rewrite the tail. (level 4) How would you prove to a skeptic that the gain is data and not model size? Expected: the reference comparison beat a larger model; replicate at one size with two data mixes and the same encoder, connector and schedule. (level 4) Where in the three-stage pipeline do dense captions pay most? Expected: alignment and the first instruction stage, where the projector and the language model learn what an image contains; task-specific data pays in the last stage. Where it is taught. The open-weight recipes lesson gives the dense-caption result and the data axis, the vision-language models lesson quantifies the ungrounded pairs, and the LLaVA lesson shows the generated instruction data that started the field. Explain the mechanism Your 7B vision-language model trails a competitor on a multimodal reasoning benchmark by several points. The team's plan is a new connector design. Argue for or against, using what the ablation literature says about where the score comes from. Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Against. Across the controlled studies, swapping the connector moved a reasoning benchmark by less than a point at a fixed token count, while swapping the encoder moved it by three or more, and doubling the language model from 7B to 13B added two to four points. The reasoning ceiling of such a model is the text reasoning ceiling of its language model; the visual side can only feed it. Spend the effort on the language model size, the encoder, the token count and the data before the connector. The decomposition. The one study that held every axis fixed but one found that the per-image visual-token count explained about 60 percent of the variance in scores, the encoder about 20 percent, the connector about 5 percent, and everything else about 15 percent. The language model sets the ceiling. Going from a 7B to a 13B language model reliably added 2 to 4 points on the flagship reasoning benchmark across the papers in the lesson, and at 70B most benchmarks saturate. The reason is structural: the encoder produces features and the connector translates them, but the reasoning happens in the language model. A 7B model cannot stand in for a 70B model through a cleverer connector. The encoder is the second lever. Swapping the common contrastive encoder for a stronger one added 3 or more points on the reasoning benchmark in one study, and self-supervised encoders led a vision-centric benchmark by about 5 to 7 points over the common contrastive one. The 2026 default pairs a strong contrastive encoder with a self-supervised one for dense features when grounding matters. The connector is a wash. At a fixed token count, an MLP, a query bridge and a resampler landed within about 1 point of each other in several independent studies. The connector is a cost question about tokens, not a quality question. What to do instead. Check the token count per image; more visual tokens up to the sweet spot helps more than any connector. Check the encoder and the resolution schedule. Check the data: detailed human captions beat distilled synthetic captions at the same token count. If the gap is in reasoning, the honest fix is a larger language model, and the budget question follows. Plausible wrong answers. "The connector is where the modalities meet, so it must matter most." Its measured share is about 5 percent of the variance; the token count and the encoder dominate. "A better connector lets a small language model reason like a large one." The reasoning ceiling is the language model's; no bridge adds reasoning the language model does not have. "More visual tokens always help." They help up to the sweet spot and then give diminishing returns at a growing compute cost; the gain is in the token count, not in the architecture that emits them. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does a bigger language model help a visual task? Expected: the benchmark asks for reasoning over what the encoder saw, and the reasoning happens in the language model; the visual side sets what it knows, not how well it thinks. (level 2) When would a connector change still be the right move? Expected: when the token budget binds, because then the connector decides how many tokens you can afford, which is the axis that matters most. (level 3) Which benchmarks move with the encoder and which do not? Expected: vision-centric benchmarks, counting and grounding, move with a self-supervised encoder, by about 5 to 7 points in one study; the reasoning benchmark also moves, by 3 or more points for a stronger contrastive encoder, so the encoder matters for both kinds. (level 3) Design the smallest ablation that settles this for your model. Expected: hold the data, the encoder, the token count, the resolution schedule and the training schedule fixed, swap the language model size in one run and the connector in another, and compare both with the baseline on the same eval. Where it is taught. The open-weight recipes lesson decomposes the variance across the five design axes, and the vision-language models lesson lays out the pattern the axes belong to. Defend a design Design a vision-language model for an on-device mobile assistant that reads the phone screen and taps, types and scrolls. Keep the language model at about 2B parameters. Choose the encoder, the bridge, the resolution plan and the data mix, justify each choice with the ablation evidence, and name the capability you would guard against over-promising. Level 4 of 4 · about 20 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Encoder: the stronger contrastive encoder at native resolution, with a self-supervised encoder's features concatenated for a dense spatial signal, because the encoder explains about 20 percent of the variance and self-supervised features lead vision-centric tests. Bridge: a two-layer MLP, since the connector explains about 5 percent, with features from several encoder depths stacked so that fine position reaches the language model. Resolution: a ramp from low to high, with dynamic resolution up to about 1280 pixels on the long side, because screens are text-dense and reading gains most from pixels. Data: dense human descriptions of screens plus grounded action traces, not distilled captions; and guard the promise on spatial relations, where general models score 50 to 60 percent and the agent must hit the right element every time. Constraints first. A 2B language model sets a low reasoning ceiling: a larger language model adds points on reasoning benchmarks, and this design cannot grow it. So every other axis must carry more, and the task must be framed as perception plus short actions, not long reasoning. Encoder. Choice Why The strong contrastive encoder at native resolution adds 3 or more points over the common one in the ablations; native resolution keeps screen text legible Concatenated self-supervised features lead vision-centric benchmarks by 5 to 7 points over the contrastive one; UI grounding is vision-centric Features from several encoder depths deep layers carry semantics and shallow layers carry fine position; stacking both tightens grounding, which an agent that taps needs Bridge. A two-layer MLP. The connector explains about 5 percent of the variance at a fixed token count, and the MLP is the simplest to retrain when the encoder or the language model changes. The token count is the knob that matters: screens are documents, so budget toward the upper end of the 576 to 1024 sweet spot, and above it for dense screens. Resolution schedule. Start low and ramp. Flat low-resolution training plateaus; a ramp trains faster and ends higher. Dynamic resolution with a minimum of 256 and a maximum near 1280 pixels on the long side handles the range of screen densities, and the document-reading gains of 3 to 5 points from splitting apply to screens. Data mix. Dense human descriptions of screens: what is on the screen, where, and what is interactive. Dense human captions beat distillation across the board in the reference comparison. Grounded action traces: screenshot, instruction, the element and the action, with coordinates. The visual-agent benchmark that frontier models lead has this shape. Task-specific instruction data for the app families you ship to. Synthetic data only where a human description anchors it, filtered for grounding. The capability to guard. Spatial relations. General models score 50 to 60 percent on above, below, left, right and counting, and an agent that taps the wrong element fails the task. Build the eval from real screens with the exact element-selection questions, measure it before any promise, and keep a verification step in the agent loop: read the screen back after the action and check the state. Serving on the device. A 2B language model and a strong encoder at a high resolution still need the visual token budget counted per screen; measure the latency per step at your resolution before you set the schedule. Plausible wrong answers. "Use a query-based bridge to save tokens on the device." It caps the tokens at a count too low for dense screen text, and the ablations put 64 tokens as too few for reading; spend tokens here and save elsewhere. "Generate the screen descriptions with a strong proprietary model." Distilled descriptions inherit hallucinations, and an agent that taps a hallucinated element fails; dense human descriptions won the reference comparison. "A 2B model with a great encoder matches a 70B agent." The language model sets the reasoning ceiling; frame the task as perception plus short actions and verify each step, instead of promising long reasoning. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why stack shallow and deep encoder layers for an agent and not for a captioner? Expected: a captioner needs semantics; an agent needs where exactly, which the shallow layers carry and the last layer blurs. (level 4) The language model is fixed at 2B. Which axis do you lean on hardest, and what is its limit? Expected: resolution and token count, because screens are text-dense; the limit is the latency per step on the device, which the token count sets. (level 4) How do you make the agent robust to being wrong about an element? Expected: a read-back after each action that compares the new screen with the expected state, and a stop when they do not match; the model's own confidence is not a safe signal. (level 4) What does the ablation evidence not tell you about this design? Expected: it comes from general benchmarks on datacenter GPUs; the device latency, the UI domain and the action format need your own ablation, one axis per run. Where it is taught. The open-weight recipes lesson supplies the ablation evidence for each axis and sets this exercise, and the vision-language models lesson covers multi-level features, visual agents and the spatial reasoning limit. Weigh a trade-off A warehouse team wants a general vision-language model to answer "which shelf is the item on" and "is the box on top of or under the pallet" from camera frames. They plan to ship as soon as a demo works on ten images. What do you tell them? Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Spatial relations are the weak spot of today's general-purpose vision-language models: on benchmarks of above and below, left and right, counting and distance they score about 50 to 60 percent, below human level. A demo on ten images proves nothing about that distribution. Build a labelled eval of a few hundred frames with the exact questions first, measure the model, and compare it with a specialised detection or depth model whose box geometry you post-process; if the general model stays, fine-tune it on the task and keep a human-review route for low-confidence answers. Why the general model struggles. The model sees projected patch tokens and reasons in language. It learned what is in an image from caption pairs that rarely say where exactly. The lesson's figure for spatial reasoning benchmarks is 50 to 60 percent, and its recommended alternatives for pure spatial tasks are a keypoint or pose estimator, a depth model, or a detector with the box geometry post-processed. What a real eval looks like. A few hundred frames from the warehouse cameras, not stock photos, with the two question types written the way the operators will ask them. Labels from two people, with the agreement measured. A split by lighting and camera position, because the demo images will not cover them. A confusion matrix per question type, not one accuracy number. The alternatives. Approach Strength Cost Detector plus box geometry exact image-plane above, under, left and right from coordinates labels for the object classes; no language interface Depth model plus detector distance and stacking calibration per camera General VLM, zero-shot any question in plain language weak on spatial relations; hallucination risk General VLM, fine-tuned a plain-language interface with the domain learned 5,000 to 50,000 labelled examples and hours of GPU time If the VLM stays. Fine-tune with low-rank adapters on the attention and projector layers, which the lesson sizes at rank 16 to 64 on one datacenter GPU for 2 to 10 hours. Then monitor hallucination in production: a cross-modal error rate flags answers where the text confidence is high but the image-text similarity is low, and routes them to review. What to tell them. Ship a measured system, not a demo. Ten images is a smoke test. The eval decides between the detector route and the fine-tuned model, and the hallucination monitor stays whichever route wins. Plausible wrong answers. "The demo worked on ten images, so it works." Ten images cannot cover the cameras, the lighting or the relation types; the benchmark figure for this kind of question is near a coin flip for some relations. "A bigger VLM will fix spatial reasoning." Size lifts language reasoning more than geometry; the lesson's advice for pure spatial tasks is a specialised model. "Fine-tune on the demo images." Tens of examples teach nothing and overfit; the fine-tuning route needs thousands of labelled frames and an eval that is separate from them. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does a model that captions well fail at which object is on top? Expected: captions describe content, not geometry; the training pairs rarely contain precise relations, and fine position fades as the language model reasons over projected tokens. (level 2) What does the detector route lose? Expected: the plain-language interface and the open vocabulary; it answers only the relations you compute from boxes, for the classes you labelled. (level 3) How many frames does the eval need, and how do you decide? Expected: enough that each question type and each camera condition has tens of examples; a few hundred in total is the floor, and you grow it where the confusion matrix is unstable. (level 3) How does a stronger encoder change the picture? Expected: self-supervised encoders carry more dense spatial features and lead vision-centric benchmarks; swapping the encoder and retraining the projector is the lesson's hard exercise for these tasks. Where it is taught. The vision-language models lesson gives the spatial reasoning figure, the fine-tuning budget and the cross-modal error rate. Defend a design Your deployed vision-language model answers questions about product photos. Support tickets say that it invents objects and misreads numbers, but the offline benchmark score is fine. Design the production monitoring and the response plan. Level 3 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Treat hallucination as a production metric, not as a model property. Score every answer with a cross-modal error rate: embed the image and the generated text with an independent contrastive checker, and flag outputs where the text confidence is high but the image-text similarity is low. Track that rate per endpoint, per prompt type and per customer, alert on a rise, and route the flagged answers to human review instead of to the user. The team that introduced the metric cut its hallucination rate by about 35 percent this way, without a model change. Why the benchmark does not see it. About 12 percent of the image and text pairs in crawled training data describe things that are not fully in the image. A model trained on them learns to say plausible things the image does not support, and benchmarks built from the same kind of data reward plausibility. In production the inputs are your photos, your questions and your numbers, and this failure is the dominant one. The metric. Copy The text confidence is the mean per-token probability of the answer. The checker is a contrastive image-text model that is independent of the generator. The two thresholds come from your own data: calibrate them on a labelled sample of grounded and hallucinated answers. The dashboard. The rate per endpoint, per prompt type and per customer, over time. The rate split by image source and resolution, because a new camera or a new upload path shifts it. A sample of flagged answers for a weekly read, with the label a reviewer gave. An alert on a rise above a baseline window. The response plan. Route. A flagged answer goes to a review queue, or returns a hedged response that shows the image region, not a confident wrong number. An answer whose numbers fail the text-recognition check also goes to the review queue, even when the whole-image rate does not flag it. Read. The weekly sample tells you which prompt types fail: numbers, counts, small text. Fix at the data level. Add grounded examples for the failing prompt types, and tiling or a higher resolution for small text and numbers. Re-measure with the same metric before and after each change. Limits of the metric. A contrastive checker scores whole-image similarity, so it misses a wrong digit in an otherwise matching description. Pair it with task checks: parse the numbers in the answer and compare them with a text-recognition pass, or ask the model for the region it read and check that the region is not empty. Plausible wrong answers. "Raise the benchmark score and the hallucinations will go away." The benchmark rewards plausible text; the production failure is confident text the image does not support, which the benchmark does not measure. "Add a system prompt that says do not hallucinate." The model does not know when it hallucinates; a prompt does not create grounding, and only a measurement and a review route reduce the harm. "Block every answer with a low image-text similarity." Low similarity with low confidence is often a right answer about a hard image; the signal is high confidence with low similarity. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why an independent checker and not the model's own confidence? Expected: the model is confident when it hallucinates, which is the failure; the checker gives a second opinion that does not share the generator's blind spots. (level 3) How do you set the two thresholds? Expected: label a few hundred answers as grounded or not, sweep the thresholds, and pick the pair that catches most hallucinations at a review load the team can afford. (level 4) The rate rises for one customer only. What do you check? Expected: their image source: resolution, lighting, a new product line with text the model misreads; the per-customer split exists for that reason. (level 4) How do you decide between a model change and a routing change? Expected: routing is cheap and immediate and protects users today; a model change needs grounded data and a re-measurement; do both in that order and let the metric arbitrate. Where it is taught. The vision-language models lesson defines the cross-modal error rate, gives the code, and reports the production result. Explain the mechanism Draw the standard architecture of a vision-language model that answers questions about an image. Name its three parts, say what each one contributes, and say which part you would expect to train when a team fine-tunes on a few thousand labelled images. Level 1 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A vision encoder, a projector and a language model. The encoder, a pretrained vision transformer, turns the image into patch tokens. The projector, a small two- to four-layer MLP or a query-based bridge, maps those tokens into the language model's embedding space, where they replace a placeholder token in the prompt. The decoder language model reads image tokens and text tokens as one sequence and writes the answer; in most fine-tunes the encoder and the language model stay frozen or get adapters, and the projector is where the training happens. The three parts. Vision encoder. A pretrained vision transformer, contrastively trained or self-supervised, produces one token per patch. With a 336-pixel input and a 14-pixel patch, the reference model gets 576 tokens of width 1024. Projector. A two-layer MLP with a GELU between the layers, from the encoder width to the language model width, 1024 to 4096 to 4096 in the reference model. The capstone's toy head, 768 to 1024 to 512, has about 1.3M parameters. Language model. A decoder-only model that receives the projected image tokens in place of an image placeholder and the text tokens after them, then generates text. How the pieces meet. The prompt holds a placeholder image token. Before the forward pass, the embeddings at those positions are overwritten with the projected vision tokens, and the batch is padded so that every sample has the same count. The language model sees one sequence; nothing else about it changes. Who trains. Stage one, alignment: freeze the encoder and the language model, and train the projector on image and caption pairs with the language-modeling loss on the caption. The capstone's version uses a cosine alignment loss between a pooled image vector and a caption vector, and that loss falls from about 1.07 to about 0.80 in 200 steps with only the projector moving. Stage two, instruction tuning: unfreeze the language model, often through adapters, keep the projector trainable, and train on image, question and answer triples. Large pretraining on interleaved image and text data sits between them in frontier recipes and is out of reach for a small team. Why the projector is enough. The encoder already represents the image, and the language model already reasons in words. The projector's job is to express one in the vocabulary of the other, which a small bend of the space can do. The capstone's encoder has 86M parameters and its projector about 1.3M; training only the projector means a few hundred steps on one GPU. Plausible wrong answers. "The language model looks at pixels through cross-attention into the image." In this pattern the image enters as tokens in the input sequence; cross-attention bridges are a different family. "Fine-tune the vision encoder first; it is the part that sees." The encoder is pretrained and frozen in stage one; the projector is where a small team's training budget goes. "The projector must be a large network to carry the image." It is a two-layer MLP far smaller than the encoder in the capstone, and it trains in minutes. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Why does the projector need two layers and not one? Expected: one linear layer rotates and scales; the non-linearity between two layers lets the map bend, which is enough to align contrastive vision features to a language model's embeddings. (level 2) What does the language model see where the image was? Expected: a run of embeddings, one per projected patch token, in place of the placeholder; the model treats them as tokens with no special handling. (level 2) What does a bridge with a fixed set of learned queries change? Expected: it compresses the patch tokens to a fixed count, which saves context at the cost of a bottleneck; the MLP keeps every patch. (level 3) Which part sets the ceiling on reasoning quality? Expected: the language model; the encoder can only feed it, so a larger language model lifts the benchmarks more than a cleverer bridge. Where it is taught. The vision-language models lesson lays out the pattern and its three training stages, the projection capstone trains the bridge alone, and the LLaVA lesson gives the reference recipe. Time : about 60 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line A depth map is a single-channel image where each pixel is a distance from the camera. Predicting it from one RGB frame used to be impossible without stereo or LiDAR. Today a large pretrained ViT encoder plus a light decoder gets close to ground truth on standard benchmarks. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Monocular depth "Single-image depth" Depth estimation from one RGB frame, no stereo or LiDAR Relative depth "Ordered depth" Ordered z-values without real-world units Metric depth "Absolute distance" Depth in metres; requires calibration or a model trained with metric supervision AbsRel "Absolute relative error" Mean of $\lvert d_{\text{pred}} - d_{\text{gt}} \rvert / d_{\text{gt}}$; standard depth metric Delta accuracy "delta < 1.25" Fraction of pixels with prediction within 25% of ground truth Pinhole camera "fx, fy, cx, cy" The camera model used to lift (u, v, d) to (X, Y, Z) DPT "Dense Prediction Transformer" The conv-based decoder used on top of frozen ViT encoders for depth DINOv2 backbone "The reason it works" Self-supervised features that generalise across domains without depth labels The problem In plain words first A depth map gives every pixel a distance from the camera. One photo has no direct distance information, but it is full of clues: far things look smaller, parallel lines converge, near objects hide far ones. A large network trained on many images learns to read those clues and predicts depth from a single photo. Most such models give relative depth (what is nearer than what), not metres, and many actually output inverse depth, where bigger means closer. Knowing which one you have matters as soon as you turn the map into 3D points. Depth is the missing axis in 2D computer vision. Given RGB, you know where things appear in the image plane; you do not know how far they are. Depth sensors (stereo rigs, LiDAR, time-of-flight) solve this directly but are expensive, fragile, and limited in range. Monocular depth estimation — predicting depth from a single RGB frame — used to produce blurry, unreliable output. By 2026 large pretrained encoders changed that: Depth Anything V2 builds on a DINOv2 backbone and produces depth maps that generalise across indoor, outdoor, medical, and satellite domains. Marigold reframes depth as a conditional diffusion problem. ZoeDepth regresses true metric distances. Depth is also the bridge between 2D detection and 3D understanding: multiply a detected box's pixels by depth and you lift the 2D object into a 3D point cloud. That is the core of every AR occlusion system, every obstacle-avoidance pipeline, and every "pick up the cup" robot. Idea 1 · Relative vs metric depth Relative depth — ordered z values without a real-world unit. "Pixel A is closer than pixel B, but the ratio of distances is not anchored to metres." Metric depth — absolute distance in metres from the camera. Requires the model to have learnt the statistical relationship between image cues and real distance. MiDaS and Depth Anything V2 produce relative (inverse) depth, with separately released metric fine-tunes; Depth Anything 3 also ships a metric variant. Marigold produces relative depth. ZoeDepth, UniDepth, and Metric3D produce metric depth. Metric models are sensitive to camera intrinsics; relative models are not. Idea 2 · The encoder-decoder pattern Depth Anything V2 pairs a DINOv2 encoder with a DPT-style decoder, fine-tuning the encoder at a much smaller learning rate than the decoder so its pretrained features are not destroyed. The encoder provides rich features; the decoder interpolates them back to image resolution and regresses depth. Idea 3 · Why a single image produces depth at all A 2D image contains many monocular cues that correlate with depth: Perspective — parallel lines in 3D converge in 2D. Texture gradient — surfaces far away have smaller, denser texture. Occlusion order — nearer objects occlude farther ones. Size constancy — known objects (cars, humans) give approximate scale. Atmospheric perspective — distant objects appear hazier and bluer in outdoor scenes. A ViT trained on billions of images internalises these cues. With enough data and a strong backbone, monocular depth hits reasonable accuracy without any explicit 3D supervision. Idea 4 · What monocular depth cannot do Absolute metric scale without intrinsics or a known object in the scene. The network can predict "the cup is twice as far as the spoon" without knowing whether the cup is 1 m or 10 m away. Occluded geometry — the back of a chair is unseen and cannot be inferred reliably. Truly untextured / reflective surfaces — mirrors, glass, uniform walls. The network reports plausible but wrong depth. Idea 5 · Depth Anything V3 in 2026 A single plain transformer (a vanilla DINO-style encoder), with no 3D-specific architecture. DPT decoder. Predicts depth together with per-pixel ray directions (a "depth-ray" target), trained with a teacher-student scheme on public academic datasets. Predicts spatially consistent geometry from an arbitrary number of visual inputs, with or without known camera poses . Reported state-of-the-art results at release on any-view geometry and camera pose benchmarks, and better monocular depth than Depth Anything V2. It ships as its own depth_anything_3 package; Depth Anything V2 remains the easiest to call through transformers , as below. Idea 6 · Marigold — diffusion for depth Marigold (Ke et al., CVPR 2024) reframes depth estimation as conditional image-to-image diffusion. Conditioning: RGB. Target: depth map. Uses a pretrained Stable Diffusion 2 U-Net as backbone. Output depth maps are exceptionally sharp at object boundaries. Trade-off: slower inference than feed-forward models (10-50 denoising steps). That is why relative-depth papers always report "scale-and-shift invariant" metrics, and why comparing a relative model's raw output to metric ground truth is meaningless. Solution B1 · An inside-out world Treating disparity as depth makes near pixels (large disparity) far away and far pixels near: in the side view the lawn right in front of the camera is placed farthest and curves downward, while the sky is pulled close. The code runs without complaint; only a plot or a sanity check (the ground should get farther towards the top of the image) catches it. a0427: Course home / Phase 4 · Teaching Machines to See Following many objects through a video Lesson 4.27 60 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Distinguish tracking-by-detection from query-based tracking and name the algorithm families (SORT, DeepSORT, ByteTrack, BoT-SORT, SAM 2 memory tracker, SAM 3.1 Object Multiplex) Implement IoU + Hungarian assignment from scratch for classic tracking-by-detection Explain SAM 2's memory bank and why it handles occlusion better than IoU-based association Read the three tracking metrics (MOTA, IDF1, HOTA) and pick which one matters for a given use case Before you start Needs : Phase 4 Lesson 06 (YOLO Detection), Phase 4 Lesson 08 (Mask R-CNN), Phase 4 Lesson 24 (SAM 3) Type : Build. Time : about 60 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Tracking is detection plus association. Detect every frame. Match this frame's detections to last frame's tracks by ID. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Tracking-by-detection "Detect then associate" Per-frame detector + Hungarian assignment on IoU / appearance Kalman filter "Motion predict" Linear dynamics + covariance for smooth track predictions and occlusion handling Hungarian algorithm "Optimal assignment" Solves the minimum-cost bipartite matching problem; scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment ByteTrack "Low-confidence second pass" Re-match unmatched tracks to low-confidence detections to recover short occlusions DeepSORT "SORT + appearance" Adds a ReID feature for cross-frame matching; better for ID preservation Memory bank "SAM 2 trick" Per-instance spatio-temporal features stored across frames; cross-attention replaces explicit association Object Multiplex "SAM 3.1 shared memory" Single shared memory with per-instance queries for fast many-object tracking HOTA "Modern tracking metric" Decomposes into detection and association accuracy; community standard The problem In plain words first A detector looks at one frame at a time and says "there is a person here". A tracker adds memory: it decides that the person in this frame is the same person as in the last frame, and gives them a stable ID. The classic recipe guesses where each known object should be now (a motion model), compares those guesses with the new detections (usually by box overlap), and picks the best one-to-one matching. The hard cases are objects that cross, hide behind each other, or vanish for a few frames. A detector tells you where the objects are in a single frame. A tracker tells you which detection in frame t is the same object as a detection in frame t-1 . Without that, you cannot count objects crossing a line, follow a ball through an occlusion, or know "car #4 has been in the lane for 8 seconds." Tracking is essential to every video-facing product: sports analytics, surveillance, autonomous driving, medical video analysis, wildlife monitoring, counting objects on a conveyor. The core building blocks are shared: a per-frame detector, a motion model (Kalman filter or something richer), an association step (Hungarian algorithm on IoU / cosine / learned features), and a track lifecycle (birth, update, death). Recent years added two memory-based patterns: SAM 2 memory-based tracking (feature-memory instead of motion-model association) and SAM 3.1 Object Multiplex (shared memory for many instances of the same concept). This lesson walks the classical stack first, then the memory-based approach. Idea 1 · Tracking-by-detection Most classical trackers are variations on this loop. The differences: SORT (2016): Kalman filter + IoU Hungarian. Simple, fast, no appearance model. DeepSORT (2017): SORT + a CNN-based appearance feature per track (ReID embedding). Handles crossings better. ByteTrack (2021): associates low-confidence detections as a second stage; no appearance features needed but top performer on MOT17. BoT-SORT (2022): Byte + camera motion compensation + ReID. StrongSORT / OC-SORT — ByteTrack descendants with better motion and appearance. Idea 2 · Kalman filter in one paragraph A Kalman filter maintains a per-track state (x, y, w, h, dx, dy, dw, dh) with a covariance. At each frame, predict the state using a constant-velocity model, then update with the matched detection. The update trusts the detection more when the predict uncertainty is high. This gives smooth trajectories and the ability to continue a track through a short occlusion (1-5 frames). Every classical tracker uses a Kalman filter in the motion-prediction step. Idea 3 · The Hungarian algorithm Given a M x N cost matrix (tracks x detections), find the one-to-one assignment that minimises total cost. Cost is usually 1 - IoU(track_bbox, detection_bbox) or negative cosine similarity of appearance features. Runtime is ) ; for up to ~1000 it is fast enough in Python via scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment . Worked example Two tracks, two detections Track A was at box , track B at box . The new frame has detections 1 and 2 with IoUs det 1 det 2 A 0.6 0.5 B 0.5 0.1 Costs are . Greedy matching takes the single best pair first (A–1, cost 0.4) and is left with B–2 (cost 0.9): total 1.3 . Hungarian checks both assignments and picks A–2 plus B–1: 1.0 . The globally best matching gives A the slightly worse detection so that B is not stranded with a near-miss. With many tracks, these trade-offs are where greedy trackers swap IDs. Idea 4 · ByteTrack's key idea Standard trackers drop low-confidence detections (< 0.5). ByteTrack keeps them around as second-stage candidates : after matching tracks to high-confidence detections, unmatched tracks try to match low-confidence detections with a slightly looser IoU threshold. Recovers short occlusions, ID switches near crowds. Idea 5 · SAM 2 memory-based tracking SAM 2 handles video by keeping a memory bank of per-instance spatio-temporal features. Given a prompt (click, box, or mask) on one frame, it encodes the instance into memory. On subsequent frames, the memory is cross-attended against the new frame's features, and the decoder produces a mask for the same instance in the new frame. No Kalman filter, no Hungarian assignment. The association is implicit in the memory-attention operation. Pros: - Robust to large occlusions (memory carries instance identity across many frames). - Open-vocabulary when combined with SAM 3's text prompts. - Works without a separate motion model. Cons: - Slower than ByteTrack for many-object tracking. - Memory bank grows; limits the context window. Idea 6 · SAM 3.1 Object Multiplex Prior SAM 2 / SAM 3 tracking keeps a separate memory bank per instance. For 50 objects, 50 memory banks. Object Multiplex (March 2026) collapses them into one shared memory with per-instance query tokens . Meta reports large speed-ups when tracking many objects at once. It targets scenes with many instances of the same concept: crowds, warehouse workers, traffic intersections. As a 2026 release, check its licence and measure it against ByteTrack on your own footage. Idea 7 · Three metrics to know MOTA (Multi-Object Tracking Accuracy) — 1 - (FN + FP + ID switches) / GT. Weighted by error type; a single metric that conflates detection and association failures. IDF1 (ID F1) — harmonic mean of ID precision and recall. Focuses specifically on how well each ground-truth track keeps its ID over time. Better than MOTA for ID-switch-sensitive tasks. HOTA (Higher Order Tracking Accuracy) — decomposes into detection accuracy (DetA) and association accuracy (AssA). The community standard since 2020; most comprehensive. For surveillance (who is who): IDF1 is what you report. For sports analytics (counting passes): HOTA. For general academic comparison: HOTA. The same idea as a formula Predict with a motion model (Kalman filter). Each track keeps a state (box centre, size and their velocities) with covariance . With a constant-velocity transition and process noise : = F x , P ^ = FP F ⊤ + Q Update with a detection (observation matrix , measurement noise ): H ⊤ ( H P ^ H ⊤ + R ) − 1 , x = x ^ + K ( z − H x ^ ) , P = ( I − KH ) P ^ The gain weighs the prediction against the measurement by their uncertainties. Match tracks to detections. Build a cost matrix ​ = 1 − IoU ( track i ​ , det j ​ ) and solve the assignment that minimises the total cost with the Hungarian algorithm, ) ; pairs with IoU below a threshold stay unmatched. ByteTrack matches high-confidence detections first, then gives the remaining tracks a second chance with low-confidence ones, recovering occluded objects. Metrics. With false negatives, false positives and identity switches summed over frames against the number of ground-truth objects : FN + FP + IDSW ​ dominated by detection quality. IDF1 scores how long identities are kept correctly, and HOTA ​ balances detection and association. Worked example MOTA by hand A 100-frame clip has 300 ground-truth object boxes in total. The tracker misses 20 (FN), reports 12 boxes where nothing is (FP) and switches identity 4 times (IDSW). 20 + 12 + 4 ​ = 1 − 0.12 = 0.88 Notice that the 4 identity switches, the errors a tracker exists to avoid, weigh almost nothing next to the detector's misses. That is why IDF1 or HOTA's association accuracy is the number to watch when identity matters. Check your mental model ✗ "A good detector makes a good tracker." ✓ Detection quality bounds tracking, but identity errors come from association: crossings, occlusions and missed frames. ✗ "IoU matching needs no motion model at 30 fps." ✓ It works while boxes overlap from frame to frame. A few missed frames or a fast object, and the old box no longer overlaps the new one. "Use it" measures it. ✗ "MOTA tells you how often IDs switch." ✓ MOTA mixes switches with misses and false positives; IDF1 and HOTA's AssA isolate identity. Show the code that draws this Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output In the crossing case the plain IoU tracker loses the hidden object: when it reappears, its last known box is where it was hidden, three frames' travel away, so the detection either matches the wrong track or starts a new one, and the colours on the top-left plot change. Predicting each box forward along its velocity puts the hidden object's track where the object actually is when it reappears, and the IDs survive. The single-object case shows the same thing without any crossing. In random scenes both trackers are perfect with few objects; with 30 objects in a small area, close encounters start producing switches for the IoU-only tracker, which is the effect Exercise 1 asks you to find. Recap What to keep from this lesson Tracking = detect every frame + associate detections with existing tracks. Association: cost matrix (1 − IoU and/or appearance distance), solved optimally by the Hungarian algorithm. A motion model (Kalman predict) carries tracks through misses and fast motion; ByteTrack also re-uses low-confidence detections. Memory-based trackers (SAM 2, SAM 3.1) associate through learned features instead of boxes. Judge identity with IDF1 or HOTA's association accuracy, not MOTA alone. Solutions Solution P1 · Switches without prediction, none with it The plain tracker produces ID switches in the crossing case (the printed count is 3 when this page was built), because the hidden object's stale box no longer overlaps its reappearance. The predictive tracker keeps both identities, because its predicted box moves with the object through the gap. The fix is one line of physics: position plus velocity times elapsed frames. Solution B1 · Every gap becomes a new identity max_age is how many frames a track may go unmatched before it is deleted. With max_age=0 the hidden object's track is removed in the first frame it is missing, so when it reappears it can only start a new track: a new ID for the same object, even for the predictive tracker, because there is no track left to predict. Real trackers keep unmatched tracks for 30 frames or more (about a second of video) for exactly this reason. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Trackers in production pipelines. ByteTrack and BoT-SORT (built into Ultralytics' model.track ) and Roboflow's supervision library are the usual tracking-by-detection choices for retail, traffic and sports video. Promptable video tracking. SAM 2 and SAM 3 keep a memory of an object across frames, so a single click or text prompt follows it through a video. a0428: Course home / Phase 4 · Teaching Machines to See World models and video diffusion Lesson 4.28 75 min Learn + Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Explain the difference between a pure video generation model (Sora 2) and an action-conditioned world model (Genie 3, DreamerV3) Describe a video DiT: spatio-temporal patches, 3D position encoding, joint attention across (T, H, W) tokens Trace how a world model plugs into robotics: VLM plans → video model simulates → inverse dynamics emits actions Pick between Sora 2, Genie 3, Runway GWM-1 Worlds, Wan-Video, and HunyuanVideo for a given use case (creative video, interactive sim, autonomous-driving synthesis) Before you start Needs : Phase 4 Lesson 10 (Diffusion), Phase 4 Lesson 12 (Video Understanding), Phase 4 Lesson 23 (DiT + Rectified Flow) Type : Learn + Build. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line A video model that predicts the next seconds of a scene is a world simulator. Condition that prediction on actions and you have a learned game engine. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means World model "Learned simulator" A model that predicts future observations given state and action Video DiT "Spacetime transformer" Diffusion transformer with 3D patchification and divided attention Latent action "Inferred control" Discrete or continuous action latent inferred from frame pairs; used to condition next-frame generation Divided attention "Time then space" Two attention operations per block — across time then across space — to keep $O(N^2)$ manageable Object permanence "Things stay real" Scene property that video models must learn; classic failure mode on food, glassware FVD "Fréchet Video Distance" Video equivalent of FID; primary visual quality metric Inverse dynamics model "Observations to actions" Given (state, next state), output the action that connects them; closes robotics loop Cosmos-Drive "NVIDIA driving sim" Open-weights autonomous-driving world model for RL and evaluation The problem In plain words first A video generator continues a scene: given a prompt or a first frame, it predicts what the next seconds look like. A world model adds controls: it predicts what happens next given an action , such as "press left" or "turn the steering wheel". Run it in a loop, feeding each predicted frame back in with the next action, and you have a learned game engine or driving simulator that a robot or an agent can practise in. The same ingredients as image generation (latent patches, transformers, diffusion or flow) are used, with time added as a third axis. Video generation and world modelling have been converging since 2024. A model that can generate a coherent long video has, in some sense, learned how the world moves: object permanence, gravity, causality, style. If you condition that prediction on actions (walk left, open the door), the video model becomes a learnable simulator that can replace a game engine, a driving simulator, or a robotics environment. The stakes are concrete. Genie 3 generates playable environments from a single image. Runway GWM-1 Worlds synthesises infinite explorable scenes. Sora 2 (September 2025) produced short clips with synchronised audio and noticeably better physics, before OpenAI announced in March 2026 that it would discontinue the Sora app and API; Google's Veo 3.1 and Kuaishou's Kling offer similar capabilities. NVIDIA Cosmos-Drive and Wayve Gaia-2 generate realistic driving video for autonomous-vehicle training data. The world-model paradigm is quietly taking over sim-to-real for robotics. This lesson is the "big picture" lesson for Phase 4. It connects image generation, video understanding, and agentic reasoning into the architecture pattern dominant research is moving toward. Idea 1 · Three families of world-modelling Sora 2 is pure video generation conditioned on prompts. No action interface. You cannot "steer" it mid-rollout. Genie 3 , GWM-1 Worlds and Mirage 2 are action-conditioned world models. Infer latent actions from observed video, then condition future frame predictions on actions. Interactive — you press keys or move a camera and the scene responds. DreamerV3 and the classic RL world-model family predict in a latent space with explicit action conditioning, trained on a reward signal. Less visual; more useful for sample-efficient RL. Idea 2 · Video DiT architecture Copy Positional encoding is 3D: a rotary or learned embedding per (t, h, w) coordinate. Attention can be: Full joint — all tokens attend to all tokens. ) with tokens. Prohibitive for long videos. Divided — alternate temporal attention (same spatial position, across time: (H*W) * T^2 ) and spatial attention (same timestep, across space: T * (H*W)^2 ). Used by TimeSformer and most video DiTs. Window — local windows in (t, h, w). Used by Video Swin. Most current video diffusion models use one of these three patterns, usually with AdaLN conditioning ( Lesson 4.23 ) and rectified flow. Worked example Why divided attention A 5-second, 24 fps, 480 × 832 clip has 121 frames. A typical video VAE compresses time by 4 and space by 8, giving a latent of , , ; 2 × 2 spatial patches leave tokens per latent frame and tokens in all. Full joint attention compares every pair: ≈ 2.34 billion pairs per head per layer. Divided attention: temporal = 1 , 560 × 961 = 1.5 million, plus spatial = 31 × 2 , 433 , 600 = 75.4 million, about 77 million . Divided attention is about 30 times cheaper here, and the gap grows with clip length. The price is that a token never directly attends to a different place at a different time in one step; it takes two hops. Check your mental model ✗ "A video generator is already a world model." ✓ Only an action-conditioned one can be steered mid-rollout. "Use it" trains both kinds on a toy world and shows the difference. ✗ "Errors in a learned simulator stay small." ✓ Each predicted frame becomes the next input, so small errors compound over a rollout; long-horizon consistency is the hard part. ✗ "Bigger video models have solved physics." ✓ They are much better, but object permanence and contact (eating, pouring, collisions) still fail. Idea 3 · Conditioning on actions: latent action models Genie learns a latent action per frame by discriminatively predicting the action between a pair of consecutive frames. The model's decoder then conditions on the inferred latent action — not on explicit keyboard keys. At inference, a user can specify a latent action (or sample one from a fresh prior) and the model generates the next frame consistent with that action. Sora skips the action interface entirely. Its decoder predicts next spacetime tokens from past spacetime tokens. Prompt conditions the start; nothing steers it mid-generation. Idea 4 · Physical plausibility Sora 2's release (September 2025) explicitly advertised physical plausibility : weight, balance, object permanence, cause-and-effect. Measured by the team via hand-rated plausibility scores; the model visibly improves on dropped objects, characters colliding, and failures-on-purpose (a missed jump) versus Sora 1. Plausibility remains the dominant failure mode. 2024-2025 videos of people eating spaghetti or drinking from glasses revealed the model's lack of persistent object representation. Newer models (Sora 2, Runway Gen-4.5, HunyuanVideo) reduce but do not eliminate these. Idea 5 · Autonomous driving world models Driving world models generate realistic road scenes conditioned on trajectories, bounding boxes, or navigation maps. Usage: Cosmos-Drive-Dreams (NVIDIA) — generates minutes of driving video for RL training. Gaia-2 (Wayve) — trajectory-conditioned scene synthesis for policy evaluation. DrivingWorld (academic, 2024) — a GPT-style video world model for driving that simulates varied conditions. Vista (OpenDriveLab, 2024) — a generalisable driving world model with action control. They replace expensive real-world data collection for corner cases — pedestrian jaywalks at night, icy intersections, unusual vehicle types — that would otherwise require millions of miles of driving. Idea 6 · Robotics stack: VLM + video model + inverse dynamics The emerging three-component robotics loop: VLM parses the goal ("pick up the red cup"), plans a high-level action sequence. Video generation model simulates what executing each action would look like — predicts observations N frames ahead. Inverse dynamics model extracts the concrete motor commands that would produce those observations. This replaces reward shaping and sample-heavy RL. The world model does the imagination; the inverse dynamics closes the loop on actuation. Genie Envisioner is one instantiation; many research groups are converging on this structure. Idea 7 · Evaluation Visual quality — FVD (Fréchet Video Distance), user studies. Prompt alignment — CLIPScore per frame, VQA-style evaluation. Physical plausibility — hand-rated on a benchmark suite (Sora 2's internal benchmark, VBench). Controllability (for interactive world models) — action → observation consistency; can you go back to a prior state? Plan -> latent-action video model -> imagined rollout. Rollout -> inverse dynamics model -> low-level actions. Actions executed -> observation fed back into step 1. See it drawn A world model you can train in a minute The "game": a ball on a 16 × 16 grid; actions move it one cell. Two identical small CNNs learn to predict the next frame, one given the action, one with the action input zeroed (a pure video predictor). Then both dream 20 frames from the same start and the same action sequence. Show the code that draws this Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The action-conditioned model follows the true path for the first 15 or so steps: given "right ×6, up ×5, left ×4, down ×5" it moves the ball exactly as the real world would, and given a different plan from the same start (last row) it produces a different future. That is what makes it steerable. Look at its later frames, though: the ball grows brighter and wider, and by step 20 its centre is about two cells off. Each prediction is very slightly wrong, and because predictions are fed back in, the errors compound. The video predictor saw the same frames but no actions, so its best guess is the average of four possible moves; that blur, fed back into itself, spreads out and fades to nothing within a few steps. Real video generators face the same ambiguity (resolved by a prompt at the start rather than an action at every step), and real world models the same compounding error over millions of pixels. Recap What to keep from this lesson A video generator continues a scene; a world model predicts the next observation given an action, so it can be steered. Video DiTs patchify space and time and use 3D positions with joint, divided or windowed attention; divided attention cuts cost by orders of magnitude. Latent action models infer actions from unlabelled video, so world models can learn from footage without control labels. Rollouts feed predictions back in, so errors compound; physics and object permanence remain the hard part. Driving and robotics use world models as simulators; check each model's licence and access terms before building on it. Solutions Solution P1 · One stays sharp, the other blurs The action-conditioned model tracks the true path exactly for the first ten steps or more (the printed errors), because the action removes all ambiguity in this toy world, but small prediction errors compound and the ball drifts by about two cells by step 20. The model without actions cannot know which way the ball will go, so under squared error it predicts the average of the four possible next frames; feeding that blur back in spreads and dims it until nothing is left. Conditioning information decides whether the future is predictable; compounding error decides how long a rollout stays trustworthy. Solution B1 · It learns to ignore the controls With shuffled actions, the action input carries no information about the move, so training drives the network to ignore it: it becomes the no-action video predictor in disguise. Its rollout blurs and drifts just like the bottom row, and changing the plan no longer changes the dream. Real latent-action models face this risk too, which is why Genie-style training makes the latent action the only way to explain the difference between consecutive frames. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Video generators people use. Google's Veo 3.1 (with synchronised audio), Runway, Kling and ByteDance's Seedance are widely used hosted systems; OpenAI announced in March 2026 that it would shut down Sora. Open-weight models such as Wan and LTX-2 run locally. World models for robots and cars. NVIDIA's Cosmos world foundation models (open weights) generate and predict scenes for training and testing robots and autonomous vehicles. Interactive worlds are still previews. Google DeepMind's Genie 3 (August 2025) generates navigable worlds in real time but is a limited research preview, not a product. Sources: Veo , Sora shutdown (Axios) , NVIDIA Cosmos , Genie 3 . Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Text-to-SQL Having a model turn a question in plain language into a database query Lesson 14.80 Content Understanding Generative extraction from documents, images, audio and video Lesson 14.156 Agent Bricks Databricks' managed builder for common agent patterns, tuned against evaluations Lesson 13.50 Vector database A store that finds the vectors nearest to a query vector quickly Lesson 14.71 A large share of enterprise knowledge sits in PDFs, scans, slides, photos and calls. Document AI (also called intelligent document processing) turns that into text and structured fields that RAG , text-to-SQL later · 14.80 and agents can use. Modern multimodal models have changed the field: a single model call can now read a messy invoice that needed a custom OCR model five years ago. But the engineering around the call (parsing, schemas, validation, measurement) decides whether the result is usable. Copy Why this came about RAG systems failed quietly when documents were scanned, laid out in columns or full of tables, because simple text extraction garbled them. Better parsers, OCR and later vision-language models became their own part of the pipeline, since everything downstream depends on clean text. In plain words first Getting the words out before anything else Before anything can be searched, documents must become clean text with their structure intact: headings, tables, page numbers. PDFs are layouts, not text; scans are pictures of text. Parsing extracts text and structure, with OCR or a vision model for scans. Errors here, such as tables flattened into nonsense or headers repeated on every page, silently poison everything downstream. What is inside a PDF, and why parsing is hard A web page or a Word file stores text as paragraphs, headings and tables. A PDF does not. A PDF is a set of drawing instructions: "put these letters at this position, in this font". It was designed to look identical on every screen and printer, and it keeps almost nothing about what the text means . That one fact explains every parsing problem in this lesson. What a person sees What the file actually contains What goes wrong for RAG A paragraph Pieces of text, each with an x and y position Usually fine A table The same: pieces of text at positions, plus some drawn lines Rows and columns are lost; numbers detach from their labels Two columns Pieces of text, in whatever order the software wrote them Lines from different columns are glued together A heading Text in a larger font The outline of the document is lost, so chunks lose their context A scanned page One picture. No text at all Nothing to extract until the picture is read by OCR A chart or photo A picture The information is invisible to text search ( Lesson 4.31 ) Two terms you will meet everywhere. The text layer is the text stored in a digital PDF, the kind you can select with a mouse. OCR (optical character recognition) is software that looks at a picture of a page and works out which letters are on it; it is the only way into a scan, a fax or a phone photo. Everything downstream depends on this step. If parsing glues two columns together or drops a table, no chunking strategy, embedding model or prompt can repair it, and the failure is silent: the system simply answers from wrong text. Step 1 · Make a realistic document, then parse it The lab creates its own invoice PDF so everything runs offline, then extracts its text the way any pipeline starts: with a PDF text layer. Document AI as a pipeline: parse layout first, read text from images where needed, turn tables into structure, extract fields to a schema, validate them with business rules, and send only the doubtful ones to a person. Copy What you should see Copy A digital PDF with a text layer is the easy case: the text is exact, but the table became lines of words and the structure is gone. Scanned documents have no text layer at all and need OCR, which Step 4 compares with the other approaches. Step 2 · Put the table back together The text is all there, but the table is now four lines of words. For a layout you know, you can rebuild it with a pattern, and then check it: an invoice has arithmetic that must hold, which is a free test of whether parsing worked. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The pattern reads each line from the right: the last number is the amount, the one before it the rate, the one before that the quantity, and whatever is left is the item name. That is why "MixPro 750W Mixer Grinder" survives even though it contains a number. The rows are printed as a Markdown table, which is the usual way to pass a table to a model or to a chunker: the header row travels with the values. The two checks are the important part. They cost nothing and they catch a misread digit, a missed row or a row split across two lines. Whenever a document has internal arithmetic (totals, counts, percentages that should add to 100), use it. A hand-written pattern like this works for one layout from one supplier. A company receives invoices from thousands. That is the job of the layout parsers and document services in Step 4: they do the same reconstruction for layouts nobody wrote a pattern for. Step 3 · Two columns: when the reading order is wrong Tables are one way structure is lost. Reading order is the other, and it is harder to notice, because the output looks like perfectly good sentences. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Read the second line of the first block: "Refunds are accepted within Metro cities: 2 to 3 days." No such sentence exists on the page. The file stored the page row by row, so the text layer came out row by row, and half a sentence from the refund column was joined to half a sentence from the shipping column. A RAG system that indexed this would retrieve it for a refund question and tell the customer something false, with a citation. The second block fixes it using the one thing a PDF does store reliably: positions. Every piece of text has an x coordinate (how far across) and a y coordinate (how far up). Sorting the left column's pieces from top to bottom, then the right column's, restores the two paragraphs. Here the column boundary (x = 100) was typed in by hand. A layout parser finds it by itself: it detects columns, headings, tables, lists, headers and footers from positions, fonts and drawn lines, often with a small vision model, and outputs Markdown or JSON with that structure marked. For anything beyond simple one-column documents, use one. The habit to keep from this step is the check: after parsing a new kind of document, read twenty parsed pages next to the originals before you index a million. Step 4 · Choosing the parsing approach Approach What it does Strengths Watch out for PDF text layer (pypdf, pdfplumber, PyMuPDF) Reads embedded text Exact, free, fast Loses tables and reading order; useless on scans Layout parsers (Docling, Unstructured, Marker, LlamaParse) Detect headings, tables, figures; output Markdown or JSON Structure for chunking ( Lesson 14.70 ); open source options Quality varies by document type; test on yours Cloud OCR and document services OCR plus layout, tables, forms and prebuilt models (invoices, IDs, receipts) Scale, SLAs, handwriting, compliance Per-page pricing; prebuilt models fit common formats Vision-language models Read the page image and return structured output Handles messy layouts, stamps, mixed languages; one prompt for many formats Cost per page, latency, occasional hallucinated values: validate every field ( Lesson 4.30 ) Hybrid OCR or text layer for the words, a model for structure and fields Accurate text plus flexible extraction Two steps to maintain Platform Document services AWS Textract (OCR, forms, tables, queries, expense and ID analysis), Bedrock Data Automation (blueprints for documents, images, audio and video) Azure Document Intelligence (layout, prebuilt and custom models), Content Understanding later · 14.156 (generative extraction across modalities) Google Cloud Document AI (OCR, Layout Parser, form and invoice processors, custom extractors) Databricks ai_parse_document , ai_extract , Agent Bricks later · 13.50 Information Extraction For Indian documents, test the specific cases that break generic tools: GSTINs and PAN numbers, Devanagari and other Indic scripts, bilingual invoices, rubber stamps over text, and low-quality phone photos. Chunks built from that text mean nothing. Layout-aware parsing restores the reading order before chunking. Solution B1 · Scans have no text layer An empty string or almost nothing, because a scan has no text layer. You need OCR or a vision-capable parser, then checks on the fields that matter ( Lesson 4.30 ). Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Multimodal embedding model A model that places images and text in one vector space Multimodal RAG Late interaction Keeping many vectors per document and comparing them with the query's vectors at search time ColBERT, ColPali ColPali Retrieval over page images, with one vector per patch of the page Multimodal RAG Vision-language model A model that takes images and text as input and writes text Multimodal About the model on this page The captions in Step 4 are written by hand Step 4 needs a vision-language model to describe each image. To keep the lesson runnable without an API key , the descriptions are written out in a dictionary, in the style such a model produces. Lesson 4.30 , Step 3 shows the real call. Everything else on this page (the images, both embedding models , the searches) is real. Why this came about The first RAG systems indexed text. Real documents are not only text: annual reports carry their numbers in charts, manuals explain with diagrams, slide decks are mostly layout, and scanned forms are pictures of text. Extracting the text from such pages throws away much of the meaning. Two developments addressed this. CLIP (2021) trained an image encoder and a text encoder together, so that a sentence and a matching picture get similar vectors, which made it possible to search images with words. And vision-language models became good enough to read a chart or a table from a picture. In 2024 the ColPali work combined the two ideas into retrieval that works directly on images of pages, with no parsing step at all. In plain words first Searching pictures and pages, not only words When the answer is in a chart, a diagram or a scanned page, a text search has nothing to find. There are two ways round this. Either have a model that can see write down what each picture shows, and search those descriptions as ordinary text. Or use a model that turns pictures and sentences into the same kind of coordinates, so that a question lands near the right picture. In both cases, once the right picture is found, a model that can see looks at it and answers. Three ways to make pictures searchable. Describing each image as text reuses the whole text pipeline and keeps fine detail, at the cost of a vision-model call per image. Embedding images directly is cheap and needs no descriptions, but matches broad content only. Embedding pages as many small patch vectors ( late interaction ) is the most accurate for visually rich documents and the heaviest to store. In all three, the retrieved image itself is then given to a vision-language model to answer from. Step 1 · Five "pages" that are pictures Draw five small figures of the kind found in business documents: a bar chart, a line chart, a pie chart, a table and a flow diagram. They are saved as image files, as pages of a PDF would be after rendering. Copy What you should see Copy Open the mm_pages folder and look at them. The bar chart shows refund requests peaking in July. Step 2 · What text extraction recovers A text extractor ( Lesson 4.29 ) reads the characters on a page. For a chart, those are the title, the axis labels and the tick marks: Copy What you should see Copy Every word of the chart is there, and the information is gone. "July" appears and "300" appears, but nothing says that the July bar is the one that reaches 310. A text-only pipeline would retrieve this page for a question about refunds and then be unable to answer it, or would answer wrongly from the axis numbers. Step 3 · Route B: one space for images and text A multimodal embedding model has two encoders, one for images and one for text, trained so that a picture and a sentence describing it get nearby vectors ( Lesson 10.40 ). Embed the five images, then embed questions as text and look for the nearest image: Copy What you should see Copy Each image became 512 numbers. The first three questions find the right page, with a clear margin over the runner-up. No description of any image was ever written: the question's vector simply landed nearest the right picture, helped by the fact that CLIP can partly read the large title text in an image. The fourth question fails. The answer ("4 to 7 days") is in a cell of the shipping table, but the model matched the question to the line chart titled "Average delivery days". One vector per image captures what the picture is broadly about. It does not capture a number in a table cell. Reading this output What the scores tell you The similarities are all between about 0.25 and 0.40. Image-to-text similarities from CLIP-style models sit in a narrow band and are not comparable with text-to-text similarities, so thresholds must be set separately, and mixing image and text results needs rank fusion ( Lesson 5.38 ). This model is also small and from 2021, and reads 224 × 224 pixels: fine print is invisible to it. Current multimodal embedding models (the SigLIP family, and hosted models from Cohere, Voyage, Google and Amazon) are much stronger and accept larger images. Step 4 · Route A: describe, then index The alternative is to turn each picture into text once, at indexing time, by asking a vision-language model to describe it for search, with every number and label it can read. Then index the descriptions with the ordinary text pipeline of the Retrieval (RAG) section: Copy What you should see Copy All four questions find the right page, including the table question, because the description contains "Other pin codes: 4-7 days". The first answer is even visible in the retrieved text: "July 310 (the highest)". The detail that the image embedding could not hold is now plain text. The price of this route is a vision-model call for every image at indexing time, and its quality depends entirely on the descriptions. "A bar chart" is a useless description; the instruction must ask for the title, every label and value, and what the figure shows. A model can also misread a value, and that error is then stored in your index. Step 5 · Answering: show the model the picture Retrieval finds the page. To answer, pass the original image (not only its description) to a vision-language model together with the question, exactly as in Lesson 4.30 . The model reads the bar heights directly and you can cite the page. This matters most for route B, where there is no text to answer from, and it protects route A against errors in the stored descriptions. Images are expensive context, often a thousand tokens or more each, so retrieve few and send only the best one to three. Route C: page images with late interaction Routes A and B have a middle ground that has become the strongest option for visually rich documents. ColPali and its successors (ColQwen and others) use a vision-language model to embed a page image as many vectors, one per patch of the page , and embed the question as one vector per token. A page's score is the sum, over the question's tokens, of each token's best match among the page's patches ( late interaction , the idea of ColBERT from Lesson 5.38 ). A question about "delivery outside metro cities" can then match the exact region of the page where that table row is. There is no OCR, no layout parsing and no captioning. The costs are storage (hundreds to a thousand vectors per page) and a specialised index; common practice is to retrieve candidates with a cheaper method first and use the page-image model to rerank . Choosing a route Your documents Start with Why Mostly text with occasional figures Parse to text ( Lesson 4.29 ); describe figures and tables and index the descriptions Reuses your text pipeline; keeps exact values Photos, product images, screenshots where the look matters A multimodal embedding model No descriptions needed; matches visual content Slide decks, reports full of charts, scanned forms, complex layouts Page-image retrieval (ColPali family), usually as a reranker Layout and figures are the content; parsing loses them Tables with numbers people will ask about Extract tables to Markdown or rows ( Lesson 4.29 ); never rely on an image embedding One vector cannot hold a table's cells A mixture Index text chunks and image descriptions together; add page images for the visual documents; fuse by rank Each route covers the others' gaps Practical points that apply to every route: Keep the link to the source. Store the document, page number and image file with every indexed item, so that the original page can be shown to the model and to the user. Evaluate separately. Build test questions whose answers are in figures and tables, and measure retrieval on those apart from text questions ( Lesson 14.72 ). Averages over a mostly-text test set hide multimodal failures. Permissions apply to pictures too. A chart from a restricted report is as sensitive as its text ( Lesson 14.73 ). Video and audio follow the same pattern: transcribe speech, sample and describe frames, and index the text with timestamps.
