Small details such as a table cell need a description, a patch-level model, or the vision model looking at the page. ✗ "Once an image is described, the image is no longer needed." ✓ Give the original to the answering model when you can; descriptions contain errors and omissions. ✗ "Images are cheap context." ✓ They cost many tokens; retrieve them selectively. Exercises Predict before you run With the CLIP model from Step 3, which page will the query "INR 99" retrieve, and will it be right? Think about what a 224-pixel view of the table page looks like to the model. (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Embed the page images with CLIP, but embed the queries with the MiniLM text model from Step 4 (cut CLIP's vectors to 384 numbers so that the sizes match). What happens to retrieval, and why? (Solution B1.) Debugging exercise Image captions generated for indexing say "a bar chart" and nothing else, and retrieval of figures is poor. Fix the captioning. (Solution D1.) Make it your own Combine the two routes: for each question, get the ranking of pages from CLIP and from the caption search, and fuse them with the rrf function of Lesson 5.38 . Does the fused ranking answer all four questions? Which route would you weight more for tables? (Solution M1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Fine print Unreliable. "INR 99" is small text inside a table cell, and after the page is shrunk to 224 × 224 pixels it is a few blurred pixels. The model has nothing to match except the general look of the pages, so the result is close to a guess. The caption route finds it, because "Express: 1 day, INR 99" is in the description; a keyword index over the captions finds it exactly ( Lesson 5.37 ). Solution B1 · Two different spaces Retrieval becomes random. CLIP's image vectors and MiniLM's text vectors come from unrelated models, and cutting one to the other's length does not make their directions mean the same thing ( Lesson 14.71 ). Image and text can be compared only when both encoders were trained together, as CLIP's two halves were. Solution D1 · Captions that carry the content Change the instruction to ask for what a searcher would need: the title, the type of figure, every axis label, legend entry and data value that can be read, the main trend or comparison, and any text in the image. Ask for Markdown tables for tables. Review a sample of captions against the images, and keep the page image available so that the answering model can check. Solution M1 · Fusing the routes Build each ranking with np.argsort(-row) , turn it into a list of page names, and call rrf([clip_ranking, caption_ranking]) . The three questions both routes get right stay right. The table question depends on how the two lists order the runners-up; with equal weights the caption route's first place and CLIP's second or third usually put the table first or second. For tables and anything numeric, trust the text route more, by giving it a higher weight or by using it alone. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism What are the main ways to do retrieval over documents with images? Worked answer. Describe each image or page with a vision model and index the text; embed images directly with a multimodal embedding model that shares a space with text; or embed page images as many patch vectors and match with late interaction (ColPali). The first keeps exact detail and reuses the text pipeline, the second is cheap and good for visual similarity, the third is strongest for visually rich pages and heaviest to store. The retrieved image is then given to a vision-language model to answer from. A plausible wrong answer. "Run OCR and index the text." That loses charts, layout and anything that is not characters. Worked answer. Whether chart pages are retrieved at all (measure retrieval on chart questions separately); whether the index holds only extracted text for those pages; whether descriptions include the data values; and whether the answering model receives the image or only the description. Fix the first stage that fails. A plausible wrong answer. "Use a larger language model." If the chart never reaches it, size does not help. Follow-ups. When would you add page-image retrieval? Defend a design Caption-and-index or ColPali for a library of 200,000 slide pages? Worked answer. Captioning costs a vision-model call per page once and then uses a standard text index; it keeps values searchable by keyword and is easy to operate. Page-image retrieval needs no captions and handles layout better, but stores hundreds of vectors per page and needs a late-interaction index. A common design: caption and index everything, and use a page-image model to rerank the top candidates. Decide by measuring both on real questions, and by storage and latency budgets. A plausible wrong answer. "ColPali, because it is the newest." Operations and cost matter as much as benchmark scores. Follow-ups. How would you keep captions up to date when documents change? Recap Text extraction keeps the words of a chart or diagram and loses what it shows. A multimodal embedding model places images and text in one space, so questions can retrieve pictures with no captions. It matches broad content, not fine detail. Describing each image with a vision model and indexing the text keeps the detail and reuses the text pipeline, at the cost of a model call per image. Page-image retrieval with late interaction (ColPali) matches regions of a page and is strongest for visually rich documents. Whatever finds the page, let a vision-language model read the original image to answer, and evaluate figure and table questions separately. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Autoencoder A network that squeezes its input into a small code and rebuilds it Generative models Variational autoencoder (VAE) An autoencoder whose codes are kept close to a simple distribution, so that new codes can be sampled Generative models Generative adversarial network (GAN) A generator trained against a discriminator that tries to tell its output from real data Generative models Latent The compressed code an encoder produces Generative models Latent diffusion Running diffusion on compressed codes instead of pixels, then decoding Image generators Classifier-free guidance Pushing each denoising step toward the prompt by comparing a prompted and an unprompted prediction Image generators Mode collapse A GAN producing only a few kinds of output GANs Flow matching A newer training objective that learns a straight path from noise to data Image and video generators FID A score for generated images: the distance between statistics of generated and real images Evaluating generators Mentioned here, taught later 2 Distillation, LoRA This lesson mentions the ideas below before the lesson that teaches them. The one-line meaning is all you need for now; each is marked later where it first appears. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Distillation Training a small student model to copy a larger teacher model Lesson 14.132 LoRA Low-rank adaptation: freeze the model and train two small matrices added to chosen layers Lesson 3.24 Why this came about Until about 2013, neural networks were used to recognise : a label for an image, a score for a sentence. Generating a new, realistic image seemed much harder, because there is no single right answer to compare with. Three ideas changed that within a few years. The variational autoencoder (Kingma and Welling, 2013) learned a compact space of codes from which new images could be decoded. The generative adversarial network (Goodfellow and colleagues, 2014) trained a generator against a critic and produced the first truly sharp synthetic faces. Diffusion models (proposed in 2015, made to work well in 2020) learned to turn noise into data by removing it in small steps, and by 2021 they produced better images than GANs and were far easier to train. In 2022, latent diffusion ran that process inside a VAE 's compressed space, which made it cheap enough to release publicly as Stable Diffusion. Almost every image and video generator since is a descendant of that design. In plain words first Three ways to make something new Suppose you want a machine that draws new handwritten digits. One way: teach it to squeeze each digit into a short description and to redraw the digit from the description; then hand it made-up descriptions ( autoencoder ). A second way: train a forger and a detective together; the forger improves until the detective cannot tell its digits from real ones ( GAN ). A third way: take real digits, smudge them with more and more random noise, and train a restorer to remove a little noise at a time; then give the restorer pure noise and let it "restore" a digit that never existed ( diffusion ). Modern generators combine the first and third: the restorer works on the short descriptions, and a text prompt tells it what to restore towards. Four ways to build a model that generates. All of them learn from examples and then turn random numbers into new data; they differ in what is trained and how sampling works. Today's image and video generators are diffusion models working in a VAE's compressed space; language models are autoregressive. Step 1 · The data, and a judge The examples use the same 8 × 8 handwritten digits as Lesson 3.21 , drawn as characters so that you can look at what each model produces. To put a number on quality, train a simple classifier ( Lesson 2.24 ) on the real digits and use it as a judge : a generated image counts as convincing if the judge is at least 90% sure which digit it is. Copy What you should see Copy Even some real digits are sloppy enough that the judge is not 90% sure, so 77% is the reference point: a generator near that number is producing digits about as clear as real handwriting. Real projects use the same idea at scale. The standard image-quality metric, FID , compares statistics of generated and real images as seen by a pretrained classifier. Step 2 · An autoencoder: compress, then rebuild An autoencoder is two networks trained together. The encoder squeezes the 64 pixel values into a few numbers, called the latent code. The decoder rebuilds the image from that code. The only training signal is "make the output equal the input". Because everything must pass through 8 numbers, the network is forced to find a compact description of what digits look like. Copy What you should see Copy Rebuilding works well: eight numbers are enough to redraw each digit recognisably. So the decoder knows how to draw digits. But when it is handed 500 random codes, almost nothing convincing comes out. The reason is in the printed code for the first image: values such as −6.5 and 6.2. Training placed the codes wherever was convenient, in scattered clumps with large gaps between them. Random points mostly land in the gaps, where the decoder has never been asked to draw anything. Step 3 · A variational autoencoder: tidy the space A variational autoencoder (VAE) makes two changes so that the latent space can be sampled: The encoder outputs not a point but a small cloud for each image (a mean and a spread per dimension), and the decoder is trained on points drawn from that cloud. Neighbouring points must therefore decode to similar images, which fills the gaps. An extra loss term, the KL divergence , pulls every cloud towards a standard bell curve centred on zero. All the codes are pushed into one compact, overlapping region with a known shape. Copy What you should see Copy The same decoder architecture, the same 8 numbers, and now random points decode to recognisable digits several times as often, across all ten classes. The cost is visible too: the samples are soft and blurry. A VAE is trained to produce an image that is good on average for a whole cloud of codes, and the average of several plausible digits is a blurry digit. Reading this output Reading the VAE code mean + torch.exp(0.5 * log_var) * torch.randn_like(mean) draws a random point from the cloud in a way that gradients can flow through. This is the reparameterisation trick . reconstruction is the rebuilding error. kl measures how far each cloud is from a standard bell curve. The weight 0.25 balances them: too low and the space has gaps again; too high and the model ignores its input and every image decodes to the same blur ( posterior collapse ). To generate, you no longer need the encoder at all: draw torch.randn(8) and decode. Step 4 · A GAN: a forger against a detective A generative adversarial network has no encoder. The generator turns random numbers directly into an image. The discriminator sees a mix of real and generated images and outputs one number: real or fake. They are trained in turns. The discriminator is rewarded for telling them apart; the generator is rewarded when the discriminator is fooled. Copy What you should see Copy The strokes are sharp and high-contrast, not blurry: the generator is never asked to average anything, only to be convincing. But many samples are malformed, and the two losses did not go down. They hover, because every improvement by one network is a setback for the other. That is normal for a GAN, and it is why they are hard to train: there is no single number that says training is going well. Reading this output Why GANs gave way to diffusion GANs produced the first photorealistic faces (StyleGAN, 2018) and are still used where speed matters, because they generate in one step. Three problems limited them. Training is unstable: small changes in settings make it diverge. They suffer mode collapse : the generator finds a few outputs that fool the discriminator and stops producing the rest of the variety. And steering them with text never worked well. Diffusion models train with a plain, stable regression loss, cover the variety of the data, and accept conditions naturally. Step 5 · Diffusion in the latent space Lesson 10.40 trained a diffusion model on points in a plane. The same recipe works on anything that is a list of numbers, including the VAE's 8-number codes. That is latent diffusion : Encode every training image to its latent code with the VAE (done once). Take a code, add a random amount of noise, and train a denoiser network to predict the noise that was added. Tell the denoiser which digit the code belongs to, so that it learns to denoise towards a requested digit . In a text-to-image model this condition is the encoded prompt. Latent diffusion, the design behind Stable Diffusion and most current image generators. The prompt is turned into vectors by a text encoder. Generation starts from random noise in the VAE's small latent space; a denoising network removes a little noise at a time, steered by the prompt; the VAE decoder turns the final latent into pixels. This lesson builds each box in miniature. Copy What you should see Copy The loss settles around 0.25 and stays there. Unlike a GAN's losses, this is a plain prediction error, and it cannot reach zero: when a code is almost entirely noise, the exact noise cannot be recovered. What matters is how the model generates. Reading this output Reading the training loop alphas_bar[t] says how much of the original code is left after t noising steps. zt is the noisy code: a mix of the original and fresh noise. The denoiser sees the noisy code, the step number t and the label, and predicts noise . The loss is the squared difference. That is the whole training objective of a diffusion model. For 15% of the examples the label is replaced by a special "no label" value. The model therefore learns both to denoise towards a specific digit and to denoise with no instruction. The next step uses both. Step 6 · Generate, and steer with guidance To generate, start from pure noise in the latent space and repeatedly remove the predicted noise. At each step, ask the denoiser twice: once with the wanted digit and once with no label. The difference between the two answers is the direction that makes the result "more like a 3". Classifier-free guidance pushes further along that direction by a chosen factor: Copy What you should see Copy These digits were generated from noise, in the VAE's latent space, steered by a label, and decoded to pixels. Read the table from the top: Guidance 0 ignores the label. The digits are random (right 10% of the time, which is chance), often unclear, and very varied. Guidance 1 uses the label plainly. Almost every sample is the requested digit. Guidance 2 to 4 exaggerates the label's direction. Every sample is the requested digit and more of them are convincing than the real handwriting was. But the variety column has halved: the samples of each digit now look alike, as the rows of 3s and 7s above show. Guidance 8 pushes too far, and quality falls again. This is the trade-off behind the "guidance scale" or "CFG" setting in every image generator: low values give variety and loose prompt-following, high values give faithful but samey and eventually distorted images. From the miniature to real systems Part In this lesson In Stable Diffusion and its relatives Compression A VAE: 64 pixels to 8 numbers A convolutional VAE: a 512 × 512 × 3 image to a 64 × 64 × 4 latent (48 times fewer numbers); newer models use 16 latent channels Condition An embedding of a digit label The prompt, encoded by one or more text encoders ( CLIP , T5); fed to the denoiser through cross-attention Denoiser A 3-layer network A U-Net ( Lesson 3.21 ) with attention, or a diffusion transformer (DiT) over latent patches; hundreds of millions to billions of parameters Noise schedule and sampler 200 steps, the basic sampler Better samplers and schedules need 20 to 50 steps; distilled later · 14.132 models (LCM, Turbo, Lightning) need 1 to 8 Guidance Scale 2 Typically 3 to 8; distilled models often build it in Training objective Predict the noise Predict the noise, or the closely related flow matching objective used by Stable Diffusion 3 and FLUX, which learns a straighter path from noise to data Ideas built on this design that you will meet in products: Image-to-image and inpainting : start from a partly noised version of an existing image, or denoise only a masked region. ControlNet and adapters : an extra network feeds a pose, an edge map or a depth map into the denoiser, so that composition can be controlled exactly. LoRA later · 3.24 for images : the low-rank adapters of Lesson 3.24 , trained on a few dozen pictures to teach a style, a product or a face. Video : the latent gains a time dimension, and the denoiser attends across frames as well as within them. Compression matters even more. Audio and music : the same recipe on compressed audio latents. Autoregressive image generation : the alternative family. An image is turned into a sequence of tokens and a transformer predicts them one after another, as with text. Multimodal language models that generate images natively work this way, sometimes with a small diffusion decoder at the end. Check your mental model ✗ "A generative model stores its training images and stitches them together." ✓ It learns a function from random numbers to data. The digits above came from 8 random numbers each. (Very large models can still memorise specific training images that were repeated many times, which is a real legal and privacy concern.) ✗ "Diffusion works on the pixels of the final image." ✓ Most systems denoise a small latent and decode to pixels once at the end. That is what made them affordable. ✗ "A higher guidance scale always gives a better image." ✓ It trades variety for faithfulness , and too much distorts the result. ✗ "GANs are obsolete." ✓ They are less used for open-ended generation, but still valued for one-step speed, and adversarial losses are used inside VAEs and distilled diffusion models. Think about which direction the update moves in, then run it and ask the judge what digits came out. (Solution P1.) Make it your own Change the VAE's KL weight from 0.25 to 2.0 , retrain, and decode 500 random points. Then try 0.01 . Report the reconstruction error, the KL value and the share of convincing digits for each. Which failure does each setting show? (Solution M1.) Practice Apply it A marketing team wants product images in a consistent brand style, with the product placed exactly where the layout needs it, and they need thousands of images a day. Using the list of ideas above, say which technique addresses each of the three requirements. (Solution X1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Negative guidance The update moves away from "3": the samples are digits, but almost never a 3. This is the mechanism behind negative prompts in image generators: the "without" branch is replaced by a prompt describing what you do not want, and guidance pushes away from it. Solution M1 · The KL weight With weight 2.0 the KL term wins: KL falls to nearly zero, the reconstruction error rises, and every random point decodes to much the same grey blur. The encoder has stopped passing information (posterior collapse). With 0.01 reconstruction is excellent but the KL value is large: the codes have spread out and left gaps, so random decodes are again mostly unconvincing, as with the plain autoencoder. A usable VAE sits between the two. Solution X1 · Style, placement, volume Style: a LoRA trained on a few dozen brand images, applied to a base model . Placement: ControlNet (an edge or depth map of the layout), or inpainting the product into a fixed scene. Volume: a distilled few-step model, which cuts the cost of each image by a factor of ten or more. Recap An autoencoder compresses data to a short latent code and rebuilds it. A VAE also organises the latent space so that random codes decode to plausible data, at the price of blur. A GAN trains a generator against a discriminator: sharp results, unstable training, limited variety. A diffusion model is trained to predict the noise added to data, and generates by removing noise step by step. Running it in a VAE's latent space makes it cheap: latent diffusion. A condition (a label here, a text embedding in practice) steers generation. Classifier-free guidance amplifies the condition, trading variety for faithfulness. Real image and video generators are this design at scale, with better samplers, distillation, ControlNet, LoRA and, increasingly, transformers and flow matching. Check your understanding Q1 Why do random codes decode badly with a plain autoencoder but much better with a VAE? A The VAE has a bigger decoder B The VAE is trained so that its codes fill one compact region with no large gaps C The VAE uses convolution D The autoencoder was trained for too few steps The KL term and the sampling during training organise the latent space so that random points land where the decoder has learned to draw. Q2 What does a diffusion model's denoiser learn to predict? A Whether an image is real or fake B The label of the image C The noise that was added to a piece of data D The next pixel Training adds a known amount of noise and asks the network to recover it; generation runs that in reverse from pure noise. A More varied images that follow the prompt less B Images that follow the prompt more literally, look more alike, and may become distorted C Faster generation D Higher resolution Guidance amplifies the condition's direction: more faithfulness, less variety, and eventually artefacts. Generative media: how diffusion models work Image, video and much audio generation uses diffusion models . Training teaches a network to remove a little noise from a noisy example; generation starts from pure noise and removes noise step by step, guided by the prompt, until an image (or audio clip, or video) remains. The guidance comes from a text encoder, and classifier-free guidance controls how strictly the output follows the prompt. Modern systems run diffusion in a compressed latent space ( latent diffusion ) and often use a transformer as the denoiser (diffusion transformers); flow matching is a closely related training method used by several recent image models. See it drawn The Illustrated Stable Diffusion : Jay Alammar: text encoder, image information creator and decoder, drawn step by step The denoising network inside Stable Diffusion. It receives the noisy image, the time step and the encoded prompt, and predicts the noise to remove. The prompt enters at every level through cross-attention, which is how the text steers the picture. Figure: Hugging Face, Diffusion Models Course , Apache 2.0 . The whole idea fits in a few lines on one-dimensional data. The "model" here is the exact denoising direction (the score), which a real system learns with a neural network: Copy What you should see Copy Ten thousand samples of pure noise were denoised, in 200 small steps, into the two clusters of the training data. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Language is continuous. Models are discrete. Preprocessing is the bridge. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Token A word Whatever unit the model consumes. Can be word, subword, character, or byte. Stem Root of a word Result of rule-based suffix stripping. Not always a real word. Lemma Dictionary form The form you'd look up. Requires grammatical context to compute correctly. POS tag Part of speech Category like NOUN, VERB, ADJ. Needed to lemmatize accurately. Morphology Word shape rules How a word changes form based on tense, number, case. Lemmatization depends on it. The problem In plain words first Before a computer can learn anything from text, the text has to be cut into pieces it can count. Tokenization decides where one piece ends and the next begins ("don't" is one piece or two?). Stemming chops word endings by rule so that "connect", "connected" and "connecting" count as the same thing, even if the result ("connect", but also "univers" for "university") is not a real word. Lemmatization looks words up properly ("ran" becomes "run", "better" becomes "good") but needs to know whether the word is a verb, a noun or an adjective. Each choice changes what the model sees. A model cannot read "The cats were running." It reads integers. Every NLP system opens with the same three questions. Where does a word start. What is the root of the word. How do we treat "run", "running", "ran" as the same thing when it helps, and as different things when it doesn't. Get tokenization wrong and the model learns from garbage. If your tokenizer treats don't as one token but do n't as two, the training distribution splits. If your stemmer collapses organization and organ to the same stem, topic modeling dies. If your lemmatizer needs part-of-speech context but you don't pass it, verbs get treated as nouns. This lesson builds the three preprocessing steps from scratch, then shows how NLTK and spaCy do the same work so you can see the tradeoffs. The idea Three operations. Each has a job and a failure mode. Tokenization splits a string into tokens. "Token" is deliberately vague because the right granularity depends on the task. Word-level for classical NLP. Subword for transformers. Character for languages without whitespace. Stemming chops suffixes with rules. Fast, aggressive, dumb. running -> run . organization -> organ . That second one is the failure mode. Lemmatization reduces a word to its dictionary form using grammar knowledge. Slower, accurate, needs a lookup table or morphological analyzer. ran -> run (needs to know "ran" is past tense of "run"). better -> good (needs to know comparative forms). Rule of thumb. Stem when speed matters and you can tolerate noise (search indexing, rough classification). Lemmatize when meaning matters (question answering, semantic search, anything the user will read). The same idea as a formula Word frequencies are extremely uneven. Rank the distinct words of a corpus by frequency; Zipf's law says the -th most frequent appears about f ( 1 ) ​ , s ≈ 1 times: the top few hundred words make up about half of all tokens, while most distinct words appear once or twice. The vocabulary keeps growing. Heaps' law: after reading tokens, the number of distinct words is about with . Ten times more text gives roughly three times more distinct words, so a word-level vocabulary never closes, which is why modern models use subword tokens (Lesson 5.4 onwards). What stemming and lemmatisation do to counts. Both map several surface forms to one key, so they shrink and pool the counts of rare forms, helping count-based models (bag of words, TF-IDF) on small data. A stemmer is a fixed set of rules: Porter's step 1a rewrites sses → ss , ies → i , keeps ss , and drops a final s . A lemmatiser is a lookup keyed by (word, part of speech): (were, VERB) → be . Tokenisation as a function. A tokenizer maps a string to a sequence, ​ , … , t n ​ ) ; every later count, vector and model input depends on it, so the same tokenizer must be used at training and at inference. Worked example One sentence through the pipeline "The cats were running" with this lesson's functions and the default NOUN tag: token stem_step_1a lemmatize(token, "NOUN") with the right POS The the the the cats cat cat cat (NOUN) were were were be (VERB) running running running run (VERB) Step 1a only strips plural s , so "running" survives it. The lemmatizer turns "were" into "be" and "running" into "run" only when they are tagged as VERBs (the -ing fallback is for verbs): the POS tag decides the lemma. That is why Step 4 calls the missing tagger "the missing piece". Two things will bite a real preprocessing pipeline, and they are almost never covered. Reproducibility drift. NLTK and spaCy change tokenization and lemmatizer behavior between versions. Even today the tools disagree: NLTK and spaCy split can't into ca + n't , while this lesson's regex keeps it whole (see "Use it"), and an upgrade can move such splits just as silently. Your model was trained on one distribution. Inference now runs on a different one. Accuracy quietly degrades and nobody knows why. Pin library versions in requirements.txt . Write a preprocessing regression test that freezes expected tokenization of 20 sample sentences. Run it on every upgrade. Training / inference mismatch. Train with aggressive preprocessing (lowercase, stopword removal, stemming), deploy on raw user input, watch performance crater. This is the single most common production NLP failure. If you preprocess during training, you must run the identical function during inference. Ship preprocessing as a function inside the model package, not as a notebook cell the serving team rewrites. None is "right"; what matters is using the same one everywhere. Porter merges "organization", "organ" and "organic" (and three "gener-" words) into one stem, which is the noise you accept for its speed. WordNet only lemmatizes "running" or "better" correctly when told the part of speech. On Emma , stemming shrinks the vocabulary by over a third, lemmatizing with the default noun tag by much less, because it only merges plurals and other noun forms. Recap What to keep from this lesson Tokenization defines the units; every library makes different choices on contractions, numbers, emails and URLs. Stemming strips suffixes by rule: fast, but can merge unrelated words; rule order matters. Lemmatization maps to dictionary forms and needs the part of speech to be right. Normalisation trades information for a smaller vocabulary; measure the trade-off on your data. Pin library versions and apply identical preprocessing at training and inference. Solutions Solution P1 · Raw > lower > lemma > stem Raw tokens give the most distinct items, lower-casing removes the capitalised duplicates, noun lemmatization merges plurals and similar forms, and Porter stemming shrinks the vocabulary the most, by over a third relative to lower-cased words (the printed counts). The stemmer's extra shrinkage is partly real merging ("walks", "walked", "walking") and partly the collisions shown above. Solution B1 · Rule order decides everything With the plain s rule first, every word ending in s loses just that letter before the more specific rules are checked: "caresses" becomes "caresse", "ponies" becomes "ponie", and "caress" becomes "cares", a different word. Only "cats" comes out the same as before. The specific suffixes ( sses , ies , ss ) must be tested before the general one; that ordering is most of what the Porter algorithm is. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) LLM pipelines skip stemming. Subword tokenizers (Lesson 5.4) replaced stemming and lemmatisation as preprocessing for neural models; normalising Unicode (NFKC) and whitespace is still worth doing. Search engines still stem. Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and Lucene analysers apply language-specific stemmers and stop-word lists for keyword (BM25) search, which is half of most hybrid search systems. spaCy and Stanza remain the standard libraries for tokenisation, lemmas and sentence splitting in production NLP pipelines. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Count first, think later. TF-IDF still holds its own against embeddings on well-defined tasks. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means BoW Word frequency vector Counts of vocabulary words in one document. Throws away order. TF Term frequency Count of a word in a document, optionally normalized by document length. DF Document frequency Count of documents containing the word at least once. IDF Inverse document frequency log(N / df) smoothed. Downweights words that appear everywhere. Sparse vector Mostly zeros Vocabulary is typically 10k-100k words; most are absent from any given document. Cosine similarity Vector angle Dot product of L2-normalized vectors. 1 is identical, 0 is orthogonal. The problem In plain words first A classifier needs a fixed-length list of numbers for every document. Bag of words makes one by counting: give every word in the vocabulary a slot, and put in each slot how often that word appears. Word order is thrown away. TF-IDF then reweights the counts: words that appear in nearly every document ("the", "was") are turned down, and words that are frequent in this document but rare elsewhere are turned up. The result is simple, fast and explainable, and on many tasks still hard to beat; its blind spot is meaning, since "excellent" and "great" share no slot. The model needs numbers. You have strings. Every NLP pipeline has to answer the same question. How do we turn a variable-length stream of tokens into a fixed-size vector that a classifier can consume. The first answer the field landed on was the dumbest one that works. Count the words. Make a vector. That vector has carried more production NLP than any embedding model. Spam filters, topic classifiers, log anomaly detection, search ranking (before BM25), the first wave of sentiment analysis, the first decade of academic NLP benchmarks. 2026 practitioners still reach for it first on narrow classification tasks. It is fast, interpretable, and often indistinguishable from a 400M-parameter embedding model on tasks where word presence is what matters. This lesson builds bag of words, then TF-IDF, from scratch. Then shows scikit-learn doing the same in three lines. Then names the failure mode that makes you reach for embeddings. The idea Bag of Words (BoW) throws away order. For each document, count how many times each vocabulary word appears. Vector length is the vocabulary size. Position i is the count of word i . TF-IDF reweights BoW. A word that appears in every document is uninformative, so scale it down. A word rare across the corpus but frequent in a single document is signal, so scale it up. ​ = TF ( w , d ) ⋅ IDF ( w ) = ∣ d ∣ count ( w in d ) ​ ⋅ lo g df ( w ) N ​ ​ Where TF is term frequency in the document, df is document frequency (how many docs contain the word), N is total documents. The log keeps the weight bounded for ubiquitous words. Key property: both produce sparse vectors with interpretable axes. You can look at a trained classifier's weights and read which words push a document toward each class. You cannot do this with a 768-dimensional BERT embedding. The same idea as a formula Bag of words. With a vocabulary of terms, document becomes a vector of counts , one entry per term; word order is discarded. Across documents this is an matrix that is almost entirely zeros (a 200-word document touches perhaps 120 of 50,000 terms), so it is stored sparse. Inverse document frequency. A term found in every document tells documents apart not at all; one in a few documents tells a lot. With the number of documents containing : N ​ , scikit-learn’s smoothed form: ln 1 + df ( t ) 1 + N ​ + 1 and . The smoothed form never divides by zero and never gives a term weight 0. Normalise, then compare. Dividing each row by its L2 norm makes long and short documents comparable; the similarity of two documents is then the dot product of their rows, which equals their cosine similarity: ​ , d 2 ​ ) = ∥ x d 1 ​ ​ ∥ ∥ x d 2 ​ ​ ∥ x d 1 ​ ​ ⋅ x d 2 ​ ​ ​ This is the scoring core of classic search engines (BM25 refines it with term-frequency saturation and document-length normalisation) and a strong baseline for text classification with a linear model. Output: {word: index} dict. Stable insertion order means word index 0 is the first word seen in the first document. Convention varies; scikit-learn sorts alphabetically. Entry [i][j] is "how many times word j appears in document i ." Doc 1 has cat twice because it did. Doc 0 has ran zero times because it did not. Step 3 · term frequency and document frequency Copy Two smoothing tricks worth naming. The (n+1)/(d+1) avoids log(x/0) . The trailing +1 ensures a word in every document still has IDF 1 (not 0), matching scikit-learn's default. Other implementations use raw log(N/df) . Both work; the smoothed version is friendlier. With a real vocabulary of thousands of words, these vectors are sparse (most entries are zero). Even in this toy, the discriminative words pop. Step 5 · L2-normalize rows Copy Without normalization, a longer document gets a larger vector and dominates similarity scores. L2 normalization puts every document on the unit hypersphere. Cosine similarity between rows is now just a dot product. (Solution B1.) Use it: the same idea with real libraries scikit-learn ships the production version. Usually boosts classification. min_df=2 Drop words in fewer than 2 docs. Trims vocabulary on noisy data. max_df=0.95 Drop words in more than 95% of docs. When TF-IDF still wins (as of 2026) Spam detection, topic labeling, log anomaly flagging. Word presence is what matters; semantic nuance does not. Low-data regimes where no pretrained encoder fits your text (unusual jargon, codes, logs). On ordinary language, pretrained embeddings often win when labels are scarce; "Use it" measures it. Anywhere latency matters. TF-IDF plus a linear model answers in microseconds. Embedding a document through even a small transformer costs milliseconds (about 4 ms per sentence, batched, for the CPU run under "Use it"). Systems that must explain their predictions. Inspect the classifier's coefficients. Top positive words are the reason. When TF-IDF fails The semantic blindness failure. Consider these two documents: "The movie was not good at all." "The movie was excellent." One is a negative review. One is positive. Their TF-IDF overlap is exactly {the, movie, was} . A bag-of-words classifier has to memorize that the word not near good flips the label. It can learn this on enough data, but never as gracefully as a model that understands syntax. The other failure: out-of-vocabulary words at inference. A BoW model trained on IMDb reviews has no idea what to do with Zoomer-approved if that token never appeared in training. Subword embeddings (lesson 04) handle this. TF-IDF cannot. Hybrid: TF-IDF weighted embeddings A common hybrid for medium-data classification: use TF-IDF weights as attention over word embeddings. Copy You get semantic capacity from embeddings, and rare-word emphasis from TF-IDF. Classifier trains on the pooled vector. Whether this beats either part alone depends on the task and the data, so measure it; "Use it" tries a simpler combination (TF-IDF features next to sentence embeddings) on a real dataset. Show the code that draws this Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output With only 200 labelled sentences the pretrained embeddings clearly win: MiniLM already knows that "dazzling" and "brilliant" are related, while TF-IDF has to learn every word from those 200 examples. With all 8,530 sentences, TF-IDF with bigrams catches up and slightly passes the small embedding model, and putting both feature sets side by side is best of all. The learned weights explain the bigram model completely: you can read the words and phrases that push a review negative or positive, including whether "not good" was frequent enough to earn its own negative weight. That readability is TF-IDF's lasting advantage; an embedding classifier's 384 weights mean nothing on their own. It also explains the strangest line: "The movie was excellent." comes out negative . The printed weights show why: in critics' one-line reviews, "movie" and "was" lean negative, and a single "excellent" cannot outvote them. Short inputs written in a different style from the training data are exactly where bag-of-words models fail, and reading the weights is how you find out. Recap What to keep from this lesson Bag of words counts each vocabulary word per document; order is lost. TF-IDF downweights words found in many documents; scikit-learn smooths the IDF and L2-normalises rows. Sparse TF-IDF plus a linear model is fast, cheap and explainable; bigrams recover some word order such as "not good". Pretrained embeddings win when labels are few; with enough labels, TF-IDF is often close, and combinations can beat both. Fit the vocabulary and IDF on training data only. Solutions Solution P1 · Embeddings early, TF-IDF late At 200 and 1,000 sentences the MiniLM embeddings win by several points; at the full 8,530, TF-IDF with bigrams is slightly ahead, and the combination is best (the printed table). Pretrained knowledge matters most when labelled data is scarce; with enough labels, counting words that actually signal sentiment in this domain is competitive. Solution B1 · A leak through the vocabulary Fitting on train plus test lets the test set decide the vocabulary and the IDF weights: words that only occur in test sentences get slots, and every IDF reflects test-set frequencies. The classifier is still trained on training labels only, so the effect is usually small, but the evaluation is no longer of a pipeline you could actually deploy, where future documents are unseen. Fit on training data, then only transform everything else. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) BM25 is the default keyword ranker. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Word embedding Word as a vector A dense, low-dim (typically 100-300) representation learned from context. The problem In plain words first A word embedding gives every word a short list of numbers, say 100 of them, chosen so that words used in similar ways get similar lists. Word2Vec learns them with a guessing game: for each word in a text, guess which words appear near it. Words that keep the same company ("dog" and "puppy" both appear near "walk", "bark", "vet") end up with nearby vectors. Directions in that space can even carry meaning, so "king" minus "man" plus "woman" lands near "queen". The weakness: each word gets exactly one vector, so "bank" the river side and "bank" the lender are forced to share. TF-IDF knows dog and puppy are different words. It does not know they mean nearly the same thing. A classifier trained on dog cannot generalize to a review about puppy . You can paper over this by listing synonyms, but that fails on rare terms, domain jargon, and every language you did not anticipate. You want a representation where dog and puppy land close together in space. Where king - man + woman lands near queen . Where a model trained on dog transfers some signal to puppy for free. Word2Vec gave us that space. A two-layer network with no non-linearity, trained on about 100 billion words of Google News, published in 2013. The architecture is almost embarrassingly simple. The results reshaped NLP for a decade. The idea Distributional hypothesis (Firth, 1957): "You shall know a word by the company it keeps." If two words appear in similar contexts, they probably mean similar things. Word2Vec comes in two flavors, both exploiting that idea. Skip-gram. Given a center word, predict the surrounding words. cat -> (the, sat, on) with window size 2. CBOW (continuous bag of words). Given surrounding words, predict the center. (the, sat, on) -> cat . Skip-gram is slower to train but handles rare words better. It became the default. The network has one hidden layer with no nonlinearity. Input is a one-hot vector over the vocabulary. Output is a softmax over the vocabulary. After training, you throw away the output layer. The hidden layer weights are the embeddings. Copy The trick: softmax over 100k words is prohibitively expensive. Word2Vec uses negative sampling to turn it into a binary classification task. Predict "did this context word appear near this center word, yes or no". Where Word2Vec fails The polysemy wall. bank has one vector. river bank and financial bank share it. table (spreadsheet vs. furniture) shares it. Recap What to keep from this lesson Distributional hypothesis: words in similar contexts get similar vectors. Skip-gram predicts context words from the center word; negative sampling turns the softmax into a few binary decisions. Embedding quality depends heavily on corpus size; analogies need billions of words. One vector per word: senses are averaged, and unseen words have no vector. Train your own with gensim for a specialised corpus; otherwise start from pretrained vectors. Solutions Solution P1 · Clusters by topic The nearest neighbours of "cat" are the other four animals, of "car" the other vehicles and of "bread" the other foods, with cosine similarities above 0.9 (the printed lists). Within a template set the five words are interchangeable, so they collect identical contexts, and skip-gram gives them nearly identical vectors. Solution B1 · Everything collapses together With no negatives, the only force pulls center and context vectors together, and nothing pushes unrelated words apart. The cheapest way to make every positive pair score high is for all vectors to point in roughly the same direction and grow, so cosine similarities between all words approach 1 and the neighbour lists become meaningless. Negative samples are what give the space structure. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Sentence embeddings replaced word vectors for most tasks. Embedding APIs (OpenAI text-embedding-3 , Gemini Embedding, Cohere Embed) and open models (BGE, GTE, Qwen3-Embedding via sentence-transformers) embed whole passages (Lesson 5.22). Word2vec ideas still run recommendations. Item embeddings learned from sessions with skip-gram (Airbnb's listing embeddings, many "item2vec" systems) remain a cheap, strong method in recommender systems; Gensim and fastText are the libraries. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Word2Vec trained one embedding per word. GloVe factorized the co-occurrence matrix. FastText embedded the pieces. BPE bridged to transformers. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Co-occurrence matrix Word-word frequency table X[i][j] = how often word j appears in a window around word i . Subword Piece of a word A character n-gram (FastText) or learned token (BPE/WordPiece/SentencePiece). BPE Byte-pair encoding Iterative merging of most-frequent adjacent pairs until vocabulary hits target size. OOV Out of vocabulary Word the model has never seen. Word2Vec/GloVe fail. FastText and BPE handle it. Byte-level BPE BPE on raw bytes GPT-2's scheme. Vocabulary starts with 256 bytes, so nothing is ever OOV. The problem In plain words first This lesson is about the pieces a model reads. Word2Vec gave each whole word one vector, which leaves two gaps: it ignores the big table of "which words appear together" that you could simply count, and it has nothing at all for a word it never saw. Three fixes followed. GloVe counts how often every pair of words appears together and fits vectors to those counts. FastText builds a word's vector from its spelling pieces ("whe", "her", "ere"…), so a new word still gets a vector from pieces it shares with known words. BPE, the method behind GPT-style tokenizers, stops treating words as the unit at all: it learns a vocabulary of frequent chunks, so any text, in any language, splits into chunks it knows. Word2Vec left three open questions. First, there was a parallel line of research that factorized the co-occurrence matrix directly (LSA, HAL) rather than doing online skip-gram updates. Was Word2Vec's iterative approach fundamentally better, or was the difference an artifact of how the two methods handled counts? GloVe answered that: factorizing the counts with a carefully chosen loss matched Word2Vec on the benchmarks of 2014, and the counting pass over the corpus happens once rather than every epoch. Later controlled comparisons (Levy, Goldberg and Dagan, 2015) found the two roughly tied once their settings were matched, so neither approach is fundamentally better. Second, neither method had a story for words it had never seen. Zoomer-approved , dogecoin , any proper noun coined last week, every inflected form of a rare root. FastText fixed this by embedding character n-grams: a word is the sum of its parts, including morphemes, so even out-of-vocabulary words get a sensible vector. Third, once transformers arrived, the question shifted again. Word-level vocabularies cap out around a million entries; real language is more open than that. Byte-pair encoding (BPE) and its relatives solved this by learning a vocabulary of frequent subword units that covers everything. Practically every modern LLM reads text through a subword tokenizer. This lesson walks all three, then explains which to reach for when. The idea GloVe (Global Vectors). Build the word-word co-occurrence matrix X where X[i][j] is how often word j appears in the context of word i . Train vectors such that v_i · v_j + b_i + b_j ≈ log(X[i][j]) . Weight the loss so frequent pairs do not dominate. Done. FastText. A word is the sum of its character n-grams plus the word itself. With 3-character pieces, where becomes <wh, whe, her, ere, re> plus the whole word <where> ; real FastText uses every length from 3 to 6, which gives 14 pieces plus the whole word. The word vector is the sum of those component vectors. Train as Word2Vec. Benefit: unseen words ( whereupon ) compose from known n-grams. BPE (Byte-Pair Encoding). Start with a vocabulary of individual bytes (or characters). Count every adjacent pair in the corpus. Merge the most frequent pair into a new token. Repeat for k iterations. Result: a vocabulary of the base symbols plus k merges ( k + 256 tokens when you start from bytes) where frequent sequences ( ing , tion , the ) are single tokens and rare words are broken into familiar pieces. Every sentence tokenizes into something. Worked example One GloVe term by hand Suppose "ice" and "solid" were counted together ​ = 10 times, with the defaults ​ = 100 and . Weight: = 0.178 . Most of what you need to know about classical text classification shows up here. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Polarity Positive or negative Binary label; sometimes extended to neutral or fine-grained (5-star). Aspect-based sentiment Per-aspect polarity Attribute sentiment to specific entities or attributes mentioned in text. Negation scoping Reversing nearby tokens Prefix tokens after "not" with NOT_ until punctuation. Laplace smoothing Adding 1 to counts Prevents zero-probability features in Naive Bayes. L2 regularization Shrinking weights Adds lambda * sum(w^2) to loss. Essential for sparse text features. The problem In plain words first Sentiment analysis means deciding whether a piece of text is positive or negative. The classic recipe has two steps: turn the text into counts of its words, then let a simple model learn which words point which way ("loved" up, "boring" down). Naive Bayes does this by counting how often each word appears in positive and in negative examples; logistic regression learns one weight per word. Both are fast and surprisingly good. They also share blind spots: "not great" contains "great", sarcasm says the opposite of its words, and "great camera, terrible battery" is two opinions at once. This lesson builds both models, measures them on 10,000 real movie-review sentences, and checks those blind spots against a modern transformer. "The food was not great." Positive or negative? Sentiment sounds simple. A reviewer said they liked or did not like something. Label the sentence. The reason it became the canonical NLP task is that every easy-looking case hides a hard one. Negation flips meaning. Sarcasm inverts it. "Not bad at all" is positive despite two negative-coded words. Emojis carry more signal than surrounding text. Domain vocabulary matters ( tight in music review versus tight in fashion review). Sentiment is a working lab for classical NLP. If you understand why every naive baseline has a specific failure mode, you understand why every richer model was invented. This lesson builds a Naive Bayes baseline from scratch, adds logistic regression, and names the traps that make production sentiment a compliance-grade problem. The idea Classical sentiment is a two-step recipe. Represent. Turn the text into a feature vector. BoW, TF-IDF, or n-grams. Classify. Fit a linear model (Naive Bayes, logistic regression, SVM) on labeled examples. Naive Bayes is the dumbest model that works. Assume every feature is independent given the label. Estimate P(word | positive) and P(word | negative) from counts. At inference, multiply the probabilities. The "naive" independence assumption is laughably wrong and yet the results are shockingly strong. The reason: with sparse text features and moderate data, the classifier cares about which side each word leans toward more than how much. Logistic regression fixes the independence assumption. It learns a weight per feature, including negative weights. Give either model the bigram not good and both will learn that it is negative. The difference shows when features overlap: Naive Bayes counts "not", "good" and "not good" as three independent pieces of evidence, while logistic regression fits all the weights together, so it can learn how much the bigram should override the word "good". The same idea as a formula Naive Bayes, derived from Bayes' rule We want the class with the highest probability given the document ​ , … , w n ​ ) . The independence assumption is false, which mostly makes the probabilities overconfident (correlated words such as "not", "good" and "not good" are counted as separate evidence), but the ranking of the two classes is often still right. Step 1 · a real mini-dataset Copy Small on purpose. Real work uses tens of thousands of examples (IMDb, SST-2, Yelp polarity). The math is identical. Step 2 · multinomial Naive Bayes from scratch Copy Additive smoothing (alpha=1.0) is Laplace smoothing. Without it, a word unseen in a class has probability zero and the log explodes. alpha=1.0 is also scikit-learn's default. Smaller values are sometimes better on large vocabularies, so treat it as a setting to tune (under "Use it", 0.1 does slightly worse on movie reviews). Worked example Naive Bayes by hand on "great story" With the regex tokenizer used under "Use it", the five positive sentences hold 26 tokens, the negative ones 25, and the vocabulary has 44 distinct tokens (the comma counts as one). Smoothed totals: positive , negative . "great" appears once in positive text and never in negative: , . "story" has the same counts. Scores (both priors are ): positive ; negative . Positive wins by in log space, a factor of ≈ 3.9 : each of the two words is about twice as likely under positive. A word seen once in each class, like "acting", is nearly neutral, and tilts very slightly negative only because the negative class has one token fewer. Step 3 · logistic regression from scratch Copy L2 regularization matters here. Text features are sparse; without L2 the model memorizes training examples. Start near 0.01 and tune it: in the sweep under "Use it", 0.01 is already too strong for movie reviews and 0.001 does best. Check your mental model ✗ "Naive Bayes works because words really are independent." ✓ They are not. It works because classification only needs the right side of the decision boundary, not calibrated probabilities. The probabilities it prints are usually far too confident. ✗ "More preprocessing always helps." ✓ Under "Use it", removing stop words costs up to three points and negation scoping slightly hurts Naive Bayes. Every step is a hypothesis to test. ✗ "Stronger regularization is the safe default." ✓ Too much L2 underfits just as surely as none overfits; the sweep under "Use it" shows both ends. Step 4 · handling negation (the failure mode) Consider "not good" and "not bad". A BoW classifier sees {not, good} and {not, bad} and learns from whichever showed up more in training. A bigram classifier sees not_good and not_bad and learns them as distinct features. That is usually enough. A cruder fix that works when you do not have bigrams: negation scoping . Prefix tokens following a negation word with NOT_ up to the next punctuation. Copy Copy Checked This session was run when the page was built: every result above is exactly what Python prints. Now good and NOT_good are different features. The classifier can weight them opposite. It is a few lines of preprocessing and often helps on short, negation-heavy text, but measure it on your data: on the movie reviews under "Use it" it slightly hurts Naive Bayes, while plain bigrams help. Predict before you run Under "Use it", the lesson's Naive Bayes is trained on 8,530 movie-review sentences, once on plain words and once after apply_negation . Will negation scoping raise test accuracy, lower it, or leave it unchanged? (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Call train_nb(docs_by_class, vocab, alpha=0) , turning smoothing off, and then classify any sentence containing a word that appears in only one of the two classes. What happens? (Solution B1.) Step 5 · evaluation metrics that matter Accuracy alone is misleading if classes are imbalanced. Benchmark sets such as IMDb and SST-2 are balanced by design, but real streams of text rarely are: product reviews skew heavily positive, support tickets heavily negative. On an 80-20 split, a classifier that always answers the majority class scores 80% accuracy and is worthless. Report every one of the following: Per-class precision and recall. One pair per class. Macro-average them to get a single number that respects class balance. Macro-F1 (primary metric for imbalanced data). Mean of per-class F1 scores, equally weighted. Use this instead of accuracy when classes are imbalanced. Weighted-F1 (alternative). Same as macro but weighted by class frequency. Report alongside macro-F1 when the imbalance itself has business meaning. Confusion matrix. Raw counts. Always inspect before trusting any scalar metric; it reveals which pair of classes the model confuses. Per-class error samples. Pull 5 wrong predictions per class. Read them. Nothing replaces reading the actual errors. For severely imbalanced data (> 95-5 ratio), report AUROC and AUPRC instead of accuracy. AUPRC is more sensitive to the minority class, which is what you usually care about (spam, fraud, rare sentiment). Common bug to avoid. Reporting micro-F1 instead of macro-F1 on imbalanced data gives a number that looks high because it is dominated by the majority class. Macro-F1 forces you to see the minority-class performance. Stop-word lists were made for search, where those words add little; for sentiment they are signal. "Camera great, battery terrible" gets one fully confident label from DistilBERT and a shrug (0.54) from TF-IDF, which is the wrong question for a two-opinion sentence. "I expected to hate it, and I did not" is called negative by both, DistilBERT with full confidence: the score next to each label is how sure the model is, not how often it is right. Those three failures are exactly the bullets below. When to reach for a transformer Sarcasm. Word-count models mostly fail here, and transformers only partly do better: the DistilBERT run under "Use it" reads an obviously sarcastic sentence as positive. Long reviews where sentiment shifts mid-document. Aspect-based sentiment. "Camera was great but battery was terrible." You need to attribute sentiment to aspects, which a single-label classifier cannot express: use an aspect-based model, or an LLM asked for structured output per aspect. Non-English, low-resource languages. A multilingual model such as XLM-R, fine-tuned on English labels, transfers to other languages without labels in them (zero-shot cross-lingual transfer); a few hundred labels in the target language usually help a lot. If you need any of the above, skip ahead to phase 7 (transformers deep dive). Otherwise, logistic regression or Naive Bayes on TF-IDF with bigrams is the strong, cheap baseline to beat first, and a fine-tuned small transformer is the usual next step when its accuracy is not enough. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Encoders still do the volume work. For millions of texts a day, teams fine-tune a small encoder. ModernBERT (December 2024; 149M and 395M parameters, 8,192-token context, about twice as fast as DeBERTa-v3) is the usual modern starting point in place of the original BERT. LLMs as zero-shot labellers. An LLM given the label definitions and a JSON schema classifies with no training data, and handles aspects ("camera: positive, battery: negative") naturally. It is slower and costlier per item, so a common pattern is to let the LLM label a few thousand examples, check a sample by hand, and train a small classifier on them. Small zero-shot models on CPU. GLiNER2 (2025, about 205M parameters) does text classification with labels given at run time, alongside entity extraction, in about 0.1 to 0.2 seconds per text on a CPU. Same rule as ever. Whatever the model, measure it on your own labelled sample with per-class scores, and keep the TF-IDF baseline as the number to beat. Sources: ModernBERT , GLiNER2 . The reproducibility trap (again) Retraining sentiment models is routine. Re-evaluating them is not. Accuracy numbers reported in papers use specific splits, specific preprocessing, specific tokenizers. If you compare your new model to a baseline without using the identical pipeline, you will get misleading deltas. Always regenerate the baseline on your pipeline, not the paper's number. Recap What to keep from this lesson The recipe: represent (counts, TF-IDF, n-grams) then classify (Naive Bayes, logistic regression). Keep negation words: never remove stop words for sentiment. Bigrams help; test every other preprocessing step. Report per-class precision, recall and macro-F1, not accuracy alone, and read the errors. A fine-tuned transformer is about eleven points better here but still misses sarcasm and mixed opinions. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Pull the names out. Sounds easy until you deal with ambiguous boundaries, nested entities, and domain jargon. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means NER Extract names Label token spans with types (PERSON, ORG, GPE, DATE, ...). BIO Tagging scheme B-X begins, I-X continues, O outside. BILOU Better BIO Adds L-X (last), U-X (unit) for cleaner boundaries. CRF Structured classifier Models transitions between labels, not just emissions. Enforces valid sequences. Nested NER Overlapping entities One span is a different entity than a sub-span of it. BIO cannot express this. Entity-level F1 Proper NER metric Predicted span must match true span exactly. Token-level F1 overstates accuracy. The problem In plain words first Named entity recognition (NER) finds the names in a text and says what kind of thing each one is: a person, a company, a place, a product. The trick that makes it learnable is to label every word: "B-ORG" for the first word of an organisation's name, "I-ORG" for the words that continue it, "O" for everything else. A model then only has to predict one label per word. This lesson climbs the ladder of models that do that, from a lookup list of known names, to a probabilistic model that counts label sequences, to a CRF that uses hand-made clues like capital letters, to BERT. Under "Use it" all of them run on the same standard news benchmark, so you can see exactly what each step bought, and a small modern model finds entity types you name on the spot. "Apple sued Google over its iPhone search deal in the US." Five entities: Apple (ORG), Google (ORG), iPhone (PRODUCT), search deal (maybe), US (GPE). A good NER system extracts all of them with correct types. A bad one misses iPhone, confuses Apple the fruit with Apple the company, and labels "US" as a PERSON. NER is the workhorse underneath every structured extraction pipeline. Resume parsing, compliance log scanning, medical record anonymization, search query understanding, grounding for chatbot responses, legal contract extraction. You never quite see it; you always depend on it. This lesson walks the classical path (rule-based, HMM, CRF) into the modern one (BiLSTM-CRF, then transformers). Each step solves a specific limitation of the one before it. The pattern is the lesson. The idea BIO tagging (or BILOU) turns entity extraction into a sequence-labeling problem. Label each token with B-TYPE (beginning of entity), I-TYPE (inside entity), or O (outside any entity). Copy Multi-token entities chain: New B-GPE , York I-GPE , City I-GPE . A model that understands BIO can extract arbitrary spans. The architecture progression: Rule-based. Regex + gazetteer lookups. High precision on known entities, zero coverage on new ones. HMM. Hidden Markov Model. Emission probability of token given tag, transition probability of tag-to-tag. Viterbi decode. Trained on labeled data. CRF. Conditional Random Field. Like HMM but discriminative, so you can mix arbitrary features (word shape, capitalization, neighboring words). Still a solid choice when labelled data is modest and inference must be cheap. BiLSTM-CRF. Neural features instead of hand-crafted. LSTM reads the sentence both directions, CRF layer on top enforces consistent tag sequences. Transformer-based. Fine-tune BERT with a token-classification head. Best accuracy. Most compute. LLM-based NER (the 2026 option) Zero-shot and few-shot NER, with LLMs or with small open-type models, is now a practical starting point. On a standard benchmark it usually scores below a fine-tuned model, but when labelled data is scarce or the entity types are new, it is often good enough, and it works on day one. Zero-shot prompting. Give the LLM a list of entity types and an example schema. Ask for JSON output. Works out of the box; accuracy is moderate on novel domains. Small open-type models (GLiNER). A ~200M-parameter encoder that takes the entity types as plain-text labels at inference time ("drug", "dose", "symptom") and runs on a CPU. GLiNER (NAACL 2024) and GLiNER2 (2025, which adds classification and structured extraction) are the usual middle ground between a fixed-type model and an LLM; one runs under "Use it". Multi-stage prompting. Split the task: first extract candidate spans, then assign types and have the model check its own answers. FETA ("First Extract, Tag Afterwards", 2026) reports state-of-the-art biomedical NER this way with general-purpose LLMs. Dynamic prompting with RAG. Retrieve the most similar labeled examples from a small annotated seed set for every inference call; build the few-shot prompt on the fly. On biomedical NER with GPT-4 and Llama 3, this raised average F1 by about 7% (5-shot) and 6% (10-shot) over a fixed set of examples (Ge et al., 2025). Per-entity-type decomposition. For long documents, a single call that extracts all entity types at once loses recall as length grows. Run one extraction pass per entity type. Higher inference cost, substantially higher accuracy. This is the standard pattern for clinical notes and legal contracts. A sensible starting point: try a zero-shot model first (GLiNER on a CPU, or an LLM with a JSON schema), score it on a hundred hand-labelled examples, and fine-tune only if that falls short. For high-volume, fixed-type extraction, a fine-tuned encoder like the BERT model under "Use it" is still faster, cheaper and usually more accurate. Where classical NER still wins Even with LLMs available, classical NER wins when: Latency budget is under 50ms. You have thousands of labeled examples and a fixed set of types, and need the highest accuracy per millisecond. The domain has a stable ontology where a pretrained CRF or BiLSTM transfers well. Regulatory constraints require an on-prem, non-generative model. Where it falls apart Domain shift. A model trained on news (CoNLL-2003) loses much of its accuracy on legal contracts, tweets or clinical notes, where both the names and the writing style differ. Fine-tune on your domain, or start from a zero-shot model. Nested entities. "Bank of America Tower" is simultaneously an ORG and a FACILITY. Standard BIO cannot represent overlapping spans. You need nested NER (multi-pass or span-based models). Long entities. "United States Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation." Token-level models sometimes split this. Use aggregation_strategy or post-process. Sparse types. Medical NER labels like DRUG_BRAND, ADVERSE_EVENT, DOSE. General-purpose models have no idea. Scispacy and BioBERT are the starting points there. Recap What to keep from this lesson BIO labels turn span extraction into one label per token; evaluate on whole spans with precision, recall and F1. Gazetteers are precise but blind to new names; every learned model's real test is entities it never saw. HMMs score whole label sequences; CRFs add arbitrary features and learn BIO constraints from data. Fine-tuned BERT is the accuracy baseline for fixed types; its types are fixed by its training data. Zero-shot models (GLiNER, LLMs with a schema) handle new types on day one; measure them before trusting them. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Three production routes. Fine-tuned encoders (spaCy transformer pipelines, Hugging Face token classification) for high volume; GLiNER models that take entity types as text at run time for zero-shot extraction on CPUs; and LLMs with a JSON schema for complex or rare types. PII detection. Microsoft Presidio combines NER models and rules to find and redact personal data, a common pre-processing step before sending text to an LLM. Cloud APIs. AWS Comprehend, Azure AI Language and Google Cloud Natural Language provide managed NER with custom-entity training. Sources: spaCy , GLiNER , Microsoft Presidio , AWS Comprehend . In plain words first The idea in one line Grammar was unfashionable for a while. Then every LLM pipeline needed to validate structured extraction, and it came back. The problem In plain words first Part-of-speech (POS) tagging labels every word with its grammatical role: noun, verb, adjective, and so on. Parsing goes one step further and works out how the words connect: which word is the subject of which verb, which adjective describes which noun. Both matter because the same word can play different roles ("I saw a saw"), and many later steps, from finding a word's dictionary form to pulling facts out of text, need to know which role it plays here. This lesson builds the two classic taggers from counts (the simplest possible baseline, then a hidden Markov model), measures them on a million words of real English, and then uses spaCy's parser to draw sentence structure and extract information from it. Lesson 5.1 promised that lemmatization needs a part-of-speech tag. Without knowing running is a verb, a lemmatizer cannot reduce it to run . Without knowing better is an adjective, it cannot reduce to good . That promise hid a whole subfield. Part-of-speech tagging assigns grammatical categories. Syntactic parsing recovers the sentence's tree structure: which word modifies which, which verb governs which arguments. Classical NLP spent twenty years refining both. Then deep learning collapsed them into a token-classification task on top of a pretrained transformer, and the research community moved on. Not the applied community. Tags and parses are still the cheap, deterministic layer under many pipelines: lemmatization, rule-based extraction ("which adjective describes which product"), query understanding, and annotation for the hundreds of languages that have treebanks but no large model of their own. Worth knowing. This lesson introduces the tagsets, the baselines, and the point where you stop implementing from scratch and call spaCy. The idea POS tagging labels each token with a grammatical category. The Penn Treebank (PTB) tagset is the English default. 36 tags with distinctions the casual reader finds fussy: NN singular noun, NNS plural noun, NNP proper noun singular, VBD verb past tense, VBZ verb 3rd person singular present, and so on. The Universal Dependencies (UD) tagset is coarser (17 tags) and language-agnostic; it became the default for cross-lingual work. Copy Syntactic parsing produces a tree. Two major styles: Constituency parsing. Noun phrases, verb phrases, prepositional phrases nest inside each other. Output is a tree of non-terminal categories (NP, VP, PP) with words as leaves. Dependency parsing. Each word has a single head word it depends on, labeled with a grammatical relation. Output is a tree where every edge is a (head, dependent, relation) triple. Dependency parsing won in the 2010s because it generalizes cleanly across languages, especially free-word-order ones. Copy Step 1 · most-frequent-tag baseline The dumbest POS tagger that works. For each word, predict the tag it had most often in training. Copy On the Brown corpus it reaches about 90% with Brown's full set of 471 tags and about 95% with the 12 coarse universal tags (both measured under "Use it"). That sounds high, but the easy words ("the", "of", ".") make up much of every sentence; the baseline is the floor below which no serious model should fall. They cannot capture that saw is a noun in "I bought a saw" but a verb in "I saw the movie." On the Penn Treebank's Wall Street Journal test set, a CRF or maximum-entropy tagger with rich features (suffix, word shape, neighbouring words) reaches about 97.3%, and BiLSTM or transformer taggers about 97.5 to 98%. The ceiling on this task is set by annotator disagreement. Human annotators agree about 97% of the time on Penn Treebank. Scores much above that mostly mean a model has learned the quirks of one test set's annotators. Step 4 · dependency parsing sketch Full dependency parsing from scratch is out of scope; the canonical textbook treatment is in Jurafsky and Martin. Two classical families to know: Transition-based parsers (arc-eager, arc-standard) act like a shift-reduce parser: they read tokens, shift them onto a stack, and apply reduce actions that create arcs. Greedy decoding is fast. Classic implementation is MaltParser. Modern neural version: Chen and Manning's transition-based parser. Graph-based parsers (Eisner's algorithm, Dozat-Manning biaffine) score every possible head-dependent edge and pick the maximum spanning tree. Slower but more accurate. Worked example An arc-standard parse by hand A transition-based parser keeps a stack , a buffer of unread words and a set of arcs, and applies one of three actions: SHIFT (move the next word to the stack), LEFT-ARC (the top word becomes head of the word below it, which is popped) and RIGHT-ARC (the word below becomes head of the top word, which is popped). For "cats chase mice": Step Stack Buffer Action Arc added 1 [] cats chase mice SHIFT 2 [cats] chase mice SHIFT 3 [cats, chase] mice LEFT-ARC chase → cats (nsubj) 4 [chase] mice SHIFT 5 [chase, mice] RIGHT-ARC chase → mice (obj) 6 [chase] done: chase is the root A sentence of words always takes actions here ( shifts and arcs; parsers that start with a ROOT symbol on the stack add one more arc, for ), so parsing is linear time. The model's only job is to pick the next action from the current stack and buffer; Chen and Manning (2014) made that choice with a small neural network, which is close to what spaCy's parser does today. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Universal Dependencies keeps growing. Release 2.19 (November 2026) has over 200 treebanks in over 150 languages, all with the same 17 POS tags and relation labels, which is what makes cross-lingual tools like spaCy, Stanza and trankit possible. Parsers next to LLMs. LLMs can tag and parse when asked, but a pipeline that needs the same structure millions of times a day, deterministically and in milliseconds, still runs a dedicated parser; the LLM handles the open-ended parts. Transformer pipelines are the default. spaCy's *_trf and Stanza's models put a pretrained transformer under the tagger and parser; the small CNN-based *_sm pipeline used here trades a few points of accuracy for speed. Source: Universal Dependencies . Where this still matters in 2026 Lemmatization. Lesson 5.1 needs POS to lemmatize correctly. Always. Structured extraction from LLM outputs. Validate that a generated sentence respects grammatical constraints (e.g., subject-verb agreement, required modifiers). Aspect-based sentiment. Dependency parses tell you which adjective modifies which noun. Query understanding. "movies directed by Wes Anderson starring Bill Murray" decomposes into structured constraints via the parse. Cross-lingual transfer. UD tags and dependency relations are language-agnostic, enabling zero-shot structured analysis of new languages. Low-compute pipelines. If you cannot ship a transformer, POS + dependency parse + gazetteer gets you surprisingly far. Recap What to keep from this lesson POS tags label grammatical role in context; UD's 17 tags work across languages, Penn Treebank's 36 are English-specific. The most-frequent-tag baseline is strong (about 95% on coarse tags); measure every tagger against it. An HMM multiplies transition and emission probabilities and decodes with Viterbi in words × tags² time. Unknown words and context-dependent ambiguity are where simple taggers fail; features (CRF) and context (transformers) fix them. A dependency parse gives each word one head and a relation; simple rules over it extract aspects, query constraints and lemmas.
