Solutions Solution P1 · The baseline wins on unknown words The most-frequent-tag baseline is right on roughly 60% of unknown words, simply because most unknown words are nouns, while the HMM gets well under half of them. With add-alpha smoothing, an unseen word's emission probability is about alpha divided by the tag's total count, which is larger for rare tags, so the HMM drifts toward rare tags exactly when it knows least. Real HMM taggers fix this with a separate model for unknown words based on suffixes and capitalisation, the same trick as the shape feature in Lesson 5.6. Solution B1 · The same tags for every sentence of the same length With no emission term, the words have no influence, and Viterbi returns the single most probable tag chain from the transition table: DET NOUN ADP DET NOUN … for any sentence of that length. "I saw the movie yesterday ." and "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog ." come out as the same repeating pattern. The transition table only knows what tag sequences look like; the emissions are what tie the tags to the actual words. In plain words first The idea in one line Convolutions learn n-grams. Recurrences remember. Both are superseded by attention. Both still matter on constrained hardware. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means TextCNN CNN for text Stack of 1D convolutions over word embeddings with global max-pool. Kim (2014). RNN Recurrent net Hidden state updated at each time step: h_t = f(W x_t + U h_{t-1}) . LSTM Gated RNN Adds input / forget / output gates + a cell state. Trains stably through long sequences. GRU Simpler LSTM Two gates instead of three. Similar accuracy, fewer parameters. Bidirectional Both directions Forward + backward RNN concatenated. Every token sees both sides of its context. Vanishing gradient Training signal dies Repeated multiplication by <1 weights in plain RNNs makes early-step gradients effectively zero. The problem In plain words first A bag of words throws word order away, so "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" look identical. This lesson covers the two neural designs that first read words in order. A convolutional network (CNN) slides small learned windows over the sentence, each one acting as a pattern detector for a short phrase such as "not good at all". A recurrent network (RNN) reads one word at a time and carries a running memory forward; its improved versions, the LSTM and GRU, add learned gates that decide what to keep and what to forget, so the memory survives longer sentences. You will see the equations behind each, train both on real movie reviews, and measure the weakness that pushed the field to attention: a signal from early in a long sequence fades away as it travels. TF-IDF and Word2Vec produced flat vectors that ignored word order. A classifier built on them could not tell dog bites man from man bites dog . Word order sometimes carries the signal. Two families of architectures filled that gap before transformers arrived. Convolutional nets for text (TextCNN). Apply 1D convolutions over sequences of word embeddings. A filter of width 3 is a learnable trigram detector: it spans three words and outputs a score. Stack different widths (2, 3, 4, 5) to detect multi-scale patterns. Max-pool to a fixed-size representation. Flat, parallel, fast. Recurrent nets (RNN, LSTM, GRU). Process tokens one at a time, maintaining a hidden state that carries information forward. Sequential, memory-bearing, flexible input lengths. Dominated sequence modeling from 2014 to 2017, then attention happened. This lesson builds both, then names the failure that motivated attention. The idea TextCNN (Kim, 2014). Tokens get embedded. A width- k 1D convolution slides a filter over consecutive k -grams of embeddings, producing a feature map. Global max-pooling over that map picks the strongest activation. Concatenate max-pooled outputs from several filter widths. Feed to a classifier head. Why it works. A filter is a learnable n-gram. Max-pooling is position-invariant, so "not good" fires the same feature at the start or middle of a review. Three filter widths with 100 filters each gives you 300 learned n-gram detectors. Training is parallel; no sequential dependency. RNN. At each time step t , the hidden state h_t = f(W * x_t + U * h_{t-1} + b) . Share W , U , b across time. The hidden state at time T is a summary of the entire prefix. For classification, pool across h_1 ... h_T (max, mean, or last). Plain RNNs suffer vanishing gradients. The LSTM adds gates that decide what to forget, what to store, and what to output, stabilizing gradients through long sequences. The GRU simplifies LSTM to two gates; performs similarly with fewer parameters. Bidirectional RNNs run one RNN forward and another backward, concatenating hidden states. Every token's representation sees both left and right context. Essential for tagging tasks. The same idea as a formula Convolution over words. Step 1 · TextCNN in PyTorch Copy The transpose(1, 2) reshapes [batch, seq_len, embed_dim] to [batch, embed_dim, seq_len] because nn.Conv1d treats the middle axis as channels. The pooled output is fixed-size regardless of input length. Step 2 · LSTM classifier Copy Max-pool over the sequence, not last-state pool. For classification, max-pooling usually beats taking the last hidden state because information at the end of a long sequence tends to dominate the last state. Step 3 · the vanishing gradient demo (intuition) A plain RNN without gating cannot learn long-range dependencies. Consider a toy task: predict whether token A appeared anywhere in a sequence. If A is at position 1 and the sequence is 100 tokens long, the gradient from the loss has to flow back through 99 multiplications of the recurrent weight. If the weight is less than 1, the gradient vanishes. If more than 1, it explodes. Copy LSTMs fix this with a cell state that runs through the network with only additive interactions (the forget gate scales it multiplicatively, but gradients still flow along the "highway"). GRUs do something similar with fewer parameters. Both make long-range learning possible : the gradient can survive 100+ steps when the forget (or update) gates learn to stay near 1. It is not automatic; under "Use it" an untrained LSTM loses its gradient almost as fast as a plain RNN. The same idea as a formula Why the gradient vanishes, in one line Backpropagation through time multiplies one Jacobian per step. Step 4 · why this still was not enough Three problems persisted even with LSTMs. Sequential bottleneck. Training an RNN on a sequence of length 1000 requires 1000 serial forward/backward steps. Cannot parallelize across time. Fixed-size context vector in encoder-decoder setups. The decoder sees only the final hidden state of the encoder, compressed over the entire input. Long inputs lose detail. Lesson 5.9 covers this directly. Distant-dependency accuracy ceiling. LSTMs outperform plain RNNs but still struggle to propagate specific information across 200+ steps. Attention solved the second and most of the third, and transformers dropped recurrence to solve the first: every position is processed in parallel during training. (Recurrence came back later in a new form; see "What's current" below.) Lesson 5.10 is the pivot. Use it: the same idea with real libraries PyTorch's nn.LSTM , nn.GRU , and nn.Conv1d are production-ready. Training code is standard. A TextCNN or small LSTM has well under a million weights besides its embedding table; with a vocabulary trimmed to tens of thousands of words, the whole model is tens to hundreds of times smaller than BERT-base (110M parameters). Streaming / online classification. An RNN updates a fixed-size state per token, so cost and memory per token stay constant however long the stream runs. A transformer can also stream with a key-value cache, but its memory grows with the length of the context. That constant-cost property is exactly why recurrent layers are back in 2025 hybrid models. Tiny models for baselines. Fast iteration on a new task. Under "Use it", a TextCNN trains on 8,530 reviews in seconds per epoch on two CPU cores. Sequence labeling with limited data. BiLSTM-CRF (lesson 06) is still a production-grade NER architecture for 1k-10k labeled sentences. Everything else goes to a transformer. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Recurrence is back in production models, in a form that also trains in parallel. Hybrid production models. NVIDIA's Nemotron-H (2025) replaces most self-attention layers with Mamba-2 layers and reports up to three times the inference speed of similar-sized transformers; IBM's Granite 4.0 (October 2025) and AI21's Jamba are hybrid Mamba-transformer models offered commercially; Qwen3-Next (2025) mixes linear-attention Gated DeltaNet layers and standard attention 3:1, with over ten times the throughput of Qwen3-32B beyond 32K tokens of context. Why it matters. A recurrent state costs the same per token however long the context grows, while attention's key-value cache keeps growing. The gating ideas in this lesson's LSTM equations are the ancestors of those layers' update rules. LSTMs still ship in small on-device models (keyboard prediction, wake words, sensor streams), where their tiny state and low latency fit. Sources: Nemotron-H , IBM Granite 4.0 , Jamba , Qwen3-Next . Recap What to keep from this lesson A text CNN filter is a learned n-gram detector; max-pooling makes it position-invariant and gives a fixed-size vector. An RNN applies the same weights at every step; backpropagation through time multiplies one Jacobian per step, so gradients shrink or blow up exponentially. The LSTM's additive cell and learned forget gate let gradients survive, if the gates learn to stay open; the GRU does the same with two gates. Pretrained embeddings matter on small datasets; pool over all positions (max or mean) rather than reading a padded last step. Recurrence is sequential to train, which is what transformers removed; its constant cost per token is why it returned in 2025 hybrids. Solutions Solution P1 · About the same: both vanish At initialisation the LSTM's gradient at the first position is as negligible as the plain RNN's (both around or smaller in the run). The LSTM's advantage is not built in; it comes from forget gates near 1. PyTorch starts the forget bias at 0, so the gate starts at about 0.5 and the cell halves its contribution every step. With the forget bias set to 3 the curve flattens immediately. In training, gates learn to open, which is why trained LSTMs handle dependencies that plain RNNs cannot. Solution B1 · It reads padding, and accuracy collapses Reviews are padded at the end with token 0, so for a 20-token review the last output comes after 30 padding steps. The padding embedding is zero, but the LSTM still updates its state at every step through its biases and recurrent weights, so the review's content must survive 30 extra multiplications to influence the output. Under "Use it" the last-step model ends far below the pooled ones. Fixes: pool over positions (max or mean with a mask), take the output at each review's true last token, or use nn.utils.rnn.pack_padded_sequence so the LSTM stops at each sequence's real length. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Two RNNs pretending to be a translator. The bottleneck they hit is the reason attention exists. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Encoder Input RNN Reads source. Produces per-step hidden states and a final context vector. Decoder Output RNN Initialized from context vector. Generates target tokens one at a time. Context vector The summary Final encoder hidden state. Fixed size. The bottleneck attention solves. Teacher forcing Use true tokens Feed the ground-truth previous token at training time. Stabilizes learning. Exposure bias Train/test gap Model trained on true tokens never practiced recovering from its own mistakes. Beam search Better decoding Keep top-k partial sequences alive at each step instead of committing greedily. The problem In plain words first Translation turns a sequence into a different sequence, with a different length and in a different vocabulary. The sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) design does it with two networks. An encoder reads the whole input and condenses it into a summary. A decoder writes the output one token at a time, each time looking at the summary and at what it has written so far. Training shows the decoder the correct previous word ("teacher forcing"). At use time it has to rely on its own guesses, which is a source of errors. Choosing the output is itself a search problem, because the best first word does not always lead to the best sentence. This lesson writes the equations behind all of that, works through greedy and beam search by hand, and runs a pretrained translation model to see where its decoder looks. Classification maps a variable-length sequence to a single label. Translation maps a variable-length sequence to another variable-length sequence. The input and output live in different vocabularies, possibly different languages, with no guarantee of length parity. The seq2seq architecture (Sutskever, Vinyals, Le, 2014) cracked this with a deliberately simple recipe. Two RNNs. One reads the source sentence and produces a fixed-size context vector. The other reads that vector and generates the target sentence token by token. Same code you wrote for lesson 08, glued together differently. This is worth studying for two reasons. First, the context-vector bottleneck is the most pedagogically useful failure in NLP. It motivates everything attention and transformers are good at. Second, the training recipe (teacher forcing, scheduled sampling, beam search at inference) still applies to every modern generation system including LLMs. The idea Encoder. An RNN that reads the source sentence. Its final hidden state is the context vector — a fixed-size summary of the entire input. Lose nothing but the source, supposedly. Decoder. Another RNN initialized from the context vector. At each step it takes the previously generated token as input and produces a distribution over the target vocabulary. Sample or argmax to pick the next token. Feed it back in. Repeat until an <EOS> token is produced or max length is hit. Training: Cross-entropy loss at each decoder step, summed over the sequence. Standard backprop through time through both networks. Teacher forcing. During training, the decoder's input at step t is the ground-truth token at position t-1 , not the decoder's own previous prediction. This stabilizes training: without it, an untrained decoder's early mistakes become its next inputs, the targets no longer line up with what it is reading, and learning is slow and unstable. At inference, you have to use the model's own predictions, so there is always a train/inference distribution gap. That gap is called exposure bias . The bottleneck. Everything the encoder learned about the source must be squeezed into that one context vector. Long sentences lose detail. Rare words get blurred. Reordering (chat noir vs. black cat) has to be memorized, not computed. Attention (lesson 10) fixes this by letting the decoder look at every encoder hidden state, not just the last one. That is the whole pitch. The same idea as a formula What the model computes. For a source ​ , … , x n ​ ) and target ​ , … , y m ​ ) ending in <EOS> , the chain rule of probability gives ∏ m ​ P ( y t ​ ∣ y 1 ​ , … , y t − 1 ​ , x ) The encoder turns into a context (here the last hidden state, e n c ​ ). The decoder keeps its own state ​ = GRU ( s t − 1 ​ , embed ( y t − 1 ​ )) with ​ = c , and predicts ​ ∣ y < t ​ , x ) = softmax ( W s t ​ + b ) . Training. Maximise the log-likelihood of the reference translation, which is the same as minimising the summed cross-entropy: ∑ m ​ lo g P ( y t ​ ∣ y < t ​ , x ) With teacher forcing, the ​ fed to the decoder are the reference tokens, so every step's loss can be computed even when the model would have guessed wrong. Exposure bias. At inference the condition becomes the model's own output, ​ < t ​ . The model was never trained on its own mistakes, so one wrong token can push it into states it has never seen. Scheduled sampling (Bengio et al., 2015) feeds the model's own predictions with a probability that grows during training. Decoding is a search. Check your mental model ✗ "Greedy decoding finds the most likely output." ✓ It finds the output made of locally best choices. The worked example's greedy answer is three times less likely than beam search's. ✗ "A wider beam is always better." ✓ Wider beams find higher-probability outputs, and the most probable output is not always the best one: for translation, very wide beams return shorter and blander outputs, and an exact search can even return an empty one (Stahlberg and Byrne, 2019). ✗ "Teacher forcing is a trick for inference." ✓ It is a training-time choice. At inference there is no reference, so the decoder always reads its own outputs. Step 1 · an encoder Copy outputs has shape [batch, seq_len, hidden_dim] — one hidden state per input position. hidden has shape [1, batch, hidden_dim] — the final step. Lesson 5.8 said "pool over outputs for classification." Here we keep the last hidden state as the context vector, and ignore the per-step outputs. Step 2 · a decoder Copy Decoder is called one step at a time. Input: a batch of single tokens and the current hidden state. Output: vocabulary logits for the next token and the updated hidden state. Step 3 · training loop with teacher forcing Copy Two knobs worth naming. ignore_index=0 skips loss on padding tokens. teacher_forcing_ratio is the probability of using the true token vs. the model's prediction at each step. Start at 1.0 (full teacher forcing) and anneal down to ~0.5 over training to close the exposure-bias gap. Step 4 · inference loop (greedy) Copy Greedy decoding picks the highest-probability token at every step. It can wander off: once you commit to a token, you cannot unsay it. Beam search keeps the top- k partial sequences alive and picks the highest-scoring complete one at the end. Beam width 3-5 is standard, with a length penalty so the search does not prefer short outputs. Predict before you run Under "Use it", the worked example's decoder table is searched exactly, over every output up to 6 tokens long, using raw probabilities with no length penalty. The decoder is not reading one compressed summary; it is looking back at every encoder state. That is the fix for the bottleneck, and the subject of the next lesson. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Decoder-only won for general LLMs. Most chat models generate from one stack that reads prompt and output together; the encoder-decoder split survives where inputs and outputs are clearly separate: speech recognition (Whisper, NVIDIA Canary), translation (NLLB, MADLAD-400, Marian models in on-device and offline translators) and some summarisation and search models. The training recipe carried over. Teacher forcing is how every LLM is pretrained (predict token from the true tokens before it), and exposure bias is one motivation for the reinforcement-learning stage after pretraining, which scores whole generated outputs. Sources: Whisper , NLLB , MADLAD-400 , Marian NMT . When to still reach for RNN-based seq2seq Almost never, for new projects. Specific exceptions: Streaming translation where you consume input one token at a time with bounded memory. On-device text generation where transformer memory cost is prohibitive. Pedagogy. Understanding the encoder-decoder bottleneck is the fastest path to understanding why transformers won. Exposure bias and its mitigations Scheduled sampling. Anneal teacher forcing ratio during training so the model learns to recover from its own mistakes. Minimum risk training. Train on sentence-level BLEU score instead of token-level cross-entropy. Closer to what you actually want. Reinforcement learning fine-tuning. Reward the sequence generator with a metric. Used in modern LLM RLHF. All three still apply to transformer-based generation. Recap What to keep from this lesson Seq2seq factorises token by token: an encoder summarises the source, a decoder generates conditioned on it. Training maximises log-likelihood with teacher forcing; inference reads its own outputs, which creates exposure bias. Decoding is a search: greedy takes local bests, beam search keeps hypotheses, and a length penalty stops it preferring short outputs. The fixed-size context vector is the bottleneck; attention lets the decoder look at every encoder state instead. The same recipe, minus the separate encoder, is how decoder-only LLMs are trained and decoded. Task Write beam_search(step_fn, bos_id, eos_id, beam_width, max_len, length_penalty=0.0) . A hypothesis is a tuple of token ids and a raw score. The search starts with one alive hypothesis: the tuple (bos_id,) with score 0. The raw score of a hypothesis is the sum of ​ ∣ t < i ​ ) over its generated tokens. Repeat at most max_len times: For each alive hypothesis, call step_fn(tokens) once. It returns the log-probs of the next token, a float array of length . Make one candidate for each alive hypothesis and each token id from 0 to . The candidate score is the parent score plus the log-prob of the token. Sort all candidates by raw score, highest first. For equal scores, the smaller token tuple comes first, in Python tuple order. Keep the first beam_width candidates. A kept candidate that ends with eos_id is finished. The other kept candidates are the new alive hypotheses. Stop when no hypothesis is alive. After the loop, the hypotheses that are still alive are also part of the result. Each hypothesis then gets its final score , where is the raw score, is the number of generated tokens (BOS does not count, EOS counts) and is length_penalty . With the final score is the raw score. The length penalty does not change the pruning in step 3. Return every finished hypothesis as a list of (tokens, final_score) pairs. Sort the list by final score, highest first. For equal scores, the smaller token tuple comes first. The first pair is the answer of the search. Reference solution and notes Copy Why beam search helps Greedy decoding commits to the best token at each step. In the toy model, token 1 has the highest first probability, but every token after it is unlikely. Token 2 is a little worse at first, and EOS after it has probability 0.9. Width 2 keeps both paths alive long enough to see this. What beam search does not promise Beam search is a heuristic. A beam wide enough to keep every hypothesis is an exhaustive search, but any narrower beam can miss the best sequence. A wider beam often finds a better sequence, but this is not a theorem: a new candidate can push out a hypothesis that a narrower beam keeps and later extends to a better finish. Length normalization Each log-prob is 0 or less, so a raw score only goes down as a sequence grows. Without a correction, beam search prefers short outputs. Division by removes part of that bias. Read it to see what the model attended to. The problem In plain words first In Lesson 5.9 the decoder only ever saw one summary vector of the whole input, and long inputs did not fit. Attention removes that limit. At every output step the decoder asks a question ("which input words matter for what I am about to write?"), scores every input position against that question, turns the scores into weights that add up to 1, and takes the weighted average of the encoder's states. The summary is rebuilt fresh for every output word. This lesson writes out the equations for the two classic scoring functions (additive and multiplicative), works through one step by hand, shows why transformers divide the scores by ​ , and looks inside a trained translation model at how its attention heads divide the work. Lesson 5.9 ended on the bottleneck. In the classic copy-task experiment, a GRU encoder-decoder that copies short inputs almost perfectly falls towards chance as the inputs grow long. The reason is structural, not a training bug: every bit of information the encoder gleaned has to fit in one fixed-size hidden state, and the decoder never sees anything else. Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio published a three-line fix in 2014. Instead of giving the decoder only the final encoder state, keep every encoder state. At each decoder step, compute a weighted average of encoder states where the weights say "how much does the decoder need to look at encoder position i right now?" That weighted average is the context, and it changes every decoder step. That is the whole idea. Transformers extended it. Self-attention applied it to a single sequence. Multi-head attention ran it in parallel. But the 2014 version already broke the bottleneck, and once you have it, the pivot to transformers is engineering, not conceptual. The idea At each decoder step t : Use the previous decoder hidden state s_{t-1} as a query . Score it against every encoder hidden state h_1, ..., h_T . One scalar per encoder position. Softmax the scores to get attention weights α_{t,1}, ..., α_{t,T} that sum to 1. Context vector c_t = Σ α_{t,i} * h_i . Weighted average of encoder states. Decoder takes c_t plus the previous output token, produces the next token. The weighted average is the point. When the decoder needs to translate "Je" to "I", it weights the encoder state over "Je" high and the others low. When it needs "not", it weights "pas" high. The context vector reshapes each step. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) The scoring function is settled; the engineering is not. Every production LLM uses scaled dot-product attention. FlashAttention (2022) and FlashAttention-3 (2024) compute exactly the same result without writing the weight matrix to memory, and grouped-query attention shares keys and values across heads to shrink the cache; both are defaults in vLLM, SGLang and PyTorch's scaled_dot_product_attention . Attention sinks are now an architecture feature. Trained transformers put large weight on the first token or other fixed tokens regardless of content; OpenAI's open-weight gpt-oss models add a learned "sink" term to every attention head, and sliding-window serving keeps the first tokens for the same reason. Linear-attention and Mamba-style layers replace the softmax over all positions with a fixed-size state; Lesson 5.8's "What's current" box lists production hybrids. You will misread it without knowing Bahdanau's convention. Fine-grained alignment analysis in MT. Raw attention weights are an interpretability tool even on transformer models, and reading them requires knowing what they are. The attention-weight-as-explanation trap Attention weights look interpretable. They are weights that sum to one across positions; you can plot them; high means "looked at this." Reviewers love them. They are not as interpretable as they look. Jain and Wallace (2019) showed that attention distributions can be permuted and replaced by arbitrary alternatives without changing model predictions for some tasks. Wiegreffe and Pinter (2019) answered that attention is not useless as explanation either: for some tasks the weights cannot be swapped freely without hurting the model, so it depends on the model and task. Never report attention weights as evidence of reasoning without an ablation or counterfactual check. Recap What to keep from this lesson Attention: score every encoder state against the decoder's query, softmax the scores, and average the states with those weights; a new context at every step. Additive (Bahdanau) scores use a small network; dot and general (Luong) scores use products; transformers use scaled dot products. Divide dot-product scores by ​ , or softmax saturates as the dimension grows; subtract the maximum before exponentiating. Mask padding with before the softmax so padded positions get zero weight. Attention gives each output a direct path to every input, which fixes the bottleneck and the long gradient path; its weights are a hint, not proof, of what a model used. Debug a failure An attention module between an encoder and a decoder runs without any exception, but the model's accuracy slowly falls behind the reference implementation. When you print the context tensor, its second dimension is the encoder length instead of the decoder length. Walk me through the diagnosis. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A module that runs and still produces the wrong shape is a broadcast bug, and a silent broadcast is the worst attention bug because it degrades accuracy instead of crashing. Write the expected shapes first: scores and weights are batch by decoder length by encoder length, and the context is batch by decoder length by the encoder state width. Then find the matmul whose operands were swapped or not transposed, fix it with one transpose or reshape, and add asserts on the shapes and on the weights summing to one. The shape table. Tensor Shape Encoder states H (T_enc, d_h); d_h is twice the hidden size for a bidirectional encoder Decoder state s (d_s,) Score for one encoder position scalar Weights after the softmax (T_enc,) for one decoder step Context vector (d_h,), the same shape as one encoder state Batched over decoder steps, the weights are (batch, T_dec, T_enc) and the context is (batch, T_dec, d_h) . How the wrong shape appears. The context is weights @ H . If the code built the scores as H @ H.T because the query tensor was replaced by the encoder states, the shapes still multiply and the result has the encoder length where the decoder length belongs. Nothing raises. Downstream layers broadcast or reshape the tensor and the loss keeps falling, just more slowly. The diagnosis steps. Print the shape of every intermediate tensor and compare with the table. Check the score formula. For the additive form the projection vector collapses an attention-dimension vector to a scalar; for the dot form the query and the key must have the same width, and a bidirectional encoder doubles the key width, so the dot form fails unless a matrix W sits between them. Check which decoder state feeds the query. One classic formulation uses the state before the current step and the other uses the state after it. Mixing them gives subtly wrong gradients that are very hard to see. Fix with one transpose, reshape or projection. Refuse any fix that only silences the mismatch by broadcasting. The regression test. Copy The third line catches a softmax taken over the wrong axis, which is the other silent bug in this layer. Plausible wrong answers. "Reshape the output to the expected shape and continue." The values inside are wrong; a reshape only hides the mismatch. "Lower the learning rate; the model is just unstable." The run is not unstable; it is computing the wrong quantity. "Add a mask to fix the shape." A mask changes which positions get weight, not the layout of the tensor. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Which single test catches most attention bugs? Expected: the weights have shape batch by decoder length by encoder length and sum to one along the last axis. (level 2) The score matrix comes out square in the encoder dimension. What happened? Expected: the keys were scored against themselves; the query tensor was replaced by the encoder states. (level 3) Why does the plain dot score fail with a bidirectional encoder? Expected: the encoder state is twice the hidden width, so it no longer matches the decoder state; use the general form with a matrix between them. (level 3) Why is the state convention a gradient problem and not a shape problem? Expected: both states have the same shape, so nothing fails; the gradient flows to the wrong step and the model learns a slightly wrong alignment. Where it is taught. The attention mechanism lesson gives the shape table and the shape-debugging prompt, and the self-attention lesson gives the projections. Explain the mechanism A paper draft shows attention heatmaps as proof that the model "reasons over the right tokens". You are the reviewer. What do you say about the heatmaps, and what would convince you that a given head does something specific? Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Attention weights are a distribution over positions, and on their own they are not an explanation: for some tasks they can be permuted or replaced by arbitrary alternatives without changing the prediction, so a heatmap shows where mass went, not that it mattered. Ask for an ablation or a counterfactual, zero or shuffle the head and show that the prediction moves. The head roles that have survived probing are specific and testable: heads that attend to the previous token, copy heads, and induction heads that find an earlier occurrence of the current token and copy what followed it. The caveat from the literature. A 2019 study showed that on some tasks the attention distribution can be permuted, or swapped for an adversarial alternative, while the output stays the same. The lesson's rule follows: never report attention weights as evidence of reasoning without an ablation or a counterfactual check. Reviewers like heatmaps because they are easy to read; that is a reason to be careful, not a reason to accept them. What a head can show you. The inspection hook in the lesson's block returns the per-head weights of shape (B, H, T, T) . In a trained model the patterns differ by head: some attend to the token just before, some to the start of the sequence, some spread almost uniformly. Those are descriptions. Turning a description into a claim takes an intervention. The evidence that convinces. Ablation. Zero the head's output or replace its weights with a uniform row and measure the change in loss or in the specific prediction. A head that matters moves the number. Counterfactual input. Change the token the heatmap points at and show that the output changes in the direction the story predicts. A behavioral test for the claimed role. For an induction head, feed a random token sequence repeated twice and show that the head attends from each token to the token that followed its first occurrence, and that ablating the head removes the copying. Replication across seeds and prompts. One heatmap on one example is an anecdote. What to write in the review. Ask the authors to keep the heatmaps as illustration and to add the intervention results as the evidence. If the ablation does not move the prediction, the heatmap was decoration. Plausible wrong answers. "A high weight means the token caused the output." Weight shows where the lookup went; causation needs an intervention. "Average the heads to get the model's attention." Heads do different things; the average hides the roles and still is not evidence. "If the heatmap matches human intuition, the model reasons like a human." Agreement with intuition is not a test; the permutation result shows intuitive maps can be irrelevant to the output. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) A head attends almost uniformly across positions. What does that tell you? Expected: little on its own; it may carry an average or nothing, and only an ablation says which. (level 3) Describe a test for an induction head in one sentence. Expected: repeat a random token sequence and check that the head attends from each token to the token after its earlier occurrence, with ablation removing the copy behavior. (level 4) Why can the weights be permuted without changing the output? Expected: the values at the attended positions may carry near-identical information, other heads may be redundant, and later layers can compensate. (level 4) What replaces the heatmap as the headline figure? Expected: the change in loss or in the target probability under ablation and counterfactual edits, with a band across seeds. Where it is taught. The attention mechanism lesson states the explanation trap, the multi-head lesson lists the probed head roles, and the attention capstone exposes the weights for inspection. Explain the mechanism A new teammate has read the word "attention" a hundred times and still cannot say what a query, a key or a value is. Explain the three to them in one minute. Then tell me what changed between the 2014 encoder-decoder version and the version inside a transformer. Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Attention is a soft lookup. Each token produces a query that asks for information, a key that says what the token holds, and a value that the token hands over when it is picked. The query is scored against every key, the scores go through a softmax, and the output is the weighted sum of the values. In the 2014 version the query was the decoder state and the keys and the values were the same encoder states; a transformer takes all three from one sequence through three learned projections. The three projections. For a sequence X of n tokens with d dimensions each: Copy Row i of the score matrix is one token's view of the whole sequence. The softmax turns the row into weights that sum to one. The output for token i is the weighted sum of all value vectors. The database picture. A real database matches a query to one key and returns one value. Attention matches a query to every key with a similarity score and returns a blend of every value. The blend is what lets the model combine information from several positions in one step. What the 2014 version had. The encoder-decoder attention of 2014 used the previous decoder state as the query and scored it against every encoder hidden state. The context vector was the weighted average of those same encoder states. In that design the keys and the values were the same thing. Two score functions were common: an additive score that passes the pair through a tanh and a learned vector, and a multiplicative score that takes a dot product. The three-line fix broke the fixed-size bottleneck of the encoder-decoder. What a transformer changed. Self-attention queries a sequence against itself, and it separates keys from values with different learned projections. Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel. The weighted sum of values is the same idea. The score function changes: the additive tanh score and the plain dot product give way to a dot product divided by the square root of the key width. Plausible wrong answers. "The key and the value must be the same vector." They were in the classic version, but a transformer learns separate projections for them. "Attention picks the single best matching token." The softmax gives a weight to every position, and the output blends all of the values. "The query comes from the encoder." In encoder-decoder attention the query comes from the decoder and the keys and the values come from the encoder. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) What shape does the output have for one token? Expected: the value dimension, because the output is a weighted sum of value vectors. (level 2) Why give keys and values separate projections? Expected: a token can be matched on one kind of information and return another kind. (level 2) Why does the plain dot-product score need the query and the key to have the same dimension? Expected: a dot product is only defined for vectors of equal length; the general form inserts a matrix W to remove that constraint. (level 3) Name the convention trap between the two classic score functions. Expected: one uses the decoder state before the current step and the other uses the state after it; mixing them produces subtly wrong gradients. Where it is taught. The attention mechanism lesson builds the classic version and the self-attention lesson builds the projections. Sources and further reading Bahdanau, Cho, Bengio (2014). Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate — the paper. Luong, Pham, Manning (2015). Effective Approaches to Attention-based Neural Machine Translation — the three score variants and their comparison. Jain and Wallace (2019). Attention is not Explanation — the interpretability caveat. Dive into Deep Learning — Bahdanau Attention — runnable walkthrough with PyTorch. a0511: Course home / Phase 5 · Working with Language Translating between languages Lesson 5.11 75 min Build Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 5 · 10 (Attention Mechanism), Phase 5 · 04 (GloVe, FastText, Subword) Type : Build. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Translation is the task that paid for NLP research for thirty years and keeps paying now. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means BLEU Translation score N-gram precision with brevity penalty. [0, 100]. chrF Character F-score Character-level F-score. More sensitive for morphologically rich languages. NMT Neural MT Transformer encoder-decoder trained on parallel text. The 2017+ default. NLLB No Language Left Behind Meta's 200-language MT model family. Constrained decoding Controlled output Force specific tokens or n-grams to appear / not appear in the output. Hallucination Invented content Model output that is not supported by the source. The problem In plain words first Machine translation (MT) is the seq2seq-with-attention design of the last two lessons, trained on millions of sentence pairs. Today you rarely build the model yourself. You pick a pretrained one, decode with beam search, and spend your effort on two harder questions. The first is how to tell whether a translation is good. Automatic scores such as BLEU and chrF count how many word or character sequences the output shares with a human reference translation; newer metrics use neural networks trained on human judgements. The second is how translations fail in ways a score will not show, such as a sentence that reads perfectly but says something the source never said. This lesson derives BLEU by hand, checks it against the standard library, runs a pretrained English-to-French model on a public news test set, and probes its typical failure modes. A model reads a sentence in one language and produces a sentence in another. Length varies. Word order varies. Some source words map to multiple target words and vice versa. Idioms refuse one-to-one mapping. "I miss you" in French is "tu me manques" — literally "you are lacking to me." No word-level alignment survives that. Machine translation is the task that forced NLP to invent encoder-decoders, attention, transformers, and eventually the whole LLM paradigm. Every step forward arrived because translation quality was measurable and the gap between human and machine was stubborn. This lesson skips the history lesson and teaches the working pipeline of 2026: pretrained multilingual encoder-decoder (NLLB-200 or mBART), subword tokenization, beam search, BLEU and chrF evaluation, and the handful of failure modes that still ship to production uncaught. The idea Modern MT is a transformer encoder-decoder trained on parallel text. The encoder reads the source in its language's tokenization. The decoder generates the target, one subword at a time, using the encoder's output via cross-attention (lesson 10). Decoding uses beam search to avoid the greedy-decoding trap. The output is detokenized, detruecased, and scored against a reference. Three operational choices drive real-world MT quality. Tokenizer. SentencePiece BPE trained on a mixed-language corpus. Shared vocabulary across languages is what enables zero-shot pairs in NLLB. Model size. NLLB-200 distilled 600M fits on a laptop. NLLB-200 3.3B is the largest dense checkpoint. The 54.5B mixture-of-experts model is the research ceiling. Decoding. Beam width 4-5 for general content. Length penalty to avoid too-short output. Constrained decoding when you need terminology consistency. Step 1 · a pretrained MT call Copy Watch out Not run on this page The NLLB-200 600M checkpoint is a 2.5 GB download, more than this page's build allows. The experiments below use the same transformers calls with a Marian model (Helsinki-NLP opus-mt-en-fr , 300 MB), which is English-to-French only and needs no language codes. Copy Three things matter here. src_lang tells the tokenizer which script and segmentation to apply. forced_bos_token_id tells the decoder which language to generate. Both are NLLB-specific tricks; mBART and M2M-100 use their own conventions and they are not interchangeable. Step 2 · BLEU and chrF BLEU measures n-gram overlap between output and reference. Four reference n-gram sizes (1-4), geometric mean of precisions, brevity penalty for too-short output. The score is in [0, 100]. Commonly used. Frustrating to interpret: rough folklore says 30 is "usable", 40 "good" and 50 "exceptional", but scores depend heavily on the language pair, the test set and how many references there are, so compare systems only on the same test set, and treat differences under about 1 BLEU as noise. chrF measures character-level F-score. More sensitive to morphologically rich languages where BLEU undercounts matches. Often reported alongside BLEU. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Always use sacrebleu . It normalizes tokenization so scores are comparable across papers. Rolling your own BLEU computation is how misleading benchmarks happen. The same idea as a formula BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002). For n-gram sizes , the clipped precision counts each hypothesis n-gram only as many times as it appears in the reference: ​ = ∑ g ∈ n-grams ( y ^ ​ ) ​ count y ^ ​ ​ ( g ) ∑ g ∈ n-grams ( y ^ ​ ) ​ min ( count y ^ ​ ​ ( g ) , count y ​ ( g ) ) ​ Precision alone would reward a one-word output, so a brevity penalty compares the hypothesis length with the reference length : e 1 − r / c ​ c > r c ≤ r ​ , BLEU = BP ⋅ exp ( 4 1 ​ n = 1 ∑ 4 ​ lo g p n ​ ) Corpus BLEU sums the clipped counts and lengths over all sentences before dividing, so it is not the average of sentence BLEUs. chrF (Popović, 2015) works on character n-grams (up to 6) with precision and recall averaged over , combined with , which weighs recall twice as much as precision: ​ = ( 1 + β 2 ) β 2 P + R P R ​ Because it matches pieces of words, "chats" and "chat" still share most of their character n-grams, which is why chrF is fairer to languages with rich morphology. The first experiment under "Use it" checks this number against sacrebleu . Check your mental model ✗ "BLEU measures whether the translation is correct." ✓ It measures n-gram overlap with one particular reference. A correct paraphrase can score low, and a fluent wrong translation that reuses the reference's words can score high. ✗ "Corpus BLEU is the average of sentence BLEU." ✓ Counts are pooled first, then divided; the two numbers differ, and sentence BLEU is very noisy. ✗ "A higher BLEU always means a better system." ✓ Only on the same test set, references and tokenization, and only for differences beyond the noise; learned metrics and human evaluation decide close calls. Predict before you run Under "Use it", the reference is "the cat is on the mat". Three hypotheses are scored: an exact copy, a correct paraphrase ("there is a cat sitting on the mat"), and the reference's words shuffled ("mat the on is cat the"). Rank them by BLEU, then by chrF. (Solution P1.) Build · The three-tier evaluation hierarchy (2026) Modern MT evaluation uses three complementary metric families. Ship with at least two. Heuristic (BLEU, chrF). Fast, reference-based, interpretable, insensitive to paraphrase. Use for legacy comparison and regression detection. Learned (COMET, BLEURT, MetricX; and the untrained BERTScore). COMET, BLEURT and MetricX are neural models fine-tuned to predict human quality judgements from the source, the translation and the reference; BERTScore instead compares contextual embeddings with no training on judgements. In the WMT metrics tasks, learned metrics agree with human judgements far better than BLEU, and COMET is the most widely reported. LLM-as-judge (reference-free). Prompt a large model to score translations on fluency, adequacy, tone, cultural appropriateness. GEMBA (Kocmi and Federmann, 2023) showed that GPT-4, prompted to score translations, ranked WMT22 systems in close agreement with human rankings; at the level of single segments it is much less reliable. Use for open-ended content where no reference exists. Practical 2026 stack: sacrebleu for BLEU and chrF, unbabel-comet for COMET, and a prompted LLM for the final human-facing signal. Calibrate every metric against 50-100 human-labeled examples before trusting it on production data. Reference-free metrics (COMET-QE, BLEURT-QE, LLM-as-judge) let you evaluate translations without a reference, which matters for long-tail language pairs where reference translations do not exist. Step 3 · what breaks in production The working pipeline above translates fluently most of the time and fails silently on a minority of inputs, and the failures are concentrated in exactly the content that matters (names, numbers, domain terms, rare languages). Named failure modes: Hallucination. Model invents content that was not in the source. Common in unfamiliar domain vocabulary. Symptom: output is fluent but claims facts the source did not state. Mitigation: constrained decoding on domain terms, human review on regulated content, monitoring for output much longer than input. Off-target generation. Model translates into the wrong language. NLLB is surprisingly prone to this on rare language pairs. Mitigation: verify forced_bos_token_id and always decode with a language-ID model check on output. Terminology drift. "Sign up" becomes "s'inscrire" in doc 1 and "créer un compte" in doc 2. For UI text and user-facing strings, consistency matters more than raw quality. Mitigation: glossary-constrained decoding or post-edit dictionary. Formality mismatch. French "tu" vs "vous", Japanese politeness levels. The model picks whichever form was more common in training. For customer-facing content this is usually wrong. Mitigation: prompt prefix with a formality token if the model supports it, or fine-tune a small model on formal-only corpora. Degenerate output on short or unusual input. Single words, UI labels and fragments are rare in sentence-level training data, and models sometimes answer them with an over-long or repetitive output. Mitigation: a hard maximum output length proportional to the source length, and a glossary for UI strings. Step 4 · fine-tuning for a domain Pretrained models are generalists. Legal, medical, or game-dialog translation benefits measurably from fine-tuning on domain parallel data. The recipe is not exotic: Copy A few thousand high-quality parallel examples beats a few hundred thousand noisy web-scraped ones. Quality of training data is the single largest production lever. Break it on purpose Compute BLEU yourself with a plain average of the four precisions, 1 ​ ∑ p n ​ , instead of the geometric mean, and with no brevity penalty. Then score the one-word hypothesis "the" against the reference "the cat sat on the mat". What do you get, and what does each missing piece of the real formula protect against? (Solution B1.) Use it: the same idea with real libraries The 2026 production stack for MT: Use case Recommended starting point Any-to-any, 200 languages facebook/nllb-200-distilled-600M (laptop) or nllb-200-3.3B (production) English-centric, high quality, 50 languages facebook/mbart-large-50-many-to-many-mmt Short runs, cheap inference, English-French/German/Spanish Helsinki-NLP / Marian models Latency-critical browser-side ONNX-quantized Marian (a few tens of MB) Maximum quality, willing to pay GPT-4 / Claude / Gemini with translation prompts General-purpose LLMs are now among the strongest MT systems: the WMT24 findings were titled "The LLM Era Is Here but MT Is Not Solved Yet", and WMT25's preliminary ranking put Gemini 2.5 Pro and GPT-4.1 at the top, with the biggest advantages on idiomatic content and whole documents. The tradeoff is per-token cost and latency. Pick an LLM when context length, stylistic consistency, or domain adaptation via prompting matters more than throughput. See it drawn BLEU and chrF up close sacrebleu checks the worked example, then scores three hypotheses against one reference, so you can see what each metric rewards. The shuffled words are nonsense but still collect 13 BLEU and 33 chrF from matching words and pieces of words. Both metrics rank the three in the right order here, but the gap between "correct but differently worded" and "word salad" is small, which is why learned metrics and human checks exist. A caution: OPUS contains public news text, so the model may have seen material like this, and its score here may be slightly optimistic. The probes are mixed. "I miss you" correctly becomes "Tu me manques", word order inverted. The customer request uses formal "vous", the model's habit, with no way to ask for "tu". "Save" becomes the verb "Enregistrer", right for a button, but only by luck, since there is no context. The medical sentence keeps dose, drug and date intact. The idiom fails: "Il pleut des chats et des chiens" is a word-for-word rendering that no French speaker would say (the idiom is "il pleut des cordes"), and it is fluent enough that a reader who does not know French would never notice. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) LLMs run commercial translation. DeepL moved its service to its own translation LLM (2024), Google Translate uses Gemini models, including live speech-to-speech translation, and general LLM APIs are a common choice for document translation with style and terminology instructions. Dedicated models remain. For high volume, on-device or offline translation, compact encoder-decoders (Marian, distilled NLLB) still win on cost and latency, and they are the default for the long tail of languages that big LLMs cover poorly. Quality estimation in production. Learned metrics such as COMET and MetricX score translations without a reference, so pipelines route low-scoring output to human post-editors. Sources: DeepL next-generation LLM , Gemini in Google Translate , NLLB , COMET , MetricX . Recap What to keep from this lesson Modern MT is a pretrained transformer encoder-decoder with a shared subword vocabulary, decoded with beam search and a length penalty. BLEU = brevity penalty times the geometric mean of clipped 1- to 4-gram precisions; chrF is a recall-weighted character n-gram F-score. Surface metrics punish valid paraphrases; use learned metrics (COMET, MetricX) and human checks for close calls, on the same test set only. Production failures are silent: hallucination, wrong language, inconsistent terms, wrong formality, damaged numbers and names. LLMs now lead quality benchmarks; dedicated models still win on cost, latency and coverage of rare languages. a0512: Course home / Phase 5 · Working with Language Making text shorter (summarisation) Lesson 5.12 75 min Build Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 5 · 02 (BoW + TF-IDF), Phase 5 · 11 (Translating between languages) Type : Build. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Extractive systems tell you what the document said. Abstractive systems tell you what the author meant. Different tasks, different pitfalls. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Extractive Pick sentences Return sentences verbatim from the source. Never hallucinates. Abstractive Rewrite Generate new text conditioned on source. Can hallucinate. ROUGE Summary metric N-gram / LCS overlap between system output and reference. TextRank Graph-based extractive PageRank over sentence similarity graph. Factuality Is it right Whether summary claims are supported by the source. Hallucination Made-up content Content in the summary that the source does not support. The problem In plain words first Summarization turns a long text into a short one. There are two ways to do it. Extractive summarization picks the most important sentences of the original and copies them out unchanged. Abstractive summarization writes new sentences, as a person would. Extractive output can never state something the source did not say, but it can be choppy and miss points spread across the text. Abstractive output reads well, but it can invent facts. This lesson builds TextRank, the classic extractive method, which scores sentences by how much they have in common with all the others, the same idea Google's PageRank used to rank web pages. It then compares TextRank with the simple "first three sentences" baseline and a small pretrained abstractive model on real news articles, and scores all three with ROUGE. Finally it shows the uncomfortable fact behind every summarization metric: a summary with a wrong number can score almost as well as a correct one. A 2,000-word news article lands in your feed. You need 120 words that capture it. You can either pick the three most important sentences from the article (extractive) or rewrite the content in your own words (abstractive). Both are called summarization. They are completely different problems. Extractive summarization is a ranking problem. Score every sentence, return the top- k . The output is always grammatical because it is lifted verbatim. The risk is missing content that is distributed across the article. Abstractive summarization is a generation problem. A transformer produces new text conditioned on the input. The output is fluent and compressive but may hallucinate facts that were not in the source. The risk is confident fabrication. This lesson builds both, with the failure mode each one owns. The idea Extractive. Treat the article as a graph where nodes are sentences and edges are similarities. Run PageRank (or something like it) over the graph to score sentences by how connected they are to everything else. Highest-scoring sentences are the summary. The canonical implementation is TextRank (Mihalcea and Tarau, 2004). Abstractive. Fine-tune a transformer encoder-decoder (BART, T5, Pegasus) on document-summary pairs. At inference, the model reads the document and generates the summary token-by-token via cross-attention. Pegasus in particular is pretrained with gap-sentence generation: whole important sentences are removed from a document and the model must write them back, a task very close to summarization, so it needs less fine-tuning data. Evaluation with ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation). ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-2 score unigram and bigram overlap. ROUGE-L scores longest common subsequence. Higher is better, but like BLEU the numbers only compare systems on the same dataset: on CNN/DailyMail news, strong systems reach ROUGE-1 in the low 40s, and even human-written alternative summaries do not score near 100. Every paper reports all three. Use the rouge-score package. The same idea as a formula TextRank builds a weighted graph with one node per sentence. Mihalcea and Tarau's similarity counts shared words, normalised by sentence length: ​ = lo g ∣ S i ​ ∣ + lo g ∣ S j ​ ∣ ∣ { w : w ∈ S i ​ and w ∈ S j ​ } ∣ ​ and the score of sentence is defined by the scores of the sentences that point to it, each sharing its score in proportion to edge weight: ​ ) = ( 1 − d ) + d i  = j ∑ ​ ∑ k ​ w ik ​ w ij ​ ​ WS ( S i ​ ) This is PageRank. Read as a random walk: a reader jumps from sentence to sentence following shared words, and with probability (0.15) jumps to a random sentence instead. The scores are the long-run share of time spent at each sentence, the stationary distribution of that walk, and repeating the update (power iteration) converges to it because the damping makes the walk mix. Sentences that share vocabulary with many central sentences are central themselves. ROUGE-N is recall of reference n-grams: ​ = ∑ g ∈ n-grams ( ref ) ​ count ref ​ ( g ) ∑ g ∈ n-grams ( ref ) ​ min ( count ref ​ ( g ) , count sum ​ ( g )) ​ with precision defined the same way over the summary's n-grams, and ​ their harmonic mean (what rouge-score reports as fmeasure ). ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence (LCS), words in the same order but not necessarily adjacent: recall , precision . Build · Beyond ROUGE (2026 summarization eval) ROUGE has been the dominant summarization metric for twenty years and it is insufficient on its own in 2026. The current landscape of alternatives: BERTScore (contextual embedding similarity) gained ground through 2023 and is now reported alongside ROUGE in most summarization papers. BARTScore treats evaluation as generation: score the summary by how likely a pretrained BART assigns it given the source. MoverScore (Earth Mover's Distance over contextual embeddings) matches summary and reference words by meaning rather than exact form, so paraphrases are not punished the way ROUGE punishes them. FactCC and QA-based faithfulness were common 2021-2023, now often replaced by G-Eval (a GPT-4 prompt chain that scores coherence, consistency, fluency, relevance with chain-of-thought reasoning). G-Eval and similar LLM-judge approaches correlate with human ratings much better than ROUGE or BERTScore: on the SummEval benchmark, G-Eval with GPT-4 reached a Spearman correlation of about 0.51 with human scores (Liu et al., 2023), still far from perfect agreement. Production recommendation: report ROUGE-L for legacy comparison, BERTScore for semantic overlap, G-Eval for coherence and factuality. Calibrate against 50-100 human-labeled summaries. Step 4 · the factuality problem Abstractive summaries are prone to hallucination. Extractive summaries carry a much lower hallucination risk because the output is lifted verbatim from the source, though they can still mislead if source sentences are decontextualized, outdated, or quoted out of order. This is the single biggest reason production systems still prefer extractive methods for compliance-adjacent content. Hallucination types to name: Entity swap. Source says "John Smith." Summary says "John Brown." Number drift. Source says "25,000." Summary says "25 million." Polarity flip. Source says "rejected the offer." Summary says "accepted the offer." Fact invention. Source does not mention the CEO. Summary says the CEO approved. Evaluation approaches that work: FactCC. A binary classifier trained on entailment between source sentence and summary sentence. Predicts factual/not-factual. QA-based factuality. Ask a QA model questions whose answers are in the source. If the summary supports different answers, flag. Entity-level F1. Compare named entities in source vs summary. Entities present only in the summary are suspect. For anything user-facing where factuality matters (news, medical, legal, financial), extractive is the safer default. Abstractive needs a factuality check in the loop. Using TF-IDF cosine similarity, or penalising length, are the usual fixes. The entity check catches the changed amount and the invented name, because neither appears in the source, but it is blind to "rejected", which reverses the meaning without adding any new entity. That is why serious summarization evaluation layers a faithfulness check (entailment-based, question-answering based, or an LLM judge) on top of overlap metrics, and why extractive methods stay the default where a false statement is unacceptable. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Summaries are a built-in product feature. Meeting, email and document summaries ship in Microsoft 365 Copilot, Google Workspace with Gemini and Zoom, all generated zero-shot by LLMs; reference-based ROUGE is least reliable exactly for these systems, so teams evaluate with human ratings and LLM judges. Grounding checks as a guardrail. Managed checks such as Amazon Bedrock Guardrails' contextual grounding check and Azure AI Content Safety's groundedness detection, or Vectara's open HHEM model, flag summary sentences not supported by the source. Extractive-then-abstractive. For long or regulated documents, a common pattern is to extract the relevant sentences first, then let a model rewrite only those, so every claim can be traced to a source sentence. Sources: Bedrock contextual grounding check , Azure groundedness detection , Vectara HHEM , G-Eval . Recap What to keep from this lesson Extractive = rank and copy sentences (safe, choppy); abstractive = generate new text (fluent, can invent facts). TextRank is PageRank on a sentence-similarity graph: the stationary distribution of a random walk with damping. ROUGE-N is n-gram recall/precision against a reference; ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence. Always compare with the lead-3 baseline; on news it is hard to beat. Overlap metrics cannot see factual errors: add entity, entailment or LLM-judge faithfulness checks. Solutions Solution P1 · t5-small, with lead-3 close behind In the run, t5-small scores highest on all three ROUGE variants, lead-3 is a few points behind, and TextRank is far behind both. The surprise for most people is how strong lead-3 is: news puts the key facts first, and CNN/DailyMail's highlights restate the opening, so copying the first three sentences was a famously hard baseline in the early abstractive-summarization papers. A model needs to be trained on the genre, as t5-small was, to beat it. TextRank optimises centrality, not position, and on this data its preference for long, word-rich sentences picks quotations. Solution B1 · Every sentence scores the same With , the update is ​ ) = 1 − 0 = 1 for every sentence, whatever the graph: the random walk always teleports and never follows an edge. All scores tie at 1.0, sorted keeps the original order for ties, and the "summary" is simply the first top_k sentences, lead-3 by accident. The damping factor is the only thing that lets the graph structure influence the scores; at the walk never teleports, which can trap all the score in a disconnected cluster, which is why PageRank uses a value in between. In plain words first The idea in one line Three systems shaped modern QA. Extractive found spans. Retrieval-augmented grounded them in documents. Generative produced answers. Every modern AI assistant is a mix of the three. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Extractive QA Find the answer span Predict start and end indices of the answer within a given passage. Open-domain QA QA over a corpus No given passage; must retrieve then answer. RAG Retrieve then generate Retrieval-augmented generation. Retriever + reader pipeline. SQuAD Canonical benchmark Stanford Question Answering Dataset. EM + F1 metrics. Hallucination Made-up answer Reader output not supported by retrieved context. Refusal calibration Know when to shut up System correctly says "I don't know" when unable to answer. The problem In plain words first Question answering (QA) means giving a direct answer to a question, such as "June 29, 2007", rather than a document that might contain it. The classic approach, extractive QA, is given a passage and points at the answer inside it. A model reads the question and passage together and scores every word as a possible start and end of the answer, and the best-scoring stretch of text is the answer. Since 2018 models can also say "this passage does not contain the answer". When there is no passage, a retriever first finds relevant ones in a large collection, which is the "R" in RAG (retrieval-augmented generation). This lesson writes out the span-prediction math, rebuilds the answer step that newer transformers versions removed, measures a real model on SQuAD 2.0 (including the questions it should refuse), and shows that in a retrieve-then-read system the retriever often limits the accuracy. A user types "When did the first iPhone launch?" and expects "June 29, 2007." Not "Apple's history is long and varied." Not "2007" sitting in isolation with no sentence. A direct, grounded, correct answer. Three architectures have dominated QA over the last decade. Extractive QA. Given a question and a passage that is known to contain the answer, find the start and end indices of the answer span in the passage. SQuAD is the canonical benchmark. Open-domain QA. The passage is not given. Retrieve the relevant passage first, then extract or generate an answer. This is the bedrock of every RAG pipeline today. Generative / Closed-book QA. A large language model answers from its parametric memory. No retrieval. Fastest at inference, least reliable on facts. The trend in 2026 is hybrid: retrieve the best few passages, then prompt a generative model to answer grounded in those passages. That is RAG, and lesson 14 covers the retrieval half in depth. This lesson builds the QA half. The idea Extractive. Encode question and passage together with a transformer (BERT family). Train two heads that predict start and end token indices of the answer. Loss is cross-entropy over valid positions. Output is a span from the passage. Never hallucinates (by construction), never handles questions the passage cannot answer (by construction). Retrieval-augmented (RAG). Two stages. First, a retriever finds the top- k passages from a corpus. Second, a reader (extractive or generative) produces the answer using those passages. The retriever-reader split lets each be trained and evaluated independently. Modern RAG often adds a reranker between them. Generative. A decoder-only LLM (GPT, Claude, Llama) answers from learned weights. No retrieval step. Excellent on common knowledge, catastrophic on rare or recent facts. The hallucination rate is inversely correlated with fact frequency in the pretraining data. The same idea as a formula Span prediction. The question and passage are encoded together, <s> question </s></s> passage </s> , giving one vector ​ per token. Two learned vectors ​ , w e ​ score every token as a start and as an end: ​ e w s ⊤ ​ h k ​ e w s ⊤ ​ h i ​ ​ , P ( end = j ) = ∑ k ​ e w e ⊤ ​ h k ​ e w e ⊤ ​ h j ​ ​ Training minimises ) − lo g P ( end = j ∗ ) for the true span , j ∗ ) . At inference, the answer is the span with the best total logit, under two constraints: it must lie inside the passage, and for a maximum length : , j ^ ​ ) = ar g i ≤ j < i + L max ​ ( w s ⊤ ​ h i ​ + w e ⊤ ​ h j ​ ) No answer. SQuAD 2.0 models are trained to put both start and end on the first token for unanswerable questions, so ⊤ ​ h 0 ​ + w e ⊤ ​ h 0 ​ . Answer only if the best span beats the null score by a margin , which you tune on held-out data to trade wrong answers against wrong refusals. Metrics. After normalising both strings (lowercase, strip punctuation and the articles a, an, the), Exact Match is 1 if they are identical. Token F1 treats them as bags of tokens: precision , recall , ​ = 2 PR / ( P + R ) . With several gold answers, take the best score over them. For an unanswerable question, both metrics are 1 only if the prediction is empty. Retrieve then read. If the retriever puts the right passage in its top with probability and the reader is right on a correct passage with probability , end-to-end accuracy is at most : the reader cannot answer from a passage it never sees. Worked example EM and F1 by hand Gold answer "June 29, 2007", prediction "on June 29th, 2007". Normalise: gold tokens june 29 2007 ; prediction tokens on june 29th 2007 (punctuation removed; "on" is not an article, so it stays). Exact Match: the strings differ, so EM = 0 . Common tokens: june , 2007 , so 2. Precision , recall . ​ = 2 × 0.5 × 0.667/ ( 0.5 + 0.667 ) = 0.571 . A correct answer earns 0 EM and 0.57 F1 because of "on" and "th". That is why SQuAD reports both, and why production QA uses human or LLM judgement for answer correctness. Explicitly telling the model to ground in the context and return "I don't know" when the context is insufficient measurably reduces unsupported answers compared with naive prompting, though by how much depends heavily on the model and the data, so measure it on your own questions. More elaborate patterns add citations, confidence scores, and structured extraction. Step 4 · evaluation that reflects the real world SQuAD uses Exact Match (EM) and token-level F1 . EM is a strict match after normalization (lowercase, strip punctuation, remove articles) — either the prediction matches exactly or it scores 0. F1 is computed over token overlap between prediction and reference and gives partial credit. Both under-credit paraphrases: "June 29, 2007" vs "June 29th, 2007" typically gets 0 EM (the ordinal breaks normalization) but still earns substantial F1 from overlapping tokens. For production QA: Answer accuracy (LLM-judged or human-judged, since metrics do not capture semantic equivalence). Citation accuracy. Does the cited passage actually support the answer? Trivial to check automatically with string match between generated citations and retrieved passages. Refusal calibration. When the answer is not in the retrieved passages, does the system correctly say "I don't know"? Measure false confidence rate. Retrieval recall. Before evaluating the reader, measure whether the retriever gets the right passage into the top- k . A reader cannot fix a missing passage. Build · RAGAS: the 2026 production eval framework RAGAS is a widely used open-source framework built for RAG systems. Its four core metrics use an LLM as the judge; three of them need no gold answer: Faithfulness. Does each claim in the answer come from the retrieved context? Measured by having an LLM split the answer into individual claims and check each one against the context. Your primary hallucination metric. Answer relevance. Does the answer address the question? Measured by generating hypothetical questions from the answer and comparing to the real question. Context precision. Of the retrieved chunks, what fraction were actually relevant? Low precision = noise in prompt. Context recall. Did the retrieved set contain all needed information? This one compares against a reference answer, so it needs a labelled set. Low recall = reader cannot succeed. Reference-free scoring lets you evaluate on live production traffic without curated gold answers. Layer LLM-as-judge on top for open-ended questions where exact-match metrics are useless. pip install ragas . Plug your retriever + reader. Get four scalars per query. Alert on regressions. The reader's F1 falls from 89 with the gold passage to 66.5 with the top retrieved one, almost exactly the gold-passage score times the recall@1 ( ): given the wrong passage, it answers confidently from the wrong text. This is the "retrieve then read" bound from the formula box, and it gets worse as the corpus grows, which is why the next lesson is entirely about retrieval, and why production systems pass several passages to the reader or rerank them first. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) RAG is the default architecture, and agentic RAG is the frontier. Instead of one retrieve-then-read pass, models now decide when to search, rewrite queries and read several sources in a loop (the "deep research" products of 2025), with citations to the passages used. Long context did not make retrieval obsolete. Models with context windows of hundreds of thousands of tokens can read whole document sets, but benchmarks keep showing accuracy dropping for facts buried in the middle of long inputs, and cost grows with every token, so retrieval still decides what the model reads. Evaluation is LLM-judged and claim-level. Frameworks such as RAGAS score faithfulness by checking each claim of the answer against the retrieved text, and the RAG evaluation literature splits errors into retrieval failures and generation failures, as the last experiment did. SQuAD 2.0 adds "no answer": compare the best span with the null score and tune the margin. EM and token F1 after normalisation; both under-credit correct paraphrases. In retrieve-then-read, end-to-end accuracy is capped by retrieval recall; measure the retriever first. RAG evaluation checks faithfulness, relevance and retrieval quality separately, increasingly with LLM judges.
