Document which question types benefit most. Solutions Solution P1 · It drops a lot On the answerable half, forcing a span changes little, since the model would have answered anyway. On the unanswerable half, every question now gets a span, and every span scores 0, because the correct answer is "no answer". With about half the questions unanswerable, overall F1 falls by tens of points (the run prints both). The lesson: when a system can be asked things its sources do not contain, the ability to abstain is worth as much as the ability to answer. Solution B1 · The answer can come from the question Without the restriction, the span can start or end in the question or on special tokens. Asked about a passage that does not mention the iPhone, the model may "answer" with a piece of the question itself, such as "the first iPhone", or with a span that runs from the question into the passage, which turns into a character range that makes no sense in the passage. The sequence_ids check is what makes extractive QA extractive: only passage tokens are valid answers, and the first token is reserved for "no answer". Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Explain the mechanism You write the search step of a retrieval pipeline. A teammate wants to rank chunks by the raw dot product between the query vector and each chunk vector. What do you use instead, and when is the dot product the right choice? Level 1 of 4 · about 5 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Use cosine similarity, which is the dot product divided by the lengths of the two vectors. It measures only the angle, so a long chunk and a short chunk compete on direction and not on size. The raw dot product is right only when the vector length carries meaning that you want to reward. Three measures. Measure What it does Behavior Cosine the cosine of the angle between two vectors, from -1 to 1 ignores length, the default for retrieval Dot product the sum of the products of each pair of values longer vectors score higher L2 distance the straight-line distance between the two points smaller is closer, sensitive to length Cosine normalizes by length, so chunks of different sizes compare on direction alone. When someone says vector search, they almost always mean cosine. The code. Copy The guard returns zero when a vector has no length, so an empty chunk does not divide by zero. When the two agree. Many embedding models return unit-length vectors, or the caller asks for normalized output. The question-answering lesson encodes with normalization on and then ranks with a plain matrix product. With unit vectors the dot product equals the cosine, so the cheaper operation gives the same order. Plausible wrong answers. "The dot product and the cosine give the same order." Only when every vector has the same length; otherwise longer vectors win on the dot product. "A smaller cosine means a closer match." A larger cosine means a smaller angle; smaller is closer only for a distance such as L2. "Use whatever the vector store defaults to." The measure must match how the vectors were produced and normalized, so check the embedder before the store. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) What do the values 1, 0 and -1 mean for cosine? Expected: the same direction, orthogonal, and opposite directions. (level 2) Your embedder returns unit vectors. Does the choice still matter? Expected: no, because with unit vectors the dot product and the cosine are equal, which is why the lesson normalizes and then uses a matrix product. (level 2) Why does L2 distance treat a long and a short chunk differently? Expected: it measures the straight-line distance, so a longer vector sits farther away even when it points the same way. (level 3) When would you keep the raw dot product on purpose? Expected: when the model was trained so that length carries a signal, such as more content in a longer document, and you want that signal in the rank. Where it is taught. The lesson RAG defines the three measures and the guard, and the lesson question answering ranks normalized vectors with a matrix product. Explain the mechanism Two answer-grade metrics sit in your RAG eval report: faithfulness and answer relevance. A teammate says they measure the same thing and wants to drop one. Explain what each one grades, and give one answer that scores high on one and low on the other. Level 2 of 4 · about 7 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Faithfulness asks whether each claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved context. Answer relevance asks whether the answer addresses the question. A grounded summary of the retrieved chunks that never gets to the question scores high on faithfulness and low on relevance, and a short direct answer from the model's own memory scores high on relevance and low on faithfulness. How each one is computed. Metric Input to the judge Output Faithfulness one claim from the answer, plus the retrieved context yes or no, aggregated to the fraction of claims that pass Answer relevance the question, plus the answer does the answer address the question The eval splits the answer into sentence-shaped claims first. Faithfulness is also called groundedness, support or attribution. In its production form, the question answering lesson describes it as entailment between claim and context, and relevance as generating hypothetical questions from the answer and comparing them with the real one. Why both stay. Each one catches a failure the other cannot see: Faithfulness catches an invented fact, because the fact has no support in the context. Relevance catches an answer that wandered, because the judge never sees the context and only asks whether the question was answered. The diagnosis table in the eval lesson uses the pair. High MRR with low faithfulness points at the generation prompt. High faithfulness with low relevance points at the query rewriter or the prompt. No gold answer needed. Both are judged against the context and the question, not against a reference answer. That lets you score live traffic without labels, next to context precision and context recall for the retrieval side. The offline stand-in. The lesson ships a deterministic judge based on token overlap above a threshold, so the eval runs with no network call. It cannot read meaning, so production swaps it for a model judge from a different family than the generator. Plausible wrong answers. "They are the same, a faithful answer is relevant." A faithful answer can summarize the context and ignore the question. "Relevance is enough when retrieval is good." Relevance never sees the context, so an answer from the model's own memory can be relevant and ungrounded. "Faithfulness needs a gold answer." It is judged against the retrieved context, which is why it works on live traffic. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Which of the two catches a hallucination? Expected: faithfulness, because an invented fact has no support in the retrieved context. (level 2) Low relevance with high faithfulness points at which stage? Expected: the query rewriter or the generation prompt; the context was about something else, or the answer drifted from the question. (level 3) Why does neither metric need a reference answer? Expected: both are judged against the context and the question, which is what makes them usable on live traffic. (level 3) What is the limit of the lesson's offline judge? Expected: it counts token overlap above a threshold, so it cannot read meaning; production uses a model judge, from a different family than the generator. Where it is taught. The lesson RAG evaluation defines both metrics and the stand-in judge, and the lesson question answering gives the production forms. Debug a failure Your faithfulness score comes from a model that reads each claim next to the retrieved context and answers yes or no. The score has sat near the top for a month, yet reviewers keep finding invented facts in sampled answers. The generator and the judge are the same model. What is going on, and what do you change? Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A judge from the same family as the generator grades its own output as more faithful than it is, so the number stays high while the samples show the truth. Switch the judge to a different model family or hand-grade a sample, and add a sample-level review, because a per-sentence check can pass while the whole answer misleads. How the metric is built. The eval splits the answer into sentence-shaped claims, asks the judge whether each claim is supported by the retrieved context, and reports the fraction that pass. The lesson ships a deterministic stand-in judge based on token overlap so the eval runs offline, and swaps in a model call in production. The question answering lesson describes the production form: entailment between each claim and the context, with no gold answer needed. Two blind spots. Judge bias. A model judges the output of its own family as more faithful than it is. The lesson's rule: use a different model family for the judge than for the generator, or hand-grade a sample. Micro-checks miss macro-claims. Each sentence can be supported while the answer as a whole draws a conclusion that the context does not. Add a sample-level qualitative review on top of the automated metric. What to change. Change the judge family, then measure the disagreement between the old judge and the new one on the same fixture. The lesson's exercise does the same between the mock judge and a real model. Hand-grade a fixed sample each week and treat it as the calibration set for the automated score. Consider graded faithfulness with three values, unsupported, partially supported and fully supported, instead of a yes or no. Keep answer relevance next to faithfulness. A grounded answer to the wrong question is strong on one metric and weak on the other. Plausible wrong answers. "The score is high, so the reviewers are wrong." The score is one model's opinion of its own family's output; the sampled answers are the ground truth. "Make the judge stricter and the problem goes away." A stricter prompt or threshold does not remove a bias toward the judge's own family; only another family or a human sample does. "Replace faithfulness with answer relevance." They measure different things; relevance asks whether the answer addresses the question and says nothing about grounding. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) How do you size the judge problem before you change anything? Expected: hand-grade a sample of claims and measure the disagreement between the judge and the human labels. (level 3) Every sentence passes but the answer as a whole misleads. Which check catches that? Expected: a sample-level qualitative review in addition to the per-claim metric. (level 4) Why can a high faithfulness score sit next to a useless answer? Expected: faithfulness compares the answer with the context and not with the question, so a grounded off-topic answer scores high on faithfulness and low on relevance. (level 4) The team wants the strongest model available as judge, and it is also the generator. What do you say? Expected: pick the judge for independence first; a strong judge of its own family is still biased, so use another family and keep a human-graded calibration sample. Where it is taught. The lesson RAG evaluation names judge bias and the macro-claim gap, and the lesson question answering describes entailment-based faithfulness in production. Explain the mechanism A user reports that the document assistant gave a wrong answer. The pipeline has a chunker, a retriever, a reranker and a generator. You get one metric to look at before anything else. Which one, and why that one? Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Recall at k on the retrieval stage. If the gold chunk is not in the top k, no reranker can bring it back and the generator usually lacks the evidence for the right answer, unless another chunk happens to hold it, so the later metrics are hard to read. Recall comes first in the order, but it is not a gate: when recall holds, or when another retrieved chunk holds the evidence, move on to the rank position and then to the generated text, because a failure there stays hidden otherwise. The two retrieval metrics. Precision at k asks what share of the top k is gold. If the gold set has three documents and the top 3 returns two of them plus one wrong one, precision at 3 is 2 / 3. Recall at k asks what share of the gold set is in the top k. If the top 5 holds all three gold documents, recall at 5 is 1.0. Production teams quote recall. The generator can ignore an extra chunk with ease. It cannot invent an answer from a chunk it never saw. The order of the checks. Symptom Likely cause What to fix Low recall and low precision the chunker cut the answer or the retriever cannot find it chunk boundaries or the retrieval modality Decent recall, low MRR the right chunk is in the top k but not at position 1 the reranker High MRR, low faithfulness the generator invents content despite the right context the generation prompt, cite or refuse High faithfulness, low relevance the answer is grounded but off topic the query rewriter or the prompt All four high, users still complain the eval set does not represent real queries add real user queries to the qrels Keep the eval cheap. Tier the qrels: a smoke set of 20 queries that runs in CI, a regression set of 200 that runs nightly, and a deep set of 2000 that runs weekly. Treat a recall regression like a failing test. Plausible wrong answers. "Read the answer and judge it." The answer alone cannot tell which of the four stages failed. "Precision at k, because the noise caused the wrong answer." Precision matters once the right chunk is present; a missing chunk is the first thing to rule out. "Faithfulness, because the model hallucinated." A faithful answer to the wrong chunks is still wrong; faithfulness only grades the generator against what it saw. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) What does precision at k add once recall is fine? Expected: it shows how much of the returned list is noise, which matters when a wrong chunk poisons the answer or wastes tokens. (level 2) Recall at 5 is fine but the gold chunk sits at rank 4 or 5. Which metric shows that, and which stage do you fix? Expected: MRR, and the reranker. (level 3) Recall averages 90 percent and one team still complains every day. What is hidden? Expected: one query class that always misses; slice the qrels by class, such as literal, paraphrased and multi-topic, and report each slice. (level 3) How do you keep the eval fast enough to run on every change? Expected: tiers, with a smoke set of 20 queries in CI, 200 nightly and 2000 weekly. Where it is taught. The lesson RAG evaluation defines the metrics and the diagnosis table, and the lesson question answering says to measure the retriever before the reader. Defend a design Your document assistant answers every question, including the ones the corpus does not cover, and the invented answers are the ones users remember. Design the path that lets the system say it does not know, and say how you measure that the path works. Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Log the reranker's rank-1 score for every query and refuse when it falls below a corpus-specific threshold, instead of handing weak chunks to the generator. Tell the generator to answer only from the snippets, to cite every claim and to say it does not know when the snippets do not answer. Measure refusal calibration: on questions whose answer is not in the store, count how often the system refuses, and track the false confidence rate. Gate 1: before generation. The reranker lesson logs the rank-1 cross-encoder score. A query whose top score sits below a corpus-specific threshold is an out-of-domain hit, and the end-to-end lesson refuses on it: the generator returns the refusal text with no citation. The production capstone calls this an unsure mode and measures the drop in false confidence. The question answering lesson starts simpler, with a threshold on the top retrieval similarity, and tunes it on a held-out set. Gate 2: inside generation. The prompt tells the model to use only the snippets, to cite every claim with its anchor, and to say it does not know when the snippets do not answer. The question answering lesson measured that the explicit grounding and refusal instruction cuts hallucination by 40 to 60 percent against a naive prompt. Gate 3: after generation. Parse the answer and check each claim against the passage that its anchor cites. A claim without an anchor, or with an anchor whose passage does not state the claim, is dropped or sent back for a re-ask. An answer that slipped past the score gate then cannot ship a claim that its cited passage does not support. How to measure it. Refusal calibration. On a set of questions with no answer in the store, the share that the system refuses. False confidence rate. The share of those questions that got an answer anyway. Wrong refusal rate. On in-corpus questions, the share refused. A threshold that is too high fails here. Move the threshold on the held-out set, never on production anecdotes, and re-tune it when the embedder, the reranker or the corpus changes. Plausible wrong answers. "Tell the model to be careful." An instruction cannot see the retrieval scores; the first gate belongs before generation. "Refuse when retrieval returns fewer than k chunks." A count is not confidence; weak chunks still fill k slots. "Set the threshold once from the fixture." It is corpus specific and moves when the embedder, the reranker or the corpus changes. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Where does the threshold come from? Expected: the distribution of rank-1 scores on a held-out set with known in-corpus and out-of-corpus questions; it is specific to the corpus. (level 3) What does the generator prompt need beyond "use only the context"? Expected: cite each claim with its anchor and say it does not know when the snippets do not answer; the explicit instruction cut hallucination by 40 to 60 percent in the question answering lesson. (level 4) Too many refusals are also a failure. How do you balance it? Expected: track the false confidence rate on out-of-corpus questions next to the wrong refusal rate on in-corpus questions, and move the threshold on the held-out set. (level 4) How does the citation post-filter work with the refusal gate? Expected: each claim is checked against the passage its anchor cites, and a claim with no anchor or with a passage that does not state it is dropped or re-asked, so a weak answer that passed the score gate cannot ship an unsupported claim. Where it is taught. The lesson end-to-end RAG builds the refuse path and the cited generator, the lesson question answering defines refusal calibration, the capstone production RAG adds the unsure mode, and the lesson cross-encoder logs the rank-1 score. In plain words first The idea in one line BM25 is precise but brittle. Dense casts a wide net but misses keywords. Hybrid is the 2026 default. Everything else is tuning. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means BM25 Keyword search Okapi BM25. Scores documents by term frequency, IDF, and length. Dense retrieval Vector search Encode query + doc into vectors, find nearest neighbors. Bi-encoder Embedding model Encodes query and doc independently. Fast at query time. Cross-encoder Reranker model Encodes query + doc together. Slow but accurate. RRF Rank fusion Combine two rankings by summing 1/(k + rank) . Recall@k Retrieval metric Fraction of queries where a relevant doc is in the top-k. The problem In plain words first Information retrieval (IR) means finding the few documents, out of thousands or millions, that answer a query. It is the first half of every search box and every RAG system. There are two families of methods. Keyword (sparse) retrieval, with BM25 as the classic, scores documents by the query words they contain, weighting rare words more. It is fast and exact, but blind to synonyms. Dense retrieval turns queries and documents into vectors with a neural network and looks for nearby vectors. It understands paraphrases, but can miss an exact code, name or number. Production systems run both, merge the two ranked lists, and then re-score the best few candidates with a slower, more accurate model. This lesson derives BM25, builds each stage, and measures every combination on a real scientific-claims benchmark with 5,000 documents and expert relevance labels. The user types "what happens if someone lies to get money" and expects to find the statute that actually covers that: cheating, Section 318 of India's Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (which replaced the long-famous Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code in July 2024). A keyword search misses it entirely (no shared vocabulary). A semantic search misses it if the embeddings were not trained on legal text. Real search has to handle both. IR is the pipeline under every RAG system, every search bar, every docs site's fuzzy lookup. The 2026 architecture that works in production is not a single method. It is a chain of complementary methods, each catching the failures of the one before. This lesson builds each piece and names which failures each catches. The idea Four layers. Pick the ones you need. Sparse retrieval (BM25). Fast, precise on exact matches, terrible on semantics. Run over an inverted index. Sub-10ms per query on millions of documents. Gets you statute references, product codes, error messages, named entities right. Dense retrieval. Encode query and documents into vectors. Nearest neighbor search. Captures paraphrases and semantic similarity. Misses exact keyword matches that differ by one character. Most of the per-query time is encoding the query with the neural model (milliseconds on a GPU, tens of milliseconds on a CPU); the nearest-neighbour search itself takes milliseconds even over millions of vectors with FAISS or a vector database. Fusion. Merge the ranked lists from sparse and dense. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) is the easy default because it ignores raw scores (which live in different scales) and only uses rank positions. Weighted fusion is an option when you know one signal dominates for your domain. Cross-encoder rerank. Take the top-30 from fusion. Run a cross-encoder (query + document together, scoring each pair). Keep the top-5. Cross-encoders are slower per pair than bi-encoders but far more accurate. You amortize by only running them on the top-30. Three-way retrieval (BM25 + dense + learned-sparse like SPLADE) has beaten two-way combinations in published comparisons (IBM's "Blended RAG", 2024), but needs infrastructure for learned-sparse indexes. For most teams, two-way plus cross-encoder rerank is the sweet spot. Check your mental model ✗ "Dense retrieval replaces BM25." ✓ They fail on different queries. Exact identifiers, rare names and new terms favour BM25; paraphrases favour dense. Under "Use it" the fusion of both beats either alone. ✗ "RRF needs the two systems' scores on the same scale." ✓ It uses only ranks, which is exactly why it is the default: BM25 scores and cosine similarities are not comparable. ✗ "A cross-encoder is just a better embedding model." ✓ It produces no reusable document vectors at all; it must run on every pair at query time, so it can only rerank a shortlist. Predict before you run Under "Use it", on 300 scientific-claim queries over 5,183 abstracts: which will score higher on nDCG@10, plain BM25 or the small dense model all-MiniLM-L6-v2 ? (Solution P1.) Step 1 · BM25 from scratch Copy Two parameters worth knowing. k1=1.5 controls term-frequency saturation; higher means more weight on term repetition. b=0.75 controls length normalization; 0 ignores document length, 1 fully normalizes. These are the common defaults (Robertson and colleagues suggested $k_1$ between 1.2 and 2.0 and $b = 0.75$); tuning them per collection gains a little, usually much less than adding a dense retriever. Step 2 · dense retrieval with a bi-encoder Copy L2-normalize embeddings so dot product equals cosine. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is 384-dim, fast, and strong enough for most English retrieval. For multilingual work, use paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2 . For top accuracy, bge-large-en-v1.5 or e5-large-v2 . Step 3 · Reciprocal Rank Fusion Copy The k=60 constant comes from the original RRF paper. Higher k flattens the contribution of rank differences; lower k makes top ranks dominate. 60 is the published default and rarely needs tuning. Break it on purpose Replace RRF with a plain sum of the raw scores: BM25 score plus cosine similarity for each document. On a typical query, BM25 scores run from 0 to about 20 and cosines from about 0.2 to 0.8. What does the "fused" ranking turn into? (Solution B1.) Step 4 · hybrid search + rerank Copy Three stages composed. BM25 finds lexical matches. Dense finds semantic matches. RRF merges the two rankings without needing score calibration. Cross-encoder rescores the top-30 using query-document pairs together, which captures fine-grained relevance the bi-encoder missed. Keep top-5. Step 5 · evaluation Metric Meaning Recall@k Of queries where the correct document exists, how often is it in the top-k? MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank) Average of 1/rank of first relevant document. nDCG@k Accounts for relevance gradations, not just binary relevant/not. For RAG specifically, Recall@k of the retriever is the most important number. Your reader cannot answer if the right passage is not in the retrieved set. Debugging tip: for failing queries, diff the sparse and dense rankings. If one finds the right document and the other does not, you have a vocabulary mismatch (fix: add the missing half) or a semantic ambiguity (fix: better embeddings or a reranker). Use it: the same idea with real libraries The 2026 stack: Scale Stack 1k-100k docs In-memory BM25 + all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings + RRF. No separate DB. 100k-10M docs FAISS or pgvector for dense + Elasticsearch / OpenSearch for BM25. Run in parallel. 10M+ docs Qdrant / Weaviate / Vespa / Milvus with hybrid support. Cross-encoder rerank on top-30. Best-quality frontier Three-way (BM25 + dense + SPLADE) + ColBERT late-interaction reranking Whatever you pick, budget for evaluation. Benchmark retrieval recall before benchmarking end-to-end RAG accuracy. A reader cannot fix what the retriever missed. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output BM25 puts Section 318 first, but look at why: the only shared word is "to" ("lies to get money" and "induce them to deliver"), a stop word that happens to be rarer in this tiny corpus than in real text. Remove stop words and BM25 scores every law 0: the query and the statute share no meaningful vocabulary. The dense model ranks cheating first because "lies to get money" and "deceiving … to deliver any property" mean similar things. The cross-encoder agrees on the order, although all its scores are strongly negative: trained on web search queries and passages, it judges none of these legal one-liners a good answer to the casual question, and only the relative order counts. Small corpora make keyword search look luckier than it is. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Embedding models are much stronger than MiniLM. The MTEB leaderboard's retrieval track is led by multi-billion-parameter embedding models (Qwen3-Embedding topped the multilingual board in June 2025), and API models (OpenAI, Gemini, Cohere, Voyage) and compact open models such as BGE and GTE beat MiniLM by a wide margin. Rerankers are a standard stage. Hosted rerankers (Cohere Rerank, Voyage, Jina) and open cross-encoders (BGE reranker) reorder the top results of hybrid search; they usually add more quality than changing the embedding model. Learned sparse and late interaction in search engines. Elastic's ELSER and OpenSearch's neural sparse models add learned term expansion to inverted indexes, and Vespa serves ColBERT-style late interaction. Agentic search. In agentic RAG a model rewrites the query, searches several times and decides when it has enough, so retrieval becomes a tool the model calls. Sources: MTEB , Qwen3-Embedding , Cohere Rerank , ELSER , Vespa ColBERT . The hard-won lessons from 2026 production RAG Many RAG failures trace to ingestion and chunking, not the model. Teams spend weeks swapping LLMs and tuning prompts while the retrieval quietly returns the wrong context every third query. Fix chunking first. Chunking strategy matters more than chunk size. Fixed-size splits break tables, code, and nested headers. Sentence-aware is the default; semantic or LLM-based chunking pays off for technical docs and product manuals. Parent-doc pattern. Retrieve small "child" chunks for precision. When multiple children from the same parent section appear, swap in the parent block to preserve context. This consistently lifts answer quality without retraining. Pass only a few reranked chunks. A handful (often 3 to 5) is a common sweet spot: every extra chunk adds token cost and latency, and irrelevant chunks can distract the reader. Measure where the curve flattens for your data; if many more chunks keep helping, the reranker is probably weak. HyDE / query expansion. Generate a hypothetical answer from the query, embed that, retrieve. Bridges the phrasing gap between short questions and long documents. Free precision lift with no training. Set a context budget. Decide a maximum number of retrieved tokens per answer; if queries keep hitting it, the reranker threshold is probably too loose. Version everything. Prompts, chunking rules, embedding model, reranker. Any drift silently breaks answer quality. CI gates on faithfulness, context precision, and unanswered-question rate block regressions before users see them. Three-way retrieval (BM25 + dense + learned-sparse like SPLADE) can beat two-way , especially for queries mixing proper nouns with meaning. Ship it when your infrastructure supports SPLADE indexes and your evaluation shows the gain. These are rules of thumb from practitioners, not laws; check each on your own evaluation set. The robust lesson underneath them: most RAG quality problems are retrieval problems, so improve and measure retrieval before tuning the model. Recap What to keep from this lesson BM25: idf times a saturating, length-normalised term frequency; precise on exact terms, blind to synonyms. Dense retrieval: cosine similarity of learned embeddings; good at paraphrase, can miss exact identifiers, depends on training domain. RRF merges ranked lists by rank alone ( ); no score calibration needed. Cross-encoders read query and document together: most accurate, too slow for anything but reranking a shortlist. Evaluate with recall@k, MRR and nDCG on labelled queries; measure retrieval before end-to-end RAG. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line LDA: documents are mixtures of topics, topics are distributions over words. BERTopic: documents cluster in embedding space, clusters are topics. Same goal, different decompositions. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Topic A thing the corpus is about A probability distribution over words (LDA) or a cluster of similar documents (BERTopic). Mixed membership Doc is multiple topics LDA assigns each document a distribution over all topics. UMAP Dimensionality reduction Manifold learning that preserves local structure; used in BERTopic. HDBSCAN Density clustering Finds variable-size clusters; produces "noise" label (-1) for outliers. c_v coherence Topic quality metric NPMI of top topic words over sliding windows, turned into context vectors and compared with cosine similarity. The problem In plain words first Topic modeling finds the themes in a pile of documents without anyone labelling them. You give it, say, two thousand forum posts. It gives back a handful of topics, each described by its most typical words ("space, nasa, launch, orbit"), and tells you which topics each post is about. LDA, the classic method, imagines that every document was written by picking topics from a personal mix and then picking words from those topics, and works backwards from the words to the mix. BERTopic, the modern method, turns each document into a meaning vector, groups similar vectors into clusters, and describes each cluster by the words that are unusually common in it. This lesson writes out LDA's generative story and its sampling update, works through the word-weighting that names BERTopic's clusters, and runs both on real newsgroup posts whose true categories are known, so you can check what each method found. You have 10,000 customer support tickets, 50,000 news articles, or 200,000 tweets. You need to know what the collection is about without reading it. You do not have labeled categories. You do not even know how many categories exist. Topic modeling answers that without supervision. Give it a corpus, get back a small set of coherent topics and, for each document, a distribution over those topics. Two algorithmic families dominate. LDA (2003) treats each document as a mixture of latent topics and each topic as a distribution over words. Inference is Bayesian. It still ships in production where you need mixed-membership topic assignments and explainable word-level probability distributions. BERTopic (2020) encodes documents with BERT, reduces dimensionality with UMAP, clusters with HDBSCAN, and extracts topic words via class-based TF-IDF. It tends to win on short text, social media, and anything where semantic similarity matters more than word overlap, because two posts can share meaning without sharing words. One document gets one topic, which is a limitation for long-form content. This lesson builds intuition for both and names which one to pick for a given corpus. The idea LDA generative story. Each topic is a distribution over words. Each document is a mixture of topics. To generate a word in a document, sample a topic from the document's mixture, then sample a word from that topic's distribution. Inference reverses this: given observed words, infer the topic distribution per document and the word distribution per topic. Collapsed Gibbs sampling or variational Bayes does the math. Key LDA output: doc_topic : matrix (n_docs, n_topics) , each row sums to 1 (document's topic mixture). topic_word : matrix (n_topics, vocab_size) , each row sums to 1 (topic's word distribution). BERTopic pipeline. Encode each document with a sentence transformer (e.g., all-MiniLM-L6-v2 ). 384-dim vectors. Reduce dimensionality with UMAP to ~5 dimensions. BERT embeddings are too high-dim for clustering. Cluster with HDBSCAN. Density-based, produces variable-size clusters and an "outlier" label. For each cluster, compute class-based TF-IDF over the cluster's documents to extract top words. Output is one topic per document (plus a -1 outlier label). Optionally, a soft membership via HDBSCAN's probability vector. The same idea as a formula LDA's generative story (Blei, Ng and Jordan, 2003), for topics and vocabulary size : For each topic : draw a word distribution ​ ∼ Dirichlet ( β ) . For each document : draw a topic mixture ​ ∼ Dirichlet ( α ) . For each word position in : draw a topic ​ ∼ Categorical ( θ d ​ ) , then a word ​ ∼ Categorical ( ϕ z d , i ​ ​ ) . The Dirichlet priors control sparsity: a small (below 1) says each document uses few topics; a small says each topic uses few words. Fitting means computing the posterior , which has no closed form, so it is approximated: scikit-learn uses variational inference; collapsed Gibbs sampling is the easiest to understand. It integrates out and and resamples each word's topic given all the others: ​ = k ∣ z − i ​ , w ) ∝ ( n d , k − i ​ + α ) ⋅ n k − i ​ + V β n k , w i ​ − i ​ + β ​ where ​ counts words in document assigned to topic , ​ counts how often word is assigned to across the corpus, and means "not counting word itself". The first factor says "this document likes topic "; the second says "topic likes this word". BERTopic's class-based TF-IDF. After clustering, all documents of cluster are joined into one long document. For term with frequency ​ in cluster , total frequency ​ across all clusters, and the average number of words per cluster: ​ = tf t , c ​ ⋅ lo g ( 1 + f t ​ A ​ ) A word frequent in this cluster and rare overall gets a high weight; a word frequent everywhere ("the", "would") gets a low one. Coherence. Normalised pointwise mutual information of two top words, l o g P ( a ) P ( b ) P ( a , b ) ​ ​ , ranges from to ; topic coherence ( ​ ) aggregates NPMI-based vectors over each topic's top words and compares them with cosine similarity. Worked example One Gibbs update by hand Two topics, , , vocabulary . We resample the topic of the word "orbit" in a document whose other words are assigned 8 to topic 1 (space) and 2 to topic 2 (cars). Across the corpus, excluding this word, "orbit" is assigned 30 times to topic 1 and once to topic 2; topic 1 has 5,000 words in total, topic 2 has 6,000. Topic 1: 30 + 0.01 ​ = 8.1 × 0.00599 = 0.0485 . Topic 2: 1 + 0.01 ​ = 2.1 × 0.000168 = 0.000353 . Normalise: . Both factors point the same way, so "orbit" almost surely goes to topic 1. Thousands of sweeps of updates like this let the topics sharpen themselves out of random initial assignments. Check your mental model ✗ "LDA finds the true topics of a corpus." ✓ It finds the word distributions that best explain the counts under its assumptions; is your choice, and different or seeds give different, equally "valid" topics. ✗ "BERTopic gives each document a mixture of topics, like LDA." ✓ Its clustering assigns each document to one topic (or to the outlier group); mixtures need extra steps. ✗ "High coherence means the topics are useful." ✓ Coherence measures whether top words co-occur; a topic of boilerplate words ("subject, writes, article") can be very coherent and useless. Predict before you run Under "Use it", both methods run on 1,800 posts from six newsgroups (graphics, autos, hockey, medicine, space, gun politics). LDA is told to find 6 topics. BERTopic chooses its own number of topics. Which will match the six true groups more cleanly, and what will BERTopic do that LDA cannot? (Solution P1.) Step 1 · LDA via scikit-learn Copy Notice: stopwords removed, min_df and max_df filter rare and ubiquitous terms, CountVectorizer (not TfidfVectorizer) because LDA expects raw counts. Step 2 · BERTopic (production) Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The table lists BERTopic's clusters with their sizes and automatic names (the top c-TF-IDF words joined by underscores). Five of the six newsgroups appear as one clean topic each: guns, space, hockey, graphics, medicine. Cars split into three, general car talk, radar and lights, oil and diesel engines, because those posts really do form separate clusters of meaning. Topic -1 is the outlier bucket: about 90 posts (5%) that HDBSCAN would not place in any dense region. One detail matters in the code: without a stop-word list in vectorizer_model , every topic is named "the_to_of", because c-TF-IDF only down-weights words that are frequent across clusters , and "the" is frequent everywhere but still dominates raw counts. The filter on Topic != -1 drops BERTopic's outlier bucket (documents HDBSCAN could not cluster). min_topic_size controls HDBSCAN's minimum cluster size; BERTopic's library default is 10. This example sets it to 15 explicitly for the lesson's scale. For corpora over 10,000 documents, increase to 50 or 100. Step 3 · evaluation Both methods output topic words. The question is whether those words cohere. Topic coherence (c_v). Combines NPMI (normalized pointwise mutual information) of top-word pairs over sliding-window contexts, aggregates the scores into topic vectors, and compares those vectors via cosine similarity. Higher is better. Use gensim.models.CoherenceModel with coherence="c_v" . Topic diversity. Fraction of unique words across all topics' top words. Higher is better (topics do not overlap). Qualitative inspection. Read the top words of each topic. Do they name a real thing? Human judgment is still the last line of defense. See it drawn LDA versus BERTopic against the true groups The lesson's fit_lda (6 topics) on the same 1,800 posts, then a cross-tabulation of each method's topics against the six newsgroups. Each row of a heatmap is a topic; each column a true group; the colour is the share of that topic's documents from that group. Show the code that draws this Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output LDA's topics line up with five of the groups (cars, space, guns, hockey, and medicine, whose topic also absorbs some general talk), but the sixth topic, "know like ve don does just make thanks", is named by generic forum chatter. The heatmap shows it is mostly the graphics group: those posts are largely questions ("does anyone know… thanks"), and LDA latched onto the question style instead of the subject, while graphics words such as "image" and "file" are too spread out to dominate. Its purity is 0.60. LDA's strength is the mixture: about half the posts get a second topic above 25%, honest for posts that mix subjects. BERTopic's rows are mostly a single bright cell, with purity 0.92 on the 95% of posts it was willing to assign, and the car split shows on its heatmap as three rows pointing at the same column. The catch is the outlier group: those 5% get no topic at all. See it drawn What makes a topic "coherent" Topic coherence ( ​ , computed with gensim over the corpus) and topic diversity (share of unique words among all topics' top 10) for both methods, plus the c-TF-IDF formula recomputed by hand for one BERTopic topic. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The by-hand c-TF-IDF list matches BERTopic's own top words for the same topic exactly, in the same order: the formula really is just "frequent here, rare overall". The coherence numbers are a useful warning: LDA scores higher (0.59 against 0.53), even though its topics matched the true groups far worse and one of them was pure chatter. Words like "know, like, don, just" co-occur constantly, so a chatter topic is very coherent. Diversity is similar for both. As the check box said, coherence measures co-occurrence, not usefulness; reading the topic words and, where you have them, checking against labels, as the heatmaps did, is what tells you which model found real structure. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) LLMs name the topics. BERTopic can pass each cluster's top documents and words to an LLM (OpenAI, local models via its representation models) to write a readable label and description; this is the usual production setup for exploring support tickets, reviews and survey answers. Embeddings got better, and the pipeline stayed. Swapping MiniLM for a stronger embedding model is the simplest upgrade; the embed, reduce, cluster, describe pipeline is now also the standard way to explore unlabelled text before building a classifier. LDA is still in use where interpretable word distributions are needed and compute is tight (Gensim, scikit-learn). Sources: BERTopic , BERTopic LLM representations , Gensim LDA . When to pick which Situation Pick Short text (tweets, reviews, headlines) BERTopic Long documents with topic mixtures LDA No GPU / limited compute LDA or NMF Need document-level multi-topic distributions LDA LLM integration for topic labeling BERTopic (direct support) Resource-constrained edge deployment LDA Max semantic coherence BERTopic The biggest practical consideration is document length. BERT embeddings truncate; LDA counts work on whatever length. For documents longer than the embedding model's context, either chunk + aggregate or use LDA. Use it: the same idea with real libraries The 2026 stack: BERTopic. Default for short text and anything where semantics matter. gensim.models.LdaModel . Classic LDA for production, mature, battle-tested. sklearn.decomposition.LatentDirichletAllocation . Easy LDA for experiments. NMF. Non-negative matrix factorization. Fast alternative to LDA, comparable quality on short text. Top2Vec. Similar design to BERTopic. Smaller community but good on some benchmarks. FASTopic (NeurIPS 2024). Newer; models topics with optimal transport between document, topic and word embeddings, and its authors report it is faster than BERTopic on large corpora with competitive quality. LLM-based labeling. Run any clustering, then prompt a model to name each cluster. Break it on purpose In fit_lda , replace the CountVectorizer with a TfidfVectorizer (keeping max_features=2000 ). scikit-learn's LDA accepts the matrix without complaint and prints topics as before. Which assumption of LDA's generative story have you broken, and what should you expect to happen to each document's topic mixture? (Solution B1.) Recap What to keep from this lesson LDA: documents are Dirichlet mixtures of topics, topics are Dirichlet distributions over words; fit by variational inference or Gibbs sampling. The Gibbs update multiplies "the document likes this topic" by "the topic likes this word". BERTopic: embed, reduce with UMAP, cluster with HDBSCAN, name clusters with class-based TF-IDF; one topic per document plus outliers. Evaluate with coherence and diversity, and always by reading the topics. Pick by document length and by whether you need mixtures (LDA) or semantic clusters (BERTopic). Solutions Solution P1 · BERTopic matches better, but leaves documents out BERTopic matches the groups far more cleanly (purity 0.92 against 0.60): five groups come out as one topic each, and cars split into three sub-themes because BERTopic chooses its own number of clusters. What BERTopic does that LDA cannot is refuse: 5% of posts land in the outlier topic -1 and get no topic. LDA instead gives every post a full mixture, with a real second topic for about half of them. Solution B1 · LDA needs counts LDA models a document as a sequence of word draws: each occurrence picks a topic, then a word, so the input must be counts of occurrences, and a document's total count is how much evidence it carries. TF-IDF rows are real-valued weights, and after the vectorizer's L2 normalisation each row's entries sum to only a few units, so a 300-word post looks to LDA like a document of a handful of words. Its posterior mixture is then dominated by the Dirichlet prior, and mixtures drift towards the flat prior (topics spread evenly), while the IDF weighting also inflates rare words inside the topics. Keep LDA on raw counts and use TF-IDF for models that expect it. Sources and further reading Blei, Ng, Jordan (2003). Latent Dirichlet Allocation — the LDA paper. Grootendorst (2022). Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line If a word is surprising, the model is bad. Perplexity makes surprise a number. Smoothing keeps it finite. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means N-gram Word sequence Sequence of n consecutive tokens. Smoothing Avoiding zeros Reallocating probability mass so unseen events get non-zero probability. Perplexity LM quality metric exp(-average log-prob) on held-out data. Lower is better. Backoff Fallback to shorter context If trigram count is zero, use bigram. Katz backoff formalizes this. Kneser-Ney Best smoothing for n-grams Absolute discounting + continuation probability for the lower-order model. Continuation probability KN-specific P(w) weighted by number of contexts w appears in, not by raw count. Entropy of text Information per symbol Average bits needed to encode the next symbol given the context. Shannon's 1951 estimate for printed English with up to 100 letters of context: 0.6-1.3 bits/letter, measured before any model existed. The problem In plain words first A language model assigns probabilities to what comes next. The oldest working kind, the n-gram model, just counts: how often did "sat" follow "the cat" in a big pile of text? Counting is easy. The hard part is everything the pile never contained. Most long phrases you will ever see are new, and a pure counter gives them probability zero. Smoothing methods move a little probability from seen events to unseen ones. The best classic method, Kneser-Ney, also asks in how many different contexts a word has appeared, not just how often. This lesson measures how often new phrases really occur, derives Kneser-Ney's formula and works an example by hand, scores the models with perplexity (how many choices the model is effectively torn between at each word), generates text from them, and compares them with a small transformer on exactly the same sentences. Before transformers, before RNNs, before word embeddings, a language model predicted the next word by counting how often it followed the previous n-1 words. Count "the cat" → "sat" 47 times, "the cat" → "jumped" 12 times, "the cat" → "refrigerator" 0 times. Normalize to get a probability distribution. That is an n-gram language model. It ran every speech recognizer, every spell checker, and every phrase-based machine translation system from 1980 through 2015. It still runs when you need cheap on-device language modeling. The interesting problem is what to do about unseen n-grams. A raw count-based model assigns zero probability to anything it has not seen, which is catastrophic because sentences are long and almost every long sentence contains at least one unseen sequence. Fifty years of smoothing research fixed that. Kneser-Ney smoothing is the result, and modern deep learning inherited its empirical tradition. The idea Idea 1 · The prediction game Before any of this machinery existed, one experiment defined what a language model is. Cover the next letter of an English sentence. Ask someone to guess it, one guess at a time, until they get it right. Write down the guess count. Repeat for a few hundred letters. The guess counts are not trivia. They are a lossless re-encoding of the text: hand the count sequence to a second, identical guesser and they can reconstruct every letter, because at each position they know exactly which guesses come first. A message you can re-encode in fewer symbols carries less information per symbol, so the guess-count statistics put a ceiling on the entropy of English. Shannon ran this in 1951 and got a number that still governs the field. A 27-symbol alphabet (26 letters plus space) could carry log2(27) ≈ 4.75 bits per letter. Human guessers with 100 letters of context landed between 0.6 and 1.3 bits per letter. English is roughly three-quarters forced moves. The structure a model must learn was measured before any model could learn it. Every language model since is a mechanical player of this game, and every evaluation number in this lesson is the game scored: Cross-entropy loss is the average number of bits the model needs per symbol. Training an LM is literally minimizing its score at the guessing game. Perplexity is 2^bits (or e^nats ): the branching factor still facing the model after its guesswork. Uniform guessing over 27 symbols is perplexity 27; a 1-bit-per-letter player has perplexity 2. Context length is the player's memory. A trigram model plays with two tokens of memory. A transformer plays the same game with 100K tokens. The rules never changed; the player got better. One unit switch to track: the game scores per letter in bits ( log2 ), while the n-gram formulas below score per word token in nats (natural log) — and since perplexity e^H in nats equals 2^H in bits, the two views are the same measurement in different units. N-gram probability: P(w_i | w_{i-n+1}, ..., w_{i-1}) . Fix n (typically 3 for trigrams, 4 for 4-grams). Compute from counts: ( context ) count ( context , w ) ​ The zero-count problem. Any n-gram not seen in training gets probability zero. How common are unseen n-grams? Measured under "Use it" on the Brown corpus with 2,000 sentences held out: a small share of held-out words never appeared in training, but most held-out trigrams and the large majority of held-out 4-grams were never seen. You cannot evaluate on any real text without smoothing. Smoothing approaches, in order of sophistication: Laplace (add-one). Add 1 to every count. Simple, terrible on rare events. Good-Turing. Reallocate probability mass from higher-frequency events to unseen ones based on frequency-of-frequencies. Interpolation. Combine n-gram, (n-1)-gram, etc., estimates with tunable weights. Backoff. If n-gram has count zero, fall back to (n-1)-gram. Katz backoff normalizes this. Absolute discounting. Subtract a fixed discount D from all counts, redistribute to unseen. Kneser-Ney. Absolute discounting plus a clever choice for the lower-order model: use continuation probability (how many contexts a word appears in) instead of raw frequency. The Kneser-Ney insight is deep. "San Francisco" is a common bigram. Unigram "Francisco" appears mostly after "San." Naive absolute discounting gives "Francisco" high unigram probability (because the count is high). Kneser-Ney notices that "Francisco" appears in only one context and lowers its continuation probability accordingly. Result: a novel bigram ending in "Francisco" gets the appropriate low probability. Evaluation: perplexity. The exponent of the average negative log-likelihood per word on a held-out test set. Lower is better. Worked example Kneser-Ney by hand: why "Francisco" is rare A toy corpus has 1,000 distinct bigram types. "Francisco" occurs 50 times, always after "San". Laplace smoothing avoids zeros but is far worse than Kneser-Ney: it hands every one of the tens of thousands of vocabulary words an equal share of each context's probability. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) n-gram models still ship in speech recognition. KenLM language models are fused into CTC beam search (NVIDIA NeMo, pyctcdecode for wav2vec 2.0) to fix spelling and domain words cheaply, and keyboards use small n-gram models on device. Counting as a data tool. Deduplication (MinHash over n-gram shingles in Hugging Face datatrove and NVIDIA NeMo Curator), benchmark-contamination checks and training-data attribution in LLM pipelines rest on n-gram matching over huge corpora. The training objective is the same game. Every LLM is still trained to minimise next-token cross-entropy, Shannon's prediction game, and perplexity remains the first number reported during pretraining. The problem In plain words first A chatbot has to work out what someone wants, ask for anything missing, sometimes act on their behalf, and remember what was said a few turns ago. Four designs have been tried, in this order. Hand-written rules match patterns in the user's words. Retrieval looks up the closest stored question and returns its prepared answer. Neural generation writes a reply word by word. LLM agents use a language model that can also call tools, such as looking up a booking or issuing a refund. Each design was adopted because the previous one failed visibly, and real systems today combine all four. This lesson builds each piece and shows where each breaks: a rule that turns "my" into nonsense, the similarity threshold that decides when a FAQ bot should give up, an agent loop driven by a scripted stand-in for the model, and a prompt-injection attack against that loop with the defence that stops it. A user says "I want to change my flight." The system has to figure out what they want, what information is missing, how to get it, and how to complete the action. Then the user says "wait, what if I cancel instead?" and the system has to remember the context, switch tasks, and preserve state. Conversation is hard for an ML system. The input is open-ended. The output has to be coherent over many turns. The system may need to act on the world (change a flight, charge a card). Every wrong step is visible to the user. Chatbot architectures have cycled through four paradigms, each introduced because the previous one failed too visibly. This lesson walks them in order. The 2026 production landscape is a hybrid of the last two. The idea Idea 1 · The scripted half-century, 1950-2001 The first paradigm did not last five years. It lasted fifty. Knowing its arc matters because every system in it is the same machine — match input, emit a canned response, update a little state — and fifty years of adding rules to that machine never produced the general case. That ceiling is why paradigms two through four exist. 1950. Turing sidesteps "can machines think?" by proposing an operational replacement: if an interrogator cannot tell the machine from a person over teletype, the philosophical question is moot. Conversation becomes the field's benchmark before the field has a name. 1956. The name arrives — a summer workshop at Dartmouth coins "artificial intelligence" on the conjecture that every feature of intelligence "can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it." The proposal budgets two months for substantial progress. 1966. ELIZA ships the reflection trick you build in Step 1: decomposition rules pull fragments from the input, reassembly rules echo them back as questions. A few hundred lines of script, zero state, zero understanding — and users confided in it anyway. Weizenbaum spent the rest of his career alarmed by how little machinery it took. 1972. PARRY, built at Stanford to model paranoia, adds the piece ELIZA lacked: internal state. Numeric variables for fear, anger, and mistrust update on every turn and gate which script fires next, so identical inputs produce different responses depending on the conversation so far. In a blinded transcript test, psychiatrists distinguished PARRY from human patients at chance. It is the direct ancestor of persona conditioning — a system prompt implemented as three floats. The same year, the two bots were pointed at each other over ARPANET: a therapist script interviewing a paranoia state machine, the first bot-to-bot conversation on a network. 1995. ALICE scales the ELIZA recipe with AIML, an XML dialect for pattern-template pairs. Roughly 40,000 hand-written categories, three Loebner Prize wins. It proved the scaling law of rule-based systems: more rules buy coverage, never generality. Every rule is a liability someone must maintain. 2001. SmarterChild puts the recipe in front of 30 million instant-messenger users and adds backend lookups — weather, stocks, movie times — spliced into templates. Squint and it is tool calling wearing a 2001 costume: parse intent, call a service, render the result into the reply. Fifty years, one mechanism, rising rule counts. The paradigm ended not because anyone disproved it but because the maintenance cost of hand-written state machines grows linearly with coverage while user expectations grow with whatever they saw last week. Rule-based (ELIZA, AIML, DialogFlow). Hand-authored patterns match user input and produce responses. Intent classifiers route to predefined flows. Slot-filling state machines collect required info. Works brilliantly inside the narrow scope it was designed for. Fails immediately outside it. Still ships in safety-critical domains (banking authentication, airline booking) where hallucination is not tolerated. Retrieval-based. A FAQ-style system. Encode every pair of (utterance, response). At runtime, encode the user's message and retrieve the nearest stored response. Think Zendesk's classic "similar articles" feature. Handles paraphrases better than rules. No generation, so no hallucination. Neural (seq2seq). Encoder-decoder trained on conversation logs. Generates responses from scratch. Fluent but prone to generic outputs ("I don't know") and factual drift. Never reliably on topic. The reason Google, Facebook, and Microsoft all had disappointing chatbots in 2016-2019. LLM agents. A language model wrapped in a loop that plans, calls tools, and verifies outcomes. Not a chatbot with a long prompt. An agent loop: plan → call tool → observe result → decide next step. Retrieval-first grounding (RAG) keeps it from hallucinating. Tool calls let it actually do things. This is the 2026 architecture. The four paradigms are not sequential replacements. A 2026 production chatbot routes through all four: rule-based for authentication and destructive actions, retrieval for FAQ, neural generation for natural phrasing, LLM agent for ambiguous open-ended queries. The same idea as a formula Rules. ELIZA's unit is a decomposition pattern that splits the input into pieces, and a reassembly template that rebuilds a reply from them, with pronouns reflected (I → you, my → your). A rule system is a function from (input, state) to (reply, new state) written by hand. Retrieval with a refusal threshold. DialoGPT-style decoder-only models need explicit turn separators and EOS handling to produce coherent replies; a FLAN-T5 text2text pipeline works out of the box for a teaching example. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output FLAN-T5-small (77M parameters) produces fluent, polite, generic replies. It cannot change a flight, it has no record of which flight, and the second turn ("cancel it instead") is answered with no memory of the first, because each call starts fresh. That is the 2016-2019 neural chatbot in miniature: natural phrasing, no state, no ability to act, which is why it survives only as the phrasing layer inside larger systems. Step 4 · LLM agent loop The 2026 production shape: Copy Three things to name. Tools are callable functions the LLM can invoke. The loop terminates when the LLM returns a final answer instead of a tool call. The step budget prevents infinite loops on ambiguous tasks. Real production adds: retrieval-first grounding (inject relevant docs before each LLM call), guardrails (refuse destructive actions without confirmation), observability (log every step), and evaluations (automated checks that agent behavior stays on-spec). Step 5 · hybrid routing Copy The pattern: deterministic rules for anything destructive, retrieval for canned FAQs, LLM agents for everything else. This is what ships in 2026 customer-support systems. Use it: the same idea with real libraries The 2026 stack: Use case Architecture Booking, payment, authentication Rule-based state machines + slot filling Customer support FAQs Retrieval over curated answers Open-ended help chat LLM agent with RAG + tool calls Internal tools / IDE assistants LLM agent with tool calls (search, read, write) Companion / character chatbots Tuned LLM with persona system prompt, retrieval on knowledge Always use hybrid routing in production. No single architecture handles every request well. The routing layer itself is typically a small intent classifier. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Without reflection, the rules echo the user's own pronouns back: "Why do you need my phone back?" asks about the bot's phone. Weizenbaum's ELIZA swapped first and second person in every captured fragment, which is what makes the reflection trick feel like listening. It is also a good picture of the rule-based ceiling: each fix is another hand-written table, and "The flight was late" still falls through to "Tell me more about that." So a threshold of 0.4 answers everything answerable and nothing else here, but with a margin of 0.01 that will not survive real traffic. The lesson's 0.5 already escalates 17% of answerable questions, and the hybrid router's 0.6 escalates half of them. Near-miss questions such as "i was charged twice" or "how do i update my credit card" are the ones that eventually land on the wrong side; in production the threshold is set from logged conversations and the escalation path is part of the design. The naive policy obeys text it reads; the defended version checks every requested action against the user's request before running it (the plan-then-verify idea). The model here is a script, but the failure is the real one: whatever a tool returns becomes part of the history the model conditions on. The guarded run uses the same model and tools; the only change is outside the model: each action is checked against the plan for the user's request (allowed tools, the user's own booking), so the refund is blocked and the date change goes through. The last line shows the step budget stopping a loop that never answers. Real systems add confirmation for money-moving actions and log every call. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Tool use is standardised. Function calling with JSON schemas is built into every major model API, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP, introduced by Anthropic in November 2024 and since adopted across the industry) standardises how agents connect to tools and data. Prompt injection is the top risk. OWASP's 2025 Top 10 for LLM Applications ranks it first; EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711, CVSS 9.3) showed a zero-click data-exfiltration path in Microsoft 365 Copilot through an attacker's email. Defences are architectural (privilege separation, action allowlists, human confirmation), as in the last experiment. Voice and real-time agents. Speech-to-speech models made low-latency voice agents practical in 2025; Phase 6 of this course covers the speech side. Sources: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 , Model Context Protocol . Failure modes that still ship Confident fabrication. LLM agent claims it completed an action it did not. Mitigation: verify outcomes, log tool calls, never let the LLM claim to have done something without a successful tool return. Prompt injection. User inserts text that overrides the system prompt. Ranked LLM01 in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025. Two flavors: direct injection (pasted into the chat) and indirect injection (hidden in documents, emails, or tool outputs the agent reads). Reported attack success rates vary enormously with the benchmark, the defences and the attacker: low single-digit percentages for fixed attack strings against well-defended frontier models, and the large majority of attempts for adaptive attackers who iterate against a specific agent. Production CVEs include EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711, CVSS 9.3) — a zero-click data-exfiltration flaw in Microsoft 365 Copilot triggered by an attacker-controlled email. Mitigations: treat user input as untrusted throughout the loop; sanitize before tool calls; isolate tool outputs from the main prompt; use the Plan-Verify-Execute (PVE) pattern where the agent plans first, then verifies each action against that plan before executing (this stops tool results from injecting new unplanned actions); require user confirmation for destructive actions; apply least-privilege to tool scopes. No amount of prompt engineering fully eliminates this risk. External runtime defense layers (LLM Guard, allowlist validation, semantic anomaly detection) are required. - Scope creep. Agent goes off-task because a tool call returned tangentially related info. Mitigation: narrow tool contracts; keep the system prompt focused; add evaluations for off-task rate. - Infinite loops. Agent keeps calling the same tool. Mitigation: step budget, tool-call deduplication, LLM judge on "are we making progress." - Context window exhaustion. Long conversations push the earliest turns out of context. Mitigation: summarize older turns, retrieve relevant past turns by similarity, or use a long-context model. Recap What to keep from this lesson Four designs: rules, retrieval, neural generation, LLM agents; production routes between them. Retrieval bots refuse below a similarity threshold that trades wrong answers against escalations. An agent loop is a policy over tool calls with a step budget; the history is its only view of the world. Prompt injection exploits the shared channel for instructions and data; defend outside the model. Never trust a model's claim that it did something; trust the tool log. The pattern i (need|want) (.+) captures "need" and "my phone back" and pastes them into "Why do you {0} {1}?", giving "Why do you need my phone back?", a question about the bot's own phone. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line One model, 100+ languages, zero training data for most of them. Cross-lingual transfer is the practical miracle of the 2020s. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Multilingual model One model, many languages Shared vocabulary and parameters across languages. Cross-lingual transfer Train on one language, run on another Fine-tune on source, evaluate on target without target-language labels. Zero-shot No target-language labels Transfer without fine-tuning on the target language. Few-shot Small target labels 100-500 target-language examples used for fine-tuning. mBERT First multilingual LM 104-language BERT pretrained on Wikipedia. XLM-R Standard cross-lingual baseline 100-language RoBERTa pretrained on CommonCrawl. NLLB Meta's 200-language MT No Language Left Behind. Includes 55 low-resource languages. The problem In plain words first There are about 7,000 languages, and labelled training data exists for a handful of them. Multilingual models are trained on text in around a hundred languages at once, with one shared vocabulary of word pieces and one shared network. Because the network keeps seeing the same meanings expressed in different languages, sentences with the same meaning end up with similar internal representations whatever the language. That makes cross-lingual transfer possible: teach a task with English examples and the model can often do it in Hindi or Swahili. It works unevenly, though. Languages far from the training mix get less model capacity and are chopped into more, smaller pieces by the shared tokenizer. This lesson explains the shared space and the "curse of multilinguality", measures the tokenizer tax on real parallel sentences, tests whether translations really land close together, and runs zero-shot classification across several languages with a model that never saw a label in most of them. English has billions of labeled examples. Urdu has thousands. Maithili has almost none. Any practical NLP system that serves a global audience has to work on the long tail of languages where task-specific training data does not exist. Multilingual models solve this by training one model on many languages simultaneously. The shared representation lets the model transfer skills learned in high-resource languages to low-resource ones. Fine-tune the model on English sentiment analysis, and it produces surprisingly good sentiment predictions on Urdu out of the box. That is zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, and it has reshaped how NLP ships to the world. This lesson names the tradeoffs, the canonical models, and the one decision that trips up teams new to multilingual work: picking a source language for transfer. The idea Shared vocabulary. Multilingual models use a SentencePiece or WordPiece tokenizer trained on text from all target languages. The vocabulary is shared: the same subword unit represents the same morpheme across related languages. anti- in English and Italian gets the same token. Shared representation. A transformer pretrained on masked language modeling across many languages learns that semantically similar sentences in different languages produce similar hidden states. mBERT, XLM-R, and NLLB all exhibit this. Embeddings for "cat" in English cluster near "chat" in French and "gato" in Spanish, and so do full-sentence embeddings. Zero-shot transfer. Fine-tune the model on labeled data in one language (usually English). At inference, run it on any other language the model supports. No target-language labels needed. Results are strong for typologically related languages and weaker for distant ones. Few-shot fine-tuning. Add 100-500 labeled examples in the target language. Accuracy usually closes much of the gap to the English baseline on classification tasks (how much depends on the language and task), and it is one of the most cost-effective levers in multilingual NLP. The same idea as a formula Why a shared space appears. Masked-language-model pretraining on many languages uses one vocabulary and one set of weights. Shared pieces (numbers, names, cognates such as "information", "información") and shared structure give the model a reason to reuse the same directions for the same meanings, and parallel sentences end up close: ​ ) , E ( x fr ​ )) ≈ 1 for a sentence and its translation. Sentence-embedding models such as paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2 are additionally trained so that a translation maps to the same vector as its source (Reimers and Gurevych, 2020). Aligning two monolingual spaces. Before multilingual pretraining, Mikolov et al. (2013) found that word vectors trained separately for two languages are related by a nearly linear map. With holding the vectors of dictionary pairs, the best orthogonal map (orthogonal Procrustes) is = ar g W ⊤ W = I min ​ ∥ W X − Y ∥ F ​ = U V ⊤ , where U Σ V ⊤ = SVD ( Y X ⊤ ) Orthogonality keeps distances, so the map only rotates one space onto the other. Train the NLI model on English (or a few languages), and the shared space carries it to others. Fertility of a tokenizer on a language is tokens per word; for parallel sentences, the ratio ​ ) # tokens ( x lang ​ ) ​ measures the extra cost of the same content. The curse of multilinguality (Conneau et al., 2020): with model size fixed, adding languages first helps low-resource languages (more shared signal) and then hurts all of them, because each language's share of the model's capacity shrinks. Bigger models and larger vocabularies (XLM-V) push the turning point out. Check your mental model ✗ "A multilingual model is equally good in all its languages." ✓ Quality follows pretraining data; low-resource languages get less capacity and worse tokenization. ✗ "Zero-shot transfer means no target-language data was ever involved." ✓ No labelled target data. The model's pretraining included unlabelled text in the target language, and that is what makes transfer work. ✗ "Token counts are a cosmetic difference." ✓ They set context length, cost and latency per sentence, and more pieces per word means each piece carries less meaning. With the multilingual MiniLM, will it find the right one for nearly all, about half, or very few? And with the English-only all-MiniLM-L6-v2 ? (Solution P1.) The models Model Year Coverage Notes mBERT 2018 104 languages Trained on Wikipedia. First practical multilingual LM. Weak on low-resource. XLM-R 2019 100 languages Trained on CommonCrawl (much larger than Wikipedia). Sets the cross-lingual baseline. Base 270M, Large 550M. XLM-V 2023 100 languages XLM-R with 1M-token vocabulary (vs 250k). Better on low-resource. mT5 2020 101 languages T5 architecture for multilingual generation. NLLB-200 2022 200 languages Meta's translation model; includes 55 low-resource languages. BLOOM 2022 46 languages + 13 programming Open 176B LLM trained multilingually. Aya-23 2024 23 languages Cohere's multilingual LLM. Strong on Arabic, Hindi, Swahili. Pick by use case. Classification works well with XLM-R-base as the sane default. Generation tasks call for mT5 or NLLB depending on translation vs open generation. LLM-style work pairs with Aya-23 or Claude using explicit multilingual prompting. The source-language decision (2026 research) Most teams default to English as the fine-tuning source. Recent research (2026) shows this is often wrong. Language similarity often predicts transfer quality better than raw corpus size, though a 2025 study across 266 languages (Blaschke et al.) found the effect depends on the task and on whether the target language was in the model's pretraining data. For Slavic targets, German or Russian often beat English. For Indic targets, Hindi often beats English. The qWALS similarity metric (2026, based on World Atlas of Language Structures features) quantifies this. LANGRANK (Lin et al., ACL 2019) is a separate, earlier method that ranks candidate source languages from a combination of linguistic similarity, corpus size, and genetic relatedness. Practical rule: if your target language has a typologically close high-resource relative, try fine-tuning on that one first, then compare to English fine-tune.
