Solutions Solution P1 · Freely, never; constrained, always valid, right 3 times out of 5 A base model continues text rather than obeying it: none of the five free outputs was a bare label. Constrained decoding always returned one of the three words, by construction, but GPT-2 small labelled a complaint about cold food and a neutral statement of opening hours as "positive". Format and correctness are separate guarantees. Solution B1 · It can only emit forbidden tokens With the mask inverted, every token the grammar allows gets and every token it forbids keeps its logit, so the sampler picks a token that breaks the format at the very first step. The automaton's transition then has no valid move: depending on the implementation it raises an error, gets stuck in a dead state, or keeps going while the output drifts arbitrarily far from the grammar. Unit-test a constraint by checking that every token it allows really advances the automaton, and that it allows at least one token in every reachable non-final state. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Debug a failure A classifier uses constrained decoding with a schema of two fields, answer and reasoning , in that order. The output is always valid JSON and the accuracy is worse than the free-text version was. What is wrong? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The field order. The model commits to the answer before it writes any reasoning, so the reasoning tokens never shape the answer, and you lose the gain that step-by-step gives. Put reasoning first and answer last; the schema stays valid, and no validator will ever flag the difference, because the order is logic and not formatting. The pitfall. The constrained decoding lesson calls it the pitfall that costs you. With answer first, the model writes the decision token at the first position where the grammar allows it, and the reasoning that follows is a story about a choice already made. With reasoning first, the chain comes before the decision, and the decision token is conditioned on it. Both documents validate. Only one is right. The lesson's skill refuses any design that puts an answer or decision field before the reasoning fields. Neighbors of the same mistake. Schema choice What goes wrong Fix A strict pattern for a value that can be missing, such as a date the model invents a value to satisfy the grammar allow null or a sentinel A field left optional that matters the model omits it when it is inconvenient make it required and allow null, so the absence is explicit Nesting four levels deep or more each level is one more place to lose the structure flatten An enum with thousands of options the grammar compiles slowly or times out predict a short list of candidates first, then constrain to it Why the unconstrained reply did better. A free-text reply tends to explain before it concludes, so it had the chain by accident. The constrained schema removed it. The fix restores it on purpose. Plausible wrong answers. "Constrained decoding guarantees a correct output." It guarantees the shape; the lesson shows valid JSON with a wrong answer. "Order does not matter in JSON." It does not matter to the parser; it matters to the model, which writes the fields in order. "Add a check that the reasoning supports the answer." That is an eval, not a fix; the fix is to generate the reasoning first. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why can no validator catch this? Expected: both orders are valid against the schema; the harm is in what the model has seen when it writes the answer token. (level 2) The schema forces a date pattern and the model fills in dates that are not in the text. Which related mistake is that? Expected: a grammar too strict for missing data; allow null or a sentinel so the model does not invent a value. (level 3) A field is optional and the model leaves it out when it matters. What do you change? Expected: make it required and allow null, so the model has to state that the value is missing. (level 3) The schema nests four levels deep and errors rise. What do you do? Expected: flatten, because each level of nesting is one more place to lose track of the structure. Where it is taught. The lesson constrained decoding names the field order pitfall and the strict grammar pitfall, and the lesson structured outputs covers nesting depth and optional fields. Defend a design Design the extraction service for purchase-order emails. The input is free text; the output is a typed record with a customer, line items and a total. Cover the schema, the enforcement mode, the retry and refusal handling, and how you prove it works before it touches the accounting system. Level 3 of 4 · about 20 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Write one JSON Schema 2020-12 with the constraints that matter: required fields, enums for closed sets, a minimum of zero on the total, additional properties forbidden, and any reasoning field ahead of any decision field. Run it in the provider's strict schema mode so that a response that finishes cannot have a parse error or a schema violation, check the stop reason so that a response cut at the token limit goes to the error path, and treat a refusal as a typed outcome that goes to a review queue. Prove it with a labeled set of real emails scored per field, a refusal check on inputs that must not extract, and a run beside the human process before any record is written. The schema. type , properties and required for the shape; every property listed as required, with null allowed where the source can lack a value. enum for closed sets such as currency or status; minimum on the total; pattern , minLength and maxLength on identifiers; items for the line items. additionalProperties: false everywhere, which blocks invented fields and which strict mode demands. Field order as logic: any reasoning field before total or status , because the model commits to the first field it writes. In Python, a Pydantic model generates this schema; the service keeps the schema as the contract and the model as its binding. The enforcement mode. Situation Pick A hosted frontier model, a flat schema the provider's strict schema mode Several providers, retries acceptable a retry library over the Pydantic model, which is portable and does not touch logits A local model, validity required a grammar engine, finite state for a flat schema and context-free for a recursive one Strict mode is the default here: a finished output parses and validates by construction. Two failures remain: the refusal, and a response cut at the token limit, which can still fail to parse. Check the stop reason before you read the output, and send an incomplete response to the error path. Retry and refusal. Outside strict mode: generate, parse, validate, inject the typed errors and retry, at most three times. More than three means the schema or the prompt is wrong for some inputs. In every mode: a refusal is a first-class outcome with a reason attached. Log it, return it typed, send it to the review queue, and never retry it, because forcing a record on an input that does not fit produces an invented record. Proof before accounting sees a record. A labeled set of real emails with gold records; the structured outputs lesson uses 50 documents. Report exact match, accuracy per field and type compliance. A refusal check. Construct inputs that must not extract, such as a lyric, a proof or a blank email, and count refusals against invented outputs. A confidence per field from repeated extraction or token probabilities, with low-confidence records routed to a human. A schema version on every record, and a schema diff that separates breaking changes from non-breaking ones before any deploy. A side-by-side run against the human process on the labeled set, with the service writing nothing until the field-level numbers clear the bar you set with finance. Plausible wrong answers. "Prompt for JSON and parse it, the model is good." That works 85 to 95 percent of the time and fails six different ways; accounting needs the contract. "Retry refusals until the model gives a record." A refusal says the input does not fit; forcing a record invents one. "Validation after generation is as good as strict mode." It is reliable but pays for every retry, and a truncated output costs a turn each time. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why forbid additional properties? Expected: it blocks invented fields, and strict mode requires it everywhere. (level 3) You expect to switch providers next year. Which mode do you pick? Expected: a retry library over the Pydantic model for portability, or keep the schema identical across providers so each strict mode receives the same contract. (level 4) How do you version the schema once records exist? Expected: a version field on each record and a schema diff that separates breaking changes from non-breaking ones. Strict mode makes every field required, so an added field is breaking too, because the records written before it do not contain it; removed fields and changed types are breaking, and relaxed constraints are not. (level 4) Which failure can this design not remove, and where does it go? Expected: a wrong value with the right type; it goes to the field-level eval and the confidence flags, and the low-confidence records go to review. Where it is taught. The lesson structured output gives the schema constructs, the strict mode rules, the retry pattern and the refusal handling, the lesson structured outputs sets the labeled eval and the schema diff, and the lesson constrained decoding gives the mode table and the field order rule. Explain the mechanism A teammate turned on the provider's JSON mode and says the extraction output is now guaranteed. What does JSON mode guarantee, what does it not, and what do you turn on instead? Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. JSON mode guarantees that a finished output parses, nothing more; a response cut at the token limit can still fail, so check the finish reason first. It does not guarantee your keys, your types, your enum values or the absence of extra fields. Turn on the schema mode, where the provider takes a JSON Schema and constrains decoding to it, and keep a check on your side for the values that a schema cannot judge. Four levels of control. Level Guarantee Typical failure A prompt that says "respond in JSON" none; about 90 percent valid code fences, preamble text, truncation, wrong structure JSON mode valid syntax extra keys, wrong types, missing fields Schema mode the output conforms to your schema a wrong value with the right type, or a refusal Constrained decoding every token is valid for the schema the same as schema mode; this is how schema mode is built The constrained decoding lesson is blunt about it: pure JSON mode guarantees valid JSON, not JSON that is valid for your use case, so always provide a full schema. What strict schema mode asks of you. The structured output lesson lists the strict mode rules: every property appears in required , additionalProperties is false everywhere, and there is no unresolved reference. A schema that breaks these is rejected at request time with a 400. What stays with you. Under strict enforcement two failures disappear for a response that finishes, the parse error and the schema violation. A response cut at the token limit can still fail to parse, so check the finish reason before you read it. Two more remain. The model can refuse when the input does not fit the schema, which your code treats as a typed outcome. And the model can fill a field with a value that has the right type and the wrong content; no format layer sees that. Plausible wrong answers. "JSON mode means the keys match my model." It only guarantees syntax; extra keys, wrong types and missing fields still happen. "Adding 'respond in valid JSON' to the prompt is the same thing." A prompt-only approach is about 90 percent reliable and fails with fences, preambles and truncation. "With schema mode I can drop validation." A schema cannot catch a wrong value with the right type; keep a semantic check. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Which failure remains under strict schema mode? Expected: a refusal, when the model decides the input does not fit the schema; handle it as a typed outcome, and route a response cut at the token limit to the error path. (level 2) What does strict mode demand of the schema? Expected: every property required, additional properties forbidden, no unresolved references; otherwise the request is rejected with a 400. (level 2) The output matches the schema and the price is wrong. Which layer failed? Expected: none of the format layers; the value is invented, and only a semantic check or an eval catches that. (level 3) A field is sometimes unknown in the source text. How do you write the schema? Expected: allow null or a sentinel; a grammar that forces a value makes the model invent one, such as a date. Where it is taught. The lesson structured outputs lays out the four levels, the lesson constrained decoding warns against JSON mode without a schema, and the lesson structured output gives the strict mode rules. Read the code Read this constrained generation loop from the lesson. Explain what the mask does to the probabilities, what the machine's state records, and why the loop can end up faster than unconstrained generation. python def mask_logits(logits, valid_token_ids): mask = [float("-inf")] * len(logits) for tid in valid_token_ids: mask[tid] = logits[tid] return mask def generate_constrained(model, tokenizer, prompt, fsm): ids = tokenizer.encode(prompt) state = fsm.initial_state while not fsm.is_accept(state): logits = model.next_token_logits(ids) valid = fsm.valid_tokens(state, tokenizer) logits = mask_logits(logits, valid) tok = sample(logits) ids.append(tok) state = fsm.transition(state, tok) return tokenizer.decode(ids) Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The mask sets the logit of every invalid token to negative infinity, so after the softmax those tokens carry zero probability and the sampler can only pick a token that keeps the output inside the grammar. The machine keeps the position in the grammar reached so far, and valid_tokens returns the tokens that advance it without leaving an accepting path. It can be faster because the search space shrinks, and because a position where only one token is valid needs no model call at all. Walk the loop. Encode the prompt and start the machine in its initial state. Until the machine accepts: ask the model for the logits of the next token over the whole vocabulary. Ask the machine which token ids are valid in the current state. Replace every other logit with negative infinity; the valid ones keep their value. Sample from the masked logits, append the token, and move the machine to the next state. Decode the ids. The piece between the model and the sampler is the logit processor. Nothing in the model changes; the edit is to one step's logits. Where the valid set comes from. A compiled grammar. A finite state machine built from a regex or a JSON Schema gives a constant-time lookup of the valid tokens per state. A context-free grammar engine handles recursion that a finite machine cannot express. Inference servers ship the same idea as guided decoding, with JSON, regex, choice and grammar modes. Why it can run faster. Two reasons from the lesson. The next-token search space shrinks. And a clever implementation skips the model call for forced tokens: when the grammar leaves exactly one valid token, such as the scaffolding of a key name, the token is appended without generation. This code does not do that yet. What this code does not fix. A grammar that is too strict makes the model invent a value, because no valid token lets it say unknown. A huge enum compiles slowly. A recursive schema does not fit a finite machine. And a retry library that validates after generation does none of this; it never touches the logits. Plausible wrong answers. "The mask changes the model's weights." It changes nothing in the model; it edits the logits of one step before sampling. "Constrained decoding always slows generation down." The lesson calls it often faster: a smaller search space, and forced tokens that skip the model call. "A retry library does the same thing." It formats the schema into the prompt and validates after the fact; it does not touch the logits. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Where does valid_tokens get its answer? Expected: from the compiled grammar; a finite state machine gives a constant-time lookup per state. (level 2) What does a production implementation do that this loop does not? Expected: skip forced tokens; when exactly one token is valid it is appended without a model call. (level 3) Which schemas defeat a finite state machine? Expected: recursive ones, such as nested comments or a syntax tree, which need a context-free grammar engine. (level 3) The grammar forces a strict date pattern and the source has no date. What does the loop produce? Expected: a well-formed invented date, because no valid token lets the model say unknown; allow null or a sentinel in the grammar. Where it is taught. The lesson constrained decoding gives this loop, the logit processor, the speed argument and the grammar pitfalls. Debug a failure An extraction pipeline with strict schema enforcement has reported zero validation errors for a month. A finance review finds that a share of the extracted invoice totals do not match the source documents, and that a status field often holds a value that is allowed by the enum and wrong for the document. The engineers say the schema guarantees correctness. What do you tell them, and what do you build? Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Schema enforcement guarantees shape, not truth. A total with the right type and the wrong number passes every format check, and an enum member can be allowed and still be the wrong one. Build a semantic eval: a labeled set of documents with gold records, exact match and field-level accuracy per field, plus a confidence signal from repeated extraction or token probabilities that sends low-confidence fields to human review. The failures a schema cannot see. The structured outputs lesson lists them even with enforcement on: Failure Example Why the schema passes it Invented value the text says one amount and the record holds another right type, wrong content Enum confusion the model picks an allowed member that does not fit the document the member is in the set Array length too many or too few line items not every provider enforces the item bounds at decode time Optional omission a field left out when it was inconvenient optional means allowed to be absent The constrained decoding lesson adds two causes that make the values worse: a grammar too strict for missing data, which pushes the model to invent, and a decision field placed before the reasoning. What to build. A labeled set. The lesson's exercise uses 50 documents with hand-labeled records. Label real invoices, including the hard cases. Field-level metrics. Exact match on the record, accuracy per field, and type compliance as a sanity row that should sit near 100 percent. A confidence per field. Run the extraction three times and measure agreement, or read the token probabilities, and flag the fields that disagree. A review queue. Low-confidence records go to a human before they reach accounting. Schema repairs. Put a reasoning field ahead of the status, give enum members descriptions that make their meaning explicit, and add a null or an "other" member if the source has cases that none of the members fit. Why size does not fix it. The structured output lesson notes that grammar enforcement lets a small model beat a much larger one on structured tasks, because the format is decoupled from the model size. The values are not. Only a labeled eval tells you how often they are right. Plausible wrong answers. "Zero validation errors means zero extraction errors." Validation checks shape; the review found value errors that no shape check can see. "Switch to a bigger model and the values will be right." Size changes the error rate, not the blind spot; without a labeled eval you cannot tell by how much. "Add a tighter pattern to the total field." A tighter grammar does not make the number true; a grammar too strict even pushes the model to invent one. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Which failure can a schema never see? Expected: a value with the right type and the wrong content, such as a total copied from the wrong line. (level 3) How do you get a confidence per field without a new model? Expected: run the extraction three times and measure agreement, or read token probabilities, and flag fields that disagree for review. (level 4) The status enum has a member the model keeps picking wrongly. What are the candidate fixes? Expected: describe the members so their meaning is explicit, put a reasoning field before the status, and check whether the source has cases no member fits, which calls for a null or an "other" member. (level 4) What does the finished eval report look like? Expected: schema compliance near 100 percent as a sanity row, then exact match and field-level accuracy per field on the labeled set, with the hardest fields named. Where it is taught. The lesson structured outputs lists the failures that survive a schema and sets the labeled extraction eval, the lesson constrained decoding covers the strict grammar and field order causes, and the lesson structured output separates format reliability from model size. Explain the mechanism A classifier prompt asks for one of three labels and the model answers with a paragraph, so the parser crashes. Three layers of fix exist. Explain how the strongest one works at the level of the logits, and why it is often faster than free generation, not slower. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Prompting asks nicely, a vendor's structured-output API does it on the server, and constrained decoding does it locally by editing the logits. At each step a logit processor computes which vocabulary tokens can advance the target grammar, a JSON schema, a regex or a context-free grammar compiled to a state machine, and sets every other logit to minus infinity, so the softmax puts probability only on valid continuations and an invalid output is unreachable. It can be faster because the search space shrinks and because tokens that the grammar forces, such as a fixed key name, are emitted without a model step. The three layers. Prompting. "Return only the JSON object." The lesson puts this at about 80 percent compliance on strong models and lower on small ones. Not a contract. Native structured output. The provider runs the constraint on its side. Reliable for supported schemas; locked to that provider. Constrained decoding. The constraint runs in your own decoding loop and works with any local model. The loop. Copy The state machine tracks how much of the grammar is satisfied. valid_tokens returns the vocabulary tokens that keep the machine on an accepting path; the mask sets the rest to minus infinity. The vocabulary is about 100k tokens, so the mask is computed per state ahead of time. State machine or grammar engine. A regex or a flat JSON schema compiles to a finite-state machine with a constant-time lookup of valid tokens per state. Recursive schemas, nested comments or a syntax tree, need a context-free grammar engine, which handles recursion at near-zero decoding overhead in current implementations. Inference servers expose both as guided decoding. Why it can be faster. Fewer candidate tokens means a smaller effective search at each step. More important, long stretches of the output are fully determined by the grammar: the opening brace, a quoted key, the colon. A good implementation skips the model for those tokens and only calls it where the grammar leaves a choice. The library that does not touch logits. A retry-based client formats the schema into the prompt, parses the output, and retries on a validation failure, 3 times by default. It works across providers, and each retry costs latency and money. It is a different mechanism, not a weaker version of the same one. Plausible wrong answers. "Constrained decoding makes the answer correct." It makes the answer valid for the grammar; a well-formed wrong answer still passes. "Checking the grammar at every token makes generation slower." The valid-token sets are precomputed per state, and forced tokens skip the model, so it is often faster. "Enough examples in the prompt reach full compliance." The lesson's figure for prompting alone is about 80 percent; a contract needs the logits or the server. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) When does a finite-state machine not suffice? Expected: for recursive schemas; the machine flattens recursion to a fixed depth, and a context-free grammar engine is needed. (level 3) What does a provider's plain JSON mode guarantee, and what does it not? Expected: valid JSON syntax, not conformance to your schema; always send a full schema. (level 3) How does the retry library differ from the logit processor? Expected: it never changes the model's distribution; it validates after the fact and retries, which adds latency and cost per failure. (level 4) The schema has an enum with 10,000 options and compilation times out. What do you do? Expected: predict a short list of candidates with a retriever first, then constrain the decode to those. Where it is taught. The structured outputs lesson builds the logit processor and compares the three layers. Defend a design You review the schema of an extraction service. It is {"answer": ..., "reasoning": ..., "date": <a strict year-month-day regex>} , enforced by constrained decoding. Compliance is perfect, yet accuracy is poor and some dates are invented. What is wrong with the design, and how do you change it? Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Two faults that no validator can catch. The answer field comes before the reasoning field, so the model commits to an answer before it has reasoned, and the strict date pattern leaves no legal way to say unknown, so the model complies by inventing a date. Put reasoning first and the answer last, and allow a null or a sentinel for a missing date; field order is logic, not formatting, and a grammar that is too strict forces a confident wrong value. Fault one: premature commitment. Generation is left to right. With answer first, the model must emit the label before it has written a single word of analysis; the reasoning that follows is a justification of a choice already made. Swap the order and the model writes its analysis into the context that the answer is then conditioned on. The JSON is equally valid either way. Only the second way is correct. Copy Fault two: a grammar with no exit. The date regex admits only well-formed dates. When the source has no date, the model cannot output "unknown", and a mask that forbids every honest token leaves only dishonest ones. Allow null or a sentinel string in the schema and instruct the model to use it. The other pitfalls to check in the same review. Recursive schemas behind a state-machine library. The machine flattens recursion to a fixed depth; nested structures need a context-free grammar engine. Huge enums. An enum of 10,000 options compiles slowly or times out; narrow the candidates with a retriever first, then constrain to those. Plain JSON mode without a schema. It guarantees syntax, not your fields. The validation plan that would have caught it. Compliance rate is one number of four. Add semantic validity, measured with a judge or a labeled set, the field coverage rate, and latency at p50 and p99. A system with perfect compliance and poor semantic validity is exactly this case. The rule for the team. Refuse any schema that puts answer or decision before its reasoning fields. Refuse bare JSON mode without a schema. Flag any recursive schema that sits behind a state-machine-only library. Plausible wrong answers. "Tighten the regex so only plausible dates pass." The grammar is already the problem; a tighter one forces more invention. "Add a line to the prompt asking the model to be honest." The mask forbids the honest tokens; no instruction can make the model emit a token with minus infinity logit. "Validation passes, so the system works." Validation checks shape; it cannot see that the answer was committed before the reasoning or that a date was made up. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) How do you measure semantic validity when compliance is already perfect? Expected: a labeled sample scored by a judge or by rules on the content, tracked separately from schema compliance. (level 3) The output needs a tree, such as nested comments. What changes? Expected: a state-machine library flattens recursion; move to a context-free grammar engine. (level 4) The product streams the answer to the user and wants it first for latency. How do you resolve the conflict? Expected: name the trade; options are two calls, reasoning in a hidden field before a visible answer, or accepting the latency; never answer-first with the same accuracy expectation. (level 4) How would the invented dates have shown up in monitoring? Expected: a field coverage rate near 100 percent on a corpus where the date is often missing is itself the alarm; compare the rate with the base rate of the field in the source. Where it is taught. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line "t entails h" means a human reading t would conclude h is true. NLI is the task of predicting entailment / contradiction / neutral. Boring on the surface, load-bearing in production. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means NLI Natural Language Inference 3-way classification of premise-hypothesis relationship. RTE Recognizing Textual Entailment Older name for NLI; same task. Entailment "t implies h" A typical reader would conclude h is true given t. Contradiction "t rules out h" A typical reader would conclude h is false given t. Neutral "undecided" No inference from t to h either way. Zero-shot classification NLI as classifier Verbalize labels as hypotheses, pick max entailment. Faithfulness Is the answer supported? NLI over (retrieved context, generated answer). The problem In plain words first Natural language inference (NLI) asks one question about two texts: given the first (the premise ), is the second (the hypothesis ) definitely true, definitely false, or undecided? These three answers are called entailment, contradiction and neutral. The task sounds academic, but it is the workhorse behind three practical jobs: checking whether a summary or chatbot answer is supported by its source, classifying text into labels the model was never trained on ("this text is about sports": true or not?), and filtering contradictory claims. This lesson defines the task precisely, shows how a cross-encoder computes the three probabilities and how zero-shot classification turns them into label scores, measures the famous dataset shortcut where the hypothesis alone gives the answer away, and runs a real NLI model on standard and adversarial test sets and as a faithfulness checker. You built a summarizer. It produced a summary. How do you know the summary does not contain a hallucination? You built a chatbot. It answered "yes." How do you know the answer is supported by the retrieved passage? You need to classify 10,000 news articles by topic. You have no training labels. Can you reuse a model? All three problems reduce to Natural Language Inference. NLI asks: given a premise t and a hypothesis h , is h entailed by t , contradicted, or neutral (unrelated)? Hallucination check: t = source document, h = summary claim. Not entailment = hallucination. Grounded QA: t = retrieved passage, h = generated answer. Not entailment = fabrication. Zero-shot classification: t = document, h = verbalized label ("This is about sports"). Entailment = predicted label. One task, three production uses. This is why NLI models, or LLMs prompted to do the same three-way judgement, sit underneath most hallucination and faithfulness checks in RAG evaluation. The idea The three labels. Entailment. t → h . "The cat is on the mat" entails "There is a cat." Contradiction. t → ¬ h . "The cat is on the mat" contradicts "There is no cat." Neutral. No inference either way. "The cat is on the mat" is neutral to "The cat is hungry." Not logical entailment. NLI is natural language inference — what a typical human reader would infer, not strict logic. "John walked his dog" entails "John has a dog" in NLI, but strict first-order logic would only admit it if you axiomatize possession. Datasets. SNLI (2015). 570k human-annotated pairs, image captions as premises. Narrow domain. MultiNLI (2017). 433k pairs across 10 genres. The standard training corpus in 2026. ANLI (2019). Adversarial NLI. Humans wrote examples specifically designed to break existing models. Harder. DocNLI, ConTRoL (2020–21). Document-length premises. Tests multi-hop and long-range inference. The architecture. A transformer encoder (BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa) reads [CLS] premise [SEP] hypothesis [SEP] . The [CLS] representation feeds a 3-way softmax. Train on MNLI, evaluate on held-out benchmarks, get 90%+ accuracy on in-distribution pairs. Zero-shot via NLI. Given a document and candidate labels, turn each label into a hypothesis ("This text is about sports"). Compute entailment probability for each. Pick the max. This is the mechanism behind Hugging Face's zero-shot-classification pipeline. The same idea as a formula The model. A cross-encoder reads both texts together, [CLS] premise [SEP] hypothesis [SEP] , so every hypothesis token can attend to every premise token. The final [CLS] vector goes through a linear layer to three logits , and ​ , y ∈ { entailment , neutral , contradiction } trained with cross-entropy on labelled pairs (MultiNLI, ANLI, ...). Zero-shot classification. For a text and labels ​ , … , ℓ K ​ , build hypotheses ​ = "This example is about ​ ." Two ways to score: - Single-label (one label is true): softmax across labels of the entailment logits, ​ ∣ x ) = ∑ j ​ e x p z ent ​ ( x , h j ​ ) e x p z ent ​ ( x , h k ​ ) ​ . Scores sum to 1. - Multi-label (any number can be true): for each label separately, softmax over just entailment and contradiction, ​ ) = e z ent ​ + e z con ​ e z ent ​ ​ . Scores do not sum to 1. Faithfulness. Split an answer into atomic claims ​ , … , c m ​ and score 1 ​ ∑ i ​ 1 [ P ( entail ∣ context , c i ​ ) > τ ] . Dataset artefacts. If the label is predictable from the hypothesis alone, = P ( y ) , then a model can score well without reading the premise; a test of how much a dataset leaks is how far ​ P ( y ∣ some feature of h ) rises above the base rate. Single-label forces the labels to compete, so "politics" looks unlikely; multi-label judges each on its own, and "politics" is more likely than not, a fair reading of a story about a central bank. What does it return, and what is wrong with checking a whole answer as one hypothesis? (Solution B1.) Pitfalls Hypothesis-only shortcuts. Classifiers that never see the premise predict the label from the hypothesis alone about 67% of the time on SNLI and 53% on MultiNLI, against about 34% by chance (Gururangan et al., 2018), because annotators wrote contradictions with "not", "nobody", "never" and entailments as vaguer paraphrases. Strong baseline for detecting label leakage. Lexical overlap heuristic. The subsequence heuristic ("every subsequence is entailed") passes SNLI but fails HANS/ANLI. Use adversarial benchmarks. Document-length degradation. Models trained on sentence pairs lose much of their accuracy on document-length premises, where the evidence may be spread over several sentences. Use DocNLI-trained models for long context. Zero-shot template sensitivity. "This example is about {label}" vs "{label}" vs "The topic is {label}" can swing accuracy by many points. Tune the template on a labelled sample. Domain mismatch. MNLI trains on general English. Legal, medical, and scientific text need domain-specific NLI models (e.g., SciNLI, MedNLI). Annotators, asked to write a false statement quickly, reached for "not" or an absolute claim; asked for a true one, they wrote something vaguer. A model can learn these cues without reading the premise, which is why adversarial datasets were built and why hypothesis-only baselines are a standard check. Solutions Solution P1 · About 60% In the run, 60% of the 1,456 hypotheses with a negation word are contradictions, and only 22% entailments, against a base rate of about a third each. Depending on the model, the unsupported clause "lunch will be provided" either drags the entailment score down, so the answer is rejected although its main content is correct (as in the museum example under "Use it"), or is swamped by the long copied part, so the answer passes with a hallucination inside it. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Word2Vec gave you a vector per word. Modern embedding models give you a vector per passage, cross-lingual, with sparse, dense, and multi-vector views, sized to fit your index. Pick wrong and your RAG retrieves the wrong thing. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Dense embedding The vector One fixed-size vector per text. Cosine similarity for ranking. Sparse embedding Learned BM25 One weight per vocab token; mostly zeros; trained end-to-end. Multi-vector ColBERT-style One vector per token; MaxSim scoring; bigger index, better recall. Matryoshka Russian doll trick First N dims are a valid smaller embedding on their own. MTEB The benchmark Massive Text Embedding Benchmark — 56 tasks at launch, 100+ in v2. BEIR The retrieval benchmark 18 zero-shot retrieval tasks; often cited for cross-domain robustness. Asymmetric encoding Query ≠ doc path Model uses different projections for queries and documents. The problem In plain words first An embedding model turns a piece of text into a list of numbers, a vector, so that texts with similar meaning get nearby vectors. Search, RAG, clustering and deduplication all rest on it, and swapping one embedding model for another often changes results more than anything else in the pipeline. There are three shapes of embedding. Dense: one vector per passage. Sparse: a weight for each vocabulary word, like a learned BM25. Multi-vector: one vector per token, compared token by token. There are also practical knobs: how many numbers to keep, at what precision, and whether queries need a special prefix. This lesson explains each shape and the Matryoshka trick for shrinkable vectors, then measures on a real retrieval benchmark what a query prefix, truncation, 1-bit quantization and token-level scoring actually do. Your RAG system retrieves the wrong passage 40% of the time. The culprit is rarely the vector database or the prompt. It is the embedding model. Choosing an embedding in 2026 means picking across five axes: Dense vs sparse vs multi-vector. One vector per passage, or one per token, or a sparse weighted bag of words. Language coverage. Monolingual English models still win on English-only tasks. Multilingual models win when corpora are mixed. Context length. 512 tokens vs 8,192 vs 32,768, and quality often degrades well before the advertised maximum, so test with your real document lengths. Dimension budget. 3,072 floats at full precision = 12 KB per vector, so 100M vectors take about 1.2 TB before any index overhead. Matryoshka truncation to 768 dimensions cuts this 4×, and int8 or binary quantization cuts it a further 4× or 32×. Open vs hosted. Open-weight means you control the stack and data. Hosted means you trade control for always-latest. This lesson names the tradeoffs so you can pick on evidence, not on whatever was popular last quarter. The idea Dense embeddings. One vector per passage (usually 384-3,072 dimensions). Cosine similarity ranks passages by semantic proximity. OpenAI text-embedding-3-large , BGE-M3 dense mode, Voyage-3. Default choice. Sparse embeddings. SPLADE-style. A transformer predicts a weight for every vocab token, then zeros out most of them. Result is a sparse vector of size |vocab|. Captures lexical matching (like BM25) but with learned term weights. Strong on keyword-heavy queries. Multi-vector (late interaction). ColBERTv2, Jina-ColBERT. One vector per token. Scoring with MaxSim: for each query token, find the most similar document token, sum the scores. More expensive to store and score, but wins on long queries and domain-specific corpora. BGE-M3: all three at once. Single model outputs dense, sparse, and multi-vector representations simultaneously. Each can be queried independently; scores fuse via weighted sum. The 2026 default when you want flexibility from one checkpoint. Matryoshka Representation Learning. Trained so the first N dimensions of the vector form a useful standalone embedding. Truncate a 1,536-dim vector to 256 dims and lose only a little accuracy for 6× less storage (OpenAI reported that text-embedding-3-large cut to 256 dimensions still beat its previous full-size model). Supported by OpenAI text-embedding-3, Cohere embed v4, Voyage 4, Jina embeddings v3 and v4, Gemini Embedding, Nomic Embed v1.5 and later. The same idea as a formula Dense. One vector per text, , normalised to length 1, scored by cosine d . Trained contrastively (InfoNCE): for a query ​ with its relevant passage + ​ and the other passages in the batch as negatives, ​ exp ( q i ⊤ ​ d j ​ / τ ) exp ( q i ⊤ ​ d i + ​ / τ ) ​ Sparse (SPLADE). For each input token and vocabulary word , the masked-LM head gives a logit ​ ; the document's weight for is ​ = max j ​ lo g ( 1 + ReLU ( z j , w ​ ) ) , pushed towards zero for most words by a sparsity penalty. The score is ​ w w ​ ( q ) w w ​ ( d ) : lexical matching with learned weights and learned expansion terms. Multi-vector (ColBERT). One unit vector per token, ​ .. q m ​ and ​ .. d n ​ ; each query token finds its best-matching document token: ∑ m ​ j max ​ q i ⊤ ​ d j ​ (MaxSim) Storage grows with document length ( vectors instead of 1), which is why it is used for reranking or with heavy compression. Matryoshka representation learning (Kusupati et al., 2022) trains the same embedding at several prefix lengths at once, ​ = ∑ m ∈ { 64 , 128 , 256 , … , k } ​ c m ​ L ( q 1 : m ​ , d 1 : m ​ ) , so the first coordinates are a good embedding on their own. A model trained without it spreads information across all coordinates, and truncation removes some of it. Quantization. int8 stores each coordinate in one byte (4× smaller than float32). Binary keeps only the sign, , 32× smaller, with similarity by Hamming distance; a common recipe retrieves candidates with bits and rescores them with full vectors. Worked example MaxSim versus one pooled vector Query tokens "apple" and "price" . Document A has tokens "apple", "cost"; document B has one token "fruit-market" (unit-ish vectors, rounded). MaxSim A: "apple" best match ; "price" best match ; total . MaxSim B: "apple" ; "price" ; total . A wins: it covers both query aspects separately. Mean-pooled dense: query , A , B . Cosines: A ; B . B wins. Pooling blurs which query word each part of the document answers; MaxSim keeps that alignment, which is why late interaction helps on multi-aspect queries. Idea 1 · The MTEB leaderboard tells a partial story Massive Text Embedding Benchmark — 56 tasks across 8 task types at launch (2022), expanded to 100+ tasks in MTEB v2. The top of the leaderboard changes every few months; in 2025-2026 it has been held by large proprietary models (Gemini Embedding and its multimodal successor Gemini Embedding 2, among others) and large open ones (Qwen3-Embedding), with smaller open models such as the BGE family far down the list but much cheaper to run. The leaderboard is necessary but not sufficient — always benchmark on your domain. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Embedding models grew and went multimodal. LLM-based embedders (Qwen3-Embedding, 2025; Gemini Embedding, 2025) lead MTEB, and Gemini Embedding 2 (2026) maps text, images, video and audio into one vector space. Matryoshka and quantization are standard. Most current API and open models support truncated dimensions, and vector databases offer int8 and binary storage with rescoring, the recipe measured above. Multi-vector went practical. ColBERT-style late interaction is now served with heavy compression (PLAID, token pooling) and extends to documents as images (ColPali, 2024), where each page is a grid of patch vectors; Lesson 5.14's reranking stage is where it usually sits. Sources: Matryoshka Representation Learning , Gemini Embedding 2 , Qwen3-Embedding , ColPali . Pitfalls Same model for query and doc. Some models (Voyage, Jina-ColBERT) use asymmetric encoding — query and document pass through different paths. Always check the model card. Missing prefix. bge-* models need "Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: " prepended to queries. Validate on your eval set. Context truncation. Most models silently truncate inputs over their max length. Long docs need chunking (see lesson 23). Ignoring latency tail. MTEB scores hide p99 latency. A 600M model might beat a 335M model by 2 points but cost 3× more per query. Recap What to keep from this lesson Dense (one vector), sparse (learned term weights), multi-vector (one per token, MaxSim): different storage, different strengths. Embedding models are trained contrastively; query and document may need different prefixes or encoders. Matryoshka training makes prefixes of the vector usable; other models lose more when truncated. Binary quantization with float rescoring keeps most quality at 1/32 of the storage. Choose by measuring on your own data; leaderboards average away your domain. A non-Matryoshka model spreads information over every coordinate, so dropping 320 of them throws away real signal, while the sign of each coordinate preserves most of the angle between two vectors. 64 floats (256 bytes) is also more storage than 384 bits (48 bytes). Solution B1 · Vector length starts to count Truncated vectors no longer have length 1, and different documents keep different shares of their length in the first few coordinates. The dot product then mixes the angle with that leftover length, so documents whose information happens to sit in the early coordinates rank higher regardless of relevance. Rankings change, and usually get worse. Re-normalising restores cosine similarity on the kept coordinates. Sources and further reading Reimers, Gurevych (2019). Sentence-BERT — the bi-encoder paper. Get chunking wrong and no amount of reranking saves you. Overlap Safety margin N tokens shared between adjacent chunks; often useless in 2026 benchmarks. Semantic chunking Smart chunking Split where adjacent-sentence embedding similarity drops. The problem In plain words first Before a RAG system can retrieve anything, long documents have to be cut into pieces ("chunks"), each embedded and stored separately. How you cut decides what can be found. Cut too small and the answer is separated from the words that identify it. Cut too large and the answer is buried in a long chunk whose single vector mostly describes other things, which also costs more context in the prompt. Cut in the wrong place and a sentence is split in half. This lesson explains why one vector per chunk forces this trade-off. It compares the common strategies (fixed-size, recursive, sentence windows, semantic, parent-child) and the "contextual" tricks that prepend surrounding information to each chunk. Then it measures them on real Wikipedia articles with hundreds of questions whose answers are known, so you can see the recall-versus-context trade-off rather than take a blog post's word for it. You put a 50-page contract into a RAG system. User asks: "What is the termination clause?" The retriever returns the cover page. Why? Because the model was trained on 512-token chunks and the termination clause sits 20 pages in, split across a page break, with no local keywords tying it to the query. The fix is not "buy a better embedding model." The fix is chunking. How big? Overlap? Where to split? With surrounding context? Published comparisons show surprising results: Vectara's 2024 study (Qu, Bao and Tu, "Is Semantic Chunking Worth the Computational Cost?") found that semantic chunking did not consistently beat simple fixed-size chunking, and concluded fixed-size is the more efficient, reliable choice for most applications. NVIDIA's 2025 comparison found page-level chunking the most accurate and most consistent default across its datasets, with about 15% overlap best among the few overlap settings it tried. Results differ by dataset and query type in all of these studies, so your own evaluation decides. The "obvious" answer (semantic chunking, 20% overlap, 1000 tokens) is often wrong. This lesson builds intuition for six strategies and tells you when to reach for which. The idea Fixed chunking. Split every N characters or tokens. Simplest baseline. Breaks mid-sentence. What problem does the two-level layout solve, what does the seen set do, and how many parents can the function return? python def retrieve_parent(child_query, mapping, encoder, top_k=3): child_embs = encoder.encode([m["child"] for m in mapping], normalize_embeddings=True) q_emb = encoder.encode([child_query], normalize_embeddings=True)[0] scores = child_embs @ q_emb top = np.argsort(-scores)[:top_k] seen, parents = set(), [] for i in top: if mapping[i]["parent_idx"] not in seen: parents.append(mapping[i]["parent"]) seen.add(mapping[i]["parent_idx"]) return parents Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Small child chunks are indexed for a precise match and the larger parent is returned for context, which removes the trade-off between a precise hit and enough surrounding text. The seen set drops a parent that several top children map to, so the prompt does not receive the same text twice. For a mapping that is not empty and a positive top_k , the function returns between one and top_k parents, fewer when children share a parent; an empty mapping or a top_k of zero returns none. The layout. Standard chunking forces a choice: small chunks match precisely but lack context, large chunks carry context but cover many topics. The two-level layout indexes small children and stores the parent each child came from. The chunking lesson splits parents at 2048 and children at 256 by default, and the advanced RAG lesson draws a 512-token parent with four 128-token children. A query about one detail matches one child precisely, and the prompt receives the whole parent, including the lines around the detail. Walk the function. Encode every child and the query with normalization on, so the matrix product equals the cosine. Sort children by score and keep the top k indices. For each top child, look up its parent index; if that parent was not seen, append the parent text and mark it. Return the parents in the order of their best child. Why de-duplicate. Several children of one parent often match the same query, because they sit in the same section. Without the set, the prompt would receive the same parent twice or three times and waste its context budget. The lesson calls this the key insight of the pattern. What production changes. The function re-encodes every child on each call. A real index stores the child vectors once and only embeds the query. The two-level layout also degrades gracefully: a poor child match still returns a reasonable parent. Plausible wrong answers. "Return the parent of every top child, duplicates included." Several children map to one parent, and the repeated text wastes the context budget. "Make the child as large as the parent." Then there is no precision gain; the point is a small match unit and a large context unit. "The function always returns exactly top_k parents." It returns fewer when children share a parent. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why index the child and not the parent? Expected: a small chunk matches a specific question precisely, while a large chunk covers many topics and its embedding points nowhere in particular. (level 2) Why a plain matrix product and no cosine? Expected: the vectors are normalized at encode time, so the dot product equals the cosine. (level 3) What does this function do on every call that production code must not? Expected: it re-encodes all the children; store the child vectors once at index time and embed only the query. (level 3) Two parents each have one matching child, and a third parent has three matching children below the cut. What does the function miss? Expected: it ranks by the best child only; a parent with several good children gets no extra credit unless you aggregate child scores per parent. Where it is taught. Two chunkers times two retrievers, every cell against the same qrels, same k values. The metrics. Recall at 5 as the primary number, precision at k beside it, MRR for the position of the first hit, nDCG if the labels are graded, and an answer hit at 5 that counts a query only when a top-five chunk contains the gold answer substring. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line "She called him. He did not answer. The doctor was at lunch." Three references to two people and nobody is named. Coreference resolution figures out who is who. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Mention A reference A span of text that refers to an entity (name, pronoun, noun phrase). Antecedent What "it" refers to The earlier mention a later one corefers with. Cluster The entity's mentions Set of mentions that all refer to the same real-world entity. Anaphora Backward reference Later mention refers to earlier ("he" → "John"). Cataphora Forward reference Earlier mention refers to later ("When he arrived, John..."). Bridging Implicit reference "I bought a car. The wheels were bad." (wheels of THAT car.) CoNLL F1 The number on leaderboards Average of MUC, B³, CEAF-φ4 F1 scores. The problem In plain words first Coreference resolution works out which words in a text refer to the same thing. In "Apple announced new phones. The company said they will ship soon", "Apple" and "the company" are one entity and "new phones" and "they" are another. The output is a set of groups (clusters) of mentions, one group per real-world entity. Search, summarization, question answering and knowledge graphs all need this: without it, "she" is a dead end and one company becomes three. This lesson describes the mention-ranking model behind modern systems, runs the lesson's rule-based resolver on easy and famously hard sentences, and builds the three standard scores (MUC, B³ and CEAF) from scratch. Scoring a clustering turns out to be subtle: the scores disagree sharply on simple degenerate systems, which is exactly why the field reports their average. Extract every mention of Apple Inc. from a 300-word article. Easy when the article says "Apple." Hard when it says "the company," "they," "Cupertino's technology giant," or "Jobs's firm." Without resolving these mentions to the same entity, your NER pipeline misses 60-80% of the mentions. Coreference resolution links every expression that refers to the same real-world entity into one cluster. It is the glue between surface-level NLP (NER, parsing) and downstream semantics (IE, QA, summarization, KG). Why it matters in 2026: Summarization: "The CEO announced..." vs "Tim Cook announced..." — the summary should name the CEO. Question answering: "Who did she call?" requires resolving "she." Information extraction: a knowledge graph with "PER1 founded Apple" and "Jobs founded Apple" as separate entries is wrong. Multi-document IE: merging mentions across articles about the same event is cross-document coreference. The idea The task. Input: a document. Output: a clustering of mentions (spans) where each cluster refers to one entity. Mention types. Named entity. "Tim Cook" Nominal. "the CEO", "the company" Pronominal. "he", "she", "they", "it" Appositive. "Tim Cook, Apple's CEO," Architectures. Rule-based (Hobbs, 1978). Syntactic-tree-based pronoun resolution using grammar rules. Good baseline, and for decades surprisingly hard to beat on pronouns (Lappin and Leass, 1994, and later learned systems took many years to pull clearly ahead). Mention-pair classifier. For every pair of mentions ​ , m j ​ ) , predict whether they corefer. Cluster by transitive closure. Standard pre-2016. Mention-ranking. For each mention, rank candidate antecedents (including "no antecedent"). Pick the top. Span-based end-to-end (Lee et al., 2017). Transformer encoder. Enumerate all candidate spans up to a length cap. Predict mention scores. Predict antecedent-probability for each span. Cluster greedily. The modern default. Generative (2024+). Prompt an LLM: "List every pronoun in this text and its antecedent." Works well on easy cases, struggles on long documents and rare referents. The evaluation metrics. Five standard metrics (MUC, B³, CEAF, BLANC, LEA) because no single metric captures clustering quality. Report the average of the first three as CoNLL F1. Check your mental model ✗ "Coreference is pronoun resolution." ✓ Pronouns are one case; names, descriptions ("Cupertino's technology giant") and appositives also have to be linked, and they are often harder. ✗ "One clustering score is enough." ✓ The scores reward different things; under "Use it", putting every mention in its own cluster scores 0 on MUC and well on B³. ✗ "Gender and number agreement settle most pronouns." ✓ Many pronouns are ambiguous on agreement alone; "The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big" needs world knowledge to resolve "it". The experiments below run the lesson's own rule-based resolver and build the evaluation metrics, which is where most of the subtlety lies. On a longer document, you get something like: - Cluster 1: [Apple, The company, it] - Cluster 2: [new products, them] Step 2 · rule-based pronoun resolver (teaching) See code/main.py for a stdlib-only implementation: Extract mentions: named entities (capitalized spans), pronouns (dict lookup), definite descriptions ("the X"). For each pronoun, look at the previous K mentions and score them by: - gender/number agreement (heuristic) - recency (closer wins) - syntactic role (subjects preferred) Link the highest-scoring antecedent. Not competitive with neural models. But it shows the search space and the decisions an end-to-end model must make. Break it on purpose In the lesson's agreement_score , remove the gender check entirely (so only number agreement and recency count), and resolve "Mary Chen joined Apple last year. She leads the AI team." What does "She" link to now, and why? (Solution B1.) Step 3 · using LLMs for coreference Copy Two failure modes to watch. First, LLMs over-merge ("him" and "her" referring to two distinct people). Second, LLMs silently drop mentions in long documents. Always verify with span-offset checks. Step 4 · evaluation The standard conll-2012 script computes MUC, B³, CEAF-φ4 and reports the average. For an in-house eval, start with span-level precision and recall on your annotated test set, then add mention-linking F1. Pitfalls Singleton explosion. Some systems report every mention as its own cluster. B³ is lenient. MUC punishes this. Always check all three metrics. Pronouns in long context. Accuracy drops on long documents, where antecedents can be pages away and models process text in windows. Chunk carefully and merge clusters across windows. Gender assumptions. Hard-coded gender rules break on non-binary referents, organizations, animals. Use learned models or neutral scoring. LLM drift on long docs. A single API call cannot reliably cluster mentions across 50+ paragraphs. Use sliding-window + merge. "It will ship in June" means the laptop, but "It" links to "The company": both candidates sit in the previous sentence, the recency score cannot tell them apart, and the tie goes to the first one. "Her" links to "AI", because the capitalisation rule treated the acronym in "the AI team" as a name of unknown gender. The hard cases fail in instructive ways. Cataphora: "she" comes before "Mary", the resolver only looks backwards, and the only earlier capitalised word is "When", so it links "she" to a sentence-initial word. Winograd: "trophy" and "suitcase" are not in the list of known nouns, so "it" gets no antecedent at all, and even with them, agreement could not decide; a reader knows that the thing that is too big is the one that does not fit. Unknown names: "they" links to "Jordan Kim" because unknown gender agrees with everything. Each fix would be another rule; this is why learned models took over. The degenerate systems expose each metric's blind spot. All singletons: MUC 0, because there are no links to get right, while B³ still gives 0.50, since every mention's cluster is "pure". One big cluster: MUC gives 0.84, because every gold link is present, while B³ (0.42) and CEAF (0.20) punish the impurity. The most striking row is the third: merging two whole entities scores higher on MUC (0.94) than the system with a single misplaced pronoun (0.88), because MUC only counts the minimum number of links needed and a merge costs few of them. CEAF, with its one-to-one alignment, is the metric that notices the merge. The CoNLL average ranks the good system first and both degenerate ones far below, which is why papers report it rather than any single number. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) LLMs as resolvers. Production pipelines increasingly prompt an LLM to resolve references within a document (or to rewrite pronouns before retrieval); they handle many easy and medium cases well but still over-merge distinct entities and drop mentions in long documents, as the lesson warns. Small trained models for volume. Libraries such as fastcoref and spaCy's experimental coreference component, and open checkpoints such as Maverick, run on CPUs or one GPU when every document must be processed. Coreference inside RAG and knowledge graphs. Resolving "she" and "the company" before chunking or extraction keeps facts attached to the right entity (Lessons 5.23 and 5.26). Sources: fastcoref , spacy-experimental coref , Maverick , End-to-end Neural Coreference Resolution . Downstream tasks see one entity per cluster, not one entity per mention. Recap What to keep from this lesson Coreference groups mentions (names, descriptions, pronouns) into one cluster per entity. Modern systems score spans and antecedents and let each span pick an earlier antecedent or none; clusters are the linked components. Rules (agreement, recency, syntax) fail on cataphora, ambiguous agreement and world-knowledge cases. MUC counts links, B³ averages over mentions, CEAF aligns clusters; each can be gamed, so report all three and their mean. Run coreference after NER and merge clusters into entities for downstream use. Solutions Solution P1 · MUC gives 0; B³ is fooled MUC counts the links a system gets right; all singletons have no links, so MUC precision, recall and F1 are all 0. B³ scores every mention: each one is "correctly" in a cluster with no wrong members, so B³ precision is perfect and its F1 stays fairly high. CEAF falls in between. The reverse trick, one big cluster, gets full MUC recall and a high MUC F1 while B³ precision collapses. Each metric has a blind spot, which is why CoNLL F1 averages them. Solution B1 · Recency takes over Without the gender check, "Mary Chen" and "Apple" both agree in number with "She", and only recency is left to decide. Both are in the previous sentence, so the decision falls to the token-position term, and "She" can attach to the company. Agreement features are cheap, strong filters; removing one shows how much the resolver leans on them, and how fragile its tie-breaking is (the lesson's own document already shows "It" choosing "The company" over "a laptop" on a tie). The real fix is not more rules but a model that represents what kind of thing each mention is. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line NER found "Paris." Entity linking decides: Paris, France? Paris Hilton? Paris, Texas? Paris (the Trojan prince)? Without linking, your knowledge graph stays ambiguous. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Entity linking (EL) Link to Wikipedia Map a mention to a unique KB entry. Candidate generation Who could it be? Return a shortlist of plausible KB entries for a mention. Disambiguation Pick the right one Score candidates using context, pick the winner. Alias index The lookup table Map from surface form → candidate entities. NIL Not in KB Explicit prediction that no KB entry matches. KB Knowledge base Wikidata, Wikipedia, DBpedia, or your domain KB. AIDA-CoNLL The benchmark 1,393 Reuters articles with gold entity links. The problem In plain words first Named entity recognition (Lesson 5.6) finds that "Jordan" is a name. Entity linking decides which Jordan: the basketball player, the actor, the machine-learning professor, or the country. It connects each mention to one entry in a knowledge base such as Wikidata, so that every mention of the same thing gets the same ID, and that ID brings facts with it. It works in two steps. First, look up which entries the mention's text could possibly mean (candidate generation). Then pick the one that fits the surrounding text best (disambiguation), helped by how often each candidate is meant in general. This lesson writes out the classic scoring formula and the modern embedding and generative versions. It then compares word overlap with embeddings on ambiguous sentences, shows how a popularity prior can override clear context, and shows how a system should answer "none of these" (NIL). A sentence reads: "Jordan beat the press." Your NER tags "Jordan" as PERSON. Good. But which Jordan? Michael Jordan (basketball)? Michael B. Jordan (actor)? Michael I. Jordan (Berkeley ML professor — yes, this confusion is real in ML papers)? Jordan (the country)? Jordan (Hebrew first name)? Entity linking (EL) resolves each mention to a unique entry in a knowledge base: Wikidata, Wikipedia, DBpedia, or your domain KB. Two subtasks: Candidate generation. Given "Jordan," which KB entries are plausible? Disambiguation. Given the context, which candidate is the right one? Both steps are learnable. Both are benchmarked. The combined pipeline has been stable for a decade — what changes is the quality of the disambiguator. The idea Candidate generation. Given the mention surface form ("Jordan"), look up candidates in an alias index. Wikipedia alias dictionaries cover most named entities: "JFK" → John F. Kennedy, Jacqueline Kennedy, JFK airport, JFK (movie). Typical index returns 10-30 candidates per mention. Disambiguation: three approaches. Prior + context (Milne & Witten, 2008). P(entity | mention) × context-similarity(entity, text) . Works well, fast, no training. Embedding-based (REL, BLINK). Encode mention + context. Encode each candidate's description. Pick max cosine, usually followed by a cross-encoder rerank of the top candidates. A common default from 2020 on. Generative (GENRE, 2021; LLM-based, 2023+). Decode the entity's canonical name token-by-token. Constrained to a trie of valid entity names so output is guaranteed to be a valid KB id. End-to-end vs pipeline. Modern models (ELQ, BLINK, ExtEnD, GENRE) run NER + candidate generation + disambiguation in one pass. Pipeline systems still dominate in production because you can swap components. The same idea as a formula Candidate generation returns ; candidate recall is the share of gold mentions with ∈ C ( m ) , the ceiling for everything after. The commonness prior. From Wikipedia's links, how often does the anchor text point to entity ? ​ count ( m → e ′ ) count ( m → e ) ​ Picking ​ P ( e ∣ m ) alone, ignoring context, is a famously strong baseline: most mentions mean their most common sense. Combining prior and context. A simple log-linear score: with similarity from word overlap (the lesson's Jaccard) or embeddings. Milne and Witten (2008) added relatedness between candidate entities of different mentions in the same text, measured by shared Wikipedia in-links: "Bulls" and "Chicago" pull "Jordan" toward the basketball player. Bi-encoder retrieval (BLINK, Wu et al., 2020): ​ ( mention in context ) ⊤ E e ​ ( entity description ) , trained contrastively so the right entity scores above others; entity vectors are precomputed for millions of entities, then a cross-encoder rescores the top 10 to 100. NIL. If ​ score ( e ) < τ , predict NIL: the mention's entity is not in the knowledge base. trades wrong links against missed links, like the FAQ threshold in Lesson 5.17. Check your mental model ✗ "Entity linking is NER with more labels." ✓ NER chooses among a few types; linking chooses among millions of entities, most of which never appear in training data, so it relies on descriptions and aliases rather than a classifier per entity. ✗ "If the right entity is not found, the system made a disambiguation error." ✓ First check candidate recall: if the right entity was never a candidate, no disambiguator could have found it. ✗ "Always link every mention." ✓ Many mentions refer to things not in the knowledge base; predicting NIL is a correct answer. The lesson's Jaccard overlap and the BLINK-style embedding similarity each pick a candidate. Which will get more right, and on which kind of sentence will Jaccard fail? (Solution P1.) Idea 1 · The two measurements Mention recall (candidate gen). Fraction of gold mentions where the correct KB entry appears in the candidate list. Floor for the whole pipeline. Disambiguation accuracy / F1. Given correct candidates, how often the top-1 is right. Always report both. A system with 99% disambiguation on 80% candidate recall is an 80% pipeline. Step 1 · build an alias index from Wikipedia redirects Copy Real alias tables are built from Wikipedia redirects, disambiguation pages, link anchor texts and Wikidata's "also known as" labels, millions of (alias, entity) pairs. Download them from the Wikipedia and Wikidata dumps and store them as an inverted index. (In the toy index above, the Wikidata IDs of Michael Jordan, Jordan the country, Paris, Apple Inc. and the apple fruit are the real ones; treat the others as placeholders to look up.) Step 2 · context-based disambiguation Copy The Jaccard overlap is a toy. Replace with cosine similarity on embeddings (see code/main.py step-2 for the transformer version). Break it on purpose Call the lesson's disambiguate with a context that shares no words with any candidate description, for example disambiguate("jordan", "Wow!", alias_index, entity_desc) . What does it return, and why is that dangerous? (Solution B1.) Step 3 · embedding-based (BLINK-style) Copy At index time, embed every KB entity once. At query time, embed the mention + context once, dot-product against the candidate pool, pick max. Step 4 · generative entity linking (concept) GENRE (De Cao et al., 2021) decodes the entity's Wikipedia title token by token with a sequence-to-sequence model. Constrained decoding (Lesson 5.20) over a prefix trie of all valid titles ensures only real titles can be output. Its modern descendants are LLM-prompted linkers that choose from a candidate list with structured output. Copy Combined with a whitelist (Outlines choice ), this is the simplest EL pipeline to ship in 2026. Step 5 · evaluate on AIDA-CoNLL AIDA-CoNLL is the standard EL benchmark: 1,393 Reuters articles, 34k mentions, Wikipedia entities. Report in-KB accuracy ( P@1 ) and out-of-KB NIL-detection rate. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Embeddings get 11 of 12, Jaccard 9. Jaccard's failures show what word overlap really measures: "starred as the boxer Adonis in Creed" goes to Jordan the country , because the country's description shares filler words ("the", "in") with the sentence; the trade agreement goes to the basketball player; "a faster chip for its laptops" goes to the fruit. The embedding linker gets all three, matching meaning rather than words, and fails on one: "launched a new fragrance and a reality show" goes to Paris, France, a reminder that a small general-purpose encoder knows celebrities less well than cities. The last two lines are the NIL problem. "Jordan Peterson" is not in the knowledge base, yet his sentence scores 0.50 against the machine-learning professor, higher than several correct links above (the lowest is 0.32). No single threshold on this score separates "not in the KB" from "correct but weakly worded". Real systems handle NIL with a dedicated classifier, with more aliases (the full name "Jordan Peterson" would retrieve a different candidate set), or by reranking with a cross-encoder. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) LLMs as linkers. Prompting an LLM with the mention, its context and a short candidate list (from an alias index or a bi-encoder) is now a common production pattern; the candidate list keeps the output a valid ID, the same idea as GENRE's trie. Efficient end-to-end linking. Amazon's open-source ReFinED links all mentions of a document in one forward pass using entity types and descriptions, which makes Wikidata-scale linking cheap enough for large corpora. Linking grounds retrieval. Knowledge-graph RAG pipelines (Microsoft GraphRAG, Neo4j, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with Neptune) depend on resolving mentions to stable entity IDs so that facts from different documents attach to the same node. Sources: ReFinED , BLINK , GraphRAG , Bedrock GraphRAG . Pitfalls NIL handling. Some mentions are not in the KB (emerging entities, obscure people). Systems must predict NIL instead of guessing the wrong entity. Measured separately. Mention boundary errors. Upstream NER misses partial spans ("Bank of America" tagged as just "Bank"). EL recall drops. Popularity bias. Trained systems over-predict frequent entities. A mention of "Michael I. Jordan" on an ML paper often links to basketball Jordan. Cross-lingual EL.
