Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line NER found the entities. Entity linking anchored them. Relation extraction finds the edges between them. A knowledge graph is the sum of nodes, edges, and their provenance. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Triple Subject-relation-object (s, r, o) tuple that is the atomic unit of a KG. Open IE Extract anything Open-vocabulary relation phrases; high recall, low precision. Closed ontology Fixed schema Bounded set of relation types (Wikidata, UMLS, FIBO). Canonicalization Normalize everything Map surface names / relations to canonical ids. AEVS Grounded extraction Anchor-Extraction-Verification-Supplement pipeline (2026). Provenance Source-of-truth link Every triple carries a doc id + char-span to its source. Distant supervision Cheap labels Align text with an existing KG to create training data. The problem In plain words first Named entity recognition (Lesson 5.6) finds the things a text talks about. Entity linking (Lesson 5.25) says exactly which thing each one is. Relation extraction finds what the text says between them: "Tim Cook became CEO of Apple" connects a person to a company through the relation "chief executive". Each fact becomes a triple, (subject, relation, object), and a pile of triples is a knowledge graph you can query: who runs Apple, where was Microsoft's CEO born, who owns GitHub. This lesson builds the three kinds of extractor (hand-written patterns, trained models, prompted LLMs) and measures where each one fails. It then shows the part that makes a graph trustworthy: tying every triple to the words that support it, mapping relations onto a fixed vocabulary with the right direction, checking types, and recording when a fact was true. An analyst reads: "Tim Cook became CEO of Apple in 2011." Four facts: (Tim Cook, role, CEO) (Tim Cook, employer, Apple) (Tim Cook, start_date, 2011) (Apple, type, Organization) Relation Extraction (RE) turns free text into structured triples (subject, relation, object) . Aggregate across a corpus and you have a knowledge graph. Aggregate and query and you have a reasoning substrate for RAG, analytics, or compliance audits. The 2026 problem: LLMs extract relations enthusiastically. Too enthusiastically. They hallucinate triples that the source text does not support. Without provenance, you cannot tell real triples from plausible fiction. The current answer is to make every triple point back to the exact words that support it, and to reject triples that cannot. AEVS (Yang et al., 2026), described below, is one published version of this anchor-and-verify design. The idea Triple form. (subject_entity, relation_type, object_entity) . Relations come from a closed ontology (Wikidata properties, FIBO, UMLS) or an open set (OpenIE-style, anything goes). Three extraction approaches. Rule / pattern-based. Hearst patterns: "X such as Y" → (Y, isA, X) . Plus hand-crafted regex. Brittle, precise, explainable. Supervised classifier. Given two entity mentions in a sentence, predict the relation from a fixed set, including "no relation". Trained on TACRED (106,264 sentences, 41 relations plus no_relation), ACE or the TAC KBP data. The standard approach from about 2015 to 2022. Generative. A sequence-to-sequence model trained to output triples (REBEL, 2021), or an LLM prompted to emit them. Works out of the box on new text. Needs provenance, or produces plausible-looking junk. AEVS (Anchor-Extraction-Verification-Supplement; Yang et al., 2026). One recent hallucination-mitigation framework for LLM extraction: Anchor. Identify every entity span and relation-phrase span with exact positions. Extract. Generate triples linked to anchor spans. Verify. Match each triple element back to the anchors: exact match first, then fuzzy, schema-based and full-text matching. Fully matched triples are accepted, partly matched ones get a second LLM check, the rest are rejected. Supplement. A coverage pass ensures no anchored span is dropped. In the paper's ablations the anchor constraint is the main reason hallucinations fall. The cost is 2.8 to 4.3 LLM calls per input instead of one, and in return every accepted triple can be traced to its source span. It is one recent paper, so treat its exact recipe as one option; the anchor-and-verify principle is the part to keep. The open-vs-closed tradeoff. Closed ontology. Fixed property list (e.g., Wikidata's more than 11,000 properties, most of them identifiers that link to other databases). Predictable. Queryable. Hard to invent. Open IE. Any verbal phrase becomes a relation. High recall. Low precision. Messy to query. Production KGs usually mix: open IE for discovery, then canonicalize relations onto a closed ontology before merging into the main graph. The same idea as a formula Relation classification. That is often wrong for one sentence, so later work moved to the weaker at-least-one assumption (Riedel et al., 2010): the bag of sentences mentioning the pair expresses at least once, and the model scores the bag, for example ​ P ( r ∣ x ) . Constraints a graph can check. Each property has a domain and a range: for , require and . Some properties are asymmetric: G . Time-bounded statements carry qualifiers, and a query at time keeps only statements with . Filling gaps (link prediction) is a related task: knowledge-graph embeddings such as TransE (Bordes et al., 2013) give each entity and relation a vector and score a candidate edge by . They predict edges that are likely ; extraction finds edges a text states . Worked example Pairs, labels and noise by hand Take "Born in Hyderabad, Satya Nadella joined Microsoft in 1992 and became its CEO in 2014." NER finds five entities: Hyderabad, Satya Nadella, Microsoft, 1992, 2014. That gives ordered pairs. The sentence states three relations: (Satya Nadella, place of birth, Hyderabad), (Satya Nadella, employer, Microsoft) and (Microsoft, chief executive officer, Satya Nadella), with the two years as qualifiers. So 17 of the 20 pairs, 85%, are "no relation". A classifier sees mostly negatives. Now distant supervision. The knowledge base holds (Satya Nadella, P19, Hyderabad). Three sentences mention both names (the second is invented for this example): "Born in Hyderabad, Satya Nadella joined Microsoft…": expresses P19. Label correct. "Satya Nadella gave a talk in Hyderabad.": does not. Label wrong. "Hyderabad-born Satya Nadella…": expresses P19. Label correct. Sentence-level labelling is right 2 times in 3. At the bag level, the at-least-one assumption is satisfied (sentences 1 and 3), so the bag's label is right, and a over the bag lets the model rely on its most convincing sentence. The relation, its direction and the entity types need checking too. ✗ "A knowledge graph stores what is true." ✓ It stores statements, with a source and, for many relations, a time span. "Tim Cook is CEO of Apple" was true from 2011 to 2026. See it drawn How far do six regexes get? main.py 's extract on fifteen sentences, each with its correct triples written by hand in the extractor's own (person-first) direction. A predicted triple counts only if subject, relation and object all match. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Precision 0.78, recall 0.47 ( ​ = 2 × 0.78 × 0.47/1.25 = 0.58 ). When a pattern fires it is usually right; most facts are simply missed. The misses are the ways English moves words around: passive voice ("was founded by", "was acquired by"), apposition ("Apple's chief executive, Tim Cook"), a fronted phrase ("Born in Hyderabad, Satya Nadella…"), a hyphen ("co-founded") and a second subject joined by "with". The two false triples show the other weakness: "Nobody" looks like a name to a regex that only checks for a capital letter, and "White Plains" is cut to "White" because the object group allows one word. "No longer works at Meta" produced nothing, but only by luck: the pattern needs the name right before "works", and "LeCun no" is not a name. Same fifteen sentences. Relations are now the verb's dictionary form, not property IDs. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The parse fixes the passive cases: "Google was founded by Larry Page and Sergey Brin" now gives both founders, in the right direction, and "GitHub was acquired by Microsoft" gives (Microsoft, acquire, GitHub). It also shows the costs of open IE. Relations are raw verbs, so ("found", "found with", "become in", "acquire in") must still be mapped onto properties, and dates come out as objects ("become in 2011"). "Became CEO of Apple" loses Apple, because "of Apple" hangs off the noun "CEO", not the verb. "Was born in" without a "by" agent is missed, and so is "co-founded". Worst, "Yann LeCun no longer works at Meta" comes out as a plain (Yann LeCun, work at, Meta): "no longer" is not tagged as a negation, so the extractor states the opposite of the sentence. Rules over a parse generalise better than regexes but still need a rule for every construction. Text in, triples out, with relation names taken from Wikidata properties. The decoded strings still carry REBEL's <triplet> , <subj> and <obj> markers, so split on them (as the model card's parser does) to get (subject, relation, object) records. Fine-tuned on distant-supervision data. Standard open-weights baseline. One subject can have several objects. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output One <triplet> opened Tim Cook as the subject; each <subj> ... <obj> pair added an object and a relation. The relation names are Wikidata labels in words, so a small lookup turns them into property IDs. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The type check does real work: (Larry Page, P112, Google) says Larry Page was founded by Google, and a person cannot be the item of "founded by". The NLI check is weaker than it looks. It accepted all the right triples, but it also gave 0.94 to "GitHub owns Microsoft." Types cannot catch that error either, since both are companies. The reverse question, "who owns GitHub?", scans for edges pointing at GitHub; real triple stores keep an index in each direction so that this is as fast as the forward lookup. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Graphs built by LLMs for RAG. Microsoft's GraphRAG has an LLM extract entities and relations from every chunk, clusters the resulting graph into communities and summarises each, so that "global" questions about a whole corpus can be answered. Extraction quality and entity merging decide how good those summaries are. Graph builders in common stacks. Small, fast extractors. GLiNER-style models with relation names given at inference time, and fine-tuned encoders, handle high-volume extraction where an LLM call per chunk is too costly. Patterns are precise but miss most phrasings; parses generalise further; generative models and LLMs cover the most and invent the most. Ground every element in the source text, then check property direction, entity types and constraints such as asymmetry. NLI checks help but can be fooled by swapped roles. Canonicalize relation phrases onto a fixed vocabulary before merging; unmapped phrases go to review, not into the graph. Score with precision, recall and hallucination rate on hand-labelled triples. Solutions Solution P1 · Two invented, three reversed Two of ten triples name something not in the text ("location", "software company"), and three of the remaining eight point the wrong way: Google "founded" Larry Page and Sergey Brin, and Microsoft "acquired by" GitHub, which the model output alongside the correct reading. Solution B1 · Evidence for one fact accepted for another verify checks that the evidence string sits at its recorded span, and that the subject and object appear somewhere in the text. A triple {"subject": "Tim Cook", "relation": "P112", "object": "Apple"} carrying the span and evidence of "Steve Jobs founded Apple" passes: the evidence is real, and "Tim Cook" occurs earlier in the document. The fix is to require subject and object inside the evidence span, and the relation's trigger words too, so that each triple is supported by its own evidence and not by the document as a whole. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Exact-match and F1 miss semantic equivalence. Human review does not scale. LLM-as-judge is the production answer — with enough calibration to trust the number. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means LLM-as-judge Scoring with an LLM Prompt a judge model to score outputs 0-1 given a rubric. RAGAS The RAG metric library Open-source eval framework with 4 reference-free RAG metrics. Faithfulness Is the answer grounded? Fraction of answer claims entailed by retrieved context. Context precision Were retrieved chunks relevant? Fraction of top-K chunks that actually mattered. Context recall Did retrieval find everything? Fraction of gold-answer claims supported by retrieved chunks. G-Eval Custom LLM judge Rubric + chain-of-thought eval steps + 0-1 score. Calibration Trust but verify Spearman correlation between judge score and human score. The problem In plain words first Once a system writes free text, "is this answer right?" stops being a string comparison. A correct answer can share few words with the reference, and a wrong one can share almost all of them. This lesson builds the scores teams use instead. Faithfulness asks whether every claim in the answer is backed by the retrieved text. Answer relevance asks whether it answers the question asked. Context precision and recall ask whether retrieval found the right passages. An LLM-as-judge scores anything you can describe in a rubric. Each of these is itself a model that can be wrong, so the lesson also covers the step people skip: checking the judge against human ratings, measuring its biases, and deciding when a drop in a score is a real regression and when it is noise. All models here run locally and only for inference: a 0.5-billion-parameter instruction model plays the LLM and the judge. Your RAG system answers: "June 29th, 2007." The gold reference is: "June 29, 2007." Exact Match scores 0. Token F1 scores 67%. A human would score 100%. Now multiply by 10,000 test cases. Multiply again by every change to the retriever, chunking, prompt, or model. You need an evaluator that understands meaning, runs cheaply at scale, does not lie about regressions, and surfaces the right failure modes. Three widely used tools address this problem: two libraries and one method. RAGAS. Retrieval-Augmented Generation ASsessment. Four RAG metrics (faithfulness, answer-relevance, context-precision, context-recall) with NLI + LLM-judge backends. Research-backed, lightweight. DeepEval. Pytest for LLMs. G-Eval, task-completion, hallucination, bias metrics. CI/CD-native. G-Eval. A method (and a DeepEval metric): LLM-as-judge with chain-of-thought, custom criteria, 0-1 score. All three lean on LLM-as-judge. This lesson builds intuition for the method and the trust layer around it. See it drawn Exact match and token F1 on answers a person would mark right or wrong SQuAD's normalisation and scores from Lesson 5.13, against the reference "June 29, 2007." Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Exact match is 0 for every line, right or wrong. Token F1 gives "June 29th, 2007." 0.67 (two of three tokens shared), the same as the wrong year "June 29, 2008.", and gives "Not June 29, 2007.", which says the opposite, 0.86. Overlap scores measure shared surface, not meaning; that is why the rest of this lesson compares meanings with models. The idea LLM-as-judge. Solutions Solution P1 · Always "A" It picks the correct answer only when it is shown first (10 of 10) and never when it is shown second, so it gives the same verdict in both orders 0 times out of 10. We give you a small instruction tuned model, a held out corpus, a set of short factual prompts with gold answers, a set of open form prompts with reference answers, and no network access. Build an evaluation pipeline that reports more than one number and explains its aggregate, and describe how it would run in CI once a network and a judge model are available. What do you deliver, and what do you leave out on purpose? Level 4 of 4 · about 60 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Deliver one runnable file with four evals: held out perplexity with honest token accounting, normalized exact match on the factual set, token F1 on the open form set, and a deterministic mock judge on a 1 to 5 scale with the same interface a real judge will have. Report every per eval number, a weighted aggregate with the weights in a config, and per example records for diagnosis. Leave out the real judge, intervals on the aggregate and anything that needs a network, and say so in the readme. The four evals. Each eval covers a dimension the others miss. Perplexity says whether the model fits the language at all. Exact match says whether it produces the gold string on short answers. Token F1 forgives paraphrase on open answers. The judge scores quality that string metrics cannot see. Each is a function from the model and a dataset to a result with the metric, the per example details and a name. The details a reviewer checks. Perplexity. Sum the loss over real target positions, exclude pad targets from the denominator, shift the targets by one, divide once at the end. Normalization. Lowercase, strip, collapse whitespace, drop trailing terminal punctuation when the sides differ only by it. Token F1 is one when both sides are empty and zero when only one is. Mock judge. A 5 when the normalized strings match, a 4 at token F1 of at least 0.8, a 3 between 0.5 and 0.8, a 2 between 0.2 and 0.5, a 1 otherwise, with a one line rationale. It is not a judge. It fixes the interface so a real model is a one function swap. The aggregate. Normalize each eval into the unit range: perplexity as one over one plus the log of perplexity, exact match and F1 as they are, the judge divided by 5. The default weights are 0.2, 0.3, 0.3 and 0.2. Put them in a config and print them in the report, because the choice is a product decision, not a fact. Write the report with stable JSON keys and a table for the terminal. The CI story. When a network exists, swap the mock judge for a real one and calibrate it against at least 50 hand labeled cases, with a Spearman correlation of 0.7 or more, before its scores gate anything. Grow the suite to about 200 cases, compare two runs with Wilson and bootstrap intervals, block on a regression beyond 0.3 on any criterion, trigger on prompt and model paths, and upload the report as an artifact. What to leave out and why. The real judge, because there is no network and no human labels to calibrate it. Intervals on the aggregate, because the weights make it a product number; put intervals on the components. Contamination checks, because the training corpus is not provided. Explain the mechanism Your question answering system returns "June 29th, 2007." The reference says "June 29, 2007." A teammate reports that this case gets a zero and asks you to replace the whole eval with token F1. What do you tell them? Level 1 of 4 · about 5 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Both metrics are right for different answer shapes. Exact match compares the whole string after normalization, so one extra character makes it zero. Token F1 compares the bags of tokens, so this pair scores about 75 percent. First add normalization to exact match, then pick the metric by the shape of the answers you grade. What each metric compares. Exact match normalizes both sides and then asks for equality. The capstone's exact match eval lowercases, strips the ends, collapses runs of whitespace and drops trailing terminal punctuation when the two sides differ only by it. After that step "Paris", "Paris." and " paris " all count as the same answer. The suffix in "29th" is not punctuation, so this pair still fails. Token F1 splits both sides into tokens, counts the multiset intersection, and takes the harmonic mean of precision and recall. It forgives word order and paraphrase. It is fooled by lexical overlap: a prediction that shares most tokens with the reference but changes one fact still scores high. Which one to use. Answer shape Metric A date, a number, a letter, a label Exact match with normalization A short phrase with several valid wordings Token F1, best score over all references A sentence or a paragraph Token F1 as a floor, a calibrated judge for meaning Why not switch everything. Token F1 pays for shared words, not for correctness. A long answer that repeats the question and then gives the wrong entity can score higher than a short correct answer. Keep exact match where the answer is deterministic. Use token F1 where paraphrase is normal. Use a judge where only meaning counts, and calibrate it first. Plausible wrong answers. "Exact match is broken, so remove it." Exact match with normalization is the right metric for dates, numbers and multiple choice letters; the missing step is normalization. "Token F1 understands meaning." It counts shared tokens; two answers with no shared tokens can both be right, and a wrong answer can share most tokens. "A human would give this 100, so always use a judge." A judge costs money and needs a calibration run; for a date, normalized exact match is free and exact. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) What does a token F1 of one mean? Expected: the prediction and the reference have the same multiset of tokens after normalization, in any order. (level 2) The reference is "Paris" and the prediction is "Paris." Which metric fails without normalization? Expected: exact match; with the trailing punctuation rule it passes. (level 2) When do you take the best score over several references? Expected: when a question has more than one valid answer string; the F1 and ROUGE-L metrics take the highest scoring target. (level 3) Token F1 is high and the answer is wrong. How did that happen? Expected: lexical overlap with wrong content, such as a wrong entity inside a sentence that shares most tokens with the reference; grade the entity with exact match or use a judge. Explain the mechanism You wrote a rubric, and a judge model now scores faithfulness for your retrieval system. The dashboard shows a high mean, and the team wants to use it as the release gate from Monday. What has to happen before this number can block or approve a release? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Calibrate the judge against people first. Hand label about 100 cases, score them with the judge, and compute the Spearman correlation between the two rankings. Below 0.7 the rubric needs work and the number is noise. Then freeze the judge model and version, and read the bottom scores as well as the mean. Why a raw judge score lies. A judge fails in three silent ways. It carries biases: it prefers longer answers, answers from its own model family and answers that match the prompt style. It can return bad JSON, which becomes a missing score that drops out of the aggregate and raises the mean. It drifts: a new judge version changes every metric at once. The calibration run. Label at least 50 cases by hand; the lesson uses 100. Cover the bottom of the distribution, not only easy cases. Score the same cases with the judge. Plot judge against human and compute the Spearman rank correlation. A correlation below 0.7 means the rubric needs work. A judge at 0.3 is noise. Use a judge from a different model family than the generator. A model that grades its own family inflates the score by about 10 to 20 percent. After the run. Freeze the judge model and version. When you upgrade, run the old and the new judge on the same baseline before you compare anything. Inspect the bottom quantile. A mean of 0.85 can hide a 5 percent slice of catastrophic failures. Version the eval set and tag it with every change, so that a score this month means the same as a score last month. Plausible wrong answers. "The rubric is clear, so the judge is right." Length and family biases survive a clear rubric; only a correlation against human labels shows their size. "It agrees with our old metric, so it is calibrated." The old metric may share the bias; calibrate against people. "Calibrate once and keep upgrading the judge." Each judge version changes every score; freeze the version or rerun the baseline in parallel. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why Spearman and not the mean difference between judge and human scores? Expected: Spearman compares rankings, so a judge that is harsh but orders the cases the same way still passes. (level 2) What is the smallest hand labeled set the lesson accepts? Expected: it refuses a judge tested on fewer than 50 human labeled examples. (level 3) The judge is the same model that writes the answers. What will the calibration run probably show? Expected: inflated scores by about 10 to 20 percent; switch the judge to another model family. (level 3) The correlation passes, but the bottom decile holds confident wrong scores. Do you ship? Expected: no; the mean correlation can hide catastrophic failures, so inspect the lowest 10 percent before the number gates anything. Where it is taught. Debug a failure Overnight every metric on the eval dashboard moved by several points, up for some criteria and down for others, with no prompt change and no model change in the product. The last merged change switched the judge to the newest version of its model. What happened, and how should such a change be made? Level 2 of 4 · about 7 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The judge is part of the measurement, so a new judge version changes every metric at once while the product stands still. Freeze the judge model and version in the pipeline. When you upgrade, run the old and the new judge on the same baseline in parallel, calibrate the new judge against the human labeled set, and reset the baseline before you compare anything new. Why everything moved. A judge score is a function of the output and of the judge. Change the judge and every stored score is in a different unit. The lesson lists judge version drift as one of the three silent failures and asks you to flag any pipeline where a judge upgrade lands without a parallel baseline eval. The upgrade protocol. Pin the judge model and version, and record both with every run. Before a switch, score a frozen baseline set with the old and the new judge. Calibrate the new judge: Spearman correlation with the hand labeled set of 0.7 or more. If the new judge calibrates better, adopt it and rescore the stored baselines so that history and new runs share one judge. Mark the switch on every chart. Other things that move every score. An edit to the eval set without a version tag. A change in how missing scores are counted. A run that dropped some tasks. Tag the dataset with every change and record the task count. Plausible wrong answers. "Newer judge, higher scores, ship it." The product did not change; the number did. A judge change needs a parallel baseline. "Follow the newest judge version automatically." Automatic upgrades make every trendline meaningless; pin the version. "A minor version does not need recalibration." Any version change can change the scores; rerun the correlation. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) What else can move every score without a product change? Expected: an eval set edit without a version tag, or a change in how missing scores are counted. (level 2) How do you tell a judge change from a product regression next time? Expected: the run metadata records the judge model and version, so a diff of the metadata answers it. (level 3) The new judge correlates better with the human labels. Do you adopt it? Expected: yes, but rescore the stored baseline with it first so that old and new numbers share one judge. (level 3) You must keep a trendline across the switch. How? Expected: score a fixed frozen set with both judges, publish the offset per criterion, and mark the switch on the chart. Debug a failure A faithfulness dashboard reports a mean of 0.85 over a thousand cases, above the 0.8 release threshold. Support tickets say the assistant invents policy details in some answers. The eval owner says the metric is green. Where do you look, and what do you change in the report? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A mean hides the tail. A mean of 0.85 is consistent with a 5 percent slice of catastrophic failures, and that slice is what becomes tickets. Sort the cases by score and read the lowest 10 percent. Then add a pass rate at a threshold and a bottom quantile alert to the report, next to the mean. Why the dashboard is green. Most cases score high while a small slice scores near zero. The average barely moves, because the slice is small. The users in that slice get an invented policy, and no average tells them it was rare. What to report. Pass rate. The fraction of cases above a threshold. It measures reliability, which is what users feel, so it is more actionable than the mean. Bottom quantile. The lesson refuses aggregate only reporting without the lowest 10 percent surfaced. Read those cases by hand every run. Per-category scores. If the tail comes from one category, the fix is local and the gate should watch that category. How to debug it. Pull the lowest scoring cases and read them. Confirm they match the tickets. Check how missing scores were counted. A judge that returned bad JSON produces a missing score, and dropping missing scores raises the mean. Check that the judge was calibrated at the low end. A hand labeled set made of easy cases says nothing about the tail. Plausible wrong answers. "The mean passed, so the release passed." A mean of 0.85 often hides a 5 percent catastrophic slice; the gate needs the tail. "Raise the mean threshold to 0.9." A higher mean threshold still hides a small slice of zeros; add a distribution measure. "The judge is noisy at the bottom, so ignore those cases." That is where the failures live; calibrate the judge on low scoring cases too. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the lesson prefer the share of cases above a cutoff to the mean? Expected: it counts how many cases are good enough, so it measures reliability. (level 2) The lowest cases all come from one category. What changes? Expected: the fix is local; report per-category scores and gate on the weakest category, not the aggregate. (level 3) Missing scores from parse failures were dropped before averaging. What did that do? Expected: it raised the mean, because the worst outputs often fail to parse; count them as failures or report them separately. (level 3) Which alert do you add to the release gate? Expected: a floor on the lowest 10 percent and a pass rate threshold, both next to the mean. Where it is taught. The LLM evaluation frameworks lesson lists the raw aggregate pitfall and the bottom quantile rule, and the evaluation lesson defines pass rate as the more actionable summary. Debug a failure Your judge returns a JSON object with a score for each case. The pipeline parses it, and mean faithfulness rose from one week to the next with no change to the product. The logs show that the judge's output failed to parse on a growing share of cases. Explain the rise and fix the pipeline. Level 3 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A parse failure becomes a missing score, and the aggregate silently drops missing scores. The cases that fail to parse are often the worst outputs, so dropping them lifts the mean. Catch the failure explicitly, record it as its own outcome, count it against the score or report it next to the mean, and alert when the failure share grows. The mechanism. Bad JSON from the judge becomes a not a number value. A mean over a column with such values excludes them. The lesson names this as the second silent failure of a judge and asks for the parse to fail loudly with its own status. Why the exclusion is biased. The judge breaks its format most often on long, odd or refused outputs. Those are also the low scoring outputs. So the exclusion removes the bottom of the distribution, and the mean rises for a reason that has nothing to do with quality. The fix. Wrap the parse in an explicit check and give every case a status: scored, parse failed, judge error. Report the parsed share with every run. A rising failure share fails the run. Publish the mean two ways: with failures counted as zero and with failures excluded. If the two differ a lot, the failures are not random. Allow one retry with a repair prompt, record that a retry happened, and cap retries. Store the raw judge text so a reviewer can read what broke. Verify the diagnosis. Recompute last week's mean with failures counted as zero. If the rise disappears, you have the cause. Plausible wrong answers. "The mean rose, so quality rose." Nothing in the product changed; the denominator did. "Retry until it parses." Retries without a record hide the failure and can change the score; record every retry and cap them. "Exclude failures, they are judge bugs." The exclusion is biased toward bad outputs; the product number is wrong whatever the cause. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why are the failed cases not a random sample? Expected: the judge breaks its format most on long, odd or refused outputs, which are also the low scoring ones. (level 3) Do you score a failed parse as a zero or leave it out? Expected: both, with the parsed share; a gate should treat a rising failure share as a failed run. (level 4) How do you design the judge output so this cannot happen silently again? Expected: a strict schema, a validator that rejects anything else, a status field per case, and a run level parse failure metric with an alert. Where it is taught. The LLM evaluation frameworks lesson lists JSON parsing failures as a silent judge failure and requires an explicit failure mode. Debug a failure You compare two prompt versions by showing a judge model both outputs and asking which one is better. Version B wins 70 percent of the pairs. You then swap the two outputs and version A wins most of them. What went wrong, and how do you run the comparison? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The judge has position bias: it prefers the option it reads first. Your first run measured the order, not the prompt. Score every pair in both orders, count a win only when the same version wins twice, and treat split decisions as ties. Then report the win rate with a confidence interval. Why pairwise at all. A pairwise judge never has to decide whether an output is a 3 or a 4 on a scale. It only picks a winner, so it avoids the scale calibration problem of a single grader. That makes it the right tool for a head to head test of two prompt versions. The bias. Judges prefer the first option presented. The lesson's rule is short: always randomize the order and run both. One order gives you a number about the layout of the prompt. The protocol. For each input, score the pair in both orders. A version wins the pair only when it wins in both orders. A pair that flips with the order is a tie. Report the win rate and its confidence interval. A win rate near one half means the judge cannot separate the versions. Also check length. If version B is longer, the judge may reward verbosity. Normalize for length or state in the rubric that length does not count, and see if the preference survives. Plausible wrong answers. "The judge is random, so use a different judge." Position bias is systematic, not random; another judge has it too, and the protocol is the fix. "Always put the baseline first." That fixes the bias in one direction and hides it; run both orders. "Pairwise comparison is only for human raters." Judges run pairwise well once the order is randomized and both orders are scored. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does a pairwise comparison avoid rubric calibration problems? Expected: the judge only picks a winner and never places an output on a numeric scale. (level 2) Version B is also longer. What else do you control? Expected: verbosity bias; normalize for length or exclude it in the rubric, then check whether the preference remains. (level 3) After both orders, 40 percent of the pairs flip with the order. What does that tell you? Expected: the judge cannot tell the versions apart on those pairs; count them as ties and expect a win rate close to one half. (level 3) How many pairs make a 55 percent win rate real? Expected: enough that the interval excludes one half; use a Wilson or bootstrap interval, and expect to need hundreds of pairs. Where it is taught. The LLM evaluation frameworks lesson names position bias and the both orders rule, and the evaluation and testing lesson explains why pairwise comparison avoids scale calibration. Defend a design Design the evaluation gate that runs on every pull request that touches prompts or model code for a support assistant. Say what runs, what blocks the merge, what it costs per month, and how you stop the gate from blocking on noise. Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Trigger on changes to the prompt and model paths, run a fixed versioned suite of about 200 cases through the proposed prompt, score four anchored criteria with a frozen calibrated judge, and compare with the stored scores of the last known good baseline. Block when any criterion drops beyond the threshold and the interval on the difference excludes zero, and store the results as artifacts. With a small judge tier a 200 case run costs about 4 dollars, so ten merges a week cost about 160 dollars a month. What runs. Trigger. A path filter on the prompt directory and the model code, so documentation commits do not pay for a run. Suite. A golden core of 50 to 100 curated cases, 20 to 50 adversarial cases such as injections, out of domain questions and harmful requests, and 100 to 200 samples of real traffic. Version the suite and tag every change. Scoring. Deterministic assertions first, such as a contains check or a regex, because they are free. Then the judge on relevance, correctness, helpfulness and safety, each on an anchored 1 to 5 scale, with the judge model and version frozen and calibrated against hand labels. What blocks. Score the baseline once, when it becomes the last known good version, and store its scores. Each pull request scores only the new prompt on the same suite version. For each criterion compute the mean difference and the pass rate at 4 or more with a Wilson interval. The lesson's code blocks on any mean drop of more than 0.3. It computes a bootstrap interval for each run separately, not an interval on the difference, so a noisy drop can block. Its written workflow asks for a statistical test, a paired t test or a bootstrap. Add a paired bootstrap on the per case differences to the code, and block only when both hold: a drop of more than 0.3 and an interval on the difference that excludes zero. The report lists the cases that degraded so the author can read them. What it costs. Suite Small judge tier Time 100 cases, 4 criteria about 2 dollars about 2 minutes 200 cases, 4 criteria about 4 dollars about 4 minutes 500 cases, 4 criteria about 10 dollars about 10 minutes 1000 cases, 4 criteria about 20 dollars about 20 minutes Ten pull requests a week at 200 cases is about 160 dollars a month, because each pull request pays for one run and reuses the stored baseline scores. If you score the baseline again on every pull request, the cost doubles. The lesson's counter example is a prompt change that cut answer completeness by 34 percent and went unnoticed for 11 days. How to keep noise out. At 50 cases the interval is 19 points wide and a 5 percent regression is invisible, so the suite needs about 200 cases. Freeze the judge, because a judge upgrade moves every score. Keep the suite versioned and never edit it inside the pull request that fails it. Add a bottom quantile alert and a per category breakdown, because a prompt can improve overall and regress on safety. Plausible wrong answers. "Run the eval nightly instead." Nightly finds the regression after the merge; the lesson's story is 11 days of a shipped drop. Run before merge. "Fifty golden cases are enough for a gate." At 50 cases the interval is 19 points wide, and a 5 percent regression cannot be detected. "Use the newest judge model on each run." Judge changes move every score; freeze the judge and change it only with a parallel baseline. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why a path filter on the trigger? Expected: the eval costs money and minutes; run it when prompts or model code change, not on every commit. (level 3) A criterion moved by 0.1 and the author calls it a regression. Expected: the threshold is 0.3 on the mean with intervals; 0.1 is inside noise at 200 cases, so report it and do not block. (level 4) The gate blocks the merge and the author says the suite is stale. What is the process? Expected: suite changes are their own reviewed and versioned change; rerun the baseline when the suite version changes, and never edit the suite inside the failing pull request. (level 4) How do you catch an aggregate improvement that regresses one category? Expected: a stratified per category report with intervals and a block rule on any category. Where it is taught. The evaluation and testing lesson gives the pipeline, the thresholds and the cost table, and the LLM evaluation frameworks lesson gives the test gate pattern and the calibration rules. Weigh a trade-off Your product generates answers with one model, and your eval pipeline grades them using that same model plus a rubric. Scores rose after the last release and the team is pleased. A reviewer asks why the gain might not be real. What is the risk, and what do you change? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A model that grades its own family prefers its own style, so self evaluation inflates scores by about 10 to 20 percent. The rise can mean the judge likes the new outputs more, not that users do. Move the judge to a different model family, calibrate it against human labels, and score the baseline and the new version again under that judge. Where the bias comes from. A judge is a model with preferences. It favors longer answers, answers from its own model family and answers that match the prompt style. When the judge comes from the generator's own family, every release that moves the output toward the judge's taste looks like an improvement. The lesson calls this self preference and measures the inflation at about 10 to 20 percent. Why the release looked better. A release changes tone, length and structure as well as content. The judge rewards the first three. Without a separate signal you cannot tell which part of the gain is content. What to change. Pick a judge from a different model family. Use the cheapest model that still meets the calibration threshold. Calibrate it: hand label at least 50 cases, the lesson uses 100, and require a Spearman correlation of 0.7 or more with the human ranking. Score the old and the new release under the same judge and report the difference, not the absolute score. Normalize for length, or state in the rubric that length does not count. Plausible wrong answers. "The judge has a rubric, so its family does not matter." The rubric does not remove the preference for its own style; the lesson measures a 10 to 20 percent inflation. "Use the strongest model we have as the judge, which is the one we ship." Strength does not remove self preference; a different family at similar strength is the fix. "Scores went up, so quality went up." The score is a proxy; the output may have moved toward what the judge rewards, such as length and tone. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Which two other judge biases does the lesson name next to self preference? Expected: position bias in pairwise comparison and verbosity bias toward longer answers. (level 2) The judge from another family is cheaper but correlates less with people. Which one do you take? Expected: the cheapest judge that still meets the calibration threshold; below the threshold the number is noise whatever the family. (level 3) You cannot change the judge family this quarter. What limits the damage? Expected: calibrate against human labels and publish the correlation, normalize for length, and read only relative changes under the frozen judge. (level 3) After the switch, how do you tell a real gain from a judge preference? Expected: both versions scored by the new judge, the difference with a confidence interval, and a human labeled slice of the cases that moved most. Where it is taught. The LLM evaluation frameworks lesson lists self evaluation as a pitfall, and the evaluation lesson names self preference among the judge failure modes. Sources and further reading Es et al. (2023). DeepEval docs — open production stack. Zheng et al. (2023). Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena — biases, calibration, limits. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Gemini 3 Pro (November 2025) accepts 1M tokens of context, yet Google's own launch table puts it at 26.3% on 8-needle MRCR at 1M tokens. Advertised ≠ usable. Long-context evaluation tells you the actual capacity of the model you are shipping on. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means NIAH Needle in haystack Plant a fact in filler, ask the model to retrieve it. RULER NIAH on steroids 13 task types across retrieval / multi-hop / aggregation / QA. Effective context The real capacity Length at which accuracy still holds above threshold. Lost in the middle Depth bias Models under-attend to content in the middle of long inputs. Multi-needle Many facts at once Multiple plants; tests attention juggling, not retrieval alone. MRCR Multi-round coref 8, 24, or 100-needle coreference; exposes attention saturation. NoLiMa Non-lexical needle Needle and query share no literal tokens; requires reasoning. The problem In plain words first A model's context window is how much text it can take in at once, measured in tokens. Vendors now advertise hundreds of thousands or millions. That number says what the model accepts , not what it uses well . Finding one planted sentence in a long document is easy for current models; connecting several facts spread through it, or finding a fact that is phrased differently from the question, is much harder, and gets harder as the text grows. This lesson builds the standard tests, a planted "needle" at different depths and lengths, several needles, a chain of facts and a needle with no words in common with the question, and runs them on a small local model so you can watch the gap between "found it" and "understood it" open up at only a few thousand tokens. You have a 200-page contract. The model claims a 1M-token context. You paste the contract in and ask: "What is the termination clause?" The model answers — but answers from the cover page because the termination clause sits at 120k tokens deep, past where the model actually attends. This is the context-capacity gap. Spec sheets say 1M tokens (Meta advertised 10M for Llama 4 Scout). How much of that is usable depends on the task, and has to be measured. Retrieval (single needle in haystack): near-perfect up to the advertised max on frontier models. Multi-hop / aggregation: degrades much earlier than retrieval, often well inside the advertised window. Reasoning over dispersed facts: the first task to fail. Long-context evaluation measures these axes. This lesson names the benchmarks, what each actually measures, and how to build a custom needle test for your domain. The idea Needle-in-a-Haystack (NIAH, 2023). Place a fact ("the magic word is pineapple") at a controlled depth in a long context. Ask the model to retrieve it. Sweep depth × length. The original long-context benchmark. Frontier models now saturate this; it is a necessary but not sufficient baseline. RULER (Nvidia, 2024). 13 task types across 4 categories: retrieval (single / multi-key / multi-value), multi-hop tracing (variable tracking), aggregation (common word frequency), QA. Configurable context length (4k to 128k+). Reveals models that saturate NIAH but fail on multi-hop. In the 2024 release, only half of 17 models claiming 32k+ context maintained quality at 32k. RULER's effective length is the longest length at which a model still beats a fixed bar: Llama-2-7B's score at 4k, 85.6%. LongBench v2 (2024). 503 multiple-choice questions, 8k-2M word contexts, six task categories: single-doc QA, multi-doc QA, long in-context learning, long dialogue, code repo, long structured data. The production benchmark for real-world long-context behavior. MRCR (Multi-Round Co-reference Resolution). Introduced in Google's Michelangelo evaluations (2024) and released in a harder open version by OpenAI (2025). A long synthetic conversation contains 2, 4 or 8 identical requests (say, "write a poem about tapirs") among similar distractor requests, and the model must reproduce one of them, for example the second poem about tapirs. Scored by string similarity to the right reply. Exposes how many near-identical items a model can keep apart. NoLiMa. "Non-lexical needle." The needle and the query share no literal overlap; retrieval requires one step of semantic reasoning (Modarressi et al., 2025). Of 13 models claiming at least 128k tokens, 11 fell below half of their short-context score at 32k; GPT-4o fell from 99.3% to 69.7%. HELMET (Yen et al., 2024). A suite of application-style tasks (retrieval-augmented QA, generation with citations, passage re-ranking, many-shot in-context learning, long-document QA, summarisation, and synthetic recall) at controlled lengths up to 128k. Built because synthetic recall scores alone did not predict how models ranked on real tasks. BABILong. Embeds bAbI reasoning chains inside irrelevant haystacks. Tests reasoning-in-a-haystack, not just retrieval. The same idea as a formula Effective length. With accuracy measured at context length and a threshold , ​ ( τ ) = max { L : a ( L ) ≥ τ } RULER uses . Report ​ separately for retrieval and for reasoning tasks. The depth × length grid. For depths and lengths , the cell value is the pass rate over trials, ( d , L ) = k 1 ​ ∑ j ​ pass j ​ . With every cell is a single coin flip; a 95% interval for a pass rate needs in the tens. Several needles. If each of needles were found independently with probability , finding all of them has probability so multi-needle accuracy falls even when nothing interacts. In practice needles also compete for attention, which makes it worse. Lost in the middle. Liu et al. (2024) found a U-shaped curve: accuracy is highest when the relevant passage is at the start or end of the context, lowest in the middle. What length costs. A transformer's prefill does about floating-point operations per token for the weights ( parameters) plus about ​ ℓ per token for attention over earlier tokens ( layers). The first term is linear in length, the second quadratic. The key/value cache needs ​ × d head ​ × n × bytes per value which is why grouped-query attention (few key/value heads) matters for long contexts. Worked example Two needles, a cache and a crossover by hand Many needles. A model finds a single needle 95% of the time. If eight needles were independent, it would find all eight with probability = 0.66 ; with , = 0.43 . A respectable single-needle score says little about an eight-needle one. KV cache for the model used below. Qwen2.5-0.5B has layers, ​ = 2 key/value heads of size 64. Per token: bytes bytes. At 32,000 tokens: GB; at 1M tokens it would need 12.3 GB, more than the model's own weights by a factor of about 12. When attention starts to dominate. The same model has about parameters, so the weights cost operations per token. Attention costs . They are equal at /86 , 000 ≈ 11 , 600 tokens. Below that, doubling the length roughly doubles the time; well above it, doubling the length roughly quadruples it. Check your mental model ✗ "The model accepts 1M tokens, so it can use 1M tokens." ✓ The window is a limit, not a measurement. Usable length depends on the task and must be tested. ✗ "It passes needle-in-a-haystack at every depth, so long context works." ✓ Plain NIAH is a lookup with a word match. Tasks that need a step of inference or several facts fail much earlier. ✗ "Filler text doesn't matter." ✓ Repeated filler makes the needle stand out; related, coherent filler makes it harder. Use realistic text from your domain. Predict before you run Under Step 3, a 0.5B model with a 32k-token window answers four kinds of question about text of 0, 1,000 and 2,000 tokens: a needle that shares words with the question, a needle that shares none ("Yuki lives next to the Semper Opera House" / "Which character has been to Dresden?"), three needles at once, and a three-step chain of variable assignments. Which will fail first, and at what length? (Solution P1.) See it drawn How big is the KV cache? The numbers in the worked example, read from the model's configuration. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Idea 1 · What to actually report Advertised context window. The spec-sheet number. Effective retrieval length. NIAH pass at some threshold (e.g., 90%). Effective reasoning length. Multi-hop or aggregation pass at that threshold. Degradation curve. Accuracy vs context length, plotted per task type. Two numbers for your spec sheet: retrieval-effective and reasoning-effective. Expect the reasoning-effective length to be much shorter than the advertised window, and measure it rather than assume a ratio. Step 1 · a custom NIAH for your domain See code/main.py . The skeleton: Copy What you should see Copy Copy Sweep depth_ratio ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0} × total_tokens ∈ {1k, 4k, 16k, 64k}. Plot the heatmap. That is the NIAH card for your target model. See it drawn The repository's toy grid main.py simulates the grid with a mock "model" that finds the needle with a regular expression whenever it sits within a fixed capacity of 20,000 words. It shows the shape of the report, not a real model. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The mock passes everything up to 20,000 words and fails past its capacity, with a hard edge no real model has: the cells at depth 0.7 and 0.9 of a 40,000-word haystack fail because the needle sits past word 20,000. The filler is random words drawn from one sentence, which also makes the needle trivially easy to spot. The run below replaces both: a real model, and real news text. See it drawn A real needle-in-a-haystack grid Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, greedy decoding, inference only. The haystack is real news prose from the SummEval articles; the needle is "The special code for the archive room is NNNN." with a different code in every cell; the question comes after the text. Three depths × four lengths, one trial per cell. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Every cell passes: the needle is found at the start, middle and end of up to 4,000 tokens of news. A small model saturates this test at these lengths, which is the point: plain NIAH is a lookup in which the question's words ("special code", "archive room") point straight at the answer. The timing line is the other result. On this page's 2-core CPU, a question took 3.8 seconds at 500 tokens and 18.9 at 4,000; from 1,000 tokens on, each doubling of length roughly doubles the time (5.2, 9.1, 18.9), as the worked example predicts for lengths below about 11,600 tokens. Step 2 · a multi-needle variant Copy What you should see Copy Copy Questions like "What are the three magic words?" require retrieving all three. Single-needle success does not predict multi-needle success. This version works on a word list, so each needle lands at its stated depth; the repository's sketch sliced a string by character counts while calling them tokens. The printed positions are 10, 42 and 74: each needle is two words long, so the later ones shift by two words per earlier needle. Step 3 · multi-hop variable tracing (RULER-style) Copy The answer requires chaining three assignments (and here, arithmetic). RULER's version only copies values ( VAR B = VAR A ) and asks for every variable that ends up holding a given value. In RULER, models that are near-perfect on simple retrieval show large drops on tasks like this as length grows. See it drawn Where the small model breaks: four tasks at three lengths Same model and haystack. Each task is asked with no filler (just the needles), and inside 1,000 and 2,000 tokens of news. Score = share of expected items that appear in the answer. The last line of each task shows the answer at 2,000 tokens. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The word-matching needle passes at every length, as in the grid above. Three needles at once also pass here: each still shares the words "special codes" with the question. The non-lexical needle collapses: with nothing but the needle, the model names Yuki (the only person mentioned), but inside 1,000 tokens of news it fails, and at 2,000 it confidently names a footballer from one of the articles, Carlos Tevez. It fails because nothing in "Which character has been to Dresden?" matches "Semper Opera House" and it must know the opera house is in Dresden and connect the two. That is NoLiMa's finding at a far shorter length. Variable tracking degrades even without filler (two of three variables), and reaches zero at 2,000 tokens. The two tasks that need a step of reasoning are the ones that fail, and they fail at 1/16 of this model's 32k window. Step 4 · LongBench v2 on your stack Copy Report per-category accuracy. Aggregate scores hide big task-level differences. Not run here: the dataset is about 465 MB, and its contexts (8,000 words to 2 million) are far beyond what a CPU can process in a lesson. Three fixes from the repository's sketch: the split is train , the category field is domain (for example "Single-Document QA"), and every question is multiple choice, so the prompt lists choices A to D and the score compares letters. Break it on purpose Plant two versions of one fact in the same haystack: "The special code for the archive room is 1111." and "Update: the special code for the archive room has been changed to 2222." Ask for the current code with the update placed after the original, then with the two sentences' positions swapped. Does the model follow the word "Update", or something else? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Million-token windows are common; using them is not. Gemini 3 Pro (November 2025) accepts 1M tokens, and Google's own launch figures put it at 26.3% on 8-needle MRCR v2 at that length. Vendors now publish multi-needle and long-reasoning scores next to the window size. "Context rot". Chroma's July 2025 report tested 18 models on deliberately simple tasks and found reliability falls as input grows, faster when the needle is phrased unlike the question, and with even one topically related distractor in the haystack. Context management is a product feature. Prompt caching (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini) makes long, repeated prefixes cheap, and agent platforms trim, summarise or clear old tool results (for example Anthropic's context editing, 2025) rather than letting the window fill. Sources: MRCR dataset , Context Rot , Anthropic context management , Anthropic prompt caching , RULER . Pitfalls NIAH-only evaluation. Passing NIAH at 1M tokens says nothing about multi-hop. Always run RULER or a custom multi-hop test. Uniform depth sampling. Many implementations only test depth=0.5. Test depth=0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0 — the "lost in the middle" effect is real. Lexical overlap with filler. If the needle shares keywords with the filler, retrieval becomes trivial. Use NoLiMa-style non-overlapping needles. Ignoring latency. Prefill time grows with length, the attention part quadratically. On this page the 0.5B model needed about 19 seconds per question at 4,000 tokens on a CPU; a 1M-token prompt is a large computation even on data-centre GPUs. Measure time-to-first-token alongside accuracy. Vendor-self-reported numbers. OpenAI, Google, Anthropic all publish their own scores. Always re-run independently on your use case. Use it: the same idea with real libraries The 2026 stack: Situation Benchmark Quick sanity check Custom NIAH at 3 depths × 3 lengths Model selection for production RULER (13 tasks) at your target length Real-world QA quality LongBench v2 single-doc-QA subset Multi-hop reasoning BABILong or custom variable-tracing Conversational / dialogue MRCR 8-needle at your target length Model upgrade regression Fixed in-house NIAH + RULER harness, run on every new model Rule of thumb for production: never trust a context window until you have NIAH + 1 reasoning task at your intended length. Recap What to keep from this lesson The context window is what a model accepts; the effective length is what it handles at a given accuracy, and it differs by task. Plain NIAH is a lookup; it saturates early. Add needles without word overlap, several needles, and a multi-step task. Sweep depth (start, middle, end) as well as length, with several trials per cell, on filler that looks like your data. Long inputs cost time and memory: prefill grows linearly then quadratically, and the KV cache grows linearly with tokens. Re-run your own harness on every model upgrade; do not rely on self-reported numbers. Build a NIAH with 3 depths (0.25, 0.5, 0.75) × 3 lengths (1k, 4k, 16k). Run on any model. Plot pass rate as a 3×3 heatmap. Medium. Add a 3-needle variant. Measure retrieval of all 3 at each length. Report effective reasoning length per model. Solutions Solution P1 · The reasoning tasks fail first Both tasks that need reasoning fail, and early. The non-lexical needle is answered when it is alone but missed from 1,000 tokens on; variable tracking is imperfect even with no filler and reaches zero at 2,000 tokens. The two needles that share words with their question, single or triple, pass at every length tested. A NIAH score would have described this model as fine at 2,000 tokens. Solution B1 · It follows position, not meaning With the update placed after the original, the model answers 2222 ("the current special code for the archive room is 2222"). Swap the positions, so that the update comes first and the old statement last, and it answers 1111. The word "Update" did not decide; the later statement did. (Read literally, the swapped text is ambiguous, but the model shows no sign of noticing that.) Tests with superseded facts, such as revised contract clauses or changed settings, need both orders, and production systems should resolve versions before the model sees them. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Weigh a trade-off A leaderboard ranks your candidate models by one aggregate score, and the top model wins by a small margin. A colleague on the code team says that the top model is the worst of the three on their work. Both read the same report. How is this possible, what does the aggregate hide, and how do you publish so that both readers are served? Level 4 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The aggregate is a weighted mean, so a model can win overall and lose in one category, and a small margin can sit inside the interval on the mean. Publish the per category means next to the aggregate, with intervals, and print the weights. If the leaderboard also mixes scales, a task with a wider range dominates the mean without anyone noticing. Where the aggregate comes from. The eval pipeline normalizes each eval into the unit range and takes a weighted mean; the default mix there is 0.2 for perplexity, 0.3 for exact match, 0.3 for token F1 and 0.2 for the judge. The aggregator in the leaderboard lesson takes the plain mean over tasks. In both cases the headline is one weighting of several numbers, and a different weighting is a different winner. What it hides. Category weakness. The per category column, such as math, reasoning, code and safety, is the only place where a model that is strong overall and weak on code shows up. Task imbalance and outliers. The mean is sensitive to both; the win rate is less sensitive and loses magnitude. Scale leakage. A task that scores from 0 to 100 next to tasks in the unit range dominates the mean, so the aggregator refuses scores outside the unit range. The margin. A small gap between the top two means nothing until the paired bootstrap of their per task difference excludes zero. The long context lesson states the same rule from another angle: report per category accuracy, because aggregate scores hide large task level differences. How to publish. Three layers on one page. The aggregate at the top with its weights printed. Below it, every per eval or per category number with intervals and the win rate. Below that, the per example records a reviewer needs to chase a regression. Add the paired difference interval for the top two models, and if a category matters to the product, a block rule on that category. Plausible wrong answers. "The aggregate is the objective answer." It is the answer to one weighting; a different weighting is a different winner. "Drop the aggregate and show only categories." The headline exists so people can decide; keep it, label its weights and put the categories under it. "Rank by win rate instead." Win rate hides magnitude; publish both and the paired interval. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) The code team wants the code category to count double. Do you change the headline? Expected: no; keep the unweighted table and, if agreed, add a second weighted view with its weights printed, as the capstone leaves weighting an explicit hook. (level 3) The top two means differ by less than their intervals. What does the leaderboard show? Expected: the paired bootstrap of the per task difference; if it includes zero the two are tied and the rank order is a coin flip. (level 4) Which single change to the report would have stopped this argument? Expected: per category means with intervals under the headline, so the code weakness was visible on the same page. Where it is taught. The eval pipeline capstone shows the three layers of a report and the weighted aggregate, the leaderboard aggregation capstone adds categories and intervals, and the long context evaluation lesson warns that an aggregate hides what each task type does. Defend a design Your team will adopt a new model next quarter and needs a long context evaluation that runs again on every future upgrade. Design the battery for a product that answers questions over long documents and sometimes has to combine facts from several places: the tests, the sampling grid, the metrics, the cutoffs and the regression procedure. Level 4 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Build a fixed in house harness with three parts: a needle grid over depth and length on your own documents, a multi hop variable tracing task at the same lengths, and a slice of real long document questions. Sample five depths at each length and record pass rates, time to first token and cost per query. Publish two cutoffs, the effective retrieval length at a 90 percent pass and the effective reasoning length at 70 percent, and rerun the same harness on every upgrade. The tests. Domain needle. Plant a fact from your domain in filler built from your documents at a chosen depth ratio and total length. Use needles that share no words with the filler, so retrieval needs one step of reasoning rather than keyword matching. Multi needle. Plant three facts at different depths and ask for all three. Single needle success does not predict this. Variable tracing. Plant a chain such as a first value, a second defined from the first and a third defined from the second, and ask for the last one. This is the task that fails first, and it is the one your product does when it combines facts. Real questions. A fixed subset of your long documents with answers, graded per category. The grid. Depths 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1.0 at each length, because models under attend to the middle. Lengths 1k, 4k, 16k, 64k and your target. Plot pass rate as a heatmap per task type. The metrics. Retrieval pass rate, reasoning pass rate, time to first token and cost per query at every length. A million token prompt can take 30 to 120 seconds to prefill, so the product's length budget comes from latency as much as from accuracy. The cutoffs. The effective retrieval length is the longest length where the needle grid passes at 90 percent. The effective reasoning length is the longest length where tracing passes at 70 percent. Expect the second to be 25 to 50 percent of the advertised window, and put both on the spec sheet. The regression rule. Keep the harness fixed and version it. Run it on every candidate model and publish the deltas per task type. Refuse the model card as evidence, refuse vendor self reported scores, and refuse a needle only result for a multi hop workload. Plausible wrong answers. "Run the needle test at the advertised length and stop." Needle only says nothing about multi hop; the lesson refuses it for any multi hop workload. "Use the vendor's published long context scores." They are self reported; rerun independently on your use case. "Test the middle depth at one length." Models under attend to the middle and degrade with length; one point hides both effects. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why a fixed harness instead of the newest public benchmark each time? Expected: a regression needs the same test on both models; a changing benchmark confounds the model change with the test change. (level 3) The new model passes the needle grid at the target length but fails tracing at a quarter of it. What do you ship? Expected: the reasoning effective length as the product limit; chunk or retrieve beyond it and say so on the spec sheet. (level 4) Prefill at the target length takes two minutes. Does it change the design? Expected: yes; the length budget is what the product can afford in latency and cost, not what the model can read. Where it is taught. The long context evaluation lesson gives the battery, the sampling grid, the two cutoffs and the regression rule. Explain the mechanism A model card advertises a context window of one million tokens and a perfect score on a needle in a haystack test at that length. Your product asks the model to reconcile figures that appear in several places across a long contract. Does the card answer your question, and what do you measure instead? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. No. A single needle test measures retrieval of one planted fact, and frontier models saturate it. Your task is multi hop aggregation, which degrades sharply past about 128k tokens on most models. Run a multi hop test at your target length and report two numbers: the effective retrieval length and the effective reasoning length. What the needle test measures. Place one fact at a controlled depth in filler text and ask for it. Sweep depth and length. It is the baseline, and it is necessary but not sufficient. Single needle success does not predict multi needle success, and neither predicts reasoning over dispersed facts, which is the first task to fail. What the harder benchmarks add. A multi task suite with 13 task types across retrieval, multi hop tracing, aggregation and question answering. In its first release only half of 17 models that claimed 32k context kept their quality at 32k. A multi round coreference test with 8, 24 or 100 needles, which shows how many facts a model can hold at once. On one advertised 10M token model, the 8 needle variant fell to 26.3 percent at 1M tokens. Non lexical needles that share no words with the query, so retrieval needs one reasoning step. The two numbers for your spec sheet. Effective retrieval length : the longest context where the needle test still passes at a threshold such as 90 percent. Effective reasoning length : the longest context where a multi hop or aggregation task passes at a threshold such as 70 percent. It is usually 25 to 50 percent of the advertised window. Build the test for your contract. Plant three linked assignments in filler, such as a value, a second value defined from the first and a third defined from the second, and ask for the last one. Test depths 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1.0 at each length. Use needles that do not share keywords with the filler. Record the time to first token with every run; a million token prompt can take 30 to 120 seconds to prefill. Plausible wrong answers. "The vendor's score is independent evidence." Vendors publish their own scores; rerun on your task at your length. "Pass at one million means pass at every shorter length and every task." Report the curve per task type; an aggregate hides large task level differences. "Test the middle depth only." Many implementations do; the middle is where models under attend, so test five depths. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does a single needle pass not predict a three needle pass? Expected: several facts need attention at several positions at once; the multi needle test measures juggling, not retrieval. (level 2) Which depths do you test? Expected: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1.0, because models under attend to the middle of the input. (level 3) The planted fact uses the same words as the surrounding text. What goes wrong? Expected: retrieval becomes trivial lexical matching; use a needle with no literal overlap. (level 3) What do you measure next to accuracy at the target length? Expected: time to first token and cost per query; a million token prompt can take 30 to 120 seconds to prefill. Where it is taught. The long context evaluation lesson names the benchmarks and the two numbers for a spec sheet. Sources and further reading Kamradt (2023). Needle in a Haystack analysis — the original NIAH repo. (2025). NoLiMa: Long-Context Evaluation Beyond Literal Matching — harder needles. Kuratov et al. (2024). BABILong — reasoning-in-haystack. Liu et al. (2024). Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts — the depth-bias paper. a0529: Course home / Phase 5 · Working with Language Keeping track of a conversation Lesson 5.29 75 min Build Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 5 · 17 (Chatbots), Phase 5 · 20 (Structured Outputs) Type : Build. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line "I want a cheap restaurant in the north... actually make it moderate... and add Italian." Three turns, three state updates. DST keeps the slot-value dict in sync so the booking works. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means DST Dialogue state tracking Maintain the slot-value dict across dialogue turns. Slot Unit of user intent Named parameter the backend needs (cuisine, date). Domain The task area Restaurant, hotel, taxi — sets of slots. JGA Joint Goal Accuracy Fraction of turns where every slot is correct. All-or-nothing. MultiWOZ The benchmark Multi-domain WOZ dataset; standard DST evaluation. Ontology-free DST No schema Generate slot names and values directly, no fixed list. Correction "Actually..." Turn that overwrites a previously-filled slot. The problem In plain words first A booking assistant has to remember what the user wants while the conversation moves: "somewhere cheap in the north", then "pizza would be great", then "actually, make it moderate". Dialogue state tracking keeps a small form up to date after every user turn: one field (a slot ) per thing the backend needs, such as cuisine, area, price range and party size. A slot can be filled, changed by a correction, cleared by "never mind", or left alone. If one slot is wrong at the end, the booking is wrong. This lesson builds a rule-based tracker and an LLM tracker with a validated schema, measures both turn by turn with joint goal accuracy, and shows why a schema guarantees well-formed output but not correct output. In a task-oriented dialogue system, the user's goal is encoded as a set of slot-value pairs: {cuisine: italian, area: north, price: moderate} . Every user turn can add, change, or remove a slot. The system must read the whole conversation and output the current state correctly. Get a single slot wrong and the system books the wrong restaurant, schedules the wrong flight, or charges the wrong card. DST is the hinge between what the user said and what the backend executes. Why it still matters in 2026 despite LLMs: Compliance-sensitive domains (banking, healthcare, airline booking) require deterministic slot values, not free-form generation. Tool-use agents still need slot resolution before calling APIs. Multi-turn correction is harder than it looks: "actually no, make it Thursday." The modern pipeline: classical DST concepts + LLM extractors + structured-output guardrails. The idea Task structure. A schema defines domains (restaurant, hotel, taxi) and their slots (cuisine, area, price, people). Each slot can be empty, filled with a value from a closed set (price: {cheap, moderate, expensive}), or a free-form value (name: "The Copper Kettle"). Two DST formulations. Classification. For each (slot, candidate_value) pair, predict yes/no. Works for closed-vocab slots. Standard pre-2020. Generation. Given the dialogue, generate slot values as free text. Works for open-vocab slots. The modern default. Metric. Joint Goal Accuracy (JGA) — the fraction of turns where every slot is correct. All-or-nothing. On MultiWOZ 2.4, the best reported results are in the low 80s: in the LDST paper's comparison, LDST (a fine-tuned 7B LLaMA) reaches 79.9% and ChatGPT 83.2%. Architectures. Rule-based (slot regex + keyword). Strong baseline for narrow domains. Debuggable. TripPy / BERT-DST. Copy-based generation with BERT encoding. Pre-LLM standard. LDST (LLaMA + LoRA). Instruction-tuned LLM with domain-slot prompting. Comes close to ChatGPT on MultiWOZ 2.4 (79.9% against 83.2%) with an open 7B model. Ontology-free (2024–26). Skip the schema; generate slot names and values directly. Handles open domains. Prompt + structured output (2024–26). LLM with Pydantic schema + constrained decoding. 5 lines of code, production-ready. The same idea as a formula State. Worked example Why JGA is so much lower than slot accuracy A tracker with 4 slots gets 95% of slots right on every turn, errors independent. A turn is fully right with probability = 0.81 . Now let errors persist: if 5% of turns introduce one error that the user never corrects, after 10 turns the state is still right with probability = 0.60 . Slot accuracy stays near 95%; JGA falls to 60%. Cost: a 20-turn chat with 30 tokens per user turn.
