Check your mental model ✗ "If the LLM's output passes the schema, the state is right." ✓ The schema checks that the slots and values are allowed , not that the user said them. ✗ "A new turn should produce a new state from scratch." ✓ Slots the user did not touch must keep their values. "For four people" changes only the party size. ✗ "JGA on the final turn of each dialogue is enough." ✓ JGA is computed on every turn. A tracker that is wrong for three turns and right on the last would book the wrong table if the user stopped earlier. Predict before you run Under Step 4, the rule-based tracker from main.py and a 0.5B LLM that regenerates a validated JSON state each turn are scored on the same 15 turns of paraphrased requests ("nothing too pricey", "a party of six", "I don't want Chinese tonight"). Which gets the higher joint goal accuracy? Which kind of mistake will the LLM make most? (Solution P1.) Idea 1 · The classic failure modes Co-reference across turns. "Let's stay with the first option." Needs to resolve which option. Over-write vs append. User says "add Italian." Do you replace cuisine or append? Implicit confirmations. "OK cool" — did that accept the offered booking? Correction. "Actually make it 7 pm." Must update time without clearing other slots. Coreference to previous system utterance. "Yes, that one." Which "that"? Step 1 · rule-based slot extractor See code/main.py . Regex + synonym dictionaries cover the canonical phrasings of a narrow domain: Copy What you should see Copy Copy Brittle outside the canonical vocabulary. Works for deterministic slot confirmations. Reading this output "Pizza" and "noodles" map correctly through the synonym lists. "Thai food please" returns nothing because Thai is not in this two-cuisine sketch ( main.py has four). The last line shows the deeper limit: "No Italian, I had pasta yesterday" returns italian , the opposite of the user's wish. Substring matching cannot see negation or whose wish a word expresses. The sketch is renamed ( SIMPLE_CUISINE_SYNONYMS ) so that it does not replace main.py 's fuller dictionary, which the later runs use. Step 2 · state update loop Copy What you should see Copy Copy Three invariants: Never reset a slot the user did not touch. Explicit negation ("never mind the cuisine") must clear. User correction ("actually...") must overwrite, not append. The repository's sketch referred to NEGATION_CLEARS and is_negated , which it never defined, and checked negation after extraction, so "Never mind the cuisine, any food is fine" would extract any and then clear it. The version above follows main.py : a value found in the turn wins, and negation clears only when the turn gives no new value. See it drawn The repository's three dialogues main.py 's own test: three dialogues, the state after every turn, and a comparison of the final state with the gold state. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output All three dialogues end in the right state: 3 of 3. The correction ("Actually make it moderate pricing") overwrites the price and nothing else, and "Never mind the cuisine, any food is fine" ends as any . Two caveats. The test sentences use exactly the words in the synonym lists, which is the case rules are built for. And the score only checks the last turn of each dialogue; standard JGA checks every turn. The run in Step 4 fixes both. Step 3 · LLM-driven DST with structured output Copy Instructor + Pydantic guarantees the shape : every returned object has only known slots, each with an allowed value, because invalid output is sent back to the model with the validation error until it passes or a retry limit is reached. It does not guarantee the values : a perfectly valid state can contain a price the user never mentioned. Not run here: Instructor wraps a hosted model's client. Step 4 runs the same idea locally: a Pydantic schema, a small model, and Instructor's validate-and-retry loop written out by hand. Step 4 · JGA evaluation Copy Calibrate: what fraction of turns does the system get ALL slots right? On MultiWOZ 2.4 the best published systems score around 80–83%. A narrow in-domain system should do better than that on its own vocabulary, or an LLM baseline will beat it. See it drawn Rules on paraphrases, scored per turn Six dialogues, 15 user turns, with the gold state after every turn written by hand for this lesson. The user says things the synonym lists do not contain ("nothing too pricey", "5 of us", "a party of six") and one negation of a value ("I don't want Chinese tonight"). Every wrong turn is listed with the wrong slots as (predicted, gold). Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Joint goal accuracy 0.60, slot accuracy 0.88. Read the misses. "Nothing too pricey" is not in the price list, so price stays empty, and the miss persists through the next two turns: one missed phrase costs three turns of JGA. "5 of us" and "a party of six" escape the people pattern. "I don't want Chinese tonight" fills cuisine with chinese , and that wrong value is carried into the next turn too. The gap between 0.88 and 0.60 is the persistence effect from the worked example. See it drawn An LLM tracker with a validated schema Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (inference only) reads the whole dialogue each turn and writes the full state as JSON. The lesson's RestaurantState schema validates it, with one addition from the pitfalls list: values are lower-cased and "centre" mapped to "center" before validation. Invalid output is sent back once with the error, as Instructor does. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The first two lines show why the normaliser is there: the strict schema rejects "Italian" and "centre", which is exactly what this model writes; without normalisation, most of its answers failed validation in testing. With it, all 15 outputs are valid on the first try. Yet JGA is 0.27, far below the rules' 0.60, with slot accuracy 0.78. The errors are almost all invented values: a cuisine on the very first turn, "expensive" and party sizes of 4 or 5 that nobody mentioned, and any for "I don't want Chinese". A validated state is a well-formed state, not a true one. A larger model makes fewer such errors; the defences that do not depend on model size are to require evidence (the slot's words in the dialogue, as in Lesson 5.26), to combine with rules, and to confirm before acting. Step 5 · handling correction Copy On a detected correction, overwrite the last-updated slot rather than appending. Hard to get right without LLM help. The modern pattern: always let the LLM regenerate the whole state from history rather than incrementally updating — this naturally handles corrections. Break it on purpose Feed the rule-based tracker the turn "I'm not paying for anything expensive, cheap is better." Which price does it store, and why? Then try "Book for two people... no wait, four people." (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) LLM-based tracking is the default for new systems. Production assistants keep state by having an LLM fill a schema each turn, and conversational platforms such as Rasa CALM and Google's Dialogflow CX / Conversational Agents combine LLM understanding with explicit flows and slots. Tool calling is DST under another name. An agent filling a function's arguments across several turns is tracking slots against a JSON schema; structured-output modes and constrained decoding (Lesson 5.20) guarantee the shape, and evaluation still needs per-turn, per-argument checks. The remaining errors are the ones in this lesson: invented values, missed corrections and lost "don't care" values. Sources: Rasa CALM , Dialogflow CX , OpenAI function calling , MultiWOZ 2.4 . Pitfalls Full-history regeneration cost. Letting the LLM regenerate state each turn costs ) total tokens. Cap history or summarize older turns. Schema drift. Adding new slots post-hoc breaks old training data. Version your schema. Case sensitivity. "Italian" vs "italian" vs "ITALIAN" — normalize everywhere. Implicit inheritance. If the user has previously specified "for 4 people," a new request for a different time should not clear people. Always pass the full history. Free-form vs closed-set. Names, times, and addresses need free-form slots; cuisines and areas are closed. Mix both in the schema. Use it: the same idea with real libraries The 2026 stack: Situation Approach Narrow domain (one or two intents) Rule-based + regex Broad domain, labeled data available LDST (LLaMA + LoRA on MultiWOZ-style data) Broad domain, no labels, prod-ready LLM + Instructor + Pydantic schema Spoken / voice ASR + normalizer + LLM-DST Multi-domain booking flow Schema-guided LLM with per-domain Pydantic models Compliance-sensitive Rule-based primary, LLM fallback with confirmation flow Recap What to keep from this lesson The state is a slot-value form updated every turn: fill, overwrite on correction, clear on negation, leave untouched otherwise. Score with joint goal accuracy on every turn, plus slot accuracy; errors persist, so JGA falls far below slot accuracy. Rules are precise on their own vocabulary and blind outside it; LLMs cover paraphrases but invent values. A schema (Pydantic, constrained decoding) guarantees valid output, not correct output; normalise case and spelling before validating. Require evidence or confirmation for slots that trigger actions. Paradigms and DST terms Rule-based : patterns, intents and slot filling. Fails outside its scope. Retrieval-based : nearest stored response. No generation, so no hallucination. Neural seq2seq : fluent, but generic replies and factual drift. LLM agent : plan, call tool, observe result, decide next step. Slot : a named parameter the backend needs, such as cuisine or date. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Transformer The neural network design behind modern language models: stacked blocks of attention and feed-forward layers Lesson 7.19 Tokenizer The program that splits text into tokens and maps each to a number Lesson 5.31 Why this came about Computers were built for numbers, but most of what people know is written in words: emails, contracts, manuals, conversations. Natural language processing (NLP) is the field that tries to get computers to work with that text. It started in the 1950s with machine translation projects and hand-written grammar rules, which proved far harder than expected. Each later wave, from counting word statistics, to neural networks, to transformers later · 7.19 , solved more of the problem by learning from more text and relying less on rules written by people. Large language models are the latest step in that line, and they still inherit its vocabulary and its hard problems. In plain words first Words are easy, meaning is hard Splitting a sentence into words is easy for a computer. Knowing what the sentence means is not. "The parcel didn't arrive, great service" is a complaint, though it contains the word "great". "Can you cancel it?" depends entirely on what "it" refers to. People resolve these using context, common sense and knowledge of the world, without noticing. An NLP system has to get all of that from somewhere: from rules a person wrote, or from patterns learned from huge amounts of text. Step 1 · Why language is hard Difficulty Example What a system needs Words with several meanings "bank" (river or money), "charge" (a fee, or a battery) the surrounding words Structure that can be read two ways "I saw the courier with the binoculars" (who had them?) world knowledge about what is likely References "The order and the refund were both delayed. Has it been sent?" tracking what it points to Saying one thing, meaning another "Oh great, late again." (sarcasm) tone and context Endless variation "where's my stuff", "order not received", "parcel missing??" recognising the same intent in different words Many languages and mixtures "Mera order kab aayega?" (Hindi in Latin letters) data in that language Every approach in this block is a different answer to the same question: where does the system get the knowledge to resolve these? Step 2 · The shapes of language tasks The main shapes of language task. Classification maps a whole text to a label. Token labelling gives every word a label. Sequence-to-sequence turns one text into another. Generation continues text. A modern language model can do all four when asked in words, which is why it replaced many separate systems. Most real NLP problems are one of these four shapes. A support desk might use all of them: classify incoming tickets by intent, pull out order numbers and names, translate replies, and draft answers. Before 2020 each needed its own model trained on its own labelled data. A large language model can do all of them when asked in plain words (the Talking to models: APIs, messages, prompts and context section), which is the main reason it replaced so many separate systems. Step 3 · Text as data: cleaning, splitting and counting The most basic NLP is plain Python. Here are eight support tickets: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output re.findall(r"[a-z0-9-]+", ...) is a regular expression ( Lesson 0.19 ): "one or more of the characters a to z, 0 to 9 or hyphen". Everything else, such as spaces and punctuation, separates words. This is a simple tokeniser later · 5.31 , a function that cuts text into units. Lowercasing first makes "Order" and "order" the same word. That is usually helpful, though it also merges "US" (the country) with "us". The most common words are mostly short glue words: "is", "my", "a". These are called stop words ; classic systems often removed them. The useful words ("order", "refund", "delivery", "damaged") come next. Removing stop words leaves the words that carry the topic: Copy What you should see Copy Counting words already tells you something: this desk's tickets are about orders, refunds, damage and delivery. Lesson 5.32 turns exactly these counts into features for a classifier. Step 4 · Rules: where they work and where they break Hand-written rules work well when the pattern is exact . Order numbers, amounts and dates follow fixed formats, and a regular expression finds them reliably: Copy What you should see Copy They break when the pattern is about meaning . Here is a rule-based intent detector of the kind built in the 1990s: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output \b means a word boundary, so \brefund matches "refund" but not "prerefund". | means "or". The first two are right. "Smashed" and "in pieces" mean damaged, but the rule only knows the words "damaged" and "broken". "Still waiting... two weeks" is clearly a missing order but matches nothing. And "No need for a refund" is tagged as a refund request: the rule sees the word and misses the "no need". You could add more patterns, and teams did, for years. Rule sets grew to thousands of lines and still missed new phrasings. That is the problem learning from examples solves ( Lesson 2.22 ), and the rest of this block shows how. Tip Rules still have a place In real systems built with language models, rules and regular expressions are still the right tool for exact formats: validating an order ID before calling a tool, masking card numbers before text is logged, or checking that a model's output is valid JSON . Use learned models for meaning and rules for format. Step 5 · Seventy years in one picture Seventy years of getting computers to handle language: from hand-written rules, to statistics counted from text, to neural networks that learn word vectors, to transformers pretrained on most of the written web. Each step needed less hand-crafting and more data and compute. Rules (1950s to 1980s). ELIZA (1966) mimicked a therapist with pattern-and-response rules, and some users believed it understood them. Grammars and rule systems worked in narrow domains and broke outside them. Statistics (1990s to 2000s). Count how often words and word sequences appear in large amounts of text, and use probabilities: n-gram language models ( Lesson 5.34 ), naive Bayes spam filters, statistical translation. Much more robust, but blind to meaning beyond a few words. Neural networks (2003 to 2016). Learn a vector for every word ( Lesson 5.33 ), and use recurrent networks that read text word by word ( Lesson 5.35 ). Encoder-decoder models and attention ( Lesson 5.36 ) made neural translation work. Transformers (2017 onwards). A design built entirely on attention, which trains efficiently on GPUs (the Transformers, step by step section). Pretrained models such as BERT and GPT-2 (2018 to 2019) learned general language skills from huge text collections, then were adapted to tasks. Large language models (2020 onwards). Scale those models up, train them to follow instructions (the From language model to assistant section), and a single model handles most language tasks when asked in words. The pattern across the eras is that each one needed less knowledge written by people and more data and compute. Lesson 3.14 tells the same story for AI as a whole. Check your mental model ✗ "If a computer can split text into words, it understands the text." ✓ Splitting and counting are easy. Meaning depends on context, references and world knowledge, which is the hard part. ✗ "Rules and regular expressions are obsolete." ✓ They are still the best tool for exact formats such as IDs, dates and amounts, and for checking outputs. They fail at meaning. ✗ "Language models replaced NLP." ✓ They are the current method of NLP. The tasks, the difficulties and many of the tools (tokenisers, embeddings , evaluation) carried over. A language model can do all four from instructions, while older systems needed a separately trained model for each. Recap Language is hard for computers because meaning depends on context, references, tone and world knowledge, and the same idea can be said in endless ways. Most tasks are one of four shapes: classify a text, label each token, turn text into other text, or generate text. Basic text handling (lowercasing, splitting with regular expressions, counting) is plain Python and already reveals what a collection of text is about. Rules are reliable for exact formats and brittle for meaning. The field moved from rules, to statistics, to neural networks, to transformers and large language models, each needing less hand-crafting and more data. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in BERT The 2018 encoder-only model trained by filling in masked words Lesson 7.22 Embedding model A model that turns a piece of text into one vector that captures its meaning Lesson 7.22 Reranker A second, slower and more accurate model that reorders the top search results Lesson 5.38 Context window The most input plus output, counted in tokens, that a model can handle in one call Lesson 10.42 Why this came about A neural network needs a fixed list of symbols, each with its own row in the embedding table ( Lesson 3.19 ). Early systems used whole words, but any word not seen in training (a new product name, a typo, "deliveries" when only "delivery" was seen) became an unknown symbol. Characters avoid that but make sequences very long. In 2016 Rico Sennrich and colleagues adapted an old data-compression trick from 1994, byte-pair encoding , to learn a vocabulary of word pieces: common words become one token, rare words are spelled out from smaller pieces. OpenAI's GPT-2 (2019) applied it to raw bytes, so any text in any language can be encoded. Variants of this scheme are used by almost every language model today. In plain words first Building a vocabulary of handy pieces Imagine writing messages using a box of rubber stamps. With only single-letter stamps you can write anything, but slowly. With a stamp for every whole word, you write fast but you need millions of stamps and still lack one for a new word. The practical answer: single letters, plus stamps for the most useful pieces, such as "the", "ing", " delivery", " customer". BPE decides which pieces deserve a stamp by finding the pairs of pieces that appear next to each other most often, and gluing them into a new stamp, again and again. Step 1 · Three ways to cut text Three ways to cut the same text into tokens. Characters need only a tiny vocabulary but make sequences very long. Whole words make short sequences but need an enormous vocabulary and cannot handle new words. Subwords , learned from data, are the compromise every modern language model uses. The bottom row is real output from the cl100k_base tokeniser (GPT-4). Unit Vocabulary size Sequence length New or rare words Characters (or bytes) tiny (about 256 bytes) very long, which costs compute ( Lesson 7.18 ) always fine Words huge (millions, with names and typos) short fail: "unknown word" Subwords chosen: 50,000 to 200,000 moderate (about 4 characters per token in English) spelled from pieces Subwords give most of the benefit of both. Common words are single tokens; rare words are split into a few known pieces; and in the worst case, any text can still fall back to single bytes. Step 2 · Text is stored as bytes Computers store text as bytes (numbers from 0 to 255) using the UTF-8 encoding. English letters take one byte each; accented letters, other scripts and emoji take two to four: Copy What you should see Copy The Hindi word for "hello" has 6 characters (letters and vowel signs) but 18 bytes, three bytes each. A tokeniser that starts from bytes, as GPT-2 and its successors do, can encode any text at all, but scripts that need more bytes start out at a disadvantage unless the tokeniser learned good merges for them (Step 5). Step 3 · Byte-pair encoding from scratch The training algorithm is short: Split the training text into words, each keeping the space in front of it (" courier"), so that pieces never cross word boundaries. Start with every word as a list of single characters. Count every pair of neighbouring tokens inside words. Merge the most frequent pair into a new token everywhere. Repeat for as many merges as you want. The list of merges, in order, is the tokeniser. Try it first: Build a tokeniser by merging the most common pairs Byte-pair encoding starts from single characters, then repeatedly merges the pair of neighbouring tokens that appears most often (never across words). Press the buttons and watch common words become single tokens. Type your own text below; start it with a space to see why the leading space matters. Now in code, on the same training text: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The first merges glue the most common pairs: "t" + "h", then "th" + "e", then " " + "the". After three merges, the most frequent word in the text, " the", is a single token. Each merge shrinks the text: from 247 characters to 96 tokens after 30 merges. Real tokenisers are trained on billions of words and do 50,000 to 200,000 merges. Counter.update(zip(w, w[1:])) counts pairs: zip(w, w[1:]) pairs every element with the next one. most_common(1) returns the top pair and its count; ties go to the pair seen first, which makes the result repeatable. !r in an f-string prints a value with quotes, so you can see the spaces inside tokens. To encode new text, split it into words and apply the learned merges in the order they were learned: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Words that were common in training ("the", " customer", " courier") come out as single tokens. "thanked" appeared only once, so it is spelled out in small pieces. " thermometer" was never seen, yet it is encoded fine, from the pieces " the", "r", "m" and so on. There is no "unknown word". "parcels" and " parcels" are encoded differently: the learned pieces include a leading space (" par", " parcel"), so the same word without a space in front uses different, smaller pieces. Real tokenisers behave the same way, which is why a stray space at the end of a prompt can subtly change a model's output. Finally, each token gets an ID number, the row it will use in the embedding table: Copy What you should see Copy Decoding is just looking the IDs up and joining the pieces. Real tokenisers work on bytes rather than characters (so they need the 256 byte values as their starting vocabulary), use a more careful pre-splitting rule, and add a few special tokens such as <|endoftext|> that mark boundaries between documents or chat messages ( Lesson 10.36 ). Otherwise this is the algorithm. Step 4 · Real tokenisers tiktoken is OpenAI's tokeniser library. It includes the GPT-2 tokeniser (50,257 tokens), cl100k_base (about 100,000, used by GPT-3.5 and GPT-4) and o200k_base (about 200,000, used by GPT-4o and later OpenAI models). Other model families ship their own tokenisers, but they work the same way. What a production tokeniser does to a string, top to bottom: clean it up (normalisation), split it roughly into words (pre-tokenisation), apply the learned merges (the model, here WordPiece , which marks word-internal pieces with ##), then add the special tokens the model expects. Recap Language models read token IDs; tokens are usually subwords, a compromise between characters (long sequences) and words (huge vocabulary, unknown words). Text is stored as UTF-8 bytes; starting from bytes means any text can be encoded. Real tokenisers (GPT-2, cl100k_base, o200k_base) have 50,000 to 200,000 tokens; English averages about four characters per token. A spam email says "free", "winner" and "click" a lot; a sports article says "match" and "goal". In 1998, Mehran Sahami and colleagues showed that a simple word-counting classifier (naive Bayes) filtered spam well, and by the mid-2000s spam filters everywhere worked this way. For search, Karen Spärck Jones's 1972 idea of inverse document frequency (a word that appears in every document tells you nothing) became TF-IDF and later BM25 later · 5.37 , the ranking formula still inside most search engines, including the keyword half of the hybrid search later · 5.38 in Lesson 5.38 . In plain words first Counting the words in a bag Tip all the words of a message into a bag, shake it, and count what is inside: "refund" twice, "order" once, "damaged" once. The order is gone, but the counts still say a lot about what the message is about. A classifier learns which words point to which kind of ticket. For search, you do the same to every document and to the query, and look for documents whose counts look most like the query's, giving more weight to words that are rare (and so informative) than to words that are everywhere. Step 1 · A dataset of support tickets You need labelled examples. Here are 48 ways customers phrase four kinds of ticket (where is my order, refund, damaged item, account), each filled in 8 times with random order numbers, items and days, for 384 tickets: Copy What you should see Copy Real ticket data would come from your help desk, labelled by agents. Generated data like this has a trap, though: eight tickets from the same template are near-duplicates. If some land in training and others in testing, the test only checks memory ( Lesson 2.26 ). So hold out whole templates : tickets from templates 2, 6 and 10 of each kind go to the test set . Those phrasings are never seen in training, which is what real new tickets are like. Copy What you should see Copy Step 2 · A bag of words A bag of words turns each text into a row of counts, one column per word in the vocabulary. Word order is thrown away, so two sentences with opposite meanings can get exactly the same row. Most entries are zero, so the rows are stored as sparse matrices. scikit-learn's CountVectorizer builds the vocabulary from the training texts and turns each text into a row of counts: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output fit_transform does two things: fit learns the vocabulary from the training texts, transform turns texts into counts. New texts must only be transformed with the same vocabulary, never re-fitted ( Lesson 2.26 's rule about fitting preprocessing on training data only). Each order number like "sk-48213" splits into "sk" and a number, and each number becomes its own column. Useless columns like that are common in raw text features. The example row counts "refund" twice and the other words once. A word the vectoriser never saw in training has no column, so it is silently ignored. That is the bag of words' biggest weakness on new text. Only about 3% of the matrix is non-zero. scikit-learn stores it as a sparse matrix , which keeps only the non-zero entries. Step 3 · Train, evaluate, inspect The counts are features; any classifier from the Machine learning from zero section can use them. Logistic regression is the standard choice: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output On unseen phrasings , accuracy is 82%. That is the honest number. With a careless random split the same model scores 100% , because every test ticket has seven near-twins in training. This is exactly the duplicate leakage of Lesson 2.26 , and it is easy to fall into with text data. The per-class report shows where it struggles. Lesson 2.25 's precision and recall apply unchanged. A linear model on word counts can be read directly: each class has one weight per word. Copy What you should see Copy Mostly sensible: "refund" and "money" for refunds, "password" and "address" for accounts. Some are artefacts of the templates ("it", "has", "but", "from"). Reading the weights is a quick way to catch a model leaning on something silly. Step 4 · Where counting fails The classifier works by counting words, so it has no idea of word order or of what "no" and "not" do to a sentence. Four messages chosen to expose that: two that contain the word "refund" while saying a refund is not wanted, and two that describe a problem without using any of the usual words. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The first is right, but partly by luck: "box" appeared in a training ticket about a crushed box. The real clues, "smashed" and "pieces", were never seen and count for nothing. "No need for a refund" and "I do not want a refund" are both labelled refund. A bag of words cannot represent "no need for" or "do not want"; it sees the word "refund". "Left it at the wrong address" is a delivery problem, but the model only half-guesses "damaged" (0.49): the words it knows ("address", "the", "it") point in different directions, and it cannot tell what the sentence is about . Adding bigrams (pairs of neighbouring words, such as "not received" or "no need") as extra features captures a little word order. Use CountVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2)) . It helps a bit, at the cost of a much larger vocabulary. The deeper fixes come later: word vectors that know "smashed" is close to "broken" ( Lesson 5.33 ), and transformers that read words in context (the Transformers, step by step section). Step 5 · TF-IDF and a first search engine For search, raw counts have a problem: words like "how", "do" and "my" appear in almost every document, so they dominate the comparison. TF-IDF fixes that by weighting each count: TF (term frequency): how often the word appears in this document. IDF (inverse document frequency): how rare the word is across all documents, log(number of documents / documents containing the word) (scikit-learn adds 1s to avoid dividing by zero). Rare words get a high weight; words found everywhere get a low one. Here is a tiny help centre with six FAQ entries. Each FAQ and each query becomes a TF-IDF vector, and the best answer is the FAQ with the highest cosine similarity ( Lesson 1.23 ) to the query: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output With common words removed, the vocabulary is just the 17 content words of the FAQs. A query is matched on those words only. The first three queries find the right FAQ: they share "track" and "order", "password", or "item arrived damaged". "the parcel came broken" scores 0 against everything : it shares no word with any FAQ, even though "broken" means "damaged" and "parcel" means "order". The argmax of all zeros is simply the first FAQ, a meaningless answer. This vocabulary mismatch is keyword search's central weakness. The fix is to compare meanings instead of words: embed the query and the FAQs with a model that places "broken" near "damaged" ( Lesson 7.22 ), which is vector search later · 14.71 ( Lesson 14.71 ). Real systems often combine both, because keyword search is better at exact terms such as order numbers and product codes: hybrid search ( Lesson 5.38 ). BM25 , the ranking formula used by Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and most search engines, is a refined TF-IDF: repeated words count less and less (the fifth "refund" adds little), and long documents do not win just by being long. Lesson 5.37 uses it for retrieval. Step 6 · When to use word counts today Use Why it still works A baseline for any text classifier trains in a second; if a large model cannot beat it, something is wrong Keyword search (BM25) exact matches on names, codes and rare terms; no GPU needed Explainable filters the weights show exactly which words drove a decision Very high volume, low cost filtering millions of texts per minute on a CPU For anything that depends on meaning, word order, or phrasings not seen before, use embeddings or a language model. The same idea as a formula bag of words: document d → vector x with xⱼ = count of word j in d TF-IDF weight: tfidf(w, d) = tf(w, d) × idf(w), with idf(w) = log((1 + N) / (1 + df(w))) + 1 in scikit-learn, where N is the number of documents and df(w) the number containing w; each row is then scaled to length 1 cosine similarity of query q and document d: ( q · d ) / (‖ q ‖ ‖ d ‖) Check your mental model ✗ "A 100% test score means the classifier is excellent." ✓ With templated or duplicated text, a random split leaks near-copies into the test set. Split by template, customer or document. ✗ "The bag of words understands negation." ✓ It only counts words. Bigrams help a little; transformers handle it properly. ✗ "TF-IDF search finds documents with the same meaning." ✓ It finds documents with the same words . Synonyms score zero. Exercises Predict before you run What will vec.transform(["SK-48213 refund"]) count for the words "sk" and "refund", given the training vocabulary? And will "48213" be counted? (Solution P1.) Make it your own Train the classifier on CountVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2)) instead. How many columns does the vocabulary have now, what is the test accuracy, and is "no need for a refund" classified any differently? (Solution M1.) Practice Apply it Add a seventh FAQ, "My parcel arrived broken, what now?", to faqs , refit the TF-IDF vectoriser and run the queries again. Which query changes its answer, and what does that tell you about how to write FAQ entries for keyword search? (Solution X1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Order numbers in the vocabulary "sk" gets a count of 1 (it was in training, from every order number) and "refund" a count of 1. "48213" is counted only if exactly that number appeared in a training ticket, which is unlikely; otherwise it is silently ignored. Unique identifiers make useless features, and some teams replace them with a placeholder such as <order_id> before vectorising. Solution M1 · Adding bigrams The vocabulary grows from 216 to 585 columns. Test accuracy rises only slightly, to about 83%. "no need for a refund, ..." is still classified as refund: the bigram "no need" never appeared in training, so it adds nothing, while "refund" and "a refund" still pull towards the refund class. Bigrams can only help with word pairs that the training data contains. Solution X1 · Matching the users' words "the parcel came broken" now matches the new FAQ, because "parcel" and "broken" are in its text. Keyword search finds what is written in the users' own words, so good FAQ entries and documents include the common phrasings and synonyms people actually use. Embedding search ( Lesson 14.71 ) relaxes this requirement, which is a big reason it became popular. Recap A bag of words turns each text into a sparse vector of word counts; word order and meaning are thrown away. Linear classifiers on word counts train in seconds and can be inspected word by word, but only know words seen in training. With templated or duplicated text, split by template or source; a random split can give a meaningless 100%. TF-IDF weights words by how rare they are across documents; with cosine similarity it ranks documents for a query, and BM25 refines it. Word counting fails on synonyms and negation; word vectors, embeddings and transformers address that, and hybrid search combines both. Check your understanding Q1 What does a bag-of-words representation throw away? A Which words appear B How often each word appears C The order of the words D The vocabulary Only counts are kept; "dog bites man" equals "man bites dog". Q2 Why does IDF give the word "my" a low weight in a help centre's FAQs? A It appears in almost every document, so it says little about which one matches B It is a short word C It is not in the dictionary D It appears only once Words found everywhere carry little information for ranking. Q3 The query "the parcel came broken" scores 0 against the FAQ "What should I do if my item arrived damaged?". Why? A The FAQ is too long B TF-IDF cannot handle short queries C They share no words, and TF-IDF only matches words, not meanings D Stop words removed the meaning Vocabulary mismatch; embeddings fix it. l2504: Course home / Phase 5 · Working with Language Word vectors: meaning from the company words keep From Zero to Agents Lesson 5.33 60 min Core Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Explain the distributional idea: words used in similar contexts have similar meanings Build word vectors from co-occurrence counts, and describe how word2vec learns them Load real word vectors from GPT-2, find nearest neighbours and solve analogies with vector arithmetic Explain the limits of one-vector-per-word embeddings, including the biases they absorb from text Before you start Needs : Lesson 3.19 (embeddings), Lesson 1.23 (cosine similarity), Lesson 5.32 (bag of words). Depth : Core. Time : about 60 minutes. Next : Lesson 5.34 starts on language models: predicting the next word, beginning with simple counts. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Word2vec The 2013 method that learns word vectors by predicting nearby words Embeddings history Skip-gram with negative sampling Word2vec's training recipe: tell real neighbouring words from random ones Embeddings history GloVe Word vectors learned from counts of how often words appear together Embeddings history Why this came about In 1957 the linguist J. R. Firth wrote, "You shall know a word by the company it keeps." The idea that a word's meaning shows in the words around it led to counting methods in the 1990s (latent semantic analysis), but the vectors were large and slow to compute. In 2013 Tomas Mikolov and colleagues at Google released word2vec , which learned compact vectors for millions of words in hours on ordinary computers, and showed a striking side effect: arithmetic on the vectors captured relations, as in king − man + woman ≈ queen . Word vectors quickly became the standard first layer of NLP systems. Today's language models still begin with an embedding table learned the same way, as part of predicting the next token. In plain words first Judging a word by its neighbours Suppose you meet a new word, "chai", in sentences like "I drink hot chai in the morning" and "she ordered a cup of chai". Without a dictionary you can guess it is a drink, a bit like tea or coffee, because it turns up in the same places they do. Word vectors make that guess mathematical: describe each word by the words that appear around it, and words that keep the same company end up with similar descriptions, and so similar vectors. Step 1 · Counting the company words keep Here is a tiny text of 14 sentences. For each word, count which other words appear within two positions of it: Copy What you should see Copy Each row of counts is now a vector describing a word by its neighbours. Compare rows with cosine similarity : Copy What you should see Copy Coffee and tea have identical neighbours in this text, so their vectors are identical (1.00); dog and cat nearly so; coffee and dog share only common words like "the"; tea and friday share nothing. Nobody told the program what any word means. Similar usage alone produced similar vectors. On real text, these count vectors are huge (one column per vocabulary word) and dominated by common words. That is where learning comes in. Step 2 · word2vec: learning short vectors The idea behind word vectors: a word is described by the words around it. Slide a window along the text; each word in the middle is paired with its neighbours. Words that keep similar company (coffee and tea both appear near 'drink', 'hot' and 'cup') end up with similar vectors. word2vec turns the counting into a training task, the same one you ran on shopping baskets in Lesson 3.19 . Slide a window along the text and collect (word, neighbour) pairs: Copy What you should see Copy Then train an embedding table so that the dot product of a word's vector with its real neighbours' vectors is high, and with randomly chosen words ( negative samples ) low. The code is exactly Lesson 3.19 's training loop with these pairs in place of basket pairs. Trained on billions of words, word2vec produced vectors of 100 to 300 numbers per word that capture remarkably fine relationships. The variant described here is called skip-gram with negative sampling ; a cousin, GloVe (Stanford, 2014), learns similar vectors directly from the co-occurrence counts. Step 3 · Real word vectors: GPT-2's embedding table You do not need to train your own. GPT-2's first layer is a table of 50,257 token vectors with 768 numbers each, learned while predicting the next token ( Lesson 3.19 ). Words with a leading space, like " coffee", are single tokens, so their rows are word vectors. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The first time, from_pretrained("gpt2") downloads the model (about 500 MB) from Hugging Face and caches it; later runs load it from disk. Lesson 7.23 explores the rest of the model. Days sit next to days, numbers next to numbers, " refund" next to " refunds", " reimbursement" and " rebate". These relationships were learned only from predicting text. Capitalised and space-less variants (" Coffee", "happy") appear as separate neighbours: they are different tokens with their own rows, but nearly the same meaning. " unhappy" is one of the closest words to " happy". Opposites are used in very similar contexts ("I am ___ with the service"), so embeddings learned from context put them close together. Similar vectors mean "used similarly", not "means the same". Step 4 · Directions in the space mean something Differences between vectors can capture relationships. The classic test is an analogy : king is to man as ? is to woman . Compute king − man + woman and look for the nearest word: The famous example. The step from "man" to "king" (blue) is nearly the same as the step from "woman" to "queen", so king minus man plus woman lands near queen. One direction in the space carries "royalty" and another carries "gender". Figure: Daniel Voigt Godoy, dl-visuals , CC BY 4.0 . Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output king − man + woman lands nearest " queen"; Paris − France + Japan nearest " Tokyo"; walking − walk + swim nearest " swimming". The difference vectors "male to female", "country to capital" and "verb to -ing form" are roughly consistent directions in the space. The last one fails: big − bigger + small should give "smaller", but gives " large" and " tiny". Analogies work for some relationships and not others, and the famous examples were partly chosen because they work. Treat them as a demonstration, not a guarantee. Explore the space yourself. The map shows 32 words placed along the main directions of variation (found by PCA , Lesson 2.27 ). Click any word to see its nearest neighbours among all 50,257 tokens. Explore real word vectors from GPT-2 Thirty-two common words, placed by their learned vectors. Each PCA direction tends to pick out one kind of word: try direction 1 against 2, then 3 against 4. Notice that each PCA direction tends to pick out one kind of word: one separates the days of the week, another places, another numbers from food, another feelings. The 768 numbers encode many such directions at once. Step 5 · Embeddings absorb what the text says, including its biases Word vectors learn associations from the text they were trained on, and text written by people contains stereotypes. One way to see it: take the direction from " she" to " he" and measure where occupation words fall along it. Copy What you should see Copy All the values are slightly negative (the direction is not perfectly centred), so compare them with each other: " nurse" and " dancer" sit noticeably further towards " she" than " engineer" and " doctor". The model was never told anything about gender and jobs; it absorbed the pattern from how people write. Research in 2016 (Bolukbasi and colleagues) found the same in word2vec, and showed that systems built on such vectors can repeat the bias, for example when ranking CVs. Large language models inherit associations like these too, which is one reason they are tested and tuned for fairness ( Lesson 10.41 and the Safety, security and governance section). Step 6 · One vector per word is not enough Static word vectors give each word one vector, whatever the sentence. But many words have several meanings: Copy What you should see Copy The neighbours are forms of the word itself and its financial meaning (" banks", " banking", " banker"); nothing about rivers. The river sense of "bank" is much rarer in text, so the single vector is dominated by the financial meaning; a word's one vector is an average of all its uses, weighted by how often each occurs. In "we sat on the river bank", that is the wrong vector. The fix is contextual embeddings : start from this table, then let every word's vector be adjusted by the words around it. That adjustment is what attention does ( Lesson 5.36 and the Transformers, step by step section), and it is why a transformer 's upper layers know which "bank" you mean. The same idea as a formula co-occurrence vector for word w: c _w with entry j = number of times word j appears within the window around w skip-gram with negative sampling: maximise log σ( v _w · u _c) + Σ log σ(− v _w · u _n) over (word, context) pairs (w, c) and random words n analogy: answer = argmax over words x of cos( v _x, v _king − v _man + v _woman), excluding the three input words Check your mental model ✗ "Words with similar vectors have the same meaning." ✓ They are used in similar contexts. Opposites ("happy", "unhappy") and related-but-different words ("tea", "coffee") are close too. ✗ "Word vectors are neutral facts about language." ✓ They reflect the text they were trained on, including stereotypes, and systems built on them can repeat those biases. ✗ "A word has one meaning, so one vector is enough." ✓ Many words have several senses; static vectors blur them together, which contextual embeddings fix. Make it your own Add three sentences to the corpus in Step 1 that use "chai" the way coffee and tea are used, rebuild the counts, and measure cosine("chai", "tea") and cosine("chai", "dog") . (Solution M1.) Practice Apply it Try two analogies of your own with GPT-2's vectors, one that you expect to work and one that you expect to fail, for example Delhi − India + France and good − better + bad . Use only words that are single tokens (the token_id check will tell you). (Solution X1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Sleeps and drink 0.00. "sleeps" appears only in "my dog sleeps on the sofa" and "my cat sleeps on the sofa", with neighbours dog, cat, my, on, the. "drink" appears with hot, coffee, tea, i, to, too. They share no neighbours within two words, so their vectors have no overlap. Solution M1 · Learning a new word For example: "i drink hot chai in the morning", "he drinks a cup of chai after lunch", "the chai is too hot to drink". After rebuilding, chai's row matches tea's almost exactly (cosine close to 1), and its similarity to dog stays low (about 0.35, from shared words like "the"). Solution X1 · Your own analogies Delhi − India + France gives " Paris" in second place, just behind the space-less token "France": capitals are a strong, consistent relationship in text, though the answer list needs reading with care. Comparative forms such as good − better + bad fail here (the top answers are " Good", "bad" and " Bad", not " worse"), as big − bigger + small did. Relationships that are written about often and consistently are captured better. Recap A word's meaning shows in the company it keeps; describing words by their neighbours gives similar vectors to similar words. word2vec learns short vectors by predicting neighbours with negative sampling, the same training as Lesson 3.19 . A language model's embedding table holds real word vectors: nearest neighbours and some analogies work by vector arithmetic. Similar vectors mean similar usage, which includes opposites; embeddings also absorb biases from their training text. Static vectors give one vector per word; contextual embeddings from attention adapt each word to its sentence. Check your understanding Q1 What does the distributional idea behind word vectors say? A Words are defined by their spelling B Words that appear in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings C Each word should be a one-hot vector D Longer words carry more meaning "You shall know a word by the company it keeps." A The tokeniser splits them the same way B Opposites are used in very similar contexts, so context-based vectors place them close together C GPT-2 does not know what happy means D Cosine similarity ignores negation words Similar vectors reflect similar usage, not identical meaning. Q3 What problem do contextual embeddings solve? A Words being too long B The vocabulary being too large C A word with several meanings getting a single vector that blurs them D Analogies being slow to compute The vector for "bank" should differ between "river bank" and "bank account". l2505: Course home / Phase 5 · Working with Language Language models from counts: n-grams, sampling and perplexity From Zero to Agents Lesson 5.34 60 min Core Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Say precisely what a language model is: a probability for the next token given the ones before Build character-level n-gram models by counting, and generate text from them by sampling Measure a language model with cross-entropy loss and perplexity on held-out text Explain smoothing, and why longer contexts eventually make counting models worse Before you start Needs : Lesson 1.25 (probability and cross-entropy), Lesson 2.26 (validation data), Lesson 0.19 (files and requests ). Depth : Core. This lesson defines the task every LLM is trained on. Time : about 60 minutes. Next : Lesson 5.35 replaces counting with neural networks that can generalise to contexts they have never seen. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up n-gram model A language model that predicts the next token from counts of the previous n-1 tokens Language model history Bigram A pair of adjacent tokens; a bigram model looks one token back Language model history Smoothing Giving unseen sequences a small probability instead of zero Count-based models Sparsity Most possible sequences never appearing in the training data Why neural models won Mentioned here, taught later 2 Transformer, Greedy decoding This lesson mentions the ideas below before the lesson that teaches them. The one-line meaning is all you need for now; each is marked later where it first appears. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Transformer The neural network design behind modern language models: stacked blocks of attention and feed-forward layers Lesson 7.19 Greedy decoding Always picking the single most likely next token Lesson 7.21 Why this came about In 1948 Claude Shannon, founding information theory, generated English-like text by picking each letter according to the letters before it, using frequency tables from books. His "n-gram" approximations got more English-like as the context grew. From the 1980s to the 2010s, word n-gram models counted from huge text collections powered speech recognition, machine translation and phone keyboards; Google released counts of n-grams from a trillion words in 2006. They were finally overtaken by neural language models, but the task, the evaluation ( perplexity ) and the sampling procedure carried straight over to GPT. In plain words first Guess the next letter Play a game: I show you "to be or not to b", and you guess the next letter. You would say "e" with confidence, because you have seen that phrase before. A language model plays exactly this game, but gives a probability for every possible next character (or token). The simplest way to get those probabilities is to count: in a big pile of text, after "to b", how often did each character come next? Then, to write text, repeatedly pick a next character according to those probabilities and add it on. Step 1 · The training text You will use Tiny Shakespeare : about a million characters of Shakespeare's plays (long out of copyright), collected by Andrej Karpathy for teaching. The same file is used again in Lesson 5.35 and for training a small GPT in Lesson 7.20 . Copy What you should see Copy This is a character-level model: the vocabulary is the 65 characters, so there is no tokeniser to worry about. Everything in this lesson works the same with BPE tokens ( Lesson 5.31 ) or words; characters just keep the counts small enough to see. Step 2 · Counting what comes next An n-gram model predicts the next character from only the previous n − 1 characters, using counts from training text. A longer context makes better guesses, but each longer context has been seen less often, until most contexts were never seen at all. An n-gram model looks at the previous n − 1 characters (the context ) and counts what followed them in the training text. A bigram model (n = 2) uses one character of context: Copy What you should see Copy defaultdict(Counter) creates an empty Counter the first time a new context appears. Dividing each count by the context's total turns counts into probabilities: P(next | context). After "q" comes "u" every time; after "t" the most common next character is "h"; after a full stop, a newline. That table is the model. Here is the bigram table for letters, built from the same text, to explore: A language model made of counts Every pair of neighbouring letters in Tiny Shakespeare, counted (punctuation and line breaks turned into spaces). Each row shows what tends to follow one character; darker means more likely. Step 3 · Writing text by sampling To generate, start from a context, pick the next character at random in proportion to its probability , append it, slide the context along, and repeat. This is exactly how GPT generates text one token at a time (Lessons 0.15 and 7.21 ). Copy What you should see Copy Word-shaped gibberish: the right mix of letters, spaces and line breaks, short "words", capital letters after line breaks. One character of context is enough to learn spelling-like patterns, but nothing longer. Step 4 · Measuring a language model: loss and perplexity How good is a model? Use the cross-entropy of Lesson 1.25 on held-out text: for each character of the validation text, ask the model what probability it gave to the character that really came next, take −log of it, and average. Lower is better. The problem: if a context-and-character pair never occurred in training, its count is 0, its probability 0, and −log 0 is infinite. Smoothing fixes that by adding a small pretend count k to every possible character, so nothing has probability exactly 0: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output A model that knows nothing gives each of the 65 characters probability 1/65; its loss is log(65) = 4.17. The bigram model's loss is 2.48. Perplexity is e^loss : about 12 here. It has a friendly meaning: the model is, on average, as uncertain as if it were choosing uniformly among about 12 characters, instead of 65. Language model papers report exactly these two numbers (often per token instead of per character). Lower perplexity on held-out text means a better model, as long as the vocabularies are the same, because perplexities from different tokenisers cannot be compared directly. Step 5 · Longer contexts, and where counting breaks More context should help: after "to b", "e" is far more predictable than after just "b". Try n from 1 (no context at all, just letter frequencies) up to 7 (six characters of context): Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output From n = 1 to n = 4 the loss falls fast: more context, better predictions. At n = 5 it stops improving (1.788 against 1.784), and from n = 6 it gets clearly worse . The model that can see more is predicting worse on new text. The reason is in the middle column. With 65 characters there are 65⁶ ≈ 75 billion possible 6-character contexts, but the training text contains only 264,623 different ones. In the validation text, many contexts were never seen, or seen once or twice, so their counts are mostly noise and smoothing. This is sparsity , the overfitting of counting models: Lesson 2.26 's U-curve again. Real n-gram systems used clever backoff (if "o not to b" was never seen, fall back to "not to b", then "to b") and huge corpora, but the wall remains: counting cannot generalise from "to be" to "to see" because it has no notion that contexts can be similar . Generated text shows the same story: Copy What you should see Copy With n = 3 you get word fragments; with n = 5, real words and Shakespeare-like layout; with n = 7, long stretches that are copied almost word for word from the training text, because most seven-character contexts appeared only once there. The model is memorising, not generalising. GPT-4 and its successors are trained on this task, with transformers later · 7.19 in place of count tables and trillions of tokens in place of a million characters. Facts show up only to the extent that predicting text well requires them. ✗ "Lower training loss means a better language model." ✓ Only held-out loss counts. The 7-gram model fits its training text better than any other and generalises worse. ✗ "Sampling always picks the most likely next character." ✓ It picks at random in proportion to the probabilities. Make it your own In val_loss , try the 5-gram model with smoothing k of 1, 0.1 and 0.01. Which works best, and why does the amount of smoothing matter more for long contexts? (Solution M1.) Debugging exercise A colleague computes perplexity on the training text instead of the validation text and reports that the 7-gram model is the best by far. What is wrong with this conclusion? (Solution D1.) Solutions Solution P1 · No context at all Characters drawn independently according to how common each one is in Shakespeare: lots of spaces and "e", "t", "o", some capitals and line breaks, but no word shapes at all, because the model has no memory of what came before. Each character is a random draw from the same distribution. Solution M1 · How much to smooth For n = 5, k of 0.1 or 0.01 does much better than 1 (validation loss about 1.77 to 1.79 versus about 2.17). Longer contexts have small counts, so a pretend count of 1 for each of 65 characters (65 in total) swamps the real evidence. With short contexts, counts are large and the pretend counts hardly matter. Choosing k is a hyperparameter decision made on validation data. Solution D1 · Measuring on training data On its own training text, a 7-gram model has seen almost every context and simply recalls what followed, so its training perplexity is very low. That measures memorisation, not prediction. On the validation text it is worse than the 4-gram and 5-gram models. Always evaluate language models on text they were not trained on, the rule from Lesson 2.26 , which also makes benchmark contamination a real concern for large models ( Lesson 10.47 ). Recap A language model gives a probability to every possible next token given the previous ones; generating means sampling from those probabilities again and again. An n-gram model estimates them by counting what followed each context of n − 1 symbols in training text. Models are measured by cross-entropy on held-out text; perplexity, e to the loss, is the effective number of equally likely choices. Smoothing avoids zero probabilities for unseen events. Longer contexts help until sparsity takes over: most long contexts were never seen, so counting models stop generalising, which neural language models fix. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Transformer The neural network design behind modern language models: stacked blocks of attention and feed-forward layers Lesson 7.19 State-space models (SSMs) Sequence models with a fixed-size running state, such as Mamba Lesson 7.24 Greedy decoding Always picking the single most likely next token Lesson 7.21 Why this came about In 2003 Yoshua Bengio and colleagues replaced the n-gram count table with a neural network: look up a learned vector for each previous word, feed them through a hidden layer, and predict the next word. Because similar words get similar vectors, the network could make sensible predictions for word combinations it had never seen. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), which read text one step at a time while carrying a memory, go back to the 1980s; the LSTM (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) made that memory last longer. By 2015, LSTM language models led the field, Andrej Karpathy's blog post "The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Recurrent Neural Networks" generated fake Shakespeare with them, and Google Translate switched to LSTM networks in 2016. A year later the transformer later · 7.19 replaced them. In plain words first From a lookup table to a pattern learner The counting model of Lesson 5.34 is a giant lookup table: it only knows contexts it has seen. A neural model learns a small vector for every character (or word), and a function that turns the vectors of the recent context into a prediction. Contexts that are similar produce similar vectors, so the model can handle a context it has never met. A recurrent network goes one step further: instead of looking at a fixed window, it reads the text one character at a time and keeps a running summary, its hidden state , like a reader who remembers the gist of what came before. Step 1 · Text as tensors The same Tiny Shakespeare text as Lesson 5.34 , turned into a tensor of character IDs: Copy What you should see Copy Step 2 · A neural language model with a fixed window A neural language model in the style of Bengio and colleagues (2003). Each of the previous characters is looked up in an embedding table, the vectors are joined end to end, a hidden layer mixes them, and the output layer gives one score per possible next character, turned into probabilities by softmax. The model looks at the previous 8 characters. Each is looked up in an embedding table (16 numbers per character), the 8 vectors are joined into one vector of 128 numbers, a hidden layer mixes them, and the output layer gives 65 scores, one per possible next character. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output unfold(0, 9, 1) cuts the validation text into every overlapping window of 9 characters: 8 of context plus the one to predict. It is a quick way to build evaluation examples. The validation loss starts at about log(65) ≈ 4.17 (a random guess) and falls to about 1.86 in some ten seconds of training. Compare with counting, using the same 8 characters of context: a 9-gram count model scores 3.24 on this validation text, because about half of the 8-character contexts in it never appeared in training. The network's 51,000 parameters handle contexts it has never seen; the count table, with over half a million entries, cannot. The best counting model in Lesson 5.34 (3 or 4 characters of context, carefully smoothed) reached about 1.78. The window network is not far off and is still improving; longer training and a bigger network would pass it. Training also gave every character a learned vector. Which characters did the model decide are similar? Copy What you should see Copy Nobody told it which characters are vowels, capitals or punctuation; characters that behave alike in text ended up with similar vectors, exactly as words did in Lesson 5.33 . Step 3 · Recurrent networks: reading with a memory A fixed window cannot use anything further back than 8 characters. A recurrent neural network (RNN) reads one character at a time and carries a hidden state , a vector that is updated at every step from the previous state and the new character: h_t = tanh(W_x · x_t + W_h · h_{t−1} + b) The same weights are used at every step, so the network can read text of any length. A recurrent network reads one character at a time. At each step it combines the new input with its hidden state, a vector that summarises everything read so far, and predicts the next character. The same weights are used at every step. The catch: step 5 cannot start until step 4 has finished. The same idea in the standard textbook drawing: one recurrent cell, shown at three consecutive time steps. The hidden state H is passed from each step to the next, and the same weights are used at every step. Figure: Zhang, Lipton, Li and Smola, Dive into Deep Learning , CC BY-SA 4.0 . Here is that update written out, for a hidden state of 4 numbers with random weights, just to see the state change as it reads: Copy What you should see Copy The state after "to be" depends on every character read so far, in order. Training adjusts W_x , W_h and b (with backpropagation through all the steps, called backpropagation through time ) so that the state keeps whatever helps predict the next character. Plain RNNs forget quickly: the gradient has to pass back through the same multiplication at every step, and it vanishes (or explodes) over long distances, the problem of Lesson 3.18 stretched along time. The LSTM ("long short-term memory") adds a separate memory cell and gates , small sigmoid layers that decide what to forget, what to write and what to read at each step. The cell can carry information over hundreds of steps. GRUs are a simpler variant. PyTorch provides both as single layers. Step 4 · Training an LSTM language model The model: an embedding table, one LSTM layer with a hidden state of 256 numbers, and an output layer. It is trained on chunks of 64 characters, predicting the next character at every position of each chunk at once: Inside one LSTM cell. Three gates (the boxes marked σ, each producing numbers between 0 and 1) control the memory cell C along the top: the forget gate decides how much of the old memory to keep, the input gate how much new information to write, and the output gate how much of the memory to reveal as the hidden state H. You will not build this by hand; PyTorch provides it as one layer. Figure: Zhang, Lipton, Li and Smola, Dive into Deep Learning , CC BY-SA 4.0 . Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Reading this code y is x shifted one place to the left: at each of the 64 positions, the target is the character that comes next. One chunk gives 64 training examples, all computed in one forward pass. GPT trains exactly this way ( Lesson 7.20 ). logits.reshape(-1, V) flattens (batch, time, 65) into (batch × time, 65) rows, because cross_entropy expects one row per prediction. Validation reads 100,000 characters as one long sequence, carrying the hidden state all the way: the LSTM can use context from much further back than 8 characters. After 1,000 steps the validation loss is about 1.64, better than the best counting model (1.78) and the window network (1.86). Lesson 7.20 's small transformer goes further still. Step 5 · Writing with the LSTM To generate, feed one character at a time, keep the hidden state between steps, and sample from the softmax : Copy What you should see Copy After two minutes of CPU training: a speaker's name in capitals, line breaks, mostly real words, and roughly the rhythm of Shakespeare's verse, though not much sense. But since 2018 nearly every leading language model has been a transformer. Solution D1 · Training loss falls, validation loss rises Overfitting : the model is memorising the training text ( Lesson 2.26 ). Recap A neural language model learns a vector per character or word and a function from the recent context to next-token probabilities; it generalises to contexts it never saw. With the same context length, a small network beats counting by a wide margin because counting has no notion of similar contexts. A recurrent network reads one step at a time, updating a hidden state with the same weights at every step; LSTMs add gates so memory lasts longer. Training predicts the next character at every position of a chunk at once; generation samples one character at a time and feeds it back in. RNNs are slow to train (sequential) and squeeze all memory into one vector; attention and transformers remove both limits. Depth : Core. Attention is the single most important idea in the rest of the course. Time : about 65 minutes, including about a minute of training. Next : the Transformers, step by step section builds the transformer, which is made of attention. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Encoder The part of a model that reads the input and turns it into vectors Translation, BERT Decoder The part of a model that writes the output one token at a time Translation, GPT Attention Letting the model look back at all the input vectors and weight them by relevance at each step Transformers Context vector The weighted average of the input vectors that attention produces for one step Attention Teacher forcing During training, feeding the correct previous token instead of the model's own guess Training sequence models Mentioned here, taught later 3 Transformer, Encoder-decoder, Attention This lesson mentions the ideas below before the lesson that teaches them. The one-line meaning is all you need for now; each is marked later where it first appears. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Transformer The neural network design behind modern language models: stacked blocks of attention and feed-forward layers Lesson 7.19 Encoder-decoder A transformer with both parts, such as T5 Lesson 7.22 Attention Letting every token gather information from the other tokens, weighted by relevance Lesson 7.17 Why this came about Translation turns a sentence of one length into a sentence of another, with words reordered. In 2014, Ilya Sutskever, Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le at Google (and, in parallel, Kyunghyun Cho and colleagues) showed that two LSTMs could do it: an encoder reads the source sentence into a vector, and a decoder writes the translation from it. It worked surprisingly well for short sentences and badly for long ones. The same year, Dzmitry Bahdanau, working with Cho and Yoshua Bengio, proposed letting the decoder look back at all the encoder's states at every step, weighting them by relevance: attention . Neural translation with attention overtook decades of statistical systems within two years. In 2017, "Attention Is All You Need" dropped the recurrent part entirely and kept only attention: the transformer later · 7.19 . In plain words first Looking back at the source while you write Imagine translating a long paragraph, but you may read the original only once and must then write the translation from memory. Short sentences are fine; long ones lose details. Now imagine you may glance back at the original while writing each word, and look mainly at the part you are translating right now. That glance is attention : at each step, score every source word for relevance, turn the scores into weights that add up to 1, and take the weighted mix of the source information. Step 1 · Encoder and decoder Two encoder-decoder designs. Top: the encoder squeezes the whole input into one final vector, and the decoder must produce every output word from it alone. Bottom: with attention, the decoder keeps every encoder state and, at each output step, takes a weighted average of them, weighted by how relevant each input position is right now. The textbook drawing of the same design, translating "They are watching ." into French. The encoder (left) reads the whole input; only its final state crosses to the decoder (right), which writes one word at a time and feeds each word back in as its next input. Figure: Zhang, Lipton, Li and Smola, Dive into Deep Learning , CC BY-SA 4.0 . The encoder is a recurrent network ( Lesson 5.35 ) that reads the input and produces a hidden state at each position (h1 to h4 in the picture). The decoder is another recurrent network that writes the output one token at a time, feeding each output back in, exactly like the generation loop of Lesson 5.35 . In the original design, the only link between them is the encoder's final state. Everything about the input, whatever its length, must fit into that one vector. That is the bottleneck . With attention , the decoder keeps all of the encoder's states and, at every step, builds a fresh summary weighted towards the positions that matter for the word it is about to write. Step 2 · Attention, by hand Attention needs three things: What attention looks like once trained, on a translation. Each row is a French word being written; each column is an English input word; a bright cell means "looked here". The model learned on its own that "zone" should look at "zone" and "économique" at "economic", even though French puts them in a different order. Figure: Daniel Voigt Godoy, dl-visuals , CC BY 4.0 . a query : what the decoder is looking for right now (its current state); keys : one per input position, to be compared with the query; values : one per input position, the information to be mixed (in this lesson the keys and values are the same encoder states; transformers separate them, Lesson 7.17 ). The recipe: score each key against the query with a dot product , turn the scores into weights with softmax , and take the weighted average of the values. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The score is high when the query and a state point the same way ( Lesson 1.23 ): "is" scores highest. Softmax turns the scores into weights that are all positive and add up to 1 ( Lesson 1.25 ). "is" gets most of the weight, but not all. The context vector is a blend of the four states, dominated by "is". The decoder uses it, together with its own state, to choose the next word. Every step of this is differentiable (multiplications, softmax, sums), so the network can learn what to look for by backpropagation . Nobody writes the queries by hand. Step 3 · A task that needs attention: reversing letters Translation needs a lot of data, so here is a small task with the same difficulty: read 12 random letters and write them in reverse order. The decoder must recall the last input letter first, which a single summary vector does poorly. The data is generated on the fly: Copy What you should see Copy The model, with attention as an option, so the two designs can be compared: Copy Reading this output Reading this code The attention lines are Step 2's recipe in PyTorch : states @ h gives one score per input position (for each example in the batch), softmax turns them into weights, and the weighted sum gives the context. During training the decoder is fed the correct previous letter ( y_in , the target shifted right with BOS in front), not its own guess. This is called teacher forcing ; it makes training fast and stable. At test time it must use its own outputs, as in Step 4. nn.GRUCell runs one step; looping over the output positions makes the step-by-step decoding explicit. Step 4 · Train both, then compare The same task, trained twice with the same settings: once with a plain encoder-decoder later · 7.22 that must squeeze the whole input into one vector, and once with attention switched on. train returns a trained model. evaluate then tests it on 500 new examples and reports two numbers: the share of single letters it got right, and the share of whole strings. Copy What you should see Copy Same data, same training, same size of network. Without attention, only about half the letters come out right and almost no string is fully correct: one vector cannot hold 12 random letters in order. With attention, about 96% of letters and 91% of whole strings are correct. Now look inside: which input position did each output step attend to? Copy What you should see Copy Real attention weights from the model trained in Step 4, reversing the word 'deliverances'. Each row is one output step; the shading shows how much attention that step paid to each input letter. Nobody told the model to read the input backwards: it learned to look at the right position at each step. Output step 1 attends to input position 11 (the last letter, counting from 0), step 2 to position 10, and so on. (The last step leans on position 1, next door to the letter it needs, yet still writes the right letter: the encoder state at each position also carries information about its neighbours.) The model discovered "read the input backwards" by itself, and the attention weights let you see it. In translation models, the same kind of picture shows which source words each target word drew on, roughly following the word order of the two languages. Step 5 · From attention to the transformer Two observations in 2016 and 2017 turned this into the transformer: Attention can replace the recurrence. If every position can look at every other position directly, there is no need to pass information along a chain of hidden states. Without the chain, all positions can be computed at the same time, which GPUs love ( Lesson 3.20 ). A sequence can attend to itself. In self-attention later · 7.17 , every word in a sentence acts as a query over all the words in the same sentence. "it" can attend to "the parcel" to work out what "it" refers to; "bank" can attend to "river" to settle its meaning. That is how the contextual embeddings of Lesson 5.33 are built. The 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani and colleagues at Google) built a translation model from self-attention and feed-forward layers only. It trained faster than recurrent models and translated better. GPT, BERT , and every large language model since are built from its blocks, which is where the Transformers, step by step section begins. Every position attends directly to the others, which is why it can be trained in parallel.
