Solutions Solution P1 · A different query The scores become 0.11, 0.61, 1.66 and 2.04, so "order" gets the most weight (about 0.48), with "my" second (about 0.33): the query now points mostly along the third number, where "my" and "order" are large. The context vector shifts towards those two states. Solution M1 · Copying instead of reversing The attention pattern becomes the main diagonal: output step 1 attends to input position 0, step 2 to position 1, and so on. Copying is learned at least as easily as reversing. The pattern always follows how output positions correspond to input positions, which is why attention weights were used to inspect word alignment in translation models. Solution D1 · Saturated softmax When scores are very large, softmax puts nearly all the weight on the largest one: e^{300} dwarfs e^{250}. The weights stop being a blend, and the gradients through softmax almost vanish, so learning stalls. Large scores come from long vectors: a dot product of two 64-number vectors grows with their length. Transformers divide the scores by the square root of the vector size ( Lesson 7.17 ) to keep them in a sensible range. Recap An encoder-decoder model reads an input sequence with one network and writes an output sequence with another, generating one token at a time. Squeezing the whole input into the encoder's final vector loses detail, especially for long inputs. Attention scores every input position against a query, turns the scores into weights with softmax, and takes the weighted average: a fresh, relevant summary at every step. On string reversal, attention lifts accuracy from about half the letters to about 97%, and its weights show the learned alignment. Self-attention, where a sequence attends to itself, with no recurrence at all, is the core of the transformer. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Vector search Finding text by meaning: embed the query and return the stored passages whose vectors are closest Lesson 14.71 Hybrid search Running keyword search and vector search together and merging the results Lesson 5.38 Vector database A store that finds the vectors nearest to a query vector quickly Lesson 14.71 Why this came about Search engines needed a way to rank documents for a query long before neural networks could read. Through the 1970s and 1980s, Stephen Robertson, Karen Spärck Jones and colleagues worked out a probabilistic account of relevance, and in 1994 it produced the ranking function BM25 ("best match", attempt 25). It became the default in Lucene, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and almost every search product. When RAG arrived, many teams used only embedding search and found that it missed exact terms such as order numbers, product codes and names. Keyword search came back, and today BM25 runs beside vector search later · 14.71 in most production retrieval systems. In plain words first Matching the exact words Keyword search finds passages that contain the words of the question. BM25 decides the order with three sensible ideas. A word that appears in few passages (an order number, "OTP") says more about a match than a word that appears everywhere ("the", "order"). A passage that uses a query word several times is probably more about it, but the tenth mention adds far less than the first. And a short passage that matches is a better sign than a long one that happens to contain the word somewhere. It needs no model and no GPU , and it is excellent for exact terms, which meaning-based search often blurs. Step 1 · Chunks as lists of words Keyword search works on tokens , here simply lowercase words and numbers. (This is a different, simpler tokeniser than the subword tokenisers language models use, Lesson 5.31 .) Split every chunk from Lesson 14.70 : Copy What you should see Copy Step 2 · Rare words carry more information Count, for each word, how many chunks contain it (its document frequency ). A word in nearly every chunk cannot tell chunks apart; a word in one chunk points straight at it. Inverse document frequency (IDF) turns that into a weight: Copy What you should see Copy "the" appears in six of the nine chunks and gets a low weight. "cod", "otp" and "sms" each appear in one chunk and get the highest weight. Look at "refund": it is also in only one chunk, although several chunks talk about refunds. They say "refunds", "refundable" and "refunded", and to a keyword index those are four different words. Keep that in mind for Step 6. Reading this output Reading the IDF line math.log((N - df + 0.5) / (df + 0.5) + 1) : with N chunks in total and df of them containing the word, the fraction is roughly "chunks without the word, divided by chunks with it". The logarithm stops very rare words from dominating completely, and the + 0.5 and + 1 keep the result positive and stable for tiny collections. This is the variant used by Lucene and Elasticsearch. Step 3 · Repetition counts, but less each time If a chunk mentions "refund" five times, is it five times as relevant as a chunk that mentions it once? Plain TF-IDF ( Lesson 5.32 ) says yes. BM25 says the first mention matters most, and applies saturation : Copy What you should see Copy One mention earns 1.0. Ten mentions earn a little over twice that, not ten times. Fifty mentions earn barely more than ten. A chunk cannot win by repeating a word. Term-frequency saturation. The first appearance of a query word in a chunk earns the most credit; each further appearance earns less, and the curve flattens. The setting k1 controls how quickly: with k1 = 0 only presence counts, and larger values let repetition keep counting for longer. Step 4 · The whole formula BM25 adds up, for every query word found in the chunk, its IDF times its saturated count. One more correction: a long chunk has more chances to contain any word, so the count is adjusted by the chunk's length relative to the average. Copy What you should see Copy The COD chunk wins clearly: it contains "cod" (rare, and mentioned several times), "refunds" does not count as "refund", and "order" is fairly common. The refund policy chunk comes second on the strength of the single word "refund". The same idea as a formula score(query, chunk) = sum over the query's words w of IDF(w) × tf × (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1 × (1 − b + b × length / average length)) tf: how many times w appears in the chunk k1 (usually 1.2 to 2.0): how slowly repetition saturates b (usually 0.75): how strongly long chunks are penalised; b = 0 switches length normalisation off Step 5 · The lab's keyword search In practice you use a library or a search engine. The rest of this chapter's lab uses the small rank_bm25 package, wrapped in one function that returns chunk IDs: Copy Reading this output Scores differ between implementations rank_bm25 uses a slightly different IDF formula from the one in Step 2 (the original 1994 form, with a floor for very common words), so its scores are not the same numbers as ours. The ranking is nearly always the same. This is normal: BM25 scores have no fixed scale, differ between engines, and change when documents are added. Never compare a BM25 score with a threshold you copied from somewhere else, and never add it to a score from another kind of search ( Lesson 5.38 ). Step 6 · What keyword search finds, and what it misses Four test questions, chosen to show the edge of what keyword search can do. Two use the same words as the documents. Two mean the same thing as a document but share no words with it. For each, print the top results and the best score: Copy What you should see Copy The first two questions share words with the right chunk ("cod"; "fee", "cash", "delivery") and it comes first. "pay when it arrives" means cash on delivery, but shares no distinctive word with that chunk. BM25 returns a shipping chunk, on the strength of small words. "stop my purchase" means cancel. No query word appears in any chunk in a way that scores, so the best score is 0.00 and the "top three" are simply the first three chunks. A score of zero means no match , and a system should treat it that way instead of passing those chunks to a model. This is the vocabulary gap : keyword search cannot connect "money back" with "refund", "stop" with "cancel", or "pasword" with "password". It is the reason the next lesson exists. Step 7 · Why it is fast: the inverted index Scoring every chunk for every query would be slow for millions of chunks. Search engines build an inverted index once: for each word, the list of chunks that contain it. A query then touches only the lists for its own words. Copy What you should see Copy Only one chunk out of nine needs scoring for this query. With a million chunks and a query of rare words, an engine still scores only a few hundred. This structure, plus compression and caching, is how keyword search answers in milliseconds over billions of documents, and it is why keyword search is so cheap compared with running a model. Keyword search in real systems Piece What it does Why it matters for RAG Analyzer The tokenising rules: lowercase, split, remove stop words , reduce words to a stem ("refunds", "refunded" → "refund") Stemming would have fixed the "refund" problem from Step 2. Analyzers are per language Synonyms A reviewed list such as "COD = cash on delivery" Closes known vocabulary gaps cheaply Fields and boosts (BM25F) Title, headings and body scored separately, with titles weighted higher A match in a title usually matters more Filters Restrict by metadata (tenant, date, product) before scoring Permissions and freshness ( Lesson 14.73 ) Identifiers Keep codes such as SK-48213 or E-4102 as single tokens The default tokeniser may split them into pieces that match everywhere Where BM25 lives: Elasticsearch and OpenSearch (the full-featured engines), Postgres full-text search and SQLite FTS5 (good enough for many applications), the built-in keyword or hybrid search later · 5.38 of vector databases later · 14.71 such as Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus and Azure AI Search, and libraries such as Tantivy, bm25s and rank_bm25 for small or embedded use. In production BM25 in practice Keyword search is the part teams most often drop and later regret: vector-only systems fail on order numbers, SKUs, error codes and people's names, which are a large share of real support and operations questions. Keep a keyword index from day one. Its weak spots are synonyms and spelling ("cancel" against "stop my order"), which is exactly what vectors cover, hence hybrid search in Lesson 5.38 . For Hindi and Hinglish text, check the tokenizer: splitting on spaces works for Hindi in Devanagari, but transliterated and code-mixed text needs normalization or it will miss matches. Go deeper (optional) Learned sparse retrieval Models such as SPLADE and Elastic's ELSER use a transformer to produce a sparse vector over the vocabulary: weights for the words in the text plus related words that were never written ("refund" also lights up "money", "return"). The result is searched with an ordinary inverted index, so it keeps keyword search's speed and exact matching while closing part of the vocabulary gap. It costs a model call at indexing and query time. Check the score: zero, or far below the usual range, means nothing matched. Solutions Solution P1 · Rare words weigh more Usually the chunk with "SK-1042": BM25 weights terms by rarity (inverse document frequency), and an order ID is rare while "refund" appears in many chunks. Term frequency also saturates, so five mentions of "refund" are worth much less than five times one. Solution B1 · No shared words, no match Nothing relevant, or something matched by accident through a small word such as "back". BM25 matches words, not meaning. That is the vocabulary gap that vector search covers ( Lesson 14.71 ), and why hybrid search combines both ( Lesson 5.38 ). Solution D1 · Tokenization destroys IDs Splitting on the hyphen turns "SK-1042" into "sk" and "1042". "sk" then appears in every order number, and "1042" may be the only useful piece. Keep IDs, codes and numbers as single tokens, for example with a pattern that matches [a-z]+-\d+ before the general rule, apply the same rule to documents and queries, and test with real IDs. Solution M1 · A stemmer changes what matches After stemming, "refunds", "refunded" and "refundable" all become "refund", so its document frequency rises from 1 to several and its IDF falls. Queries about refunds now reach every chunk that discusses them, which raises recall. The questions about paying on arrival and stopping a purchase do not change: stemming fixes word forms , not different words for the same idea. Real analyzers use tested stemmers (Porter, Snowball) or lemmatisers instead of rules like these. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism How does BM25 work, and when does it beat vector search? Worked answer. BM25 scores a document by the query terms it contains, weighting rare terms more (IDF), saturating repeated terms, and normalizing for length. It beats vector search on exact tokens: IDs, product codes, error messages, names and rare jargon, which embeddings blur. It needs no model and is fast. A plausible wrong answer. "BM25 is obsolete since embeddings." Production systems still combine it with vectors for exactly these cases. Follow-ups. What are k1 and b in BM25? Debug a failure Keyword search works for English and fails for Hindi queries. What do you check? Worked answer. The tokenizer and the text: whether Devanagari is tokenized correctly, whether queries and documents use the same script (Hinglish in Latin letters against Hindi in Devanagari), and stemming or stop-word rules built for English. Fix tokenization per language, or rely on multilingual embeddings for those queries. A plausible wrong answer. "Hindi does not work with BM25." It works with a suitable tokenizer. Follow-ups. How would you evaluate multilingual retrieval? Defend a design Elasticsearch or OpenSearch for keyword search, or a vector database's built-in keyword search? Worked answer. A search engine when keyword search must be excellent: analyzers per language, synonyms, filters and operations at scale. A vector database's built-in keyword or hybrid search when it is good enough on your eval and one system is simpler to run. Measure both on your questions. A plausible wrong answer. "Whatever the vector database offers." It may lack analyzers your languages need. Follow-ups. How would you test analyzers? Recap BM25 ranks chunks by the query words they contain: rare words weigh more (IDF), repetition saturates (k1), long chunks are penalised (b). It needs no model, runs in milliseconds through an inverted index, and is the best tool for exact terms, codes and names. It cannot bridge different words for the same meaning; a zero or very low score means nothing matched. Analyzers (stemming, stop words, synonyms, keeping identifiers whole) decide much of its quality. Keep keyword search in every retrieval system; Lesson 5.38 combines it with vector search. A "OTP" is written in capitals B "OTP" appears in fewer chunks, so it tells chunks apart better C "OTP" is shorter D BM25 has a list of important words Inverse document frequency rewards words that few chunks contain. A The three chunks are equally relevant B No chunk matched the query's words; the results are arbitrary C The index is corrupted D The query was too long Search returns a ranking even when nothing matches; the score tells you whether to trust it. A Finding an exact order number B Finding an error code C Matching "money back" to a passage that says "refund" D Ranking a short matching chunk above a long one Different words for the same meaning need embeddings, synonyms or learned sparse models. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Hybrid search Running keyword search and vector search together and merging the results Retrieval Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) Merging ranked lists by adding 1 / (k + rank) for each list an item appears in Hybrid search Reranker A second, slower and more accurate model that reorders the top results Retrieval ColBERT A retriever that keeps one vector per token and compares them late Late interaction Mentioned here, taught later 2 Semantic ranker, ColPali This lesson mentions the ideas below before the lesson that teaches them. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Semantic ranker Azure AI Search's cross-encoder reranker Lesson 14.155 ColPali Retrieval over page images, with one vector per patch of the page Lesson 4.31 Why this came about By 2020 it was clear that neither kind of search was enough alone. Keyword search missed paraphrases; embedding search missed exact terms. Adding their scores did not work, because the scores are on unrelated scales. Reciprocal rank fusion , published in 2009 for combining search engines, turned out to be a simple and robust answer: combine the positions , not the scores. At the same time, cross-encoders , models that read a question and a passage together, proved far more accurate than either method at judging relevance, but too slow to run over a whole collection. Putting the pieces in order (search wide with both methods, fuse, then rerank a short list) became the standard retrieval stack. In plain words first Two searches, then a careful reader Imagine finding a document in a large office. One assistant looks for folders with your exact words on the label. Another knows roughly where each topic is kept. Each misses things the other finds, so you ask both and merge their lists, trusting most the folders that both of them picked. That is hybrid search . Then a third person actually reads the dozen folders on the merged list and puts the truly relevant ones on top. That careful reader is a reranker : much slower per folder, which is why it only ever sees the short list. Step 1 · The two searches disagree Run both searches from the last two lessons on three questions: Copy What you should see Copy On the first and third questions both methods put the same chunk first and disagree below it. On "pay when it arrives" they disagree completely: vector search finds cash on delivery, keyword search finds shipping. Neither list is always right, and their mistakes are different. That is exactly the situation in which combining helps. Step 2 · Why you cannot add the scores The obvious way to combine is to add each chunk's two scores. Look at the scores themselves: Copy What you should see Copy BM25 scores here run from 0 to about 1.6; for another query they might reach 12. Cosine similarities live between about 0 and 1. Adding them lets one method drown out the other, differently for every query. You could rescale each list to 0 to 1 first ( min-max normalisation ), and some systems do, with a weight between the two. It works when tuned and is fragile when the score distributions shift. Step 3 · Reciprocal rank fusion Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) ignores the scores and uses only positions. A chunk at position rank in a list earns 1 / (60 + rank) from that list; its total is the sum over lists. This is the lab's hybrid search: Copy Hybrid search with reciprocal rank fusion: keyword search and vector search each return a ranked list; each document scores 1/(60 + rank) per list, so documents that both lists like rise to the top. Work one example by hand to see what RRF rewards: Copy What you should see Copy warranty#1 is first in both lists: 1/61 + 1/61 = 0.0328. The next two chunks each have one good and one middling position and tie. Chunks that appear in only one list get a single contribution and fall to the bottom. RRF rewards agreement : a chunk both methods like beats a chunk one method loves and the other never found. Reading this output Why 60, and other details The constant 60 comes from the original paper and is rarely changed. A smaller number makes first place count for much more than second; a larger one flattens the differences. Each list can be given a weight (multiply its contribution) if evaluation shows one method deserves more trust on your data. RRF works for any number of lists: keyword, several embedding models , several rewrites of the question ( Lesson 14.75 ). search_hybrid uses the stand-in search_dense so that later lessons give identical numbers everywhere. The worked example used the real model. Swap as you like. Step 4 · A reranker: reading the question and the passage together An embedding model reads the question and each passage separately and compares two vectors. It never sees them side by side. A cross-encoder takes the question and one passage as a single input, lets attention ( Lesson 7.17 ) connect every question word with every passage word, and outputs one relevance score. It is much more accurate, and it cannot be precomputed: every (question, passage) pair needs its own run of the model. Bi-encoder versus cross-encoder: the bi-encoder embeds question and passage separately (fast, precomputable, used to retrieve the top 50); the cross-encoder reads them together (slow, more accurate, used to rerank those 50). Retrieval as a funnel. Cheap methods look at everything and keep a short list; an expensive, careful model reads only that short list. Each stage can only reorder or drop what the stage before it found, so the first stage must be wide enough to contain the right passage. So it is used only on a short list. Take the top six chunks from hybrid search and rerank them: Copy What you should see Copy Hybrid search had a shipping chunk first and the right chunk, cod#0 , in third place: neither search connected "paying at the door" with cash on delivery strongly enough. The reranker, reading the question next to each passage, gives cod#0 the highest score and moves it to the top. The numbers are the model's raw scores: higher means more relevant, and only their order and the gaps between them matter. cod#0 stands clearly apart, while the five irrelevant chunks are bunched together below it. A gap like that is what you look for when choosing a cut-off score. What does that accuracy cost? Copy What you should see Copy (Your numbers depend on your processor.) Embedding the question is one small model run, however large the collection. Reranking is one run per candidate , so its cost grows with the length of the short list. This is why the usual settings are to retrieve 50 to 100 candidates and rerank them down to 5 or 10, on a GPU or a hosted reranking service where each pair takes about a millisecond. In production you rarely host the cross-encoder yourself at first. Hosted rerankers include Cohere Rerank, Voyage rerankers, Amazon Rerank on Bedrock, Google's Ranking API and Azure AI Search's semantic ranker later · 14.155 ; open models such as the BGE rerankers run on your own hardware. In production Rerankers: when they help and when they don't A reranker fixes ranking problems: the right chunk is retrieved but sits at position 15. It cannot fix recall problems: a chunk that was never retrieved cannot be reranked to the top. So widen retrieval first (50 to 100 candidates), then rerank. Costs to watch: tens to hundreds of milliseconds per query, which matters for voice and chat; and rerankers that only read the chunk text, so pass the title and section too. Some teams find that a good reranker lets them use a cheaper embedding model, which is a useful trade to test. The retrieval stack, and what to tune Stage What it is for Typical setting Keyword search Exact terms, codes, names Top 50 to 100 Vector search Paraphrases, meaning Top 50 to 100 Fusion (RRF) One list that both methods agree on k = 60, equal weights to start Reranker Precise ordering of the short list Rerank 50 to 100, keep 5 to 10 Cut-off Do not pass weak results to the model A minimum reranker score, chosen on your evaluation set Reranker choices include hosted services (Cohere Rerank, Voyage, Amazon Rerank on Bedrock, Google's Ranking API, the semantic ranker in Azure AI Search) and open models (the BGE and Qwen reranker families, and small MS MARCO cross-encoders like the one used here). Go deeper (optional) Between the two extremes: late interaction ColBERT and its successors keep one vector per token instead of one per passage, and score a passage by matching each question token to its closest passage token. It is more accurate than a single vector and far cheaper than a cross-encoder, at the price of a much larger index. The same idea applied to images of pages ( ColPali later · 4.31 ) lets you search PDFs without parsing them ( Lesson 4.31 ). Solution M1 · Weighted fusion and the full stack In rrf , multiply each list's contribution by its weight before summing: scores[item] += w / (k + rank) . search_best is rerank(query, rrf([search_bm25(query, 9), search_minilm(query, 9)])[:6]) . Tune weights only on an evaluation set, and be wary of a weight that wins on a handful of questions: check it on new questions before keeping it. Keyword search catches exact terms; vectors catch paraphrases; their failures rarely overlap, so the fusion is more robust than either. A reranker then reorders the top candidates for precision. Look at per-question results to see where the keyword list hurts. A plausible wrong answer. "Hybrid is always better, so the eval is wrong." Measure, then fix the weak component. Follow-ups. How would you split the eval by question type? Defend a design Is a reranker worth its latency and cost? Worked answer. Not when the eval shows little gain or latency budgets are tight; then improve chunking or use a smaller reranker. A plausible wrong answer. "Always add a reranker." Recap Keyword and vector search make different mistakes, so running both and merging the lists is more robust than either. Their scores are on unrelated scales. Reciprocal rank fusion merges by position: each list contributes 1 / (60 + rank). A cross-encoder reranker reads the question and a passage together. It is the most accurate judge and needs one model run per candidate, so it only sees a short list. The production pattern is a funnel: retrieve 50 to 100 with both methods, fuse, rerank to 5 or 10, cut off weak results. A reranker fixes ordering, never recall. Check your understanding Q1 Why does hybrid search usually beat either method alone? A It uses a bigger embedding model B Keyword search catches exact terms and codes; vector search catches paraphrases; fusion gets both C It searches twice as many documents D It removes the need for chunking They fail on different queries, so combining them raises recall. Q2 What does reciprocal rank fusion use from each result list? Every modern ASR and TTS pipeline walks this ladder, and the first rung is understanding sampling and Fourier. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Sample rate How many samples per second Frequency in Hz at which the ADC measures the signal. Aliasing Weird frequency ghosts Energy above Nyquist mirroring down to lower bins. The problem In plain words first Sound is air pressure changing over time. A microphone turns it into a voltage, and an analogue-to-digital converter measures that voltage thousands of times a second; each measurement is a sample , and the number per second is the sample rate . Everything a speech model sees is that list of numbers. Two facts decide whether it is usable. First, a sample rate can only describe frequencies up to half of itself; anything faster is not lost but disguised as a lower frequency ( aliasing ). Second, the useful structure of sound is easier to see as a mix of frequencies than as a wiggle in time, and the Fourier transform converts one view into the other. This lesson loads a real recording, builds the discrete Fourier transform by hand, checks it against the fast library version, and measures aliasing, spectral leakage and quantisation noise with numbers you can reproduce. A microphone produces a pressure-vs-time signal. Your neural net consumes tensors. Between them sits a stack of conventions that, when violated, produce silent bugs: the model trains fine but the WER doubles, or TTS ships a hiss, or a voice cloning system memorizes the microphone instead of the speaker. Every bug in speech systems traces back to one of three questions: What sample rate was the data recorded at, and what does the model expect? Is the signal aliased? Are you operating on raw samples or on a frequency representation? Get these right and the rest of Phase 6 is tractable. Get them wrong and even Whisper large-v3 produces garbage. The idea Waveform. A one-dimensional array of floats in [-1.0, 1.0] . Indexed by sample number. To convert to seconds, divide by the sample rate: t = n / sr . A 10-second clip at 16 kHz is an array of 160,000 floats. In plain words first The idea in one line Neural nets do not consume raw waveforms well. They consume spectrograms. They consume mel spectrograms even better. Every ASR, TTS, and audio classifier in 2026 lives or dies by this single preprocessing choice. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Frame A slice 25 ms chunk of waveform fed to one FFT. Hop Stride Samples between consecutive frames; 10 ms is ASR default. Window Hann/Hamming thing Point-wise multiplier that tapers the frame edges to zero. STFT Spectrogram generator Framed + windowed FFT; yields time × frequency matrix. Mel Warped frequency Log-perception scale; m = 2595·log10(1 + f/700) . Filterbank The matrix Triangular filters that project STFT onto mel bins. Log-mel Whisper's input log(mel_spec + eps) ; standardized in 2026. MFCC Old-school feature DCT of log-mel; 13 coeffs, decorrelated. The problem In plain words first A raw recording is 16,000 numbers a second, and the same word said twice gives completely different numbers. What stays similar is which frequencies are loud, moment by moment . A spectrogram measures exactly that: cut the sound into short overlapping slices (frames), take the Fourier transform of each, and stack the results into a picture with time across and frequency up. Speech models then make two adjustments that match hearing. They group frequencies into bands that are narrow at the low end and wide at the high end (the mel scale), and they take the logarithm, because loudness is heard on a ratio scale. The result, the log-mel spectrogram, is what Whisper and most other speech models read. This lesson builds each step, checks the result against Whisper's own feature extractor, and measures the trade-offs: frame length against time and frequency detail, and log-mel against MFCC. Take a 10-second 16 kHz clip. That is 160,000 floats, all in [-1, 1] , almost perfectly uncorrelated with the label "dog barking" or "the word cat". The raw waveform has the information but in a form the model cannot easily extract. Two identical phonemes spoken 100 ms apart have completely different raw samples. A spectrogram fixes this. It collapses the temporal detail where human perception ignores it (microsecond jitter) and preserves the structure where perception attends (which frequencies are energetic, over time windows of ~10–25 ms). Mel spectrograms push further. Human pitch judgments are not linear in Hz: the same step in Hz sounds smaller and smaller as frequency rises. The mel scale, built from listening experiments in the 1930s, is roughly linear below about 1 kHz and roughly logarithmic above, and spectrograms warp their frequency axis to match it. A mel-scaled spectrogram is the single most important feature in speech ML from 2010 through 2026. The idea STFT (Short-Time Fourier Transform). Slice the waveform into overlapping frames (typical: 25 ms window, 10 ms hop = 400 samples / 160 samples at 16 kHz). Multiply each frame by a window function (Hann is the default; Hamming slightly different tradeoff). FFT each frame. Stack the magnitude spectra into a matrix of shape (n_frames, n_freq_bins) . That is your spectrogram. Log-magnitude. Raw magnitudes span 5-6 orders of magnitude. Take log(|X| + 1e-6) or 20 * log10(|X|) to compress dynamic range. Every production pipeline uses log-magnitude, not raw magnitude. Mel scale. Frequency f in Hz maps to mel m by ​ ( 1 + f /700 ) . The mapping is roughly linear below 1 kHz and roughly logarithmic above. 80 mel bins covering 0–8 kHz is the standard ASR input. Mel filterbank. A set of triangular filters spaced equally on the mel scale. Each filter is a weighted sum of adjacent FFT bins. Multiplying the STFT magnitude by the filterbank matrix gives the mel spectrogram in one matmul. Log-mel spectrogram. log(mel_spec + 1e-10) . Whisper, NVIDIA's Parakeet models and Meta's SeamlessM4T all start from log-mel or closely related log filterbank features. It is the standard speech front end. MFCCs. Take the log-mel spectrogram, apply a DCT (type II), keep the first 13 coefficients. Decorrelates the features and compresses further. Dominant feature until about 2015 when CNNs/Transformers on raw log-mels caught up. Still used where compute is tiny (keyword spotting) and in classic speaker recognition: Kaldi's x-vector recipes use MFCCs, while ECAPA-TDNN usually takes log-mel filterbanks. Resolution trade. Larger FFT = better frequency resolution but worse time resolution. 25 ms / 10 ms is the audio-ML default; 50 ms / 12.5 ms for music; 5 ms / 2 ms for transient detection (drum hits, plosives). The problem In plain words first Audio classification puts one or more labels on a clip: siren or dog, yes or no, English or Hindi, speech or music. Every method in this lesson has the same shape: turn the sound into features (MFCCs or a log-mel spectrogram from Lesson 6.2), squeeze them into a fixed-size summary, and map the summary to labels. What changed over the years is who designs the summary: first people (averages of MFCCs), then convolutional networks, then transformers pretrained on millions of clips. This lesson builds the classic baseline, inspects a small CNN, and runs a real pretrained model (the Audio Spectrogram Transformer) on real and synthetic sounds. It also covers the parts that decide results in practice: imbalanced classes, augmentation (SpecAugment and mixup), and the metrics that do not lie about rare classes. No model is trained here; the pretrained model is used as it is. You get a 10-second clip. You want to know: "what is it?" Audio datasets have brutal class imbalance, strong domain shift (clean vs noisy), and label noise (who decided "urban babble" vs "restaurant noise"?). Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Speech recognition is audio classification at every timestep, glued together by a sequence model that knows English and silence. CTC, RNN-T, and attention are the three ways to do it. Pick one and understand why. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means CTC The blank-token loss Marginal over all frame-to-token alignments; non-AR. RNN-T The streaming loss Adds a prediction network over earlier output tokens, removing CTC's independence assumption; streamable. Attention enc-dec Whisper-style Encoder + cross-attending decoder; best offline quality. WER The number you report (S+D+I)/N at word level. Blank The emptiness Special token in CTC signalling "no emission this frame". LM fusion External language model Add weighted LM log-probs during beam search. VAD The silence gate Voice activity detector; trims non-speech. The problem In plain words first A speech recogniser turns about 100 frames of audio features per second into a few words per second, and nobody tells it which frames belong to which letter. Three designs solve that. CTC lets the network output a symbol or a special "blank" for every frame and defines the answer as whatever remains after merging repeats and deleting blanks; training adds up the probability of every frame-by-frame path that gives the right text. RNN-T (transducer) adds a small network that remembers what has been written so far, so each new symbol can depend on the previous ones. Attention encoder-decoders such as Whisper read the whole clip and then write the text token by token, like a translator. This lesson decodes real model outputs: a CTC model (wav2vec 2.0) and an encoder-decoder (Whisper) on LibriSpeech recordings, with greedy decoding, a correct beam search, the CTC probability computed two ways, and word error rate measured with and without text normalisation. Nothing is trained; both models are used as published. You have a 10-second 16 kHz clip. You want a string: "turn on the kitchen lights". The challenge is structural: audio frames do not align one-to-one with characters. The word "okay" might take 200 ms or 1200 ms. Silence punctuates the utterance. Some phonemes are longer than others. The number of output tokens is not known in advance. Three formulations solve this: CTC (Connectionist Temporal Classification). Emit per-frame token probabilities including a special blank . Collapse repeats and blanks at decode time. Non-autoregressive, fast. Used by wav2vec 2.0, MMS. RNN-T (Recurrent Neural Network Transducer). Joint network predicts next token given encoder frame and previous tokens. Streamable. Used by Google's on-device ASR, NVIDIA Parakeet. Attention encoder-decoder. Encoder compresses audio to hidden states, decoder cross-attends to generate tokens autoregressively. Used by Whisper, SeamlessM4T. On LibriSpeech test-clean the best open models are now below 2% WER (NVIDIA's Parakeet-TDT-0.6B v2: 1.69%). Across many datasets the accuracy differences between top models are small; the differences in speed, streaming and languages are large. The idea CTC intuition. Let the encoder output T frame-level distributions over V+1 tokens (V chars + blank). For a target string y of length U < T , any frame alignment that collapses to y counts. CTC loss sums over all such alignments. Inference: per-frame argmax, collapse repeats, remove blanks. Advantages: non-autoregressive, streamable, zero lookahead. Drawback: conditional independence assumption — each frame prediction is independent of the others, so there is no internal language model. Fix with an external LM via beam search or shallow fusion. RNN-T intuition. Adds a predictor network that embeds the token history and a joiner that combines predictor state with encoder frame into a joint distribution over V+1 (the +1 is a null / no-emit). Explicitly models the conditional dependence CTC ignored. Streamable because each step conditions only on past frames and past tokens. Advantages: streamable + internal LM. Drawback: training is more complex and memory-hungry (3D loss lattice); RNN-T loss kernels are a whole library category on their own. Attention encoder-decoder. Encoder (6-32 transformer layers) over log-mel frames. Decoder (6-32 transformer layers) cross-attends to encoder outputs to generate tokens autoregressively. No alignment constraint — attention can look anywhere in the audio. Non-streamable unless you restrict attention or re-run on growing chunks (Whisper-Streaming, 2023). Advantages: highest quality on offline ASR, easy to train with standard seq2seq tooling. Drawback: autoregressive latency is proportional to output length; cannot stream without engineering. In plain words first The idea in one line Whisper is a 30-second-window transformer encoder-decoder, trained on 680k hours of multilingual weakly-supervised audio-text pairs. One architecture, multiple tasks, robust across 99 languages. The most widely used open ASR model family. Hallucination The silent failure Whisper produces fluent English from noise/silence. The problem In plain words first Whisper is one neural network that listens to 30 seconds of audio and writes what was said. Its first half (the encoder) turns the log-mel spectrogram into a sequence of vectors, 50 per second; its second half (the decoder) writes text one token at a time, looking back at those vectors through cross-attention. A few special tokens at the start of the text tell it what to do: which language, whether to transcribe or translate into English, whether to write timestamps. Because the window is fixed at 30 seconds, longer recordings have to be cut up and stitched back together, and how you do that changes the result. This lesson opens the model up on real recordings: its sizes and shapes, what the decoder attends to as it writes each word, how three ways of handling a two-minute recording compare, what happens if the input features are computed even slightly differently, and what fine-tuning with LoRA would change. No model is trained here. Whisper, released by OpenAI in September 2022, was the first ASR model to ship as a commodity: paste audio, get text, 99 languages, robust to noise, runs on a laptop. By 2024 OpenAI had shipped Large-v3 and Turbo variants; Whisper remains the most common open baseline for everything from podcast transcription to voice assistants to subtitles. But Whisper is not a pipeline you can treat as a black box forever. Domain shift kills it — technical jargon, speaker accents, proper nouns, short clips, silence. You need to know: What it actually is inside. How to give it chunked, streaming, or long-form audio correctly. When to fine-tune and how. The idea Architecture. Standard transformer encoder-decoder. Input: 30-second log-mel spectrogram, 80 mels (128 for large-v3 and turbo), 10 ms hop → 3000 frames. Clips shorter are zero-padded, clips longer are chunked. Encoder: conv-downsample (stride 2) + N transformer blocks. For Large-v3: 32 layers, 1280-dim, 20 heads. Decoder: N transformer blocks with causal self-attn + cross-attn to encoder output. Same size as encoder. Output: BPE tokens over a vocabulary of about 51,865 (51,864 for the English-only models, 51,866 for large-v3). Large-v3 has 1.55B params. Turbo keeps large-v3's encoder and cuts the decoder from 32 layers to 4 (809M params); OpenAI's README lists it at about 8× the speed of large, with a small accuracy loss, and notes that it was not trained for translation. The prompt format. Whisper is a multitask model steered by special tokens in the decoder prompt: Copy <|en|> : language tag; names the language spoken in the audio. Leave it out and Whisper detects the language first. <|transcribe|> or <|translate|> : task tag; transcribe the speech in its source language, or translate it to English text. <|notimestamps|> : skip word-level timestamps (faster). The prompt is what lets one model do many tasks. Change <|en|> to <|fr|> and it transcribes French. 30-second window. Everything is pinned to 30 seconds. Longer clips need chunking; shorter clips are padded. Windows are not streamed natively — this is why WhisperX, Whisper-Streaming, and faster-whisper exist. Log-mel normalisation. Whisper takes $\log_{10}$ of the mel power, clips everything more than 8 below the clip's own maximum, and maps the result with $(x + 4)/4$ (rebuilt exactly in Lesson 6.2). No corpus statistics are involved. You must use Whisper's preprocessing ( whisper.audio.log_mel_spectrogram ), not librosa.feature.melspectrogram . The same idea as a formula Encoder. The log-mel input (128 for large-v3) passes two 1-D convolutions (kernel 3, the second with stride 2) and GELU, giving vectors of width , one per 20 ms; sinusoidal position embeddings are added, then ​ transformer blocks. Decoder. ​ P ( y u ​ ∣ y < u ​ , Enc ( X )) . Each decoder block has causal self-attention over the tokens so far, then cross-attention, / d h ​ ​ ) V with queries from the text and keys and values from the 1,500 encoder vectors, then an MLP. Prompt. The text starts with control tokens, ; with timestamps enabled, the model writes time tokens for s, 1,501 of them, around each segment. Decoding safeguards in OpenAI's transcribe : a window's output is rejected and re-decoded at a higher temperature if its gzip compression ratio exceeds 2.4 (repetitive text compresses well) or its average token log-probability is below ; it is treated as silence if and the log-probability is also low. Word timestamps. A few cross-attention heads (the alignment heads ) look at the frames being spoken as each token is written. Dynamic time warping finds the monotonic path through that token × frame matrix that maximises total attention; token 's time is where the path crosses row . LoRA. A frozen weight is used as α ​ B A with trainable , , initialised to zero so training starts from the original model. Each adapted matrix adds parameters. Cross-attention therefore compares every text token with 1,500 positions: for large-v3 (20 heads, 32 decoder layers) that is attention weights per generated token. In plain words first The idea in one line ASR asks "what did they say?" Speaker recognition asks "who said it?" The math looks the same — embeddings plus cosine — but every production decision hinges on a single EER number. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means EER The headline metric Threshold where False Accept = False Reject. Verification 1:1 "Is this Alice?" Identification 1:N "Who is speaking?" Open-set Unknown possible Test set can contain unenrolled speakers. Enrollment Registering Computing a speaker's reference embedding. AAM-softmax The loss Softmax with additive angular margin; forces cluster separation. PLDA Classic scoring Probabilistic LDA; likelihood-ratio scoring on top of embeddings. DER Diarization metric Diarization Error Rate — miss + false alarm + confusion. The problem In plain words first A voice carries the speaker as well as the words. Speaker recognition turns a recording into a list of numbers, an embedding , chosen so that recordings of the same person land close together and recordings of different people land apart, whatever they are saying. Then everything is distances. Verification ("is this Alice?") compares one embedding with Alice's stored one against a threshold. Identification ("who is this?") picks the closest of many stored speakers. Diarization ("who spoke when?") clusters the embeddings of a recording's segments. The threshold decides how many impostors get in and how many genuine users are turned away, and the point where those two rates are equal, the equal error rate , is the standard score. This lesson measures all of that on real speaker embeddings (x-vectors of seven speakers reading the same 1,130 sentences): how EER falls with more enrolment audio, what centring does, how accurate identification is, and how a clustering threshold makes or breaks diarization. No model is trained. A user says a passphrase. You want to know: is this the person they claim to be ( verification , 1:1), or is it the first person in your enrollment bank ( identification , 1:N)? Or neither — is this an unknown speaker ( open-set )? Pre-2018: GMM-UBM + i-vectors. Reasonable EER but fragile to channel shift (phone vs laptop) and emotion. 2018–2022: x-vectors (a TDNN backbone with statistics pooling, trained as a speaker classifier). 2022+: ECAPA-TDNN and WavLM-large embeddings. Today most systems use ECAPA-TDNN-style or self-supervised (WavLM-based) embeddings, and they are compared by one metric. The metric is EER — Equal Error Rate. Set your decision threshold so False Accept Rate = False Reject Rate. The crossover is EER. Used in every paper, every leaderboard, every procurement call. The idea The pipeline. Enrollment: record 5–30 seconds of the target speaker; compute a fixed-dimension embedding (192-d for SpeechBrain's ECAPA-TDNN, 512-d for classic x-vectors). Sources: pyannote.audio README , SpeechBrain ECAPA model card , WavLM paper . Pitfalls Channel mismatch. Model trained on VoxCeleb (web video) ≠ phone-call audio. Always evaluate on target channel. Short utterances. EER degrades sharply below 3 seconds of test audio. Enrollment with noise. One noisy enrollment poisons the anchor. Use ≥3 clean samples and average. Fixed threshold across conditions. Always tune the threshold on a held-out dev set from the target domain. Dot products on raw embeddings. Cosine divides by the lengths, but a plain dot product (as in many vector databases) does not: L2-normalise first, or the magnitude dominates. Centring (subtracting the mean embedding) also helps, as the run under Step 3 shows. Recap What to keep from this lesson Speaker embedding + cosine + threshold = verification; nearest centroid = identification; clustering = diarization. EER is where false accepts equal false rejects; deployments choose their own operating point. Average several clean enrolment utterances; centre embeddings before cosine. Re-tune thresholds for each channel and for each enrolment protocol. Diarization quality hinges on the clustering threshold or speaker-count estimate. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line ASR inverts speech to text; TTS inverts text to speech. The 2026 stack is three parts: text → tokens, tokens → mel, mel → waveform. Each part has a default model that fits in a laptop. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Phoneme Sound unit Abstract sound class; 39 in English (ARPABet). Duration predictor How long each phoneme lasts Non-AR model output; integer frames per phoneme. Vocoder Mel → waveform Neural net mapping mel-spec to raw samples. HiFi-GAN Standard vocoder GAN-based; dominant 2020–2024. MOS Subjective quality 1–5 mean opinion score from human raters. SECS Voice-clone metric Cosine similarity between target and output speaker embedding. F5-TTS 2024 open cloning model Flow-matching diffusion transformer; zero-shot cloning from a short reference. Kokoro Small fast open TTS 82M-param StyleTTS 2-based model, Apache 2.0. The problem In plain words first Text-to-speech runs speech recognition backwards: from a string to a waveform. Classic systems do it in three stages that are still the best way to debug any modern one. A front end cleans the text ("Dr." becomes "Doctor", "6 pm" becomes "six p m") and often converts it to phonemes. An acoustic model predicts a mel spectrogram, the same picture of sound as Lesson 6.2, including how long each sound lasts. A vocoder turns the mel spectrogram back into samples, inventing the phase information the mel throws away. Newer models merge the stages, but the same jobs still have to be done somewhere. This lesson runs two real open models on a CPU: SpeechT5 with a HiFi-GAN vocoder (the three stages made visible) and an end-to-end VITS model. It measures their output the way papers do, by transcribing it with Whisper and comparing speaker embeddings, and shows what happens when the front end is skipped. Nothing is trained. You have a string: "Please remind me to water the plants at 6 pm." You need a 3-second audio clip that sounds natural, has correct prosody (pauses, stress), pronounces "plants" with the right vowel, and runs in under 300 ms on a CPU for a live voice assistant. You also need to swap voices, handle code-switched input ("remind me at 6 pm, daijoubu?"), and not embarrass yourself on names. Modern TTS pipelines look like this: Text frontend. Normalize text (dates, numbers, emails), convert to phonemes or subword tokens, predict prosody features. Acoustic model. Text → mel spectrogram. Tacotron 2 (2017), FastSpeech 2 (2020), VITS (2021), F5-TTS (2024), Kokoro (2024). Vocoder. Mel → waveform. WaveNet (2016), WaveRNN, HiFi-GAN (2020), BigVGAN (2022), neural codec vocoders in 2024+. In 2026 the acoustic + vocoder split blurs with end-to-end diffusion and flow-matching models. But the mental model of three parts still holds for debugging. The idea Tacotron 2 (2017). Seq2seq: char-embedding → BiLSTM encoder → location-sensitive attention → autoregressive LSTM decoder emits mel frames. Slow (AR), wobbly on long text. Still cited as a baseline. FastSpeech 2 (2020). Non-autoregressive. Duration predictor outputs how many mel frames each phoneme gets. 1-pass, 10× faster than Tacotron. Loses some naturalness (monotonic alignment) but ships everywhere. VITS (2021). Jointly trains encoder + flow-based duration + HiFi-GAN vocoder end-to-end with variational inference. High quality, single model. Dominant open-source TTS 2022–2024. Related open systems: YourTTS (VITS-based, multi-speaker, zero-shot) and Coqui's XTTS v2 (late 2023, a GPT-style model), long a popular open voice-cloning choice. F5-TTS (2024). Diffusion transformer over flow matching. Natural prosody, zero-shot voice cloning with 5 seconds of reference audio. One of the most widely used open voice-cloning models; about 335M params. Kokoro (2024). Small (82M), CPU-runnable, best-in-class English TTS for real-time use. Apache-2.0 weights, built on StyleTTS 2 with a fast ISTFT-based decoder; English first, with more languages since its 1.0 release (2025). Commercial APIs. ElevenLabs (its v3 model adds inline audio tags such as [whispers] and [laughs]), OpenAI's gpt-4o-mini-tts (speaking style set by a text instruction) and Google Cloud's Chirp 3 HD voices are widely used in products and audiobook production. The same idea as a formula Autoregressive acoustic model (Tacotron 2): ​ P ( y t ​ ∣ y < t ​ , x ) over mel frames ​ ∈ R 80 , with attention deciding which input symbols each frame is about, and a stop token deciding when to end. Non-autoregressive with durations (FastSpeech 2): predict an integer duration ​ for every phoneme , repeat its hidden vector ​ times (the length regulator ), and predict all ​ d i ​ frames at once. Durations, pitch and energy are separate predicted targets, so they can be edited. VITS trains end to end as a variational autoencoder: a posterior encoder maps real audio to a latent , a normalising flow maps to a prior conditioned on the text, monotonic alignment search finds the best text-to-frame alignment during training, and a HiFi-GAN-style decoder turns into a waveform, trained with reconstruction, KL and adversarial losses. Flow matching (F5-TTS): draw noise ​ and data ​ , set ​ = ( 1 − t ) x 0 ​ + t x 1 ​ , and train a network to predict the velocity: ​ , x 1 ​ ​ ​ v θ ​ ( x t ​ , t , text , reference ) − ( x 1 ​ − x 0 ​ ) ​ 2 At inference, integrate ​ from noise to a mel spectrogram in a few dozen steps. Vocoder. A mel frame summarises one hop of samples, so a neural vocoder upsamples by : HiFi-GAN's . Without a neural vocoder, Griffin-Lim estimates the missing phase by alternating ← STFT ( ISTFT ( ∣ X ∣ e i ∠ X ^ )) . Evaluation. Mean opinion score from listeners (1–5); intelligibility as character error rate of an ASR transcript, ​ ; speaker similarity (SECS) as the cosine between speaker embeddings of the reference and the output. Worked example Frames, samples and speed by hand Frames. SpeechT5 works at 16 kHz with a hop of 256 samples, 16 ms per mel frame. Its 170 frames for the sentence under Step 5 are ms of audio. Samples. The vocoder multiplies by the hop: samples, exactly the length the run reports. If the vocoder had been trained with a different hop or sample rate, it would play back too fast or too slow. Durations. A FastSpeech-style model predicts durations of, say, 5, 7, 4 and 9 frames for four phonemes: frames, 400 ms at a 16 ms hop. Multiply every duration by 1.2 and the same words take 480 ms, slower speech with unchanged pitch. Real-time factor. Idea 1 · Vocoder evolution Year Vocoder How it works Speed 2016 WaveNet Autoregressive: one sample at a time, conditioned on all previous ones Far slower than real time at first 2018 WaveRNN A single small RNN, still sample by sample Real time on CPUs with sparsity tricks 2020 HiFi-GAN Convolutional upsampler trained with discriminators 167.9× real time on one V100 GPU (paper) 2022 BigVGAN HiFi-GAN-style, trained to generalise across speakers, languages and recording conditions Similar to HiFi-GAN 2022–2024 Codec decoders (EnCodec, DAC, SNAC) Decode discrete audio tokens produced by a language model Part of token-based TTS and speech LLMs By 2026 most "TTS" models are end-to-end from text to waveform; the mel spectrogram is an internal representation. Idea 2 · Evaluation MOS (Mean Opinion Score). 1–5 scale, crowd-sourced. Still the gold standard; painfully slow. CMOS (Comparative MOS). A-vs-B preference. Tighter confidence intervals per annotation. UTMOS, DNSMOS. Reference-free neural MOS predictors. Used for leaderboards. CER (Character Error Rate) via ASR. Run TTS output through Whisper, compute CER against the input text. Proxy for intelligibility. SECS (Speaker Embedding Cosine Similarity). Voice-cloning quality. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Voice cloning reads your text in someone else's voice. Voice conversion rewrites your voice into someone else's while preserving what you said. Both hang on the same decomposition: separate speaker identity from content. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Zero-shot clone 5 seconds is enough Pretrained model + speaker embedding; no training. PPG Phonetic posteriorgram Per-frame ASR posteriors used as language-agnostic content rep. KNN-VC Nearest-neighbor conversion Replace each source frame with nearest target-pool frame. Neural codec TTS VALL-E style AR model over EnCodec/SoundStream tokens. Watermark Inaudible signature Bits embedded in audio, survive re-encode. SECS Cloning fidelity Cosine between target and clone speaker embeddings. AASIST Deepfake detector Anti-spoof model; detects synthesized speech. The problem In plain words first A recording mixes three things: what is said (content), who says it (speaker identity) and how (prosody: timing, pitch, emotion). Voice cloning takes content from text and identity from a short sample of someone's voice. Voice conversion takes content from one recording and identity from another person, so a sentence spoken by A comes out sounding like B. Both work by pulling those factors apart and recombining them. The same technology powers dubbing and voices for people who have lost theirs, and also phone scams, so the engineering includes consent checks, inaudible watermarks and detectors, and since August 2026 the EU requires generated audio to be marked. This lesson runs a real open voice-conversion model on a LibriSpeech recording and measures what it keeps and what it changes, then builds a working audio watermark from scratch and attacks it. Nothing is trained. In 2026, a 5-second audio clip is enough to produce a high-quality clone of anyone's voice with a consumer GPU. ElevenLabs, F5-TTS, OpenVoice v2 and XTTS v2 all offer zero-shot or few-shot cloning (Meta described Voicebox in 2023 but did not release it, citing misuse risk). The technology is a blessing (accessibility TTS, dubbing, assistive voices) and a weapon (scam calls, political deepfakes, IP theft). Two closely-related tasks: Voice cloning (TTS-side): text + 5-second reference voice → audio in that voice. Voice conversion (speech-side): source audio (person A saying X) + reference voice of person B → audio of B saying X. Both factor a waveform into (content, speaker, prosody) and recombine content from one source with speaker from another. Key constraints: since 2 August 2026, the EU AI Act (Article 50) requires providers of systems that generate synthetic audio to mark the output in a machine-readable, detectable way (systems already on the market before that date have until 2 December 2026), and deployers must disclose deepfakes of real people. California's AB 2905 (signed 2024) requires calls that use AI-generated voices to say so. Laws such as Tennessee's ELVIS Act (2024) protect a person's voice as part of their likeness, and platforms require consent to clone a real voice. Build marking and consent checks into the pipeline, not around it. The idea Zero-shot cloning. Pass a 5-second clip to a model that has been trained on thousands of speakers. The speaker encoder maps the clip to a speaker embedding; the TTS decoder conditions on that embedding plus text. Used by: F5-TTS (2024), YourTTS (2022), XTTS v2 (2023), OpenVoice v2 (2024). Few-shot fine-tuning. Record 5-30 minutes of the target voice. LoRA-fine-tune a base model for an hour. Quality leaps from "okay" to "indistinguishable". ElevenLabs offers this as Professional Voice Cloning; open communities do it with F5-TTS and XTTS v2. Voice conversion (VC). Two families: Recognition-synthesis. Run ASR-like model to extract content representation (e.g., soft phoneme posteriors, PPGs), then resynthesize with target speaker embedding. Robust to language and accent. Used by PPG-based VC systems and Diff-HierVC (2023); kNN-VC (2023) does the same with self-supervised WavLM features in place of phoneme posteriors. Disentanglement. Train an autoencoder that separates content, speaker, and prosody in latent space at the bottleneck. Swap speaker embedding at inference. Lower quality but faster. Used by AutoVC (2019), VITS-VC variants. Neural codec-based cloning (2024+). VALL-E, VALL-E 2, NaturalSpeech 3, VoiceBox — treat audio as discrete tokens from SoundStream / EnCodec, train a large autoregressive or flow-matching model over codec tokens. These were research systems from Microsoft and Meta, mostly not released because of misuse concerns; the token-based idea lives on in open models and in speech LLMs (Lessons 6.10 and 6.13). The same idea as a formula Factorisation. Write an utterance's features as a function of three latent factors, : content , speaker , prosody . Worked example A watermark budget by hand Bits per second. 32 bits in 19 seconds of speech is about 1.7 bits per second, 9,500 samples per bit at 16 kHz. Correlation gain. Check your mental model ✗ "Voice conversion changes the voice and keeps everything else." ✓ It changes the speaker factor; prosody and some content often change too. Measure WER after conversion. ✗ "A watermark proves audio is fake." ✓ It proves the audio came from a system that marked it. Unmarked synthetic audio exists, so detection and provenance (signed metadata) are separate layers. ✗ "A cloning model only needs the reference audio." ✓ Many (F5-TTS among them) also need the reference transcript, exactly matching, to align the prompt. Will the converted audio match the target voice better than the original speaker? Will Whisper still get every word? (Solution P1.) Idea 1 · The ethics bit, not a bolt-on Watermarking. Meta's AudioSeal (2024, a 16-bit message), Sony's SilentCipher (2024) and Resemble AI's PerTh (open-sourced as resemble-perth ) embed a short ID imperceptibly in the audio and are designed to survive common re-encoding and edits, to varying degrees. The run under Step 4 builds a simple one from scratch. Consent gates. Must pair every cloned output with a verifiable consent record. "I, Rohit, on 2026-04-22, authorize this voice for X purpose." Store in a tamper-evident log. Detection. AASIST, RawNet2 and wav2vec 2.0-based classifiers are the standard open detectors, benchmarked in the ASVspoof challenges (ASVspoof 5 ran in 2024). They do well on generators like those they were trained on and worse on new ones (Lesson 6.16), so detection complements watermarking rather than replacing it. Idea 2 · Numbers (2026) Published SECS and WER figures for cloning models come from different test sets, prompts and speaker-verification models, so they cannot be compared across papers, and SECS values depend strongly on which embedding model computes them. Recap What to keep from this lesson Cloning and conversion both separate content, speaker and prosody, then recombine. Measure identity (SECS with a speaker-verification model) and content (ASR WER) together; conversion trades one against the other. Consent records and EU marking requirements belong inside the pipeline. The technical problem is mostly solved. The legal problem reshaped the field: Universal settled with Udio in October 2025 and Warner Music with Suno in November 2025, and both companies moved to licensed models. The problem In plain words first Music generators turn a text description (and sometimes a hummed melody or lyrics) into audio. Two designs dominate. One treats audio like text: a neural codec turns sound into a few streams of discrete tokens, and a transformer predicts those tokens one step at a time, as MusicGen does. The other is diffusion: start from noise in a compressed audio representation and refine it towards music that matches the prompt, as Stable Audio does. Commercial song generators (Suno, Udio) add vocals and song structure on top, with architectures they do not publish. Two practical questions sit around the models: how to measure output that has no single right answer (embedding distances such as FAD, text-audio agreement such as the CLAP score, and listeners), and who owns the rights, which changed sharply with the 2025 label settlements. This lesson computes the token budgets behind MusicGen with a real codec, and builds CLAP scoring and FAD on generated test signals. No music model is trained or run: the open generators are multi-gigabyte downloads. Text → a 30-second to 4-minute music clip, with lyrics, vocals, and structure. Three sub-problems: Instrumental generation. Text like "lo-fi hip-hop drums with warm keys" → audio. MusicGen, Stable Audio, AudioLDM. Song generation (with vocals + lyrics). "Country song about rainy Texas nights" → full song. Suno, Udio, YuE, ACE-Step. Conditional / controllable. Extend an existing clip, regenerate a bridge, swap genre, stem-separate, or inpaint. a0610: Course home / Phase 6 · Sound and Speech Models that listen and talk about audio Lesson 6.10 45 min Learn Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 6 · 04 (ASR), Phase 12 · 03 (Vision-Language Models), Phase 7 · 10 (Audio Transformers) Type : Learn. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Audio-language models reason over speech, environmental sound and music in one model. On the MMAU-Pro benchmark (2025), the best model tested, Gemini 2.5 Flash, scored 59.2% and the best open model, Audio Flamingo 3, 51.7%, and even leading models were close to random in several skill categories. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means LALM Audio ChatGPT Audio encoder + projector + LLM decoder. Projector Adapter Small MLP mapping audio features into LLM embedding space. MMAU The benchmark 10k audio-QA pairs across speech, sound, music. MMAU-Pro Harder MMAU 5,305 instances testing 49 skills, including multi-audio, long-audio and spatial reasoning. LongAudioBench Long-form eval Multi-minute clips with semantic queries. Voice-in / voice-out Speech-native Model ingests speech and emits speech without text detour. The problem In plain words first An audio-language model is a chat model that can listen. You give it a recording and a question in words ("Is anyone in danger?", "What instrument plays the melody?", "Summarise this meeting") and it answers in words, sometimes in speech. Almost all of them are built the same way: an audio encoder (often Whisper's) turns sound into vectors, a small projector translates those vectors into the "word vectors" a language model reads, and an ordinary LLM does the rest. Before such models existed, products chained separate parts instead: speech recognition and a sound tagger produce text, and a text-only LLM reasons over that text. This lesson builds both shapes from real parts on a CPU: Whisper's encoder feeding a projector into a small LLM's embedding space, to see the sizes and token counts involved, and a working cascade (Whisper + CLAP tags + a 0.5B LLM) to see what text throws away. The large models themselves are too big to run here, and nothing is trained. You have 5 seconds of audio: dog barks, someone yells "stop!", then silence. Useful questions span multiple axes: Transcription. "What was said?" — ASR territory. Semantic reasoning. "Is the person in danger?" — requires joint understanding of the bark + yell + silence. Music reasoning. "What instruments play the melody?" Long-audio retrieval. "Where in this 90-minute lecture did the instructor explain gradient descent?" A single model that answers all of these with one prompt is an audio-language model (LALM / ALM). Separate from pure ASR: LALMs produce free-form natural-language answers, not just transcripts. The idea The same idea as a formula The pipeline. An encoder maps audio to frame vectors ​ , optionally pooled in time; a projector maps each to the LLM's width, × d ; the LLM reads a sequence that mixes text-token embeddings and the rows of , and generates the answer: ∏ ​ P LLM ​ ( y u ​ ∣ y < u ​ , [ E ( q pre ​ ) ; A ; E ( q post ​ )] ) Training stages. Stage 1 trains only (encoder and LLM frozen) with cross-entropy on paired text, usually transcripts or captions: ​ lo g P ( y u ​ ∣ y < u ​ , A ) . Later stages fine-tune more of the network (often with LoRA) on instructions such as "answer the question about this clip". Token budget. With an encoder at frames per second and pooling by , a clip of seconds costs tokens. Text is far denser: speech at about 2.5 words per second is roughly 3 text tokens per second. Multiple-choice evaluation. With options, chance is . With questions, the standard error of an accuracy near is ​ , so differences of a few points on a few hundred questions are noise. Worked example Token budgets and chance levels by hand Whisper features. Whisper's encoder gives 50 frames per second; pooling by 2 (as Qwen2-Audio does) gives 25. A 12.5 s clip: audio tokens, as the run under Step 2 finds. Its transcript is 33 text tokens, so the audio form is about 9.5 times longer. An hour of audio. At 25 tokens per second, tokens; Google documents 32 tokens per second for Gemini, tokens per hour. Long recordings fill context windows fast, which is one reason meeting tools transcribe and chunk first. Chance. Four options: 25%. A model at 30% on 200 such questions has standard error ​ = 3.2 points, so 30% is only about 1.5 standard errors above chance. Check your mental model ✗ "An audio-language model hears everything a person would." ✓ It hears what its encoder represents and what its training data asked about. a0611: Course home / Phase 6 · Sound and Speech Processing audio as it arrives Lesson 6.11 75 min Build Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 6 · 02 (Spectrograms), Phase 6 · 04 (ASR), Phase 6 · 07 (TTS) Type : Build. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Batch pipelines process a file. Real-time pipelines process the next 20 milliseconds before the next 20 arrive. Every conversational AI, broadcast studio, and telephony bot lives and dies by this latency budget. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Ring buffer The circular queue Fixed-size, lock-free (or SPSC-locked) FIFO for audio frames. VAD Silence gate Model or heuristic marking speech vs non-speech. Streaming ASR Real-time STT Emits partial text as audio arrives; bounded lookahead. Jitter buffer Network smoother Queue reordering out-of-order packets; usually tens of ms, adaptive. AEC Echo cancellation Subtracts speaker-to-mic feedback path. Barge-in User interrupt System detects user speech mid-TTS; must cancel playback. Full duplex Simultaneous both ways User and bot can talk at the same time; Moshi is full duplex. The problem In plain words first Everything so far processed a finished recording. A live system gets audio 20 milliseconds at a time and must finish with each piece before the next arrives, forever, while a person waits for an answer. Three ideas carry it. A ring buffer holds the most recent audio in a fixed amount of memory. A voice activity detector decides, frame by frame, whether anyone is talking, so the expensive models only run when needed. And every model downstream works in streaming mode: it produces partial results from the audio seen so far, accepting some loss of accuracy for not knowing what comes next. The craft is a latency budget: how long each stage may take, and what you give up to meet it. This lesson measures two of those trade-offs on real speech: two voice activity detectors in rising noise, and a speech recogniser fed in chunks of different sizes, with and without look-ahead. Nothing is trained. You want a voice assistant that feels alive. In conversation, the typical gap between one person stopping and the next starting is about 200 ms, across languages (Stivers et al., 2009). Delays well beyond that feel increasingly unnatural, and a second or more feels broken. A typical target budget for a full hear → understand → respond → speak loop: Stage Budget Mic → buffer 20 ms VAD 10 ms ASR (streaming) 150 ms LLM (first token) 100 ms TTS (first chunk) 100 ms Render → speaker 20 ms Total ~400 ms Moshi (Kyutai, 2024) reports about 200 ms in practice, full-duplex. OpenAI reported GPT-4o answering spoken input in 320 ms on average (May 2024), against 2.8 s and 5.4 s for its earlier cascaded Voice Mode with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. The 10× improvement came from three techniques: (1) streaming everywhere, (2) asynchronous pipelining with partial results, (3) interruptible generation. The idea Frame / chunk / window. Real-time audio flows as fixed-size blocks. Common choice: 20 ms (320 samples at 16 kHz). Everything downstream must keep up with this cadence. Ring buffer. Fixed-size circular buffer. Producer thread writes new frames, consumer thread reads. Prevents allocations in the hot path. Size ≈ maximum-latency × sample-rate; a 2-second 16 kHz ring = 32,000 samples. VAD (Voice Activity Detection). Gates downstream work when nobody is speaking. Silero VAD (v5, 2024) processes a 30 ms chunk in under 1 ms on one CPU thread. webrtcvad is the older alternative. Streaming ASR. Models that emit partial transcripts as audio arrives. NVIDIA NeMo's cache-aware streaming FastConformer models are trained with limited look-ahead, so they stay accurate on chunks of a few hundred milliseconds; the run under Step 3 shows what happens to a model not trained that way. Whisper-Streaming (Macháček et al., 2023) re-runs Whisper on a growing buffer for near-streaming with a few seconds of latency. Interruption. When the user speaks while the assistant is talking, you must (a) detect the barge-in, (b) stop the TTS, (c) discard the remaining LLM output. All within 100 ms, or the user perceives deaf assistant. WebRTC Opus transport. Typically 20 ms frames at 48 kHz with adaptive bitrate (Opus supports 6 to 510 kbps). Standard for browser and mobile. LiveKit, Daily (with its open-source Pipecat framework) and Pion are common foundations for voice apps. Jitter buffer. Network packets arrive out of order / late. The jitter buffer reorders and smooths; too small → audible gaps, too large → latency. Adaptive jitter buffers usually hold a few tens of milliseconds. The same idea as a formula Frames and buffers. A frame of seconds at sample rate ​ holds ​ samples (20 ms at 16 kHz: 320). A ring buffer that can hold seconds needs ​ samples, and its fill level is the queueing delay it adds. Keeping up. If each chunk of seconds takes seconds to process, the real-time factor is . With the system keeps up; with the backlog after chunks grows as and latency rises without bound. Streaming delay. A word that ends at the start of a chunk is ready after the chunk fills, the look-ahead arrives and the model runs: ​ = C + R + c Larger chunks and look-ahead give the model more context and lower error; smaller ones give lower delay. End-to-end latency is the sum of the stages in the user's path: ​ + t VAD/end-of-turn ​ + t ASR ​ + t LLM, first token ​ + t TTS, first audio ​ + t playback ​ + t network ​ . Streaming overlaps the stages so that each starts on partial input, which is how pipelines get under 500 ms. VAD as detection. Each frame is a binary decision with a miss rate (speech labelled silence: clipped words) and a false-alarm rate (noise labelled speech: wasted compute, phantom turns), traded off by a threshold, like the speaker verification of Lesson 6.6. VAD end-of-turn 300 ms + ASR final 150 ms + LLM first token 200 ms + TTS first audio 150 ms + network 100 ms = 900 ms. Streaming the LLM into the TTS and starting the LLM on a confident partial transcript are the usual ways to cut it in half. WebRTC's VAD looks at the spectrum, not just the level, so it degrades gradually (27% false alarms at 10 dB) until 0 dB, where it too flags everything. The buffer is your latency floor. Shrink it. Not pinning threads. Audio callback on a priority-lower-than-UI thread = glitches under load. TTS chunks too small.
