Time : about 120 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Everything from lessons 01-11, stitched together. Build a voice assistant that listens, reasons, and talks back. In 2026 that is a solved engineering problem, not a research problem — but the integration details decide whether it ships. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Turn A user + assistant round-trip One VAD-bounded user speech + one LLM-TTS response. Barge-in Interruption User speaks while assistant talks; assistant stops. Wake word "Hey assistant" Short keyword detector; Porcupine or openWakeWord (Snowboy is discontinued). End-pointing Turn ending VAD + min-silence decision that user has finished. Pre-roll Pre-speech buffer Keep 200-400 ms of audio before VAD fires to avoid first-word clip. Tool call Function invocation LLM emits JSON; runtime dispatches; result feeds back in-loop. The problem In plain words first This capstone joins the phase together. A voice assistant listens to a microphone in 20 ms pieces, notices when someone starts and stops talking (voice activity detection), writes down what they said (speech recognition), decides what to do, possibly by calling a tool such as a timer or a weather service (an LLM with tool calling), says the answer (text-to-speech), and stops talking at once if the user interrupts. Each part was covered in an earlier lesson; the hard part is the joins: when exactly a turn starts and ends, how long each step may take, and what happens when one step is wrong. This lesson runs a complete assistant on this page with small open models on a CPU (WebRTC VAD, Whisper base.en, Qwen2.5-0.5B with tool calling, SpeechT5), feeds it spoken requests, and measures every stage. It also finds two real bugs along the way. Nothing is trained. Build an end-to-end assistant: Captures mic input (16 kHz mono). Detects start/end of user speech. Transcribes streaming. Passes transcript to an LLM that can call tools (timer, weather, calendar). Streams LLM text to a TTS. Plays audio back to the user. Stops if the user interrupts mid-response. Latency target: first TTS audio byte within 800 ms of the user finishing their utterance on a laptop CPU. Quality target: no missed words, no hallucinated subtitles on silence, no voice cloning leakage, no prompt injection success. The idea The same idea as a formula Latency to first audio. From the end of the user's speech: ​ + t STT ​ + t LLM ( first sentence ) ​ + t tools ​ + t TTS ( first chunk ) ​ + t network ​ ​ is a choice, the silence the system waits before deciding the user has finished; shorter waits answer faster and cut people off mid-sentence more often. Turn detection as a small state machine. States idle → speaking → idle . Enter speaking after consecutive speech frames (minimum speech duration ms) and include the pre-roll; leave after consecutive non-speech frames. With per-frame false-alarm probability on noise, a single-frame trigger fires on noise at rate per frame, while requiring frames in a row lowers that to roughly (if frames were independent). Barge-in delay = ms of speech needed to trust the detection + the time to cancel playback, LLM and TTS. Larger ignores coughs and background voices; smaller stops faster. Tool calling is a loop: the LLM emits a structured call that matches a JSON schema, the runtime executes it, and the result is appended to the conversation as a tool message before the LLM continues. Each round trip adds an LLM call to . Worked example A turn's budget by hand Target. 800 ms to first audio. Spend it: end-of-turn wait 500 ms leaves 300 ms for everything else, so on a CPU this target is out of reach (the run under Step 5 measures several seconds). Typical production answers: a shorter end-of-turn wait with a turn-detection model, GPU or hosted STT, an LLM with fast first tokens, and TTS started on the first clause. False triggers. If background noise makes a fresh VAD fire on 4 of the first 5 frames, a single-frame trigger starts a turn at once. Requiring 10 consecutive frames (200 ms) ignores that burst; the price is 200 ms of extra delay before a real turn is confirmed, recovered by the pre-roll so no audio is lost. Barge-in. At 20 ms per frame, requiring 5 speech frames means the assistant keeps talking for at least 100 ms after the user starts, plus the time to stop playback. LiveKit Agents and Pipecat provide the turn state machine, interruption handling, tool calling and streaming plumbing; teams plug in their choice of STT, LLM and TTS. Turn detection models. Both frameworks offer small models that judge from the words (and in some cases the audio) whether the user has finished, so the assistant can reply after a short pause when a sentence is complete and wait longer when it is not. Speech-to-speech as an alternative. OpenAI's Realtime API and Gemini's Live API replace STT + LLM + TTS with one streaming model; the cascade remains common because each part can be chosen, tested and logged on its own (Lesson 6.15). a0613: Course home / Phase 6 · Sound and Speech Compressing audio into tokens (neural codecs) Lesson 6.13 60 min Learn Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 6 · 02 (Spectrograms), Phase 10 · 11 (Quantization), Phase 5 · 19 (Subword Tokenization) Type : Learn. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line 2026 audio generation is almost all tokens. EnCodec, SNAC, Mimi, and DAC turn continuous waveforms into discrete sequences that a transformer can predict. The semantic-vs-acoustic token split, first codebook for content and the rest for sound, is one of the most important design ideas in audio generation since 2023. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means RVQ Residual quantization Cascade of small codebooks; each quantizes the previous residual. Frame rate Codec speed How many token-frames per second. Lower = faster LM. Semantic codebook Codebook 0 (Mimi) Codebook distilled from SSL features; encodes content. Acoustic codebooks Everything else Timbre, prosody, noise, fine detail. PESQ / ViSQOL Perceptual quality Objective metrics correlating with MOS. EnCodec Meta codec The RVQ baseline; used by MusicGen. Mimi Kyutai codec 12.5 Hz frame rate; semantic-acoustic split; powers Moshi. The problem In plain words first Language models predict the next item from a fixed vocabulary. Audio has no vocabulary: it is a stream of numbers. A neural audio codec creates one. An encoder squeezes each short slice of sound (13 to 75 slices per second) into a vector; a quantizer replaces that vector with the nearest entries from small learned "codebooks", so every slice becomes a handful of integers; a decoder turns the integers back into sound. Stacking codebooks, each fixing what the previous ones missed, is residual vector quantisation . Those integers are the tokens that music, speech and voice models predict. Two design choices matter most: how many slices per second (fewer means shorter sequences), and whether the first codebook is trained to capture what is said rather than how it sounds . This lesson runs two real codecs on LibriSpeech speech: EnCodec at five bitrates, scored by a perceptual metric and by Whisper, and Kyutai's Mimi with its first or last codebook scrambled. Nothing is trained. Language models work on discrete tokens. Audio is continuous. If you want an LLM-style model for speech / music — MusicGen, Moshi, Sesame CSM, Orpheus — you first need a neural audio codec : a learned encoder that discretizes audio into a small vocabulary of tokens, and a matching decoder that reconstructs the waveform. Two families have emerged: Reconstruction-first codecs — EnCodec, DAC. Optimize perceptual audio quality. Tokens are "acoustic" — they capture everything including speaker identity, timbre, background noise. Semantic-first codecs — Mimi (Kyutai), SpeechTokenizer. Force the first codebook to encode linguistic / phonetic content (often by distilling from WavLM). Subsequent codebooks are acoustic detail. The 2024-2026 insight: a pure reconstruction codec gives you blurry speech when you try to generate from text. The LLM over codec tokens has to learn both language structure AND acoustic structure in the same codebook, which doesn't scale. Separating them — semantic codebook 0, acoustic codebooks 1-N — is what makes Moshi and Sesame CSM work. The idea The same idea as a formula Residual vector quantisation. Idea 1 · The core trick: Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ) Rather than one big codebook (which would need millions of codes for good quality), all modern audio codecs use RVQ : a cascade of small codebooks. The first codebook quantizes the encoder output; the second quantizes the residual; etc. Each codebook is 1024 codes. 8 codebooks = effective vocabulary of = 1 0 24 . At inference time, the decoder sums all chosen codes per frame to reconstruct. Idea 2 · The four codecs that matter in 2026 EnCodec (Meta, 2022). The baseline. Encoder-decoder over waveform, RVQ bottleneck. The 24 kHz model runs at 75 frames per second with 1,024-entry codebooks: 2 codebooks at 1.5 kbps up to 32 at 24 kbps. A convolutional encoder and decoder with LSTM layers, trained with reconstruction and adversarial losses. Used by MusicGen. DAC (Descript, 2023). RVQ with L2-normalized codebooks, periodic activation functions, improved losses. Among the highest-fidelity open codecs; the 44.1 kHz model uses up to 9 codebooks (8 kbps). 44.1 kHz full-band. SNAC (Hubert Siuzdak, 2024). Multi-scale RVQ — the coarse codebooks operate at a lower frame rate than fine ones. Effectively models audio hierarchically: for the 24 kHz speech model, codebooks at about 12, 23 and 47 Hz (0.98 kbps in total): a coarse sketch plus finer detail. Used by Orpheus-3B because the hierarchical structure maps well onto LM-based generation. Mimi (Kyutai, 2024). 12.5 Hz frame rate, very low for a codec. Moshi uses 8 codebooks of 2,048 entries: 1.1 kbps (the run under Step 3 computes it). Codebook 0 is distilled from WavLM — trained to predict WavLM's speech-content features. Codebooks 1-7 are acoustic residuals. This split powers Moshi ( Lesson 6.15 ) and Sesame CSM. Idea 3 · Frame rates matter for language modeling Lower frame rate = shorter sequence = faster LM. Codec Frame rate 1 s = N frames Good for EnCodec-24k 75 Hz 75 music, general audio DAC-44.1k 86 Hz 86 high-fidelity music SNAC-24k (coarse) ~12 Hz 12 AR-LM efficient Mimi 12.5 Hz 12.5 streaming speech At 12.5 Hz, a 10-second utterance is only 125 codec frames — a transformer can easily predict them. Idea 4 · Semantic vs acoustic tokens Copy Semantic token (codebook 0 in Mimi). Encodes what was said — phonemes, words, content. Distilled from WavLM via an auxiliary prediction loss. Acoustic tokens (codebooks 1-7). Encode timbre, speaker identity, prosody, background noise, fine detail. An AR LM predicts the semantic token first (conditioned on text), then predicts acoustic tokens (conditioned on semantic + speaker reference). This factorization is why modern TTS can zero-shot-clone voices: the semantic model handles content; the acoustic model handles timbre. Opus, a classic codec, remains the choice for transmitting audio; neural codecs win where a model needs discrete tokens (which Opus does not produce) to generate from. Lower frame rates. The trend is fewer frames per second (Mimi's 12.5 Hz) and a semantically trained first codebook, so that speech language models can handle minutes of audio. Classic codecs still carry the audio. Opus remains the codec for transmitting audio (WebRTC, VoIP); neural codecs are chosen for generation, where discrete tokens matter more than bits per second. Frame-rate mismatch. Training LM on 12.5 Hz Mimi then fine-tuning on 50 Hz EnCodec fails silently. Assuming all codebooks equal. In Mimi, codebook 0 carries content; losing it destroys intelligibility. Losing codebook 7 is barely noticeable. Using reconstruction quality as the only metric. A codec can have great reconstruction but be useless for LM-based generation if the semantic structure is bad. Recap What to keep from this lesson A neural codec = encoder + residual vector quantiser + decoder; its integers are the tokens audio LMs predict. Bitrate = frame rate × codebooks × bits per code; tokens per second = frame rate × codebooks. Judge codecs by perceptual quality, intelligibility and speaker similarity, not waveform SNR. Earlier codebooks matter more; Mimi's first codebook carries content by design. Low frame rates make long audio tractable for language models. Solution B1 · Wrong rate, no error The codec accepts any array; it assumes 24 kHz. Treating 16 kHz samples as 24 kHz speeds the speech up by 1.5× and raises every frequency by the same factor, and the reconstruction, read back at 16 kHz, is the codec's version of that distorted sound. Whisper sees speech at the wrong speed and pitch and its transcript degrades. In plain words first The idea in one line Every voice agent lives or dies on two decisions: is the user speaking now, and are they done? VAD answers the first. Turn-detection (VAD + silence-hangover + semantic endpoint model) answers the second. Get either wrong and your assistant either cuts users off or never shuts up. The problem In plain words first A voice assistant hears a continuous stream of sound and must decide, many times a second, two things: is someone speaking right now? and have they finished? The first is voice activity detection (VAD): a small model labels each 20–32 ms frame as speech or not. The second is turn detection, and it is harder, because people pause in the middle of sentences. The simple rule, "wait for N milliseconds of silence", forces a trade: a short wait interrupts people, a long wait makes the assistant feel slow. Production systems add a third piece, a model that judges from the words or the sound of the voice whether the thought is complete. This lesson measures each piece on real LibriSpeech speech: an energy threshold, WebRTC VAD and Silero VAD in three kinds of noise; how often fixed silence timers cut a speaker off; and Pipecat's open Smart Turn model, plus the scoring rule behind LiveKit's text model. Nothing is trained. Three distinct decisions a voice agent makes on every 20 ms chunk: Is this frame speech? — VAD. Binary, per-frame. Has the user started a new utterance? — onset detection. Has the user finished? — end-pointing (turn-end). The naive answer (energy threshold) fails on any noise — traffic, keyboards, crowd babble. The 2026 answer: Silero VAD (open, deep-learned) + a turn-detection model (semantic endpointing) + a VAD-calibrated silence hangover. The idea The same idea as a formula Frame decisions. At 5% false positives, roughly what share of speech frames will the energy threshold catch: 90%, 60% or 25%? And Silero? (Solution P1.) Idea 1 · The three-tier VAD cascade Tier 1: energy gate. Cheapest. Threshold RMS at -40 dBFS. Filters obvious silence but fires on any noise above the threshold. Tier 2: Silero VAD (MIT licence; the silero-vad package is at version 6). About 0.46 million parameters, trained (its authors say) on data covering over 6,000 languages, and under 1 ms per 32 ms chunk on one CPU thread (0.7 ms on this page's machine). The open-source default, and the VAD that LiveKit Agents and Pipecat ship with. Tier 3: semantic turn detector. LiveKit's turn-detection model (text, reads the transcript), Pipecat's Smart Turn (audio, hears intonation and pace), the end-of-turn signals built into streaming STT services, or your own small classifier. Distinguishes "pause mid-sentence" from "done talking." Uses linguistic context (intonation + recent words), not just silence. Idea 2 · Key parameters and their defaults Threshold. Silero outputs a probability; classify speech at > 0.5 (default) or > 0.3 (sensitive). Lower threshold = fewer first-word clips, more false positives. Minimum speech duration. Reject speech shorter than 250 ms — usually coughs or chair noise. Silence hangover (end-pointing). After VAD returns to 0, wait 500-800 ms before declaring end-of-turn. Too short → interrupt user. Too long → feels sluggish. Pre-roll buffer. Keep 300-500 ms of audio before VAD fires. Prevents "hey" being clipped. Idea 3 · The flush trick (Kyutai 2025) Streaming STT models have a look-ahead delay (500 ms for Kyutai STT-1B, 2.5 s for STT-2.6B). Normally you'd wait that long after end-of-speech for the transcript. Flush trick: when VAD fires end-of-speech, send a flush signal to the STT that forces immediate output. STT processes at ~4× realtime, so the 500 ms buffer finishes in ~125 ms. End-to-end: 125 ms VAD + flush STT = conversational latency. But at the natural pauses of audiobook narration it says "done" 64% of the time, almost as often as at true ends (AUC 0.57, where 0.5 is chance): a reader's pause at a clause boundary sounds final. Used as the only turn signal, it would cut off 40% of these utterances, worse than a fixed 500 ms timer (25%), although its mean wait at true ends is shorter. What happens, and why? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Silero VAD remains the default open VAD; LiveKit Agents and Pipecat both ship it as their VAD. Semantic turn detection is standard in voice-agent frameworks. LiveKit's turn detector (text; fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, distilled from a 7B teacher; licensed for use only within LiveKit Agents) and Pipecat's Smart Turn v3 (audio; 8 MB, BSD-2; run once the VAD reports silence). Hosted APIs build it in. OpenAI's Realtime API offers server_vad (silence-based) and semantic_vad (a classifier on the user's words, with an eagerness setting); Deepgram's Flux STT emits EndOfTurn and an optional early EagerEndOfTurn so the LLM can start speculatively. Kyutai's flush trick (in Unmute): on end of speech, process the STT's buffered audio at about 4× real time, so a 500 ms delay costs about 125 ms. Typical defaults: LiveKit waits at least 0.5 s and at most 3 s of silence and treats speech of 0.5 s or more as an interruption; Deepgram Flux forces an end of turn after 5 s of silence by default. Sources: Silero VAD , LiveKit turn detector , LiveKit turn tuning , Pipecat Smart Turn , OpenAI Realtime VAD , Deepgram Flux , Kyutai STT , Picovoice VAD . Pitfalls Fixed threshold. Works in quiet, fails in noisy. Either calibrate on-device or switch to Silero. Too-short silence hangover. Agent interrupts mid-sentence. 500-800 ms is the sweet spot for conversational speech. Too-long hangover. Feels sluggish. A/B test with target users. No pre-roll buffer. First 200-300 ms of user audio lost. Always keep a rolling pre-roll. Ignoring semantic endpointing. "Hmm, let me think..." contains long pauses. Users hate being cut off mid-thought. Use LiveKit's turn-detector or similar. Recap What to keep from this lesson VAD answers "is this speech?"; turn detection answers "are they done?", and needs more than VAD. Compare VADs at a fixed false-positive rate, in noise like your users'; energy thresholds fail in noise, Silero holds up. A silence hangover trades interruptions against latency; read speech shows a quarter of turns cut off at 500 ms. Semantic turn models (audio or text) shorten the wait when a turn sounds complete; check them on your own domain. Pre-roll, minimum speech duration, a maximum wait and the flush trick complete the design. Silero catches about 95%: it has learned what speech sounds like, not just how loud it is. Solution B1 · Silero needs 512 samples Silero raises ValueError: Input audio chunk is too short . At 16 kHz it expects exactly 512-sample (32 ms) chunks, 256 at 8 kHz. Re-buffer the stream: collect incoming frames into a buffer and hand Silero 512 samples at a time, or use get_speech_timestamps / a framework's VAD wrapper, which does this for you. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Moshi (Kyutai, 2024) is a single model that listens and speaks at the same time, with about 200 ms latency. Hibiki translates speech to speech as you talk. Both replace the ASR → LLM → TTS pipeline with one transformer over Mimi codec tokens. Hosted speech-to-speech APIs (OpenAI gpt-realtime , Gemini native audio) apply the single-model idea in production; most production voice agents still use pipelines. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Full-duplex Hear-and-speak at once Two audio streams active simultaneously on the same model. Inner monologue Model's text stream Moshi emits text tokens alongside its audio output. Depth transformer Inter-codebook predictor Small transformer that predicts 8 codebooks within one 80 ms frame. Mimi Kyutai's codec 12.5 Hz × 8 codebooks; semantic+acoustic; powers Moshi. Streaming S2S Audio → audio live Chunk-by-chunk translation/dialogue, no pipeline stages. Back-channeling "Mhm" reactions Moshi can emit small acknowledgments without breaking its turn. The problem In plain words first The voice agents of Lessons 6.11 and 6.12 are pipelines: wait for the user to finish, transcribe, think, then speak. Each stage adds delay, and the agent cannot listen while it talks except through barge-in tricks. A full-duplex model removes the stages. Both people's audio is turned into codec tokens on a shared 80 ms clock (Mimi, Lesson 6.13), and one transformer reads the user's tokens and writes its own, every 80 ms, whether or not anyone is talking, so it can overlap, interrupt and say "mhm" like a person. Kyutai's Moshi is the open reference design; OpenAI's gpt-realtime and Google's Gemini native-audio models are the production speech-to-speech services. A 7B model cannot run on this page's two CPU cores, so the runs below build the exact token layout Moshi reads from real speech, and stream the Mimi codec frame by frame as a Moshi server does. Every voice agent built from Lessons 11 + 12 has a fundamental latency floor around 300-500 ms: VAD fires, STT processes, LLM reasons, TTS generates. Each stage has its own minimum latency. You can tune and parallelize, but the pipeline shape caps you. Moshi (Kyutai, 2024-2026) asks a different question: what if there is no pipeline? What if one model takes audio in and emits audio out directly, continuously, with text as an intermediate "inner monologue" instead of a required stage? The answer is full-duplex speech-to-speech . Theoretical latency 160 ms (80 ms Mimi frame + 80 ms acoustic delay). Practical latency about 200 ms on a single L4 GPU (Kyutai's figure), below what a pipeline usually achieves (Lesson 6.12's worked budget was several hundred milliseconds before the first audio). The idea The same idea as a formula One step of the clock. Moshi runs 12.5 steps per second, so a step is ms. At step it has read the user's tokens ​ , its own audio tokens ​ and its text ​ , and it factorises the next output as ​ , a t 0 : 7 ​ ∣ ⋅ ) = p ( w t ​ ∣ ⋅ ) q = 0 ∏ 7 ​ p ( a t q ​ ∣ w t ​ , a t < q ​ , ⋅ ) The temporal transformer computes the context once per step and predicts the text token ​ first; the depth transformer then produces the product, one codebook at a time. The acoustic delay. Codebooks are shifted by step, so at step the model writes the semantic token 0 ​ and the acoustic tokens 1 : 7 ​ . The latency floor is one frame plus the delay: Tokens read. 17 streams at 12.5 steps per second is tokens per second per conversation, whether anyone is talking or not. Worked example The budget of one full-duplex conversation What one conversation costs, from the numbers in this lesson. Temporal transformer: about 7 billion parameters, one forward pass per step. A forward pass costs about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token: × 12.5 ≈ 175 GFLOP/s, continuously, even in silence. Depth transformer: 8 short passes per step through 6 layers of width 1,024, roughly ≈ 75 million parameters per pass: × 8 × 12.5 ≈ 15 GFLOP/s, under a tenth of the temporal transformer. Memory traffic: serving one conversation, each step reads every weight once. In bf16, 7 billion parameters are 14 GB, so 12.5 steps per second need about 175 GB/s of memory bandwidth, more than half of the 300 GB/s NVIDIA lists for an L4. A server batches several conversations into one step, so the weights are read once for all of them. Deadline: every step must finish within 80 ms, or the model falls behind real time and the user hears gaps. Check your mental model ✗ "Full-duplex means very fast turn-taking." ✓ There are no turns. Every 80 ms the model reads the user's tokens and writes its own, even while both are speaking; the run under Step 3 has 0.4 s of overlapping speech, which a turn-based pipeline cannot represent. ✗ "The inner monologue is a transcript written after the speech." ✓ Within each step the text token comes first, before that frame's audio, so the words lead the sound. Most text steps are padding, because words arrive more slowly than frames. ✗ "Streaming the codec frame by frame changes its tokens." ✓ Mimi is causal: encoding 80 ms at a time gave exactly the same tokens as encoding the whole utterance (the run under Step 2). ✗ "Speech-to-speech models have replaced pipelines." ✓ Hosted speech-to-speech APIs are in production, but tool-heavy voice agents still mostly use pipelines, which can be swapped, logged and tested stage by stage. Predict before you run Under Step 3, the agent's 24 spoken words become its inner monologue on the 12.5 Hz clock. While the agent is speaking, roughly what share of its text steps will be PAD, carrying no new word piece: 10%, 50% or 90%? (Solution P1.) Idea 1 · The Moshi architecture Inputs. Two Mimi codec streams, both at 12.5 Hz × 8 codebooks: Stream 1: user audio (Mimi-encoded, constantly arriving) Stream 2: Moshi's own audio (generated by Moshi) The transformer. A 7B-parameter Temporal Transformer processes both streams and a text "inner monologue" stream. At each 80 ms step, it: Consumes the latest user Mimi tokens (8 codebooks). Consumes the most recent Moshi Mimi tokens (8 codebooks, as produced). Generates the next Moshi text token (inner monologue). Generates the next Moshi Mimi tokens (8 codebooks via a small Depth Transformer). All three streams — user audio, Moshi audio, Moshi text — run in parallel. Moshi can hear the user while speaking; can interrupt itself when the user interrupts; can back-channel ("mhm") without breaking its main utterance. The depth transformer. Within a frame, the 8 codebooks are not predicted in parallel — they have inter-codebook dependencies. A small "depth transformer" (6 layers of width 1,024 in Kyutai's released configuration, against the temporal transformer's 32 layers of width 4,096) predicts them one after another within each 80 ms step. Sesame's CSM uses the same split: a large backbone for codebook 0, a small decoder for the rest. Idea 2 · Why inner-monologue text helps Without explicit text, the model has to implicitly model language in its acoustic stream. Moshi's insight: force it to emit text tokens alongside audio. The text stream is essentially the transcript of what Moshi is saying. This improves semantic coherence, makes it easier to swap out a language model head, and gives you transcripts for free. Idea 3 · Hibiki: streaming speech-to-speech translation Same architecture, trained on translation pairs. Source audio in, target-language audio out, continuously. Hibiki-Zero (Feb 2026) eliminates the need for word-level aligned training data — uses sentence-level data + GRPO reinforcement learning for latency optimization. The paper covers five languages into English; the released 3B model translates French, Spanish, Portuguese and German into English (weights CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, non-commercial), and the authors adapt it to a new input language with under 1,000 hours of speech. Idea 4 · The broader Kyutai stack (2026) Moshi — full-duplex dialogue (French first, English well-supported) Hibiki / Hibiki-Zero — simultaneous speech translation Kyutai STT — streaming ASR (500 ms or 2.5 s look-ahead) Kyutai Pocket TTS — 100M-param TTS runs on CPU (Jan 2026) Unmute — full pipeline combining these on public servers Kyutai reports that its STT server, used by Unmute, serves 64 simultaneous connections on one L40S GPU at 3× real time. Idea 5 · Sesame CSM — the cousin Sesame CSM (2025) uses a similar idea — a Llama-3 backbone with a Mimi codec head. But CSM is single-directional (takes context + text, produces speech) rather than full-duplex. It is a conversational TTS with strong "voice presence" (Sesame's term), not a full-duplex model. Recap What to keep from this lesson Full-duplex models read the user's codec tokens and write their own on a shared 80 ms clock, with no turn boundaries. Per step: 17 streams (1 text + 8 own + 8 user); a big temporal transformer once, a small depth transformer per token. The inner monologue (text first, mostly padding) carries the language; the acoustic delay lets the semantic token lead. The codec is cheap enough to stream on a CPU; the 7B model needs a GPU per conversation. In production, hosted speech-to-speech APIs or pipelines; open Moshi is the design to learn from. a0616: Course home / Phase 6 · Sound and Speech Spotting fake voices and marking real ones Lesson 6.16 75 min Build Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 6 · 06 (Speaker Recognition), Phase 6 · 08 (Voice Cloning) Type : Build. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Voice cloning shipped faster than defenses. 2026 production voice systems need two things: a detector (AASIST, RawNet2) that classifies real vs fake speech, and a watermark (AudioSeal) that survives compression and editing. Ship both or do not ship voice cloning. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means ASVspoof The benchmark Biennial challenge; 2024 = ASVspoof 5. CM (countermeasure) Detector Classifier: real speech vs synthetic / converted. SASV Speaker verif + CM Integrated biometric + spoof detection. AudioSeal Meta watermark Localised (per-sample) detection, 16-bit payload, single-pass detector. Bit Recovery Accuracy Watermark survival Fraction of payload bits recovered after attack. C2PA Provenance manifest Cryptographic metadata about creation / authorship. AASIST Detector family Graph-attention anti-spoofing model; the standard baseline in ASVspoof. The problem In plain words first Lesson 6.8 showed that a few seconds of someone's voice is enough to clone it. Two defences answer two different questions. Detection asks "does this recording sound synthetic?" and must work on audio from anyone, including attackers who do nothing to help. Watermarking asks "did our system make this?": the generator hides a faint, inaudible pattern in every output, and a matching detector finds it later, even after the file has been compressed or re-recorded. A third layer, provenance , attaches signed metadata to the file. This lesson runs Meta's open AudioSeal watermark against ten everyday and hostile edits, and the standard detection baseline, AASIST, against fake speech it was never trained on. Nothing is trained. Three related defenses: Anti-spoofing / deepfake detection. Given an audio clip, is it synthetic or real? ASVspoof benchmarks (ASVspoof 2019 → 2021 → 5) are the gold standard. Audio watermarking. Embed an imperceptible signal in generated audio that a detector can extract later. AudioSeal (Meta) and WavMark are the open options. Authenticated provenance. Cryptographic signing of audio files + metadata. C2PA / Content Authenticity Initiative. Detection handles adversaries who don't cooperate. Watermarking handles compliance — AI-generated audio should be identifiable as such. Both are required in 2026. The idea The same idea as a formula Detection as a score. A countermeasure maps audio to a score , higher meaning more likely bona fide. With threshold , false acceptance and false rejection . The equal error rate is the value where they meet, ) = FRR ( θ ∗ ) ; 50% is chance. Additive watermark. A generator produces a signal from the audio and a message : = x + G ( x , m ) , imperceptibility: SNR = 10 lo g 10 ​ ∥ G ( x , m ) ∥ 2 ∥ x ∥ 2 ​ dB A detector outputs, for every sample , a probability ​ that the watermark is present and 16 bit probabilities . Training adds random edits (noise, filtering, compression) between and and minimises detection and message losses on )) , so the pattern survives the edits that were in training. Bit accuracy. 1 ​ ∑ j ​ [ m ^ j ​ = m j ​ ] ; random guessing gives 50%, and with 16 bits the chance of decoding the whole payload by luck is ≈ 1.5 × 1 0 − 5 . Worked example EER and false alarms by hand EER from four scores. Real scores , fake scores . At : one fake of four is accepted (0.9), FAR = 25%; one real of four is rejected ( ), FRR = 25%. They are equal, so EER = 25%. Why per-sample scores matter. AudioSeal scores every sample. Averaging over a 2 s span of 32,000 samples with a 0.5 threshold, a watermark spliced into part of a long recording is located to within a fraction of a second, so an edit that pastes a generated phrase into a real recording can be found. Payload collisions. A 16-bit payload names 65,536 values: enough for a model version and a coarse date, not for a user ID across millions of users; production systems map the payload to a database record. Check your mental model ✗ "A watermark proves a recording is real when absent." ✓ Absence only means this generator did not mark it, or the mark was removed; detection and provenance are separate defences. ✗ "A detector with 0.8% EER on a benchmark is reliable." ✓ That figure is in-domain; on ASVspoof 5 and real-world deepfakes the same AASIST checkpoint scores 35–43% EER, and even on easy fakes a phone-call codec raises its error (the run under Step 3). ✗ "Compression is what breaks watermarks." ✓ AudioSeal survives MP3 and Opus well; pitch and speed changes break it (the run under Step 2). Predict before you run Under Step 2, AudioSeal-marked speech is sent through MP3 at 64 kbps, Opus at 16 kbps, a 2-semitone pitch shift and a 10% speed-up. Rank the four from least to most damaging to the watermark. (Solution P1.) Idea 1 · ASVspoof 5 — the 2024-2025 benchmark Biggest change from prior editions: Crowdsourced data (not studio clean) — realistic conditions. ~2000 speakers (vs ~100 before). 32 attack algorithms. TTS + voice conversion + adversarial perturbation. Two tracks. Countermeasure (CM) standalone detection; Spoofing-robust ASV (SASV) for biometric systems. The gap between in-domain and real-world results is the main fact of this field. The official AASIST checkpoint, trained on ASVspoof 2019 LA, scores 0.83% EER there, but 12.4% on ASVspoof 2021 LA, 17.0% on 2021 DF, 35.5% on ASVspoof 5 and 43.0% on the In-the-Wild set of real-world deepfakes, according to the Speech Anti-Spoofing Benchmarks evaluation (50% is chance). The run under Step 3 shows the same on new fakes. Idea 2 · AASIST and RawNet2 — detection model families AASIST (Jung et al., ICASSP 2022). A sinc-filter front end over the raw waveform, a RawNet2-style encoder, and graph attention across spectral and temporal sub-graphs; 0.3 M parameters. ASVspoof 5's organisers supply it as a baseline, and most stronger systems keep its back end. RawNet2. Convolutional front-end over raw waveform + TDNN backbone. Simpler baseline; still competitive with fine-tuning. Self-supervised front ends. Replacing the hand-designed front end with a pretrained speech model (wav2vec 2.0, WavLM) plus an AASIST-style back end is the usual way to generalise better to unseen attacks; it is the pattern among stronger ASVspoof 5 submissions. Idea 3 · AudioSeal — the 2024 watermark default Meta's AudioSeal (Jan 2024, v0.2 Dec 2024). Key design: Localized. Detects the watermark per-frame at 16 kHz sample resolution (1/16000 s). Generator + detector jointly trained. Generator learns to embed inaudible signal; detector learns to find it through augmentations. Robust. Survives MP3 / AAC compression, EQ, speed-shift ±10%, noise mix +10 dB SNR. Fast. One forward pass detects the watermark, which the paper reports as up to two orders of magnitude faster than WavMark's brute-force synchronisation search. Capacity. 16-bit payload (can encode model ID, generation timestamp, user ID) embeddable in each utterance. Idea 4 · WavMark The pre-AudioSeal open baseline. Invertible neural network, 32 bits/sec. Problems: Synchronization brute-force is slow. Can be removed by Gaussian noise or MP3 compression. Not real-time friendly. Idea 5 · WaveVerify (July 2025) Addresses AudioSeal's weaknesses — specifically temporal manipulations (reversal, speed). Uses FiLM-based generator + Mixture-of-Experts detector. Competitive with AudioSeal on standard attacks; handles temporal edits. Idea 6 · The gap adversaries exploit AudioMarkBench (NeurIPS 2024) found that pitch shifting removes the watermarks it tested, and the run under Step 2 shows the same for AudioSeal: bit accuracy falls to chance. Pitch shift and speed change are the universal attacks. No 2026 watermark is fully robust to aggressive pitch modification. This is why you need detection (AASIST) alongside watermarking. Idea 7 · C2PA / Content Authenticity Initiative Not an ML technique — a manifest format. Audio files carry cryptographically signed metadata about creation tool, author, date. ElevenLabs, for example, attaches C2PA credentials to its audio alongside a watermark. Good for provenance; does nothing if a bad actor re-encodes and strips metadata. These are older open systems (SpeechT5 from 2022 and MMS-TTS from 2023, both with 16 kHz neural vocoders), close to the kinds of vocoder among AASIST's 2019 training attacks; EnCodec resynthesis of real speech is the hardest of the three. Passing both real and fake audio through a 16 kbps Opus call channel raises the EERs to 17%, 8% and 8%, because the codec erases some of the artefacts the detector relies on. With 12 clips per class each error moves the EER by about 8 points, so read these as indications. On newer generators and real-world deepfakes the same checkpoint does far worse in published evaluations (35.5% on ASVspoof 5, 43.0% on In-the-Wild). The roll-off feature scores 92%, worse than chance: the toy's assumption that fakes have more high-frequency energy is backwards for these 16 kHz vocoders, which have less. Flipped, it would score about 8%. A hand-picked feature captures one generator's quirk, not "fakeness". Step 4 · the production integration Copy Every generation ships: (1) watermark, (2) signed manifest, (3) retention-policy-compliant audit log. What changes, and why? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Watermarks in shipping products. Google's SynthID marks audio from Lyria and NotebookLM's audio overviews; ElevenLabs added SynthID to its TTS output alongside C2PA credentials and a public audio detector; Resemble's open PerTh watermark (MIT) is embedded in every output of its Chatterbox TTS; Meta's AudioSeal (MIT) is the common open option. Detection services (ElevenLabs' classifier, Google's SynthID Detector portal) check for their own marks; general deepfake detection for call centres and media is sold by specialist vendors such as Pindrop and Reality Defender, and should be validated on your own traffic, as the run above shows. Regulation (Lesson 6.8): the EU AI Act's Article 50 requires machine-readable marking of AI-generated audio. Sources: AudioSeal , AASIST , AASIST benchmarks , ASVspoof 5 , SynthID , ElevenLabs and SynthID , Resemble PerTh , Pindrop , Reality Defender , C2PA . Pitfalls Watermark without detector ever running. Pointless. Ship the detector in your CI. Detection without calibration. AASIST trained on ASVspoof LA overfits; real-world accuracy drops. Calibrate on your domain. Pitch-shift gap. Aggressive pitch shift removes most watermarks. Have a detection fallback. Metadata strip-and-rehost. C2PA is trivially bypassable by re-encoding. Always add cryptographic + perceptual (watermark) defense together. Liveness as detection. Ask user to say a random phrase. Prevents replay attacks but not real-time cloning. Recap What to keep from this lesson Detection works on anyone's audio; watermarking only on your own; provenance only while metadata survives. Use all three. Measure detectors on fakes they have not seen: in-domain EERs say little about real-world performance. AudioSeal survives codecs, resampling and volume changes; noise at low SNR, pitch shift and speed change remove it. Per-sample watermark scores locate generated spans inside real recordings. Every generation: watermark, signed manifest, audit log; run the detector in CI. Solutions Solution P1 · Codecs mild, pitch and speed fatal From least to most damaging: MP3 at 64 kbps (detection 1.00, all bits), Opus at 16 kbps (0.99, all bits), then the 10% speed-up (0.01, 44% of bits) and the pitch shift (0.00, about 50%). Codecs keep the spectral regions the watermark uses, and compression is among AudioSeal's training augmentations; pitch and speed changes move every frequency and stretch time, so the detector no longer finds the pattern where it expects it. Solution B1 · The detector trusts the rate you give it Both calls give the same result: a detection probability near 0.001 and about a third of the bits right. Since version 0.2, AudioSeal ignores sample_rate (it logs a deprecation warning) and always assumes 16 kHz. Read as 16 kHz, a 24 kHz file plays slower and lower, and Step 2 showed that the watermark does not survive pitch or speed changes. Resample to 16 kHz yourself before embedding and before detecting. a0617: Course home / Phase 6 · Sound and Speech Measuring speech and audio quality Lesson 6.17 60 min Learn Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 6 · 04, 06, 07, 09, 10; Phase 2 · 09 (Is the model any good? Measuring it) Type : Learn. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line You cannot ship what you cannot measure. This lesson names the 2026 metrics for every audio task: ASR (WER, CER, RTFx), TTS (MOS, UTMOS, SECS, WER-on-ASR-round-trip), audio-language (MMAU, LongAudioBench), music (FAD, CLAP), and speaker (EER). Plus the leaderboards where you compare. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means WER ASR score (S+D+I)/N at word level after normalization. CER Character WER For tone languages or char-level systems. MOS Human opinion 1-5 rating; 20+ listeners × 100 samples. UTMOS ML MOS predictor Learned model predicting listeners' 1–5 ratings; reliable for averages over many clips, less for single clips. SECS Voice-clone similarity ECAPA cosine between reference and clone. EER Speaker verif score Threshold where FAR = FRR. DER Diarization score (FA + Miss + Confusion) / total. FAD Music-gen quality Fréchet distance on VGGish embeddings. RTFx Throughput Audio seconds per wall-clock second. The problem In plain words first Every lesson in this phase ended with a number: a word error rate, a speaker similarity, an equal error rate, a distance between sets of music. This lesson puts them side by side. The core idea is that each metric measures one axis, such as intelligibility, naturalness, speaker identity or speed, and a system can be excellent on one and poor on another. The second idea is that a metric is a recipe, not just a formula: how text is normalised, how errors are averaged over utterances, and which test set is used can move a score more than a better model would. The runs score Whisper on LibriSpeech under three normalisations with a confidence interval, then score real, degraded and synthetic speech with UTMOS (a learned MOS predictor), round-trip WER and speaker similarity together. Nothing is trained. Every audio task has multiple metrics, each measuring a different axis. Using the wrong metric is how you ship a model that looks great on your dashboard and terribly in production. The 2026 canonical list: Task Primary Secondary ASR WER CER · RTFx · first-token latency TTS MOS / UTMOS SECS · WER-on-ASR-round-trip · CER · TTFA Voice cloning SECS (ECAPA cosine) MOS · CER Speaker verification EER minDCF · FAR / FRR at operating point Diarization DER JER · speaker confusion Audio classification top-1 · mAP macro F1 · per-class recall Music generation FAD CLAP · listening panel MOS Audio language model MMAU-Pro LongAudioBench · AudioCaps FENSE Streaming S2S latency P50/P95 WER · MOS The idea The same idea as a formula Word error rate. Align the hypothesis to the reference of words with the fewest edits: substitutions, deletions and insertions. Equal error rate. For a threshold on a similarity score, is the share of different-speaker pairs accepted and the share of same-speaker pairs rejected. The EER is their common value at the threshold where ) = FRR ( θ ∗ ) . Worked example Normalisation and averaging by hand One contraction. Reference "what's the weather today" (4 words), hypothesis "what is the weather today". The cheapest alignment is one substitution (what's → what) and one insertion (is): . After Whisper's normaliser turns "what's" into "what is", both sides match: . Two ways to average. A 4-word utterance with 4 errors (100%) and a 46-word utterance with 1 error (2.2%). Corpus WER: . Mean of per-utterance WERs: . One short utterance dominates the average, which is why the run's 30 utterances give 7.8% as a corpus but 12.5% averaged. Check your mental model ✗ "A lower WER always means a better model." ✓ Only with the same normaliser, averaging and test set. Changing the normaliser alone moved Whisper from 100.3% to 7.8% in the run under "Scoring Whisper properly". ✗ "Real recordings will get the highest UTMOS." ✓ Both TTS systems scored higher than the audiobook recordings (4.29 and 4.21 against 3.73). UTMOS predicts what its training listeners liked, so it is a proxy, not ground truth. ✗ "A speaker similarity of 0.89 means the same speaker." ✓ WavLM-SV cosines run high for any speech: MMS-TTS's different, synthetic voice scored 0.89. Thresholds come from real same-speaker and different-speaker pairs (Lesson 6.6). ✗ "Thirty utterances are enough to rank two ASR systems." ✓ The bootstrap interval was 4.7% to 11.8%; two systems a point or two apart cannot be told apart on a set this small. Predict before you run In the five-system run under "Three metrics, five kinds of speech", white noise at 10 dB SNR is added to the real recordings. Roughly how much does each score move (UTMOS, round-trip WER, speaker similarity), and which one does the noise hurt most? (Solution P1.) Idea 1 · ASR metrics WER (Word Error Rate). (S + D + I) / N . Lowercase, strip punctuation, normalize numbers before scoring. Use jiwer or OpenAI's whisper_normalizer . For scale, professional transcribers made 5.9% errors on the Switchboard conversational test set in Microsoft's 2016 "human parity" study (11.3% on the harder CallHome set). CER (Character Error Rate). Same formula, character-level. Used for tone languages (Mandarin, Cantonese) where word segmentation is ambiguous. RTFx (inverse real-time factor). Audio seconds processed per wall-clock second. Higher is better. On the Open ASR Leaderboard's GPU measurements, NVIDIA's Parakeet-TDT-0.6B v2 reaches an RTFx of about 3,386 and Whisper large-v3 about 146 (Lesson 6.4). First-token latency. Wall-clock from audio input to first transcript token. Critical for streaming. Vendors publish their own figures; measure from your own region and network. Idea 2 · TTS metrics MOS (Mean Opinion Score). 1-5 human rating. Gold standard but slow. Collect 20+ listeners per sample, 100+ samples per model. UTMOS (2022-2026). Learned MOS predictor. UTMOS22 (University of Tokyo) scored highest on several metrics of the VoiceMOS Challenge 2022; it predicts system averages well and single clips less well, and it was trained on English TTS and voice-conversion samples. Many TTS papers and model cards report it next to round-trip WER. SECS (Speaker Encoder Cosine Similarity). For voice cloning. Cosine between speaker embeddings (ECAPA, WavLM-SV) of the reference and the cloned output. The threshold for "same speaker" depends on the embedding model; calibrate it on real same-speaker and different-speaker pairs (Lesson 6.6). WER-on-ASR-round-trip. Run Whisper over TTS output, compute WER against the input text. Catches intelligibility regressions. 2026 SOTA: < 2% WER on English test sets (Mandarin sets report CER instead). TTFA (time-to-first-audio). Wall-clock latency from request to the first audio sample; it depends on hardware and streaming support more than on the model card, so measure it (Lesson 6.12). Idea 3 · Voice-cloning-specific SECS + MOS + CER as a triple. Cloning that scores high SECS but low MOS means timbre-right-but-unnatural; the opposite means natural voice but wrong speaker. Idea 4 · Speaker verification EER (Equal Error Rate). The threshold where False Accept Rate equals False Reject Rate. SpeechBrain's ECAPA-TDNN checkpoint reports 0.80% on VoxCeleb1-O (cleaned trial list; Lesson 6.6). minDCF (min Detection Cost). Weighted cost at a chosen operating point (often FAR=0.01). More production-relevant than EER. Idea 5 · Diarization DER (Diarization Error Rate). (FA + Miss + Confusion) / total_speaker_time . Missed speech + false-alarm speech + speaker-confusion, each as a fraction. On AMI meetings, pyannote's open community-1 pipeline reports 17.0% DER and its hosted precision-2 12.9% (Lesson 6.6). JER (Jaccard Error Rate). Alternative to DER, robust to short-segment bias. Idea 6 · Audio classification Multi-label: mAP (mean Average Precision) over all classes. AudioSet-2M: 0.486 mAP for BEATs (iter3), 0.506 for an ensemble (BEATs paper; Lesson 6.3). Multi-class exclusive: top-1, top-5 accuracy . Speech Commands v2: 98.3% top-1 for BEATs (iter3) and Audio-MAE (BEATs paper). Imbalanced: macro F1 + per-class recall . Report per-class — aggregate accuracy hides which classes fail. Idea 7 · Music generation FAD (Fréchet Audio Distance). Distance between VGGish-embedding distributions of real vs generated audio. Lower is better. Values are comparable only with the same embedding model (VGGish, CLAP, ...) and the same reference set; Lesson 6.9 measured FAD with CLAP embeddings. CLAP Score. Text-audio alignment score using CLAP embeddings. > 0.3 = reasonable alignment. Listening panel MOS. Still the final word for consumer-grade music. At its launch (September 2025) Suno reported an ELO of 1,293 for v5 on its own paired-preference benchmark (v4.5+: 1,208); the method was not published, so it is a vendor number. Independent arenas with blind votes, such as Artificial Analysis's music leaderboards, are the comparable alternative; TTS Arena ranks speech, not music. Idea 8 · Audio-language benchmarks MMAU (Massive Multi-Audio Understanding). 10k audio-QA pairs. MMAU-Pro. 5,305 instances testing 49 skills across speech, sound, music and their mixtures, including multi-audio and open-ended questions. In the paper the best model, Gemini 2.5 Flash, scored 59.2% and the best open model, Audio Flamingo 3, 51.7% (Lesson 6.10). LongAudioBench. Multi-minute clips with semantic queries. Introduced with Audio Flamingo 2; results come mostly from model authors, so check the evaluation setup. AudioCaps / Clotho. Captioning benchmarks. SPICE, CIDEr, FENSE metrics. Idea 9 · Streaming speech-to-speech Latency P50 / P95 / P99. Wall-clock from end-of-user-speech to first audible response. Moshi: about 200 ms on an L4 GPU (Kyutai's figure); hosted speech-to-speech APIs depend on region and network (Lesson 6.15). WER / MOS on the output. Barge-in responsiveness. Time from user interrupt to assistant mute. Target < 150 ms. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Without normalisation the WER is about 100%: LibriSpeech references are upper-case and unpunctuated while Whisper writes cased, punctuated text, so nearly every word "differs". Lower-casing and stripping punctuation gives 8.8%; Whisper's English normaliser, which also standardises spellings, contractions and number formats, 7.8%. Averaging per-utterance WERs gives 12.5% instead of the corpus 7.8%, because short utterances, where one error is a large fraction, count as much as long ones: the shorter half of the utterances has 13.0% WER against 5.5% for the longer half. The worst utterance is four words long: "not exactly returned kaliko" became "not exactly we have turned calico", four errors in four words, 100% (the reference's spelling of a name counts as an error too). Half the utterances are perfect. The bootstrap interval, 4.7% to 11.8%, is wide: with 30 utterances, two systems a point or two apart cannot be told apart. Whisper base.en runs at RTFx 5.9 on two CPU cores, with a p50 latency of 0.93 s per utterance and a p95 of 1.26 s. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The three metrics disagree, which is the point. White noise at 10 dB SNR collapses UTMOS from 3.73 to 1.37, more than doubles round-trip WER (10.9% to 26.7%) and barely moves speaker similarity (0.92): the voice is still recognisable but unpleasant. EnCodec at 1.5 kbps (Lesson 6.13) does similar damage. Both TTS systems score higher UTMOS than the real recordings (4.29 and 4.21 against 3.73): clean, evenly read synthetic speech is what the predictor was trained to like, while the audiobook recordings carry room sound. SpeechT5 is also more intelligible to Whisper than the real reader (5.9% WER). Speaker similarity separates the systems differently: SpeechT5 speaks with an ARCTIC voice (0.45 to the reader), while MMS-TTS scores 0.89 despite being a different, synthetic voice. WavLM-SV cosines run high for any speech, so 0.89 does not mean "same speaker"; thresholds must be calibrated on real pairs, as in Lesson 6.6. With 8 sentences, treat differences of a few points of WER as noise. Three cardinal rules: Normalize before scoring. Lowercase, punctuation-strip, number-expand. Report the normalization rule. Report distributions, not averages. P50/P95/P99 for latency. Per-class recall for classification. Per-category for MMAU. Run one canonical public benchmark. Even if your production data differs, reporting on Open ASR / TTS Arena / MMAU lets reviewers compare apples-to-apples. Break it on purpose Score Whisper's transcripts against references that still contain LibriSpeech's upper case but with the hypotheses lower-cased by Whisper's normaliser (normalise only one side). What WER do you get, and what does it tell you about checking a scoring script? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Leaderboards in use: the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard (WER and RTFx across eight English sets, plus multilingual and long-form tracks); TTS Arena and Artificial Analysis's speech and music arenas (blind pairwise votes, ELO); MMAU-Pro for audio-language models. Automatic quality metrics in TTS model cards: UTMOS (naturalness), round-trip WER or CER with Whisper or Paraformer (intelligibility), speaker similarity with a WavLM-based verifier (cloning); human preference tests remain the final word. Speech-enhancement and call-quality teams use Microsoft's DNSMOS (ITU-T P.808 / P.835 style predicted MOS for signal, background and overall quality). Normalisers: OpenAI's Whisper English normaliser (in transformers as tokenizer.normalize ) is the de facto standard for English WER on leaderboards. Sources: Open ASR Leaderboard , TTS Arena , Artificial Analysis , UTMOS paper , UTMOS22 port , DNSMOS , Human parity study , jiwer . Pitfalls UTMOS extrapolation. Trained on VCTK-style clean speech; scores noisy / cloned / emotional audio poorly. MOS panel bias. 20 Amazon Mechanical Turk workers ≠ 20 target users. Pay for a domain panel if stakes are high. FAD depends on reference set. Compare against the same reference distribution across models. Aggregate WER. A 5% WER overall can hide 30% WER on accented speech. Report by demographic slice. Public benchmark saturation. Most frontier models are near the ceiling on standard benchmarks. Build an in-house held-out set that reflects your traffic. Recap What to keep from this lesson Each metric measures one axis: intelligibility (WER), naturalness (MOS, UTMOS), identity (SECS, EER), distribution (FAD), speed (RTFx, latency). A metric is a recipe: normalisation, averaging and test set must be reported with the number. Report intervals and slices, not just averages. Learned predictors (UTMOS) are proxies; confirm important decisions with listeners. Public leaderboards for comparison, your own held-out set for decisions. Solutions Solution P1 · Noise hurts naturalness most UTMOS: from 3.73 to 1.37, a fall of about two-thirds. Round-trip WER rises from 10.9% to 26.7%, and speaker similarity barely changes (0.97 to 0.92). Noise mostly damages perceived quality; the words and the voice survive better. Solution B1 · Normalise both sides About 100%, like the raw row: every reference word is upper-case and every normalised hypothesis word lower-case, so nearly every word counts as a substitution. A WER near 100% from a model known to work almost always means a scoring bug, not a bad model. Test a scoring script on a hypothesis identical to the reference (it must give 0%) and on one known error, and apply the same normaliser to both sides. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Guardrail A check that runs on what goes into or comes out of a model and blocks, edits or flags it Lesson 15.23 Prompt injection Text that tricks a model into following an attacker's instructions instead of yours Lesson 15.24 Most of this course is about text agents, because most enterprise agents are text agents. Two other kinds of generative AI show up in real projects often enough to deserve their own module: voice agents , which put an agent on a phone line or in an app's microphone, and generative media , which creates images, audio and video. Both reuse everything else in the course (tools, retrieval, guardrails later · 15.23 , evals ), and both add constraints of their own. Why this came about Voice assistants existed for years but were rigid. In 2024 realtime speech models made natural, low-latency spoken conversations with language models possible, creating voice agents with their own latency and interruption challenges. In plain words first A conversation where a second of silence is too long Voice agents must answer within about a second, so latency drives the design. The pipeline design chains speech-to-text, a normal text agent and text-to-speech, streaming at every stage; it gives control and any model. Speech-to-speech models hear and speak directly, with fewer parts and lower latency, but fewer choices. Both must handle interruptions, when the user starts talking over the agent. Voice agents: two architectures Two ways to build a voice agent. The cascade is debuggable and swappable; speech-to-speech is faster and more natural. The latency budget decides, and turn detection sits in front of both. The cascaded design as a concrete device: a small model listens for the wake word, speech-to-text transcribes the question, a language model writes the answer, and text-to-speech reads it out. The legend shows which steps can run on the device and which in the cloud. Figure: Hugging Face, Audio Course , Apache 2.0 . Architecture How it works Strengths Trade-offs Cascaded pipeline Speech-to-text (STT), then a text LLM with tools, then text-to-speech (TTS), all streaming Use any LLM and your existing text agent; transcripts for logging and evals; swap each part independently More hops, so more latency; tone of voice is lost in the transcript Speech-to-speech model (realtime) One model hears audio and speaks audio, with tool calling Lowest latency; hears tone, hesitation and interruptions; more natural prosody Fewer model choices; harder to inspect and evaluate; audio tokens cost more Realtime speech models and APIs include OpenAI's Realtime API, Gemini Live, Amazon Nova Sonic on Bedrock and Azure's Voice Live. Frameworks that handle the media plumbing (streaming audio, voice activity detection , interruptions, telephony) include Pipecat , LiveKit Agents and Vapi-style managed platforms; telephony arrives through providers such as Twilio, Exotel or Amazon Connect. Transport matters: WebRTC handles jitter and packet loss for browsers and mobile apps; WebSockets are simpler for server-to-server audio. Streaming end to end, barge-in and turn detection before any feature work. Read-back confirmation before every action, and identity verification before account data. A human handoff path that is always one sentence away. Recording and AI disclosure at the start, and PII redaction in stored transcripts. An eval set of real call audio in your callers' languages, accents and noise levels. Step 1 · The latency budget People expect a reply within roughly a second of finishing a sentence; much more and they start talking again or assume the line dropped. Add up a turn stage by stage: Copy What you should see Copy Three lessons. Streaming everything is not optional: waiting for each stage to finish more than doubles the delay. Endpointing (deciding that the caller has finished) is often the biggest single cost, which is why voice stacks add a small turn-detection model that listens for the end of a thought, not just silence. And the LLM's time to first token matters far more than its total generation time, which favors fast models, short system prompts with prompt caching, and tools that answer in milliseconds. Speech-to-speech models win on raw latency; cascades win on control. Step 2 · Speak while the model is still thinking TTS should start on the first natural phrase, not the full answer. A small chunker sits between the LLM stream and the TTS engine: Copy What you should see Copy Chunking at punctuation keeps intonation natural; chunks of one or two words sound robotic. Write voice prompts differently from chat prompts: short sentences, no markdown, no lists or URLs, numbers and order IDs in a form the TTS reads well ("A, ten oh one"), and a confirmation read back before any action ("I'll cancel order A-1002. Shall I go ahead?"). Step 3 · Turn-taking and interruptions Voice activity detection (VAD) finds speech in the audio stream. The silence threshold that ends a turn is a trade-off: short thresholds cut people off mid-thought, long ones feel sluggish. Here is energy-based VAD on synthetic audio: Copy What you should see Copy The caller stopped at 1.1 seconds; every rule adds its silence on top. Production systems use trained VAD models (Silero VAD, WebRTC VAD) that ignore background noise, plus semantic turn detection that waits longer after "my order number is..." than after a complete question. Barge-in is the other half: when the caller starts speaking while the agent talks, stop TTS playback immediately, cancel the pending LLM generation, and keep only what the caller actually heard in the conversation history, or the agent will "remember" saying things the caller never heard. Voice agents in production Evaluate on audio, not just text : word error rate on names, order IDs, addresses and numbers in your callers' accents and languages (Indian English, Hindi and code-mixed Hinglish behave very differently from benchmark audio); task completion; latency percentiles per turn; interruption handling. Simulated callers ( Lesson 14.143 ) can be voiced with TTS to test end to end. Languages : check STT and TTS quality per language and dialect before committing; Azure Speech, Google Cloud Speech, Amazon Transcribe and Polly, and Indian providers such as Sarvam AI cover Indian languages to different degrees. Safety and compliance : announce recording and AI use at the start of the call, verify identity before revealing account data, redact PII in transcripts, hand off to a person on request or on emergencies, and guard against voice prompt injection later · 15.24 (a caller can say "ignore your instructions" as easily as type it). Cost : audio is billed per minute or per audio token at each stage; long calls with long contexts add up, so trim history and summarize. Check your mental model ✗ "Voice agents are text agents with a microphone." ✓ Latency, interruptions and spoken-style answers change the design. ✗ "Speech-to-speech is always better." ✓ It is simpler and faster; pipelines give more control and easier tracing . ✗ "Long, detailed answers are fine in voice." ✓ Short sentences and no tables or lists suit speech. Exercises Predict before you run The latency budget allots 300 ms each to speech recognition, the model's first token and speech synthesis. If the model needs 900 ms for its first sentence, where can you win time without a faster model? (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Use a fixed 1.5-second silence to decide that the caller finished speaking. What do callers experience? (Solution B1.) Debugging exercise The agent keeps talking when the caller interrupts. What is missing? (Solution D1.) Make it your own Change speakable_chunks to never split inside numbers or order IDs such as SK-1042, and test it on a reply that contains both. (Solution M1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Overlap the stages Stream: start synthesizing the first speakable chunk as soon as it is complete (Step 2), and start recognition early with streaming ASR. Fillers or short acknowledgments also hide latency. Solution B1 · Turn-taking needs more than silence Long pauses before every reply, and interruptions when callers pause mid-sentence. Use voice activity detection with adaptive or semantic end-of-turn detection, as end_of_turn begins to do. Solution D1 · Barge-in Detecting speech while the agent speaks, stopping playback, cancelling pending synthesis, and telling the model it was interrupted, with what was actually heard. Solution M1 · Speak whole units Treat numbers, IDs and abbreviations as unbreakable, and split on sentence or clause boundaries.
